title: மருதம் decade 1
theme: The decade of wishes (வேட்கைப் பத்து, marutham, Orampokiyar): in each poem the mother wishes long life and prosperity for the king Aadan Avini and his land, and the girl's side answers with wishes for the man of the field town, rising from his welfare and his house to an open suitor's chariot, marriage, his kept oath, freedom from gossip and the bride taken to his town (1-10).
source_issues: 1-10: the colophon has no thurai for this decade and the e-text prints no decade title; the speaker (thozhi, speaking with the girl as 'we', யாமே) and addressee are inferred from the poems, so occasion words are null.
9 line 1: ஆதன்வாழி is printed without the space found in line 1 of the other nine poems.

reading: The speaker reports that the mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, abundant paddy and great gold, while she and her companion wished that the man of the thriving town, where the kaanji is in bud and the small fish are full of roe, may live long, and his bard with him.
nuance: The decade's frame is set here: one line of the mother's wishes for the king and the land, one line of 'we' wishing for the lover, so a private love is set inside a public prayer for the realm. Wishing the bard well too places the lover among the bards who carry his messages and his fame. The budding tree and the fish heavy with roe are read by some as a promise of a fruitful house, but the poem itself draws no match, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: budding kaanji, roe-filled fish and the lord of a watered town are things of the field country

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that the fields may yield and alms-seekers may come, while the speaker and her companion wished that their bond with the man of the cool ford, where the neythal rivals the many-petalled blue lily, may grow from generation to generation.
nuance: The mother's wish that suppliants come is a king's virtue, giving; the girls' wish answers it with a bond that lasts 'line after line' (வழிவழி), a marriage that outlives the lovers. The two lilies matching each other at the ford sit beside the wish for a lasting bond as an image of a well-matched pair, though the poem does not say so.

thinai_evidence.note: water lilies at the cool ford of a town fix the field country

comparisons.tenor: the neythal lily at the ford

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that milk may flow and the bulls thrive, while the speaker and her companion wished that the household of the man of the flower-crowded town, where the ploughmen who sowed go home with their paddy, may flourish.
nuance: The wish is for his மனை வாழ்க்கை, the life of a house, which the girls can only share if he marries: so the blessing is also a claim. The ploughmen who sowed and now carry home the grain fit that claim (what was begun is brought home), but the poem leaves the match unspoken.

thinai_evidence.note: ploughmen returning with the harvest are the labour of the field country

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that his enemies be reduced to eating grass and the brahmins chant their learning, while the speaker and her companion wished that the chest of the man of the field town, where sugarcane flowers and paddy bears grain, may never become a common pond.
nuance: பழனம் is the town's shared water and field, open to all; to wish that his chest not become one is to fear in advance the straying husband of the field country, whose embrace every woman of the town might use. The mother's wish that enemies be brought to grass and the girls' wish against a shared chest both ask that something stay in its rightful place.

thinai_evidence.note: flowering cane, grain-bearing paddy and the wet field are things of the field country

comparisons.tenor: the lover's chest

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that there be no hunger and disease go far away, while the speaker and her companion wished that the chariot of the man of the cool ford, where the male crocodile swallows fish whole, may stand at their front gate.
nuance: A chariot standing openly at the front gate is the sign of a man who comes as a suitor by day, not a secret lover by night, so the wish asks for marriage without naming it. The male crocodile gulping whole fish is sometimes read as a warning about a greedy lover, but nothing in the poem matches it to him, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the crocodile and fish of the town's ford are things of the field country

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that the king's wars cease and his years increase, while the speaker and her companion wished that the man of the cool ford, where lotus buds rise in a pond already in flower, may marry her and that their father may give her to him.
nuance: This is the decade's plainest wish: வரைக, let him marry, and எந்தையும் கொடுக்க, let our father give, naming both halves of the rite. The 'our father' (எந்தை) shows the speaker speaks as one with the girl. The pond in flower with lotuses still in bud sets a scene of ripeness about to open.

thinai_evidence.note: the lotus pond at the town's ford is of the field country

tamil: உளைப் பூ மருதத்துக் கிளைக் குருகு இருக்கும்
reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that virtue flourish greatly and all else perish, while the speaker and her companion wished that the man of the cool ford, where a heron sits with its kin in the tufted-flowered marutham tree, may take her and go to his own town.
nuance: To be taken to his town is the bride's departure from her father's house; the heron settled among its kin (கிளை) in the tree of the field country shows what she is to have there, a place in his kindred.

thinai_evidence.note: the marutham tree and the heron of the ford are things of the field country

iraicchi.act: the heron dwells with its kin in the marutham tree
iraicchi.sense: as the heron lives among its own flock, the man should bring her to live among his kin in his own town

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that he rule justly and there be no theft, while the speaker and her companion wished that the oath sworn here by the man of the flower-crowded town, where a lovely peacock sits on the swaying bough of a mango, may come true.
nuance: சூள் இவண் is 'the oath here': the vow was sworn in this place, to the girl, and the wish is that it 'prove true' (வாய்ப்பதாக), which admits it might not. The mother's wish against theft (களவு இல் ஆகுக) uses the same word as hidden love, களவு, so the decade's two wish-lines touch: let there be no stealing in the land, and let the lover's stolen union be made good by his word.

thinai_evidence.note: the mango in a town of many flowers sets the field country; the peacock is a hill bird out of place

tamil: என வேட் டோ ளே யாயே யாமே
reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that good increase greatly and harm vanish, while the speaker and her companion wished that their bond with the man of the cool ford, where the heron that has fed on kayal fish sleeps on the straw stacks, may not become the talk of the town.
nuance: அம்பல் is the first low murmur of gossip, before it becomes open அலர்; the wish is that the secret bond be settled before the town can name it. The heron that has eaten its fill and sleeps on the stack in plain view of the field may hint at a love that should not be left lying in the open, but the poem draws no match, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron and the threshed straw stacks of the ford town are of the field country

reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that the rains come in season and wealth greatly increase, while the speaker and her companion wished that the man of the cool ford, where small fish smelling of flesh lie under the flowering mango, may take her with him and go.
nuance: The decade closes as poem 7 did, with the wish that he take her and go (கொண்டனன் செல்க), but here 'with him' (தன்னோடு) replaces 'to his town': the last wish is simply to be with him. The mother's wish for timely rain is the oldest of a king's blessings.

thinai_evidence.note: the mango by the water and the small fish of the ford fix the field country

title: மருதம் decade 2
theme: Ainkurunuru 11 to 20, the marutham reed decade of Orampokiyar: every poem opens on the reed (வேழம்) of the husband's ford-town, flowering like sugarcane, a horse's plume or a heron, serving as kohl tube or bathing float, and closes on the wife's body (shoulders, eyes, bangles, heart) bearing the cost of his other women.
source_issues: 13: line 4 reads துயலறியலரே; if the word is துயில் (sleep) the lord's women lie awake, if துயல் (distress) the line is sarcasm; the sense turns on it.
14: line 3 reads மணித்துறை வீரன் where every other poem of the decade has ஊரன்; வீரன் may be a misreading of ஊரன் (not confirmed against another edition).
19: line 2 reads மெய்ம்மணங்க் கமழும், with a stray க் after the nasal, likely an e-text slip for மெய்ம்மணங் கமழும்.
11-20: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (and the e-text no decade title), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.

reading: The wife says that, ashamed of the cruelty of the lord of the ford-town where the vayalai of the house-yard and the reed twine together, she keeps saying he is good, but her broad soft shoulders say he is not.
nuance: Her words and her body take opposite sides: shame (நாணி) makes her defend him, and the wasting shoulders give the verdict she will not. Line 1 can be read as the house creeper twining round the reed of the ford, the wife still holding to a man who belongs outside, but which plant clasps which is not fixed by the syntax, so it is left as scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the reed of the watered ford and the ford-town lord fix the field land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from யாமே and என் தோளே: the wife speaks of her own shoulders

reading: The wife says: let the lord of the ford-town, where the reed on the bank flowers like sugarcane, keep up his cruelty as much as he likes; as for her, let her broad soft shoulders lose.
nuance: The optatives (ஆற்றுக தில்ல, தோற்கதில்ல) give up the contest rather than make it: she grants him his cruelty and her shoulders their defeat. The traditional reading of the worthless reed that flowers like the sugarcane as the other woman passing for the wife has only one clear correspondence and no stated other woman, so it is not tagged as ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: the bank reed and the ford-town fix the field land

reading: Of the lord of the cool ford, where the reeds of the north bank put out white flowers like the frothing plume of a fine horse, the speaker says that his women know no rest even at midnight, when the town sleeps.
nuance: The whole sense turns on துயல் in the last line: taken as துயில் (sleep) the lord's women lie awake while the town sleeps; taken as distress, they are untroubled, which would make the line sarcasm. The reed's white plume is set beside a war-horse's crest, a puram ornament on a field weed.

nuance: The only poem of the decade with no complaint. The reed touching the young mango's shoots (வடுக்கொண் மாஅத்து வண்தளிர்) could hint at a man drawn to a young girl, but nothing in the poem states it, so it stays scene.

reading: The wife says that the lord of the old reed town, whose reed serves as a float and partner to the leaf-skirted women who bathe in the swelling flood, is lord of a town but not lord of her.
nuance: The pun ஊரன் ஆயினும் ஊரனல்லன் empties his title: he lords it over a town but is no husband. புனலாடு with a reed float is the marutham man's water-play with other women.

nuance: Two kohls meet: the girls fill the reed tubes with collyrium, and her own kohl eyes (உண்கண்) are covered over with gold, so the town's play with the reed is set against the ruin of her painted eyes.

reading: The wife says that since the lord of the town, where the white reed flower swaying on the bush looks like a heron flying in the sky, now desires new women, her simple heart has become empty.
nuance: The reed flower only looks like a flying heron, and the new women (புதுவோர்) are named in the next breath; the image of a showy look-alike fits them, but only one correspondence can be named, so it is a near miss for ullurai. மடங்கெழு, full of simplicity, makes her trust the cause of the emptiness.

title: மருதம் கள்வன் பத்து decade 3
theme: Ainkurunuru 21 to 30, the crab decade of the marutham hundred: ten four- and five-line poems in which the friend asks the mother, each time ending எவன்கொல் அன்னாய், why the girl pales and wastes for the man of the field town, while the field crab cuts lilies, creepers, sprouts and paddy, abandons its mate or hoards in its hole as the figure of what he does.
source_issues: The colophons give no thurai for this decade; every thurai_akam (the friend speaking to the foster mother, அன்னாய்) is inferred from the poems (நின்மகள் in 29, இவள் in 28 and 30), and occasion stage and words are left null.
30 line 1 reads நெடுங்கள் களவன்; the same formula in Akananuru 176 line 8 reads நெடுங்கண், and 'long-eyed' is the sense, so நெடுங்கள் is probably a misprint for நெடுங்கண்; marked as written.
The decade title is கள்வன் பத்து while the repaired lines read களவன்; both spellings of the crab are in use and the poems are marked as written.
22 line 4 நீயேன் is read as 'I will not leave'; the verse is marked uncertain.
24 lines 2-3 (முதலைத்து அவனூர் எய்தினன் ஆகின்று கொல்லோ) are compressed and the construction is uncertain; line 3 is the tamilvu.org reading flagged by show.
28 line 1 (உண்துறை அணங்கிவள் உறைநோய் ஆயின்) is a compressed conditional; the verse is marked uncertain.
23 line 2 prints அணி யூரன் split; read as அணியூரன்.

reading: The friend asks the mother why, although the man of the cool-ford town, where the speckled crab cuts the water lily on the banks of old water overgrown with mulli, gives his assurances, the girl's darkened eyes still turn pale.
nuance: The whole poem turns on the concession in தெளிப்பவும், 'even as he assures': the pallor answers his words and contradicts them. The crab cutting the lily can be felt as the ooran harming the girl, but the scene offers only that one correspondence, so it is left as scene (a near miss for ullurai).

thinai_evidence.note: the field crab, the water lily and the man named as lord of a watered town

reading: The friend asks the mother why the man of the town where the speckled crab, having wallowed in the mire, goes back into its hole at the mulli's roots, after speaking fair words and joining her, said that now he would never leave her.
nuance: நீயேன் is read as the negative first person of நீ, 'I will not leave'; the question is then why he made a promise his conduct now belies. The crab's return to its own hole after the mud can be read as the man going back to his own house after his pleasures, but only that one match holds, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: mire, field crab and the lord of a town

reading: The friend asks why the man of the town adorned by floodwater, which stirred the crab out of its hole in the mulli roots and came on plucking flowers, having given his assurance and joined with us, should now become a goddess that strikes.
nuance: தாக்கணங்கு, a deity that strikes those who approach it, is the word for what the lover has become: the one who should heal is now the cause of the sickness, which is why the friend speaks to the mother, who would otherwise look for the god. நப், 'us', joins the friend to the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: flood, field crab and the lord of a watered town

comparisons.tenor: the man who assured and embraced her, now the cause of her affliction

reading: The friend asks whether the husband has come to share the nature of his town, the town of the speckled crab whose birth kills its mother and of the crocodile that eats its own young, since he takes the beauty of the women he embraced till their gold bangles rang and then abandons them.
nuance: The two creatures are both kin-destroyers, the young that kill the parent and the parent that eats the young, so the friend charges the man with destroying those who are his own. Because she states the link (அவனூர் எய்தினன் ஆகின்று கொல்லோ), it is an open juxtaposition, not ullurai.

title: மருதம் தோழிக்கு உரைத்த பத்து decade 4
theme: Ainkurunuru 31 to 40, the marutham decade spoken to the friend: by our reading the other woman's voice throughout, holding the lord to an oath sworn at the bathing ford, mocking his wives who weep a week for one day's absence, watching her own eyes and skin turn the colour of the water lily as he forgets her, and hearing at last that he has settled back in his wives' town, where the leaping fish opens the closed lily.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; the speaker (the other woman) is inferred from 32 and 40 and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
38 line 4 reads ஒள்தோடி where the same half-line in 40 line 2 reads ஒள்தொடி; தோடி is likely a misprint for தொடி (bangle).
38 line 3 writes வெளவும் with the two-part vowel sign (ெ + ள) rather than ௌ; it is the verb வௌவும்.
37 line 4 divides the words as சூள்வாய்த் தல்லே, for சூள் வாய்த்தல்லே.
33 line 3 என்பதன் is likely என்ப + தன் written together.

reading: The other woman asks her friend whether the lord will now say he owes nothing on the oath he swore at the great ford of their town, by the old bent marutham tree, in front of the band of women bathing together.

title: மருதம் புலவிப் பத்து decade 5
theme: Ainkurunuru 41 to 50, the decade of sulking (புலவிப் பத்து) in Orampokiyar's marutham hundred: the wife and her friend refuse the husband who comes back from the courtesan, mocking his chest, his oaths and his bard, setting their pallor against his rich river town, and using the bard-women's barter of fish for grain and the tortoise and crocodile of the pond as images of his care and his cruelty.
source_issues: 41-50: the colophon gives no thurai; every speaker and addressee in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and so noted, and occasion.words is null.
41: line 2 variant at sangamtamil.com (spelling only: அவன் ஊர் என்ப); our reading kept.
42, 47, 48: lines repaired from tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), agreeing with sangamtamil.com (text flags 42 line 2, 47 line 4, 48 lines 2 and 5).
45: line 4 had encoding junk and line 1 a conversion fault; both repaired (text flags). 46 line 2 and 49 line 4: conversion faults corrected by rule (text flags).
43: அம்பணம் (a measuring vessel) and whose young sleep on the tortoise are uncertain. 50: the sense of துணையோர் செல்வமும் in line 1 is uncertain.

reading: Speaking of the man in the third person, the woman says his town is said to have a pond of white flowers with a loveless crocodile that eats its own young, and that is why the lord of that town turns gold-pale the bodies of those who took his word as true.
nuance: The crocodile that devours its own young is the hidden image a reader expects in marutham, but here அதனால் (therefore) states the inference outright: the town breeds such a lord. So it fails ullurai condition 2 and stands as a juxtaposition; the plural உணர்ந்தோர் makes her one of several women he has paled.

reading: The friend asks the man of the rich town whether his well-jewelled wife has lost her wits from too much joy, that she has begun to thrust away his chest, broad as the full flood of the Kaviri.
nuance: The question is ironic: what the friend calls a joy-drunk delusion is the wife's deliberate sulk. The flood simile flatters his chest and at the same time marks it as something that sweeps over everything in its path.

nuance: The old belief that the tortoise feeds its young by its gaze makes the claim exact: she needs only his presence, not his provision. The last words turn a love complaint into a matter of அறன், duty as well as feeling.

nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the bard-woman bringing her catch into the wife's house could stand for the bard's go-between work, but the poem names only one situation (lying) and the barter gives no second pair; record it as scene. The witnesses are the companions, so the lie is public.

title: மருதம் தோழி கூற்றுப் பத்து decade 6
theme: Ainkurunuru 51 to 60, the friend's speech decade of the marutham hundred: the friend faces the straying husband, calling him home to a pregnant wife, asking at whose door his chariot stands, laying the girl's sickness to his broken oath, measuring her fading beauty by the rich towns of the Pandya, the Chola and Viraan, mocking his rival woman, grieving that she who once cured his love has no cure for the wife, and in the last poem warning a night visitor of the father's spear.
source_issues: 51-60: the colophon has no thurai; the decade title தோழி கூற்றுப் பத்து gives only the speaker, so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and occasion words are null.
53 line 3 recurs as Ainkurunuru 94 line 4 (flagged by show); marked as written, a shared formula.
54 lines 4-6: the construction of ஊரின் ஊரனை and of whom the man brought is uncertain; the verse is marked uncertain.
55 line 1 and 59 line 1 are repaired readings (flagged by show); marked as repaired.
60 line 2: கழனியுரநின் should read கழனி ஊர நின் (vocative ஊர, the long vowel lost in the e-text).
60 line 3: துங்சுமனை is a misspelling of துஞ்சுமனை (ங் for ஞ்).

reading: The friend tells the lord of the town where the sharp-clawed hen of the blue water-cock has her pregnancy cravings that this girl's craving is not a longing for sour tamarind but a sickness that only his opened chest will cure.
nuance: The town epithet already shows a pregnant bird with her mate; the friend then sets the woman's craving against the bird's and names the cure as the husband's embrace, so the pregnancy becomes her claim on a man who is elsewhere. The usual craving of pregnant women for tart fruit is denied in order to say what she really wants.

reading: The friend asks the lord of the town of ponds, where the field lotus blooms though stirred muddy when the new flood breaks the dam and pours in, why anyone should think the ford's spirit afflicts them: the sickness they suffer is the oath he swore.
nuance: The household's diagnosis is possession by the deity of the ford (துறை அணங்கும்); the friend replaces it with his broken oath, which was presumably sworn at that ford. The flood that breaks its bank and the lotus that blooms though muddied invite a hidden reading (his broken bound, her troubled faithfulness), but only one pair is clear, so it stays scene. Line 3 recurs in Ainkurunuru 94.

nuance: The fear is not for the wife but for the new women: what has happened to her will happen to them in its order (அம்முறை). The Pandya's town that never runs dry is the measure of the beauty that has now run dry in her. The construction of lines 4 to 6 is uncertain (ஊரின் ஊரனை, and whom the man 'brought').

nuance: The question is mocking: the friend assumes no rival can equal her, so his leaving can only be folly. நின் பெண்டே turns the other woman into his, with the wife left without a word for herself.

nuance: A marutham poem with a kurinji situation: the night visit to an unmarried girl's house and the father's spear are the stock pressures of kalavu toward marriage. The water-hen calling openly to its mate in the field is set against the lover who comes by stealth at night.

title: மருதம் கிழத்தி கூற்றுப்பத்து decade 7
theme: Ainkurunuru 61 to 70, the wife's speeches of Orampokiyar's marutham: ten short retorts to a husband who goes to other women, built from the pond, the flood, the lily and the lotus, in which she mocks his new women as children and upstarts, counts the witnesses of his bathing, and turns her own body after childbirth into the ground of her refusal.
source_issues: The whole decade has no colophon thurai; the speaker (the wife) is known only from the decade title கிழத்தி கூற்றுப்பத்து, so thurai_akam occasion words are left null.
66: line 1 (உடலினேன் அல்லேன் பொய்யாது உரைமோ) is not in sangamtamil.com's text; marked as our text has it.
69: line 4 repeats ainkurunuru 125 line 3 (a stock line, not an error).

reading: The wife tells her husband that he is set on seeking out good women, one fine woman after another, women as rich as Kazhar of open-handed Matti, where the sweet ripe mango falls with a plop into the deep pond, and on celebrating marriage with them.
nuance: The doubled நல்லோர் நல்லோர் is the sting: not one new woman but a series. The falling ripe fruit belongs to Kazhar, not to the husband, so it is description of the town, not a hidden comparison; but Kuruntokai 8 opens with the same formula line, where the courtesan has the vaalai fish snatch the fruit, so a reader of the anthologies hears the fruit that drops into whatever water lies below as the man who falls to whoever is near (one pair only, a near miss on ullurai).

reading: The wife tells the lord of the town of great floods, where the water-lily that sprang up in the sugarcane bed relieves the hunger of the bees, not to embrace her body, which has borne him a son, since it would spoil his chest.
nuance: 'It would spoil your chest' is sarcasm: his chest is kept fine for other women, and her body after childbirth is offered as the excuse. The lily that grew unplanted in a bed meant for cane and feeds the bees invites a hidden reading (the other woman, not planted in the household, feeding his appetite), but the poem never states his straying, so it fails the anchor condition and stays scene.

nuance: The new woman's pride is answered with a count: she is one of a crowd of rivals, so her claim to rank with the wife is the naivety the opening word மடவள் names.

reading: The wife tells the lord of the town of the great-watered, ever-yielding pond, where the heron, having eaten the many fish of the field pools, rests on the crown of the marutham tree in the field, that his women are clean and fragrant while she, who has borne a son, is like a ghoul.
nuance: Self-mockery as accusation: the 'ghoul' is the mother whose body has served the household. The heron that feeds on many fish and then sits clean aloft is close to an ullurai (the many fish to his many women), but a second pair is not clear, so it stays scene.

title: மருதம் புனலாட்டுப் பத்து decade 8
theme: The decade of water-play (புனலாட்டுப் பத்து, marutham, Orampokiyar): the husband bathes in the river floods with another woman; the wife and her friend meet the gossip with charges (71, 75, 76, 79, 80), the man praises the woman of the water-play (72-74), and the rival invites him to the flood and away from his house (77, 78).
source_issues: 71-80: the colophon has no thurai for this decade; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems, so occasion words are null. In 72-74 no addressee is named and pira stands for that.
73 line 1: ஒந்தழை is probably a misprint for ஒண்தழை (bright leaf skirt); marked as printed.
73 line 4: புனவே is probably a misprint for புனலே (the water of the ford); marked as printed.
78 and 79: the speaker is not certain; 78 may be the wife rather than the other woman, and 79 may be the wife or another woman at the water.

reading: The wife tells the lord of revels that people say he embraced his beloved, the woman of small fine bangles and bewitching sway, and bathed with her in the flood yesterday; such gossip can no more be hidden than the light of the sun can be buried.
nuance: The charge rests on what people say (என்ப), so the wife accuses him through the town's voice rather than her own sight; the sun image turns gossip into a force of nature that no one, least of all he, can stop. The two parallel questions (மறைத்தல் ஒல்லுமோ, புதைத்தல் ஒல்லுமோ) let the second answer the first.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's bathing with another woman and the wife's charge are the field country's quarrel

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about his bathing with the other woman

reading: The man says that the soft, lovely woman, wearing a swaying leaf skirt of field water-lilies on her mottled waist, with swinging hair and kohl-lined eyes like the kuvalai, became his partner in the water-play when the flood came brimming with flowers.
nuance: The portrait runs from waist to hair to eyes before the verb arrives in the last line, so the woman is all ornament until she becomes a 'joined partner' (புணர்துணை). The poem never says whether she is his wife or another woman; set in this decade of charges about his bathing, his praise reads as his answer to them.

thinai_evidence.note: field water-lilies, the flower-laden flood and water-play belong to the watered fields

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes

reading: The man says that when the bright-browed young woman in fine jewels leapt into the water-play, her bright-coloured leaf skirt swaying, the water of the great ford became cool and smelt of honeyed, fragrant kuvalai.
nuance: The hyperbole runs backwards from what one expects: the river does not cool or scent the woman; her leap gives the whole great ford her coolness and fragrance. The kuvalai is not said to grow there; the water simply smells of it once she is in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the kuvalai and the bathing ford of a river town are things of the fields

reading: The man says that the cool, fragrant hair of the woman who climbs the marutham tree on the bank and leaps into the water-play, her bright gold jewels glinting softly, is like the grace of a peacock gliding down from the sky.
nuance: The whole poem is one sentence that ends on the hair (கதுப்பே): the leap from the branch is seen through the spread of her hair as she falls, which is why the vehicle is a peacock descending rather than one dancing. The peacock is a bird of the hills brought into a field poem only as a simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the marutham tree on the river bank and the water-play place the scene in the fields

comparisons.tenor: her cool fragrant hair as she drops from the branch into the water

reading: The friend tells the lord of revels that because he is not one of the many here, the town has begun to gossip, its talk spreading wide: that she bathed with him in the cool water at the great ford of the ancient marutham tree.
nuance: Line 1 can be taken as praise (no one here is your equal, so you are watched) or as reproach (you do not fit among us); either way his standing is what turns a bath into news. மலர puns on அலர் in the same line: the gossip blooms like the flowers of the ford.

thinai_evidence.note: gossip about the husband's bathing with another woman is the field country's quarrel

reading: The speaker tells the man that the girl of bright bangles, with hair soft as panjaay sedge and freckles like fresh flowers, bathed with him in the cool water and grew in beauty until she looked like a goddess even to the women of the heavens.
nuance: The praise is the reproach: the other woman's beauty rose 'with you' (நின்னோடு), and the climb from earthly to heavenly comparison is pushed so far that it reads as mockery of his infatuation. பஞ்சாய் may also point to the sedge of which girls' dolls were made, so the hair would be a doll's hair.

thinai_evidence.note: the bathing pool and the waterside sedge belong to the fields; the quarrel is over his companion

comparisons.tenor: her soft hair
the pale spots on her skin
the girl after bathing with him

reading: The woman tells the lord of revels she has something to say: so that gossip rises through the great town, let us bathe with you in the cool water, tossed by its waves; come with us, do not go to your house.
nuance: Here the gossip that the wife and her friend dread in 71 and 75 is what the other woman wants: the public bath is meant to be seen. The last line sets 'with us' against 'your house' and makes the bath a choice between them.

thinai_evidence.note: the other woman drawing the husband from his house is the field country's quarrel

reading: The woman asks the man to bathe with her in the new flood that has burst its dam and come rushing down its course like the wall-breaking elephant of Killi, he of the leaf-bladed long spear and swift horses, and to take her shoulders as his raft.
nuance: A king's war elephant battering a fort wall is the image of a flood breaking a dam (சிறையழி), and the broken restraint carries over to the invitation itself. The speaker may also be the wife calling him back to her own water-play; the colophon gives no thurai to decide it.

thinai_evidence.note: a new flood breaking the dam of a watered field and bathing in it are things of the fields

comparisons.tenor: the new flood breaking its dam
her shoulders

reading: The woman tells the lord of revels, who seized her asking whose daughter this was, the girl whose eyes had reddened from bathing in the new flood: whoever's daughter she may be, who is he, whose son, to seize her without knowing?
nuance: She throws his own question back word for word (யார்மகள், யார் மகனை): a man who grabs women at the water without knowing their families has no family name worth asking about. If the speaker is the wife, the barb is sharper still: he did not know his own wife with her reddened eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's careless advance at the water-play and the woman's retort are the field country's quarrel

reading: The wife tells the lord of revels that she is not sulking and asks him to say truly why, after becoming the shoulder-companion of fine women and bathing in the red flood of the first rains, his eyes have turned so very red.
nuance: 'We are not sulking' opens a sulk. She offers the red, muddy first-rain flood as the reason for his red eyes and leaves him to deny the other reason, the women whose shoulders he held.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's denied sulk over the husband's bath with other women is the field country's quarrel

title: மருதம் புலவி விராய பத்து decade 9
theme: The decade of the other woman's sulking (புலவி விராய பத்து, marutham, Orampokiyar): the courtesan answers the husband, the bard and her own friend about the wife's anger, mocking the husband's straying, the wife's jealousy and the title of wife, and ending with the husband as a bee (81-90).
source_issues: 81-90: the colophon has no thurai for this decade; the speaker (parathai) and addressees are inferred from the poems and the decade title புலவி விராய பத்து, so occasion words are null.
81 line 1: உடைத் தூண்ட is printed split; read as உடைத்து உண்ட.
88 line 4 and 89 lines 2 and 4: the e-text joins and splits words (வேண் டுதுமே, பெரி தளிக்கும்) so the exact sense of the wish and of பெண்டென விரும்பின்று is uncertain.

tamil: குருகு உடைத் தூண்ட வெள் அகட்டு யாமை
reading: The other woman tells the lord of the town, where field workers with their rattling drum add to their evening meal the white-bellied turtle a heron has cracked open, by a pond whose mouth is decked with flowers, that if his wife heard him say 'I desired you' to her, she would grieve greatly.
nuance: Her concern for the wife is mock concern: she turns his declaration of love back on him as something he could not say at home, so the line that seems kind is a taunt. The heron that cracks the turtle and the workers who gather what is left can be read as the man who takes his pleasure and the women who live on his leavings, but the poem names no second match and draws no moral, so it fails condition 3 and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: field workers, a pond turtle and a flowered pond are things of the watered fields

reading: The other woman tells the bard that, they say, his mistress flew into a rage because the bees that fed on the pollen of the fragrant garland of open clusters on her husband's chest came and settled in her own flower-filled hair.
nuance: The proof against him is so slight that it is comic: a few bees moving from his garland to her hair. She lets the bard carry back that the wife's anger is out of proportion, while admitting the closeness the bees reveal. The bees are not iraicchi: strike them and the wife's anger has no cause, so they are the poem's subject (the deletion test fails).

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's anger at a husband who has been with another woman is marutham's sulking

reading: The other woman tells the man who joined with her and now shows no grace that he should at least draw away gently and let her survive, so that even the bright-bangled girls of his town may say of the lord of the cool ford that he was hers once.
nuance: She does not ask him to stay, only to leave slowly, so that the break looks like a fading and not a dismissal; what she guards is how she will be spoken of among the town's girls, her standing rather than his love.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the cool ford is the marutham man

reading: The other woman says that the wife, who rages beyond words when she only hears of it, what will she become when she sees with her own eyes his philandering chest, which many plunge into and enjoy like the cool pond of the month of Thai where women with fragrant flowers in their braids bathe.
nuance: She includes herself among the many who bathe in that pond, so the simile is a boast as well as a charge: the chest is common, and she has had her share. The Thai bath was a girls' vow for a good husband, which makes the pond an ironic image for a husband shared by all.

thinai_evidence.note: the bathing pond of the Thai festival is the field country's water

comparisons.tenor: his philandering chest

reading: The other woman tells the lord of the town of flawless, overflowing new wealth, where the white-browed water-hen's rattling-voiced mate calls among her kin in the cool fragrant field-pond, that he does things like a little boy: won't those who see him laugh?
nuance: The address swings from the grand (பெரும, lord of rich new wealth) to the belittling (like little boys), and the mockery lives in that gap. The hen calling among her kin could be read as a woman secure in her household, but it does nothing a person of the situation does, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-hen of the field-pond is a marutham bird

reading: The other woman tells the lord of the town, where the soft-winged white-headed heron's calling voice echoes across the long fields, that it is hard for him to grace her here, so let him go and join the young woman of his house.
nuance: Sending him home is her sulk: she calls the wife a மடந்தை, a young girl, which both concedes the wife's claim and belittles it.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron calling over long paddy fields fixes the field country

reading: The other woman tells the lord of the rich town, where cowherds of many cattle, wearing pakanrai chaplets, knock down mangoes using sugarcane as a stick, that his wife sulks at everyone, so why single her out?
nuance: A town so rich that herdsmen use sugarcane to beat down mangoes is a town of careless plenty, and the wife who sulks at all comers is pictured as just as indiscriminate; a reader may see the cane-stick as the wife's anger spent on anyone, but only one match can be named, so it is a near miss on condition 3 and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: sugarcane, mango and a rich town are marutham plenty; the cowherds are guests from the pasture

reading: The other woman says that they report our sister, his wife, wanting the lord of the cool ford of the rich flowered pond where the bees dwell to come to her; she too, as if she were one of his old ones, wants just that.
nuance: Calling the wife எவ்வை, our sister, places the two women in one family of his women; the claim to want him 'like old ones' (தொல்லேம் போல்) mocks the wife's claim of seniority by borrowing it.

thinai_evidence.note: a bee-haunted flower pond at a cool ford is the field country

reading: The other woman tells the bard that people ask what great grace the lord of the town, where bees sip pollen in the field-pond, shows our sister: it is her own nature that wished to be called his wife.
nuance: The barb is that the wife has the name of wife (பெண்டு) and is content with it; the grace she is said to receive is her title, not his love. The bee sipping pollen in the epithet foreshadows the bee image of poem 90 but does nothing a person does here beyond the epithet, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: bees in the field-pond fix the field country

reading: The other woman wonders whether the bees took on the husband's fine nature or the husband took on the bees', and says that the mother of his son, not knowing he is so, sulks with her.
nuance: The 'fine quality' (மாண்குணம்) shared by bee and husband is flitting from flower to flower, so the praise is the sharpest insult in the decade; and the wife is named only as the mother of his son, the one bond the other woman cannot share.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulk at the husband's other woman is marutham's situation

comparisons.tenor: the husband's roving nature

title: மருதம் எருமைப் பத்து decade 10
theme: Ainkurunuru 91 to 100, the buffalo decade of the marutham hundred (எருமைப் பத்து, Orampokiyar): each short poem opens on a buffalo of the field town, trampling lilies, nursing its calf, resting with its mate, snapping its rope, bathing like a raft or digging up a bather's jewel, and turns to the girl, mostly as the man's praise of the field-lord's daughter, once as the friend's warning that her parents guard her, and once as the complaint of a woman the rope-breaking lord has left sick even by day.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
91 line 1 reads நீலைரும், apparently நீல் இரும் (dark blue-black) written with ை for the sandhi; the sense is clear.
91 line 4 வெதிர் (bamboo) is unexpected for a field creeper used in a garland; the word may be corrupt.
93 line 3 செய்த இனைய மன்ற does not construe easily with what precedes and follows; the line may be corrupt.
99 line 2 writes யெருமை, the glide-initial spelling of எருமை after கழனி.

reading: The man points out the girl: she is the daughter of the lord of the field town, where the dark curved-horned buffalo bull tramples and tangles the water lilies of the fragrant pond, and she wears a twined garland made from a creeper of the field.
nuance: The closing word வெதிர் normally means bamboo, an odd plant for a marutham field and for a garland; what creeper of the field it names cannot be fixed from the line, so the garland's exact material is left open.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, the pond lilies and the field town are all of the watered fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the closing formula (... ஊரன் மகள் இவள்) points to the girl and praises her, which is the man's voice in courtship, telling his companion

reading: The man tells the bright-bangled girl that, if he may have her, he will come to her father's town, where the red-eyed cow of the black-horned buffalo, newly calved, gives her flowing udder to the calf she loves.
nuance: 'If we get you' (நின்னையாம் பெறினே) makes the visit a suitor's: to come to the father's town is to ask for her openly, and the nursing cow in that town is the home the asking would found.

reading: Because the good buffalo bulls have grazed the fresh red flowers and water lilies bare, the bees, though they have fed their fill of pollen in many groves, now come humming to the crown of this girl's head, where buds are opening.
nuance: The grazed field explains the bees' move only on the surface: a reader is meant to hear that the bees, sated on every grove, still choose her flower-dressed hair, the claim the man makes for her fragrance. Line 3 (செய்த இனைய மன்ற) is hard to construe, so how the grazing and the bees are joined is uncertain.

reading: This girl, daughter of the lord of the field town, where gem-blue neythal flowers thrive with water lilies in the mire the graceful buffalo wallowed in, is the sweet bed companion of the lord of the pond town.
nuance: Two lords are named: her father, the man of the field town (கழனி ஊரன்), and the man of the pond town (பழன ஊரன்) whose bed she shares; to call her his companion of the bed is to declare the union, which is why the speaker is likely the friend making it known to the household. title: நெய்தல் தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து decade 11
theme: Ainkurunuru 101 to 110, Ammuvanar's neythal decade told to the mother (தாய்க்கு உரைத்த பத்து): every poem opens on the refrain அன்னை வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை and the friend lays the girl's secret love before her mother, first as cure (the chariot, its bell, the matched pair), then as symptom (gold brow, pale chest, sleepless nights), then as grievance (the shoulders he left) and a plea to fate.
source_issues: 101-110: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the refrain and the decade title.
104: line 1 reads அன்னை வழிவேண் டன்னை where the other nine poems have வாழிவேண்; a dropped vowel sign, likely an e-text slip (not confirmed against another edition).
104: line 4 செல்வனஃ தூரே (செல்வன் அஃது ஊரே) is obscure; whether செல்வன் is 'the rich one' or 'he will go' decides the closing sense.
105, 106: the shown text carries repaired lines (flags in show); the readings follow the repaired text.

reading: The friend tells the mother to look: the shore lord's chariot has come, tearing through the green adumbu creepers, riding up and down and trampling the neythal, the chariot that is the medicine for the sickness her daughter's flower-like kohled eyes have caught.
nuance: The poem names the cure before the illness is admitted: the friend does not tell the mother her daughter loves, she tells her the medicine is arriving, so the disclosure is made as a diagnosis. The chariot crushing the shore plants shows a man coming openly and in haste, not by stealth.

nuance: Line 2 can also be read as the bell sounding without pause like the sea birds; either way the sea birds' unending noise is set against one sound that ends the noise of grief. A bell heard openly in the town is the sign of a suitor, not a secret lover.

reading: The friend tells the mother that the lord of the cool ford, where punnai and njaazhal flower together, has become fit for this girl, and her dark beauty has become fit for him alone.
nuance: The two trees flowering together look like a hidden image of the matched pair, but it is one correspondence (the pair matched), not two, so it fails condition 3 and is left as scene: a near-miss ullurai. The claim of mutual fitness (அமைந்தனன், அமைந்தன்று) is the friend's argument for marriage put to the mother.

reading: The friend tells the mother to look at the girl's lovely chest as she thinks of him: it gleams brighter than the conch of the cool sea in his land, which the swan with its trunk-like legs treads on, taking it for its mate.
nuance: The swan that mistakes a white conch for its mate is a near-miss iraicchi: it acts as a lover would, but no single sense for the girl follows from it, so it stays scene. title: நெய்தல் தோழிக்கு உரைத்த பத்து decade 12
theme: Ainkurunuru 111 to 120, Ammuvanar's neythal decade spoken by the heroine to her friend (தோழிக்கு உரைத்த பத்து): each poem opens அம்ம வாழி தோழி and sets one moment of the shore love, from the baited kayal and the fear of parting, through gossip, the mother's guard and the closing lilies of evening, to anger that relents and shoulders that bloom again when he comes.
source_issues: 111-120: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the decade title and the poem.
112: line 4 (மறந்தோம் மன்ற நாணுடை நெஞ்சே) is a repaired line in our text; what is forgotten is not stated, and the sense is marked uncertain.
116: line 4 (காலை யன்ன காலைமுந் துறுத்தே) repeats காலை and is hard to construe; the reading is marked uncertain.
118: line 3 is the tamilvu.org reading, agreeing with sangamtamil.com; no doubt remains about the words.
118: the colophon thinai is நெய்தல் but the poem names no land and its situation is oodal; my thinai is marutham.

reading: The woman tells her friend that she could not live parted from her bond with the lord of the ford where the fisherman fixes bait on a line at the edge of the winding backwater and kills the roe-heavy kayal, since she is not one who can carry out hard penance.
nuance: Separation is measured against தவம்: to live apart from him would take an ascetic's power to bear pain, and she says she has none (ஆற்றாதேமே). பாணன் here is the fisher of the shore, not the bard; the fish killed is one that carries roe, so the catch destroys more than itself.

reading: The woman tells her friend that today, on seeing the man without justice, she went meaning to rage at him and hold him back, but thinking it over she relented and came away.
nuance: அறனிலாளன், the man without aram, is her charge, and line 3 lists what she meant to do; line 4 undoes it. Whether she pitied him or herself (இரங்கி) is left open. The poem stands in a neythal decade, but its situation is the quarrel of the fields, so my thinai differs from the colophon.

title: நெய்தல் கிழவற்கு உரைத்த பத்து decade 13
theme: Ainkurunuru 121 to 128, the neythal decade spoken to the lord of the shore: by our reading the friend answering a husband who denies another woman, each poem opening 'did we not see your woman?' and showing her as a child at sea play, asking a heron for a lost jewel, filling the sea with sand to avenge a stolen doll, weeping red-eyed for it, and feeding a doll from a breast that has no milk.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; the speaker (the friend, to the husband) is inferred from the decade title and the refrain, and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
Only eight poems (121 to 128) of the decade survive in our text; 129 and 130 are absent.
122 line 1 reads கண்டகும் where every other poem of the decade has the refrain கண்டிகும்; likely a misprint.
122 line 3 வினைவு வோளே gives no clear sense; read as வினவுவோளே (she who asks), uncertain.
125 line 1 lacks the refrain's last word கேளே, present in every other poem of the decade.
126 line 2 begins யுண்கண், carrying the glide from the refrain's கேளே across the line break; the word is உண்கண்.
127 line 3 விலங்கு வோளே is divided; the sense of விலங்குவோள் is uncertain.

reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore whether they did not see his woman, the one who leapt into the clear-waved sea and stood there with her sea-holly garland soaking.
nuance: The opening question is a rebuttal: கண்டிகும் அல்லமோ presumes he has denied her, and the friend proves the woman exists by describing her at play, so the evidence and the insult are the same picture.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-holly of the backwater and the open sea

title: நெய்தல் பாணற்கு உரைத்த பத்து decade 14
theme: Ainkurunuru 131 to 140, Ammoovanar's neythal decade spoken to the bard (பாணற்கு உரைத்த பத்து): the woman (once the man, once turning to the lord himself) uses the hero's bard as the ear for gossip, wasted shoulders and slipped bangles, rebukes him for carrying words instead of the man, and twice bids him look (காண்மதி பாண), once at beauty returned and once at bangles gone.
source_issues: 131-140: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (பாணற்கு உரைத்த பத்து), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and the decade title.
139: the poem stands in two lines, the first unusually long (அம்ம வாழி கொண்க ... நின்னினும்); the line division looks like an e-text join, and the anthology's poems have 3 to 6 lines.
140: line 3 reads விறைகேழ் எல்வளை; the வ் is the glide after பிரிந்தென, and the word is இறைகேழ் (cf. Natrinai 167 இறை ஏர் எல் வளை), split at the wrong place.
135: line 2 repeats ainkurunuru:176 line 3 (ஐதுஅமைந்து அகன்ற அல்குல்).

reading: The woman tells the bard that the friendship of the shore lord is good indeed, so long as no loud gossip rises in this town hedged with thillai.
nuance: The praise is hedged by its last line: the bond is good only at a time (காலே) when the town is quiet, so the opening நன்றே turns into a complaint that it cannot survive being known. The thillai hedge makes the town an enclosure that hears everything.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord (கொண்கன்) and the thillai hedge of the coastal town fix the seashore

nuance: What the town talks about is not his neglect but his kindness (அருளும் ஆறே): his visits are the scandal. The punnai is only in bud (அரும்புமலி), and the gossip already blooms (அலர் also means a blossom).

title: நெய்தல் ஞாழற் பத்து decade 15
theme: Ainkurunuru 141 to 150, Ammuvanar's neythal decade on the njaazhal of the sand dune: every poem opens on the dune's njaazhal tree (its scent, clusters, birds, tide and waves) and turns to the shore lord, through pallor, sleeplessness and wasting to his return, the bride price and the friend's warning not to leave.
source_issues: 141-150: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
143: the sense of முனிவு செய்த (weariness given to him, or distress to her) cannot be fixed from the text; marked uncertain.
142, 144, 148: lines repaired from tamilvu.org per the text flags; the marks follow the repaired lines.

reading: The heroine says that the shore, where the njaazhal of the dune and the cherunthi spread their scent and the cold spray is flung in drops under the falling dew, has given her the pallor of longing.
nuance: She blames the place, not the man: the scented, cold, wet shore is made the agent (செய்தன) of her pallor, so the lover is accused only through his landscape.

thinai_evidence.note: the sand dune, its njaazhal and the shore fix the sea-coast land

reading: The heroine tells her friend she will not think of the lord of the shore, where birds settle on the low branch of the dune's njaazhal with its drooping clusters, so that her eyes may sleep.
nuance: The resolve is an admission: she must decide not to think of him precisely because thinking keeps her awake. The birds coming to roost on his shore while she cannot rest could be read as an implied contrast, but they do nothing a person of the situation does beyond resting, and the poem's sense does not need them, so they stay scene.

title: நெய்தல் வெள்ளங் குருகுப் பத்து decade 16
theme: Ainkurunuru 151 to 160, Ammuvanar's neythal decade of the white heron: every poem opens on the simple-gaited stork that went to see what it took for the white heron's chick, and turns to the lord of the shore, with the woman refusing a melted heart, the friend reporting that he will marry, the woman complaining of the town's lies and of a sedge doll borne to a man who leaves with the tide, and the friend demanding back her beauty and begging him to embrace her.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives the thinai only, no thurai; every speaker is inferred from the poem and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
The decade title as printed reads வெள்ளங் குருகுப் பத்து, while the refrain in every poem reads வெள்ளாங் குருகின்; the title appears to have lost the long vowel.
156 line 4 reads தெள்கழிப், where the sandhi of தெள் + கழி would give தெண்கழி or தெட்கழி; the form looks unassimilated.
158 line 4 reads கண்டிக்கும், where the sense 'we saw' wants கண்டிகும், as in the refrain of decade 13; possibly a misprint.
157 lines 4 and 5 can be parsed two ways (எம் காதலோன் as the lover or as the son), and the sense of the poem changes with it.

reading: The woman says that for the lord of the shore, where the neythal that opened like an eye when the simple-gaited stork trod on it, going to see what it took for the white heron's chick, keeps on breathing out its honey scent, she will not give in to the heart that has melted.
nuance: The decade's refrain turns on செத்தென, which can mean 'taking it for' or 'having died': either the stork mistook something for the heron's chick or went to see a chick that had died; this poem's reading does not depend on which. The flower that blooms under the foot that crushes it is the poem's whole argument: the hurt itself made her open to him, which is why she must refuse with her will what her heart has granted.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

reading: Where the simple-gaited stork cries out helplessly in the lonely seaside grove, they say the lord of the shore will marry her; he seems a man of virtue, and that too is grace.
nuance: போலும் here is the particle of seeming, not a comparison: the speaker will believe he is virtuous only when the marriage happens. The helpless cry of the stork in the lonely grove is the grief the news is meant to end, set beside it without comment.

reading: Will the intimacy of the lord of the shore, whose heaped sand gets a covering from the down shed by the shaking stork, seek out the girl of the fine long hair?
nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the shore gains its covering from feathers the bird drops without meaning to, and one may hear the lord's affection as just as idle a gift, but only one pair maps, so condition 3 fails. reading: For the lord of the shore who goes away with the tide, where neythal flowers crushed as the stork flutters float down the backwater, I have borne a doll of green sedge, the woman says.
nuance: The sedge doll is a girl's toy, so to say she has 'borne' one to him is to say their union has left her a child still, with no issue and no standing. A near miss for ullurai (the flowers the stork crushes and the tide carries off, the man who comes and goes with it) fails condition 3 on a second clear pair.

title: நெய்தல் சிறுவெண் காக்கைப் பத்து decade 17
theme: Ainkurunuru 161 to 170, the neythal decade of the small white gull: each poem opens on the gull of the great sea's shore at rest, feeding, sleeping, nesting or taking fright, and by our reading the woman (twice her friend) weighs the shore lord's word against her wasting body: bangles that leave as he left, words that have changed, gossip bred by his good name, pallid eyes that do not obey her trust.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the poem and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
165 line 4 reads இறையோர் where 163 line 4 has இறையேர் (fair-wristed) in the same phrase; likely a misprint for இறையேர்.
165 line 2 divides அறு கழிச் (the drying backwater) as two words; read as அறுகழி.
166 line 2 வரிவெண் தாலி: what the gull mistakes for a net is unclear (a striped white shell or a shore plant); the reading of the poem does not depend on it but the iraicchi's image does.
168 line 4 is divided பாலா ரும்மே; read as பால் ஆரும் (will drink milk).

reading: The woman says that for the lord of the ford where the small white gull of the great sea's shore rests on the black-branched punnai, her forehead, once spread with pallor, has wasted away, and the heart that desired him has gone over to sickness.
nuance: The gull has a fixed perch on the punnai while her heart has none; the decade's refrain sets every poem against this bird that always has somewhere to rest. Read as scene: the gull only rests, it does nothing a person of the situation does.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore gull resting on the punnai

nuance: Near miss for ullurai: the gull that feeds in one place and sleeps in another fragrant one can be read as the man who takes his pleasure elsewhere, but only one correspondence can be named, so condition 3 fails and the bird stays scene.

nuance: The verb துற is used twice, துறந்தென துறந்து: the bangles copy his act, so her wasting body becomes a second desertion, and the pun on துறைவன் (lord of the ford) makes his title name the deed.

title: நெய்தல் தொண்டிப் பத்து decade 18
theme: Ainkurunuru 171 to 180, Ammuvanar's Thondi decade, a linked chain in which each poem opens with the last words of the one before and every poem likens the girl to the Chera port of Thondi: by our reading the man, struck by her, loses his heart and his sleep, is granted a tryst, pleads with her and her friend, and then the friend turns his own word, grace, back on him and asks for marriage.
source_issues: Every colophon of the decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
175 line 4 பண்புல gives no clear word; read as பண்பு பல (many qualities), uncertain.
174 line 4 அம் கலிழ் மேனி அசைஇய எமக்கே is hard to construe: கலிழ் may be glowing or weeping, and அசைஇய may refer to the man's weariness or the girl's rest.
173 line 2 அரவுறு may be from அரம் (a file) or அரவு (a snake); the sense of pain is clear, the image is not.
The decade is a linked chain (each poem opens with the last words of the one before) except at 180, which opens with சிறுநனை after 179 ends with சிறு நுதலே, taking up only சிறு.

reading: The man says the young woman with bright bangles and shoulders full as bamboo, lovely as Thondi where the sweet sound of the waves mingles with the sweet sound of drums beaten along every street, has carried off his heart.
nuance: The town is heard before it is seen: the sea's music and the drums of the streets blend into one sound, and that is what the girl is likened to. The last words, the girl who took my heart, are taken up as the first words of 172, beginning the decade's linked chain.

nuance: He speaks of himself in the third person plural, as if stating a law: whoever is struck by such hair suffers so. The hair is named as the அணங்கு, the afflicting power, so the girl is a danger as well as a beauty. அரவுறு துயரம் may be the pain of a file's cut or of a snake's bite; either way a bodily wound.

nuance: The just sceptre is not idle praise of the king: a town under a just ruler gives to all who come, and the lover who calls her such a town is asking for that same grace. Praise alone, he says, cannot keep him alive.

title: நெய்தல் நெய்தற் பத்து decade 19
theme: Ainkurunuru 181 to 190, Ammuvanar's decade on the neythal flower: in every poem the blue lily of the shore appears, as the girls' eyes, a garland, a closing flower at evening, dawn bloom like a lover's eyes, or a flower cut down with the paddy, and the speakers move from the hope of marriage and the friend's disclosure to the heroine's grief and the eyes he heals or makes weep.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and says so in its note.
187 is obscure: what இவை (line 1) refers to and the sense of உடலகம் கொள்வோர் (line 4) are not fixed by the text; read as the friend refusing a leaf gift, marked uncertain.

tamil: நெய்தல் உண்கண் ஏர் இறைப் பணைத் தோள்
reading: The speaker says that if the lord of the shore, where unfailing girls with neythal-like eyes and lovely bamboo shoulders play sand games and set up the kuravai dance on heaps of white sand, would only grant his grace, living in this clamouring town would be sweet.
nuance: அழுங்கல் ஊர் is a town full of noise, and the noise is double: the girls' kuravai on the sand and the talk about her; one condition, நல்கின், would turn both into the sound of a wedding town.

thinai_evidence.note: the white sand of the ford and the shore lord

thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the conditional நல்கின் and the complaint about the clamouring town fit the heroine wishing for marriage while the town talks

comparisons.tenor: the girls' kohl-lined eyes

reading: The friend says that the one who struck this girl when she saw him at the great ford is no god of fearsome power but a man whose chest smells of a hand-woven garland of fragrant neythal mixed with cherunthi.
nuance: The household reads her sickness as a god's seizure (அணங்கு); the friend keeps the word but gives it a human subject, அணங்கியோன், and the garland is her evidence: a god would not wear a shore man's hand-made wreath.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal garland and the great ford of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; denying that a god caused the girl's sickness is the friend's disclosure of the affair (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்) to the foster mother

reading: Since the man who is lord of the land of falls and forests, of the small hills, of the town of good fields and of the cool sea has left her, the woman tells the helpless evening that it comes, unlike before, in the harsh daytime, as the neythal of the curved backwater closes, and that even when morning comes there is no one to take away her pain.
nuance: She gives him the titles of all four lands in a row, so the man has no landscape that is not his, while she has only the closing hour of the shore; and the last line refuses the usual comfort that night's end brings relief.

thinai_evidence.note: evening by the backwater, the shore's hour of lament

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the heroine, after the man has left (பிரிந்தென), addresses the evening itself (மாலை, வருதி)

reading: The speaker says his town, where flocks of fish-eating herons leave the neythal of the dark backwater to rest in the seaside grove, is adorned by the sea, but greater than the sea is our friendship with him.
nuance: The sea is first his town's ornament, then the measure her love exceeds: the thing that most defines his place is the very thing she sets below their bond.

thinai_evidence.note: herons, seaside grove and the sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the heroine affirms the bond (எமக்கு அவருடை நட்பே) against any doubt about the man of another shore town

comparisons.tenor: our friendship with him

reading: The man says the young girl at the front ford of Korkai of swaying-petalled neythal, with red lips set with teeth that shine like gleaming pearls and lovely saw-cut conch bangles, has speech as sweet as tuned lute strings.
nuance: Every ornament is a Korkai product: pearl from its sea, conch cut by the saw into bangles; the girl is described in the town's own wares, and only her voice needs an image from outside the shore.

thinai_evidence.note: neythal, the harbour ford and pearls

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the man describing the girl he has seen at the ford in the third person (குறுமகள் ... கிளவியளே) fits his telling his companion

comparisons.tenor: her teeth
her sweet speech

reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where women shake out their wet hair like a fine flock of herons, that their mother has said: a chariot comes many times to this ford where neythal drips on the swelling water, so do not go there.
nuance: The mother's sentence is quoted whole, so the hero hears the prohibition from the mother's own mouth; the chariot that betrays him is his own, and the visits it repeats (பல்கால்) are what ended them.

thinai_evidence.note: heron, neythal and the lord of the ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the friend addresses the hero as துறைவ and reports the mother's ban (என்றனள் யாயே), the confinement that urges marriage

comparisons.tenor: women shaking out their wet hair

reading: The friend tells the man that strangers do not accept these leaves: even the girls who come with us to bathe in the sea do not make dolls of the green-mixed neythal leaves, and for want of anyone to wear them on the body they carry only a few flowers set in a garland.
nuance: The 'these' of line 1 are best taken as the leaf garment the man offers as a courting gift; the friend refuses it by saying her company wears no stranger's leaves, so the refusal is also a reproach that he is still a நொதுமலாளர், a stranger, until he asks for her.

thinai_evidence.note: neythal leaves and sea bathing

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; refusing gifts from strangers (நொதுமலாளர் கொள்ளார் இவையே) fits the friend turning back the man's leaf gift

reading: The man says that his love's eyes have great beauty, like the neythal that opens at dawn at the great ford of Korkai of the lord of Korkai, where flocks of birds feed on red prawns of the dark backwater.
nuance: The flower is the dawn neythal, newly opened, not the evening one that closes (183); the time word makes the eyes fresh as well as blue.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns of the backwater and neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the man praising காதலி கண் in the third person speaks to himself or his companion

comparisons.tenor: his love's eyes

reading: The woman tells her friend that since the lord of the gentle shore, where the neythal dusted with fine punnai pollen looks as lovely as a gem set in gold, has come, her eyes have become good again.
nuance: The flower dusted with gold and the eyes made good are one image: her neythal-like eyes, grown pale in his absence, regain their colour as the blue flower takes on the punnai's gold.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai and neythal, the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the heroine tells her friend (தோழி) that he has come (வந்தென), read as his coming to marry or his return

comparisons.tenor: neythal dusted with punnai pollen

reading: The woman says that the lord of the gentle shore, where the reapers of white paddy cut down the fragrant cool neythal's opened white flower along with the grain, is surely the one who has made her many-petalled kohl eyes weep.
nuance: The reapers do not aim at the neythal; it falls because it grows among the paddy they want, so the harm in the image is careless, not cruel, and the eyes it spoils are named with the flower's own word, பல்லிதழ்.

thinai_evidence.note: the weeping of the shore woman decides it, though the field things are marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the woman names her own eyes (எம் பல்லிதழ் உண்கண்) and blames the man, as in a complaint to her friend

comparisons.tenor: her eyes
the man spoiling her flower-like eyes in passing
