he harms her in passing, while about his own gain, not aiming at her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the neythal and the reapers of the fields beside her own shore town, things she knows (porul 7.26)

title: நெய்தல் வளைப் பத்து decade 20
theme: Ainkurunuru 191 to 200, Ammuvanar's neythal decade of the bangle: the conch shell of the shore sawn into bangles, which the man sees on the girl he cannot reach, the friend weighs as a lover's gift and as a reason to marry, and the woman reads as a gauge that loosens when the lord of the shore leaves and tightens when he returns.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
194 line 2 and 198 line 4 read கண்டிக்கும், with a doubled க், where the refrain elsewhere in Ainkurunuru is கண்டிகும் (we have seen); likely a misprint.
192 line 1 கோடுபுலம் கொட்ப is obscure (கோடு as shore or as conch); the sense of the opening scene is taken loosely.
195 line 4 படலின் பாயல் is unclear (படல் as lying down or as a woven mat); the sense, his sleep on his bed, is not affected.
199 line 4 lacks the final full stop the other poems carry; no effect on the sense.

reading: The man says that the girl with bangles of sea conch on her long forearms, backwater flowers strung through her dark heavy hair and a fine leaf skirt of the shore grove's njaazhal, harder to win than the nymphs of the mountain, has taken his heart that could not hold itself and hidden it away.
nuance: Everything she wears is of the shore, conch at the wrist, backwater flowers in the hair, a skirt of njaazhal leaves, and only the measure of her is brought down from the mountain: she is a fisher girl, yet rarer than its goddesses. The theft runs the other way from the decade's usual loss: here it is the man's heart, நிறையரு (past holding), that is carried off and hidden.

thinai_evidence.note: conch, backwater flowers and njaazhal of the shore grove dress her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the man describes the girl and speaks of his own heart, so he is taken to speak to it or to his companion

comparisons.tenor: the shore girl

reading: The woman tells her friend that when the lord of the cold roaring ford, where the sea rises and thunders so the shores seem to whirl and running boats are driven out, went away, her bangles slipped loose, and now they have grown tight again.
nuance: The two verbs stand side by side with no clause between them, நெகிழ்ந்தன (loosened) then வீங்கின (swelled, grew tight): the bangle is a gauge that reads both ways, and the second verb, ending in the exclamation மாதோ, reports his return without naming it. Whether வீங்கின means the arm has filled out again with his coming is the reading the sense turns on.

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring sea, the boats and the lord of the ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; she says தோழி and என் வளை

reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore, where the right-whorled conch ploughs the long sand of the bank and pearls with shining rays glitter so the darkness is gone, whether the white bangles from the dashing sea that he has given are good, then.
nuance: The question நல்லவோ தாமே can be plain or barbed: on a shore where conch and pearl lie about lighting the dark, a gift of shell bangles is a small thing, and the friend may be asking whether such gifts can stand in for the marriage he delays. The sense turns on the tone, which four lines do not fix.

thinai_evidence.note: conch and pearl on the sea bank

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the hero is addressed as கொண்க and asked about the bangles he gave, which suits the friend weighing a lover's gift

reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore that they have seen the young girl with bright bracelets, with lovely bangles sawn from sea conch, and because her fine brow is today clouded with longing, the mother has suspected some wrong cause, and that is how the mother stands.
nuance: கொன் ஒன்று (some cause, in vain) is the whole of the mother's mistake in two words: she reads the girl's pallor as something other than love, the misreading that in longer poems brings the diviner and the veri rite, and the friend reports it to the man as the danger that only marriage will end.

thinai_evidence.note: conch sawn into bangles, and the shore lord addressed

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the hero is addressed as கொண்க and told of the girl and her mother, which is the friend's warning

reading: The man says that the dear young daughter of the sea lord, on whose shore fishermen sell the pearls born of the conch, has given him a grief that will not pass and stolen his sleep on his bed.
nuance: நல்கி, the verb of a patron's gift, is used for a sorrow, and the pearl that fishermen cry for sale sits beside the daughter no one may buy: a reader may hear in the pearl born of the conch the girl born of the chief, but the poem draws no second pair, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen selling pearls on the sea shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the man speaks of the girl as the sea lord's daughter, as one does to the friend whose help he needs

reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool sea shore, where red prawns are caught in the clear backwater, that if he wants the girl with bright bangles cut from conch, rich heavy hair and fine bracelets, he should marry her and take her.
nuance: The condition is put coolly, வேண்டுதி யாயின் (if you want her), so the demand to marry comes as the only terms on offer; the prawns caught in the clear backwater may suggest a catch to be landed properly, but a single image makes no ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns of the backwater and the lord of the sea shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the hero is told வரைந்தனை கொண்மோ (marry and take her), the friend's demand

reading: The man says that the girl who stood bowed with her face hidden in her hair, her shining bangles jingling as she chased the crabs, will give him her lovely breast so that the lonely evening is gone.
nuance: Two moments are set against each other: the girl caught at a child's game, then bowing and hiding her face once she is seen, and the man's certainty that the same girl will ease his evening. Her shame (முகம்புதை, இறைஞ்சி) is the sign he reads as consent.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore crab and the lonely evening, neythal's hour

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the man speaks of what the girl will give எனக்கே, to his own heart or companion

reading: The friend says that they have seen the tall-shouldered noble man who stood asking about the small ford, in the shore grove where loose-budded flowers open and young girls with bangled forearms, white teeth and gentle smiles play.
nuance: A man of tall shoulders stops to ask about a small ford: the question is the pretext of the first approach, and the friend's கண்டிக்கும் (we have seen) says she has seen through it.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the small ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; யாமே (we) and the report of a man seen at the grove fit the friend telling the girl what she noticed

reading: The woman asks her friend to come with her and climb the sky-high long sand dune that the roaring waves beat at the great ford of the shore grove, and gaze without end at the land of the wave-dashed sea of him who loosened her close bangles.
nuance: She names him only by what he has done to her, செறிவளை நெகிழ்த்தோன் (he who loosened the close bangles), and the remedy she proposes is not to hide the sign but to climb the highest dune in view of all and look at his country, ஆனாது (without stopping).

thinai_evidence.note: parted, she can only gaze toward his land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; she says தோழி and names him by her loosened bangles

reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord with the golden chariot has now come, so that her shining bangles fit tight and her fine brow grows lovely; let her long eyes with their red lines ease, and let them laugh at the pallor that took her beauty.
nuance: The decade ends by reversing its token: the bangle that slipped is வீங்கு (swelling, tight) again, and the pallor that ruled her is turned into something to mock. பொலந்தேர் (the golden chariot) suggests he comes openly, in state, not by stealth.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord comes and the bangles tighten

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives the thinai and the decade title வளைப் பத்து only, no thurai; the girl is told her lover has come and invited to laugh with the speaker (நகுக நாமே)

title: குறிஞ்சி அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து decade 21
theme: Ainkurunuru 201 to 210, Kapilar's kurinji decade to the mother (அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து): under the refrain அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை the friend lays the girl's secret love before her mother through things of his hill, a leaf skirt from his slope, his tufted horses, the muddy water of his land, the gear he wears wet from the rains, and above all his hill itself, whose sight brings the girl tears when hidden and cure when seen.
source_issues: 201-210: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the refrain and the decade title.
209: the refrain's addressee and the speaker are unclear; யான் அவர் மறத்தல் makes the girl the speaker, against the friend-to-mother frame of the decade.
204: the subject of நோக்கி and என்ப is unstated, and தீயேன் may be the friend's or the girl's word; the sense of the poem turns on it.
207: உணங்கல கொல்லோ (drying or withering) and நிணம்பொதி வழுக்கில் are obscure; the readings are uncertain.
201: என்னை may be 'my lord' (the lover) or 'my father'.
203, 204, 205, 206, 208, 210: the shown text carries repaired lines (flags in show); the readings follow the repaired text.

reading: The friend asks the mother, as if idly, what tree it can be on his slope whose golden flowers and gem-like buds my lord himself wore and which became leaf skirts for us as well.
nuance: A leaf skirt given by a man is a token of courtship, so the friend's botanical question is a disclosure dressed as ignorance: the flowers belong to his slope and nowhere in theirs, and only the giver can explain them. Whether என்னை is the lover (my lord) or the girl's father decides how bold the hint is.

thinai_evidence.note: the slope of his hill, the kurinji land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; எமக்கும் (for us too) speaks for herself and the girl together, and என்னை (my lord) is read as the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the yellow of the flowers
the dark gleam of the buds

reading: The friend tells the mother that the horses the lord of the tall mountain rode here surely have tufted heads, just like the little Brahmin boy of our town.
nuance: The horses are proof that the lord has come to their town (ஊர்ந்த, rode), and the friend lets the mother see them through a homely, laughable likeness, the tufted head of a boy she knows, so the evidence arrives without alarm. மன்ற (surely) marks the friend as having seen them herself.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the tall mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer

comparisons.tenor: the plumed heads of the hill lord's horses

tamil: அன்னாய் வாழி வேண்டு அன்னை நம் படப்பை
reading: The friend tells the mother that the muddy water left over after deer have drunk, in a pit well under leaf litter in his land, is sweeter than the honey-mixed milk of our own garden.
nuance: The water is the poorest a hill can offer, dregs that beasts have left in a hole under rotting leaves, and the home drink is the richest; the inversion is the disclosure, for only a heart already given to his land could rank them so. Speaking of tasting it implies she has been, or means to go, there.

thinai_evidence.note: deer and leaf litter of the hill forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; the preference may be the girl's own, reported by the friend; the poem does not say whose taste it is

comparisons.tenor: the muddy water of his land

reading: The friend asks the mother what it means that, wherever the girl moves among her companions gathered like the mountain nymphs, he gazes at her without pause and says 'she is good, she is good', while to the lord of the mountain I am, alas, the wicked one.
nuance: The subject of நோக்கி and என்ப is not named; read with மலை கிழவோற்கு, it is the hill lord who watches and praises, and the friend tells the mother so by complaining that she is the obstacle. Another reading makes the townswomen the watchers.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; தீயேன் is read as the friend's own complaint that she, who keeps guard, is the hindrance in the lover's eyes; it could also be the girl speaking

comparisons.tenor: the girl and her companions in their row

reading: The friend tells the mother that her girl is very modest and fears even her, yet longs to sleep on the broad chest of the lord of the high mountain with its loud white waterfall, and the friend grieves for her.
nuance: The friend explains why she, not the girl, is speaking: the girl's shame and her fear of her mother keep her silent, so the disclosure must come from a second mouth. The two halves, great shame and open desire, are set side by side without a 'but', as the girl holds both at once.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's longing for union with the hill lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; என் தோழி names the girl as the speaker's friend

reading: The friend bids the mother look there: he is like a watchman of the rainy hill, his bright sword wet in its strap from the spray, his great anklet ringed with moss, his striped belt beaded with cold dew.
nuance: Every detail of his gear is a record of nights spent out in the wet hill: spray on the sword, moss grown on the anklet from wading, dew settled on the belt. The friend lets the mother read his constancy from his clothes, and the likeness to a field watchman makes the stranger look like one of their own hill people.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill in the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; உவக்காண் (look there) points the mother to the man himself

comparisons.tenor: the hill lord standing wet with his gear

reading: The friend asks the mother whether her millet is not drying at all, and bids her look: his tall gem-dark hill shows with rain cloud on its head like a wrapping of caul fat.
nuance: Whether உணங்கல means the millet will not dry because rain is coming from his hill, or that it is withering for want of rain that his hill's cloud promises, the friend turns the mother's eye from her crop to his hill; on the second reading the drying millet stands for the pining girl, as the Kalittokai says openly, but no stated situation anchors that pairing, so it is not tagged ullurai. வழுக்கு as the sense of the fat-wrapped likeness is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet crop and the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

reading: The friend tells the mother that whenever the gem-coloured great mountain of his land, where golden new vengai flowers fill the deep pits the hunters dug for tubers, is hidden from view, the girl's long flower-like eyes fill with tears.
nuance: The vengai's golden bloom is the kurinji sign of the wedding season, and its flowers filling the hollows the hunters left can be felt as a promise that his land is ready; but no second correspondence or stated situation completes it, so it stays scene. The girl weeps not when he is away but when his hill is out of sight, so the sight of the land stands in for the man.

comparisons.tenor: the blue of the far mountain
her long eyes

reading: If you want me to forget him, the speaker tells her, his tall gem-dark hill never stops appearing, crowned with a white-headed dark cloud like the flower of the bean that blooms in the east wind.
nuance: She does not refuse to forget; she says the landscape will not let her, putting the cause outside herself. The white-topped dark cloud is a bean flower in the cold east-wind season, so the image also tells the time of year, when the hill is most often cloud-crowned and so most often seen.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title அன்னாய் வாழிப் பத்து and the refrain's address அன்னை, as in the mother decade 101 to 110, make the friend the speaker and the mother the hearer; but யான் அவர் மறத்தல் (that I forget him) makes the girl the speaker here, answering one who urges her to forget; அன்னை may be the friend, as the address often is, or the mother herself

comparisons.tenor: the white-headed dark cloud on his hill

reading: The friend tells the mother that the girl's sickness might abate, and her gem-like bright jewels stay in place, if she climbed the flesh-smelling boulder in our garden and stood looking at the flowering hill of his land.
nuance: Jewels that stay in place mean a body that is no longer wasting, since slipping bangles are love-sickness's sign; the friend prescribes the cure while naming its source, his land, so the remedy is itself the disclosure. The boulder smells of flesh from the hunters' kills dried on it.

comparisons.tenor: her bright jewels

title: குறிஞ்சி அன்னாய்ப் பத்து decade 22
theme: The decade of 'mother' (அன்னாய்ப் பத்து, kurinji, Kapilar): every poem ends on அன்னாய், a girl and her friend speaking of the hill man of secret love, his wilting gift of leaves, his virtue, his coming and going, the omens of his return and the pallor his absence brings, each set against a scene of his hill (211-220).
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai (குறிஞ்சி) only, no thurai; speakers are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
211 line 3 பகைத்தழி is read as பகைத்தழை (a skirt of contrasting leaves); the form as printed gives no sense.
213 line 2 பாலையிற் is unclear in context (a paalai tree, or a misreading); the poem's sense does not turn on it.

reading: On the hill where the vayalai creeper grows pale as black-gram flour kneaded with ghee, the lovely leaf-skirt of mixed asoka leaves from its top is fading, mother.
nuance: The leaf-skirt (தழை) is the lover's gift of secret courtship; that it wilts is all the poem says, and the reader is left to set the withering gift beside a love that is not being renewed. The line has பகைத்தழி, read as பகைத்தழை, a skirt of contrasting leaves.

thinai_evidence.note: the asoka leaf-skirt and the vayalai creeper of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the pale vayalai creeper

reading: Why should we be parted from the man of the land where smoke rising from the fragrant wood among the sandal trees smells of blended perfume, a man of virtue, mother?
nuance: The girl calls him அறவன், a man of virtue, and that word is the whole of her argument: the fragrance that rises even from the smoke of his land is offered as a sign that nothing ill comes from him.

thinai_evidence.note: the sandal trees and the fragrant wood of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

reading: If the man of the good land high on the slopes comes, where hill people gather the cool big young mangoes that the fragrant mango drops when their stalks break, as one gathers hail fallen with the rain, I can go on living, mother.
nuance: The windfall the hill people only have to pick up is set against a life that hangs on his coming. The word பாலையிற் in line 2 is not clear as written and is left unread.

thinai_evidence.note: the mango of the slope and the hill people

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

comparisons.tenor: the fallen young mangoes

reading: The man of the land where a ripe, fragrant jackfruit from its rich cluster on the slope falls into a cleft of the dark rock and tears open a great honeycomb on the hill goes off to his own fine country, making my wide, cool eyes run with tears, mother.
nuance: The fruit does not mean to break the comb; it simply falls, and the honey runs. So the man does no deliberate wrong: he goes back to his own land, and her tears follow from his going as the honey does from the fall.

ullurai.tenor: the man's going and the girl's tears

pairs.situation: he drops away from her to his own country
her store of sweetness is broken and her eyes run

ullurai.speaker_fit: the girl uses the jackfruit and honeycomb of her own hill slope, things she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: In the evening of bush flowers, when the gem-dark bee, black as a touchstone, goes to the narrow-cut ford and hums sweeter than the musicians' flute playing the ambal tune behind the clapper and drum, those who part from us now will do things crueller still, mother.
nuance: The evening is not cruel in itself: every sound in it is sweet, the bee sweeter even than the flute. The cruelty is measured by the man who can leave at such an hour, and from that she reasons that he can do worse.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet-field clapper and the bee among bush flowers

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai, only the decade title அன்னாய்ப் பத்து; the girl speaks of those who part (பிரிவோர்) as men who leave her

comparisons.tenor: the bee's dark colour
the bee's humming

reading: Why should your body change, wilting like a plucked shoot, for the man of the land where the strong male of the short-legged great tiger hides in the rich shade of a fruit-laden jackfruit to seize the trembling calf a young she-elephant has borne in the forest of tall bushes, mother?
nuance: The friend's question half-answers itself: his land is one where a tiger lies in wait for a newborn calf, so the danger of his road, or of trusting such a man, is in the picture though never said. That reading is not tagged, since no second pair to the situation can be named.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger, the elephant calf and the jackfruit of the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

comparisons.tenor: the girl's body

reading: Even though the man of the forest land comes here, where great herds of deer graze on the fragrant gold-like flowers of the vengai on the high hill, why does the body turn pale, mother?
nuance: The puzzle is that the pallor comes while he is still coming: secret visits do not cure it. The vengai in flower is the season when marriages were made, which sharpens the question without answering it.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai of the high hill and the deer herd of the forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

comparisons.tenor: the vengai flowers

reading: My eyes under the fine brows throb and the bangles on my downy forearm grow tight: will the man of the great rocky land come, where a tiger that missed its seizure of a bull elephant rises in fury and roars like rising rain clouds, mother?
nuance: Throbbing eyes and bangles that grow tight are good signs, the reverse of the slipping bangles of separation, and she reads them as news of his coming. Yet the land she names is one of a baffled, roaring tiger, so hope and the danger of his road arrive in the same breath.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger and the bull elephant of the rocky hill

reading: Since the man of the good hill went away, where the bright flowers of the black-stemmed vengai with its dark calyx fall and stripe the wide rock, why does that bright forehead turn pale, mother?
nuance: The friend asks why, yet states the cause in the same sentence (பிரிந்தென, since he went), so the question is a gentle naming of the grief. The flowers striping the rock recall a tiger's coat, as the tree's name does.

reading: On the days she has not embraced the broad, mighty chest, like a great mountain, of the man of the land where a wide waterfall fed by swaying clouds comes down the slopes of waving bamboo, her cloud-cool eyes, their lids bewildered, run with tears, mother.
nuance: Clouds pour the waterfall, and the girl's eyes, called cloud-eyes (மழைக்கண்), pour tears: the hill's water and her weeping are matched by the same word, with no marker joining them.

title: குறிஞ்சி அம்மவழிப் பத்து decade 23
theme: Ainkurunuru 221 to 230, Kapilar's kurinji decade in which every poem opens அம்ம வாழி தோழி: the heroine and her friend talk of the secret lover's comings and goings measured on her body, her brow paling and shoulders slackening when he speaks of leaving or stays away, and her golden beauty returning when he comes by night or comes at last for the wedding.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain and from the poems' own pronouns (என் for the heroine speaking, நின் for the friend speaking), and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
222 line 3 இன் இனி is divided in our text; read as இன்னினி (now) or இன் (sweetly) with இனி, the sense uncertain.
223 line 2 வரையாம் இழிய is unclear; read as வரை ஆம் இழிய (water running down the peaks), uncertain.
227 line 3 ஆற்றலம் யாம் is read as the lover's own words (we could not bear it), uncertain.

reading: The woman tells her friend that her lover says he will go back to his hill country, and at that word her chosen beauty, fine as a doll's, begins to fade and her lovely dark body to pale.
nuance: The harm is done by the announcement, not the journey: செல்வல் is a first-person future quoted, and the fading and paling are set against the saying itself.

thinai_evidence.note: his land is the land of hills; the parting is to his own country, not across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

comparisons.tenor: her beauty

reading: The woman asks her friend whether it is because the man of the fragrant cool chest, who used to come close and stay in their town, no longer comes as sweetly now, that her brow under its small rows of hair is turning pale.
nuance: She offers the cause as a question, as if the pallor were a riddle to be solved, though she names the answer herself; the question form lets her accuse him without saying it.

thinai_evidence.note: the secret lover's visits to her town falling off, a kalavu situation

reading: The woman tells her friend that on their hill, as water runs down the peaks and the glory lily grows tall, their lover has come back ahead of the cold dew season and its north wind that torment those parted from their lovers.
nuance: The season is named only to be beaten: the poem lists everything the cold time does to the parted, and the last line says he arrived before it.

nuance: மன் marks the ease as something past and gone; the bewilderment is at the change in him, not at any obstacle she can see.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and its falls, the place of the lovers' play

comparisons.tenor: the dark hill

reading: The woman asks her friend whether their lover does not perceive that the bright lovely brow of the soft one, whose hair is fragrant within with the cool blue lily that rises above the green leaves of the hill pool, is turning pale.
nuance: The heroine speaks of herself in the third person as மெல்லியல், setting her beauty out as if for him to see; the fragrance of the lily-filled hair is still there while the brow fails.

thinai_evidence.note: the blue lily of the hill pool

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; the soft one may be the heroine naming herself, or the friend may be speaking of her

reading: The friend tells the woman that the heartless man who took her strong, conquering beauty and then turned his back like the bee that drinks the pollen of the fragrant-clustered glory lily on the cool slope of their hill and leaves, has now come.
nuance: The bee simile fixes what kind of lover he was, one who took and went; his arrival is reported without forgiveness, so the friend's news is also a charge. Because the tenor is stated, the bee is a simile, not ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: the glory lily of the hill slope

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நின் கவின் makes the heroine the one addressed

comparisons.tenor: the man who enjoyed her beauty and turned away

reading: The woman asks her friend whether she has let go the oath he swore, since the man who won their trust by saying he could not bear to see her brow pale and her shoulders slacken day by day now lives apart from them.
nuance: The oath was sworn to the friend as witness, so only the friend could release it; the question turns his absence into the friend's doing, which is reproach and irony at once.

thinai_evidence.note: no native thing; the kalavu oath and the decade's place in the kurinji hundred decide

reading: The woman asks her friend what will become of their dear life if the lord of the long hill with its falls spreading and shining goes away without pleading for their favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the long hill and its falls

reading: The friend asks the woman whether the man without virtue, who stayed away many days while they wept, came to her in the night, since her brow has taken on a golden, conquering beauty.
nuance: The friend reads the brow as evidence: the pallor's lifting betrays a night visit the heroine has not told of, so the question teases and also lets her know the secret is seen.

title: குறிஞ்சி தெய்யோப் பத்து decade 24
theme: Ainkurunuru 231 to 240, Kapilar's kurinji decade with the refrain தெய்யோ: by our reading the friend (once the girl) presses the hill lover in courtship, pointing to the girl's pallor and slipping bangles, the dream that shows him only asleep, the cold north wind, the ewe that waits and the tusker that embraces a stone, the scent of her hair on his chest, and at last proposing to go with him to his town now the mother knows.
source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees in thurai_akam are inferred from the poems' pronouns and recorded with a note.

235 line 1 கையுற வீழ்ந்த மையில் வானமொடு is obscure; we read it as a comparison, 'as rare as a clear sky dropping into one's hand', with ஒடு marking the likeness; the sense of the poem turns on it, so 235 is marked uncertain.
236 line 3 மலையும் may be the verb (it assails) or the noun (the mountain); we take the verb.

reading: The friend asks the lord of the high mountain how he can bring himself to a parting that wears away the spotted gold of his girl's skin and spreads pallor over it.
nuance: யாங்கு வல்லுநையோ asks how he is able: the strength he shows in staying away is set against the strength draining from her, so the question is a reproach that pushes him toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero is addressed as lord of the high mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; she speaks of the girl in the third person to the hill lord, urging him to end the parting

reading: The girl tells her lover that because he, a stranger to her still, has parted from her, the flower-filled hair loses its natural grace and her eyes rain without ceasing until the fire-bright gem jewel on her breast is soaked.
nuance: ஏதிலாளனை calls him a stranger: in courtship he has no bond she can name, so his leaving is the act of an outsider, and the word itself presses for marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: an unwed lover's parting in courtship, kurinji's union and its occasions

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the first person என் கண்ணே and the second person நீ show the girl speaking to the lover

comparisons.tenor: her tears

reading: The friend tells the hill lord that he does not come and the north wind is very cruel, so he should not go back to his rocky land where the waterfall rushes down the hard slope sweeping away choice gems.
nuance: The waterfall that strips the mountain of its gems as it runs away may suggest the lover who takes the girl's beauty with him when he goes, but the image does no act of a person in the situation, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard mountain and the cold north wind

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

nuance: The dream is not a comfort here but the measure of the lack: the closeness she has asleep (துன்னி) makes the waking absence the cause of the pallor.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers of courtship meet only in her dreams

nuance: Read with the next poem, எழுகமோ (shall we rise) is the first hint of going away with him; the two choices are to keep him here or to leave with him.

thinai_evidence.note: embrace and the refusal to part

comparisons.tenor: the rarity of the lovers' time together

reading: The friend tells the lover that the mother has come to know, gossip has risen, and the cruel north wind assails the good house till its tall mansion is desolate, so they will go to his town: shall they set out?
nuance: மலையும் is best taken as the verb (it assails) with the wind as subject; read as 'and the mountain', the line would add the hill to the wind among the things that make home unbearable.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend proposes leaving home with the lover, the paalai situation of elopement, against the colophon's kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

reading: The friend asks the lover where his town lies in relation to that high mountain rising tall, should a time come when desire drives them and the heart aches enough to come and see him.
nuance: The innocent question about the way to his town is a threat and a plea at once: if he will not come, they may come to him, which the courting girl cannot do without disgrace.

nuance: The scent on his chest is the secret union made public to the friend; in a marutham poem the same words would accuse a husband of another woman, but in this kurinji decade the fragrant woman is the friend's own girl, and the friend's knowing is the step before pressing for marriage.

title: குறிஞ்சி வெறிப்பத்து decade 25
theme: Ainkurunuru 241 to 250, Kapilar's kurinji decade on the veri rite (வெறிப்பத்து): mother calls the diviner, who casts his beads and names Murugu as the cause of the girl's sickness, and the friend and the girl answer with irony, asking whether the diviner can know the hill man, whether Murugu is his name, and saying the cure is union, not offering.
source_issues: 241-250: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (வெறிப்பத்து), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
245: the repeated_line flag on line 3 lists ainkurunuru:245 itself among its repeats; the line (முருகென மொழியும் ஆயின்) repeats only in 247 line 3.
245, 247: கன்னம் தூக்கி is a rare ritual phrase (the raised offering or measure); the reading turns on it.
246: lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe (கழங்கு மெய்ப்படூஉ inside the tiger scene; the simile புனவர் புணர்த்த மெய்ம்மை அன்ன).
248: line 2 (மலைவான் கொண்ட சினைஇய) was repaired from sangamtamil.com and remains obscure.
249: line 3 reads வாழிய விலங்கு மருவிச்; the sense wants வாழிய இலங்கு அருவிச் (shining falls), the வ் being the glide after வாழிய, split at the wrong place as in 140.

reading: The friend tells the girl that if mother, seeing the grief that has come on them, has brought the diviner, then that diviner can hardly know of her bond with the man of the fragrant hill country.
nuance: வெறிகமழ் describes the man's land with the very word that names the mother's rite, so the land's fragrance and the diviner's veri share a name while the diviner, by the friend's question, cannot know which of them is at work.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner of Murugu called to read the girl's sickness belongs to the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she addresses the girl as செறியெயிற்றோயே

reading: The friend tells the girl that mother, not knowing and confused into taking it for the god's seizure, has herself suffered sore grief, so it is cruel to leave her unknowing of the sickness the man of the far hill gave, which has paled her flower-like eyes.
nuance: The argument for disclosure is made on the mother's behalf (அன்னையும் அருந்துயர் உழந்தனள்): the friend counts the mother's needless grief, not only the girl's, as the harm of silence.

thinai_evidence.note: the misread sickness and the rite of veri belong to the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she speaks of the girl's own eyes and urges that the truth be told

comparisons.tenor: the girl's kohl-lined eyes

reading: The friend tells mother that she will take to heart what the ignorant diviner says after worshipping the god of the pepper-vine slope, that it is the god's seizure, as the cause of the sickness that has left her daughter's fresh-flower eyes tearful and forlorn.
nuance: அறியா வேலன் puts the diviner's ignorance first and the mother's belief second (மனம் கொள்குவை), so the friend's words to the mother already turn her from the rite toward the cause she has not been told.

thinai_evidence.note: the pepper vine of the slope and the god of the hill fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: அனை is taken as the vocative for mother, and the girl is spoken of as இவள்

comparisons.tenor: the girl's rain-wet eyes

reading: The girl tells her friend that unless the diviner sings the hill of the noble man of the land of fragrant cool groves full of flowers, his veri rite will do no good.
nuance: She does not reject the rite but rewrites its song: the diviner's praise of the god's hill would cure her only if it were the man's hill, so the rite is useless exactly because it is aimed at the wrong lord.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowered groves and the hill fix the land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: she opens with அம்ம வாழி தோழி

reading: If the old diviner of the town, of a tradition that does not lie, casts his beads, raises the offering and says it is Murugu, the friend asks, is that a kindness to the one who has afflicted her?
nuance: பொய்யா மரபின் praises the diviner's lineage only to let it fail here: naming Murugu lets the real afflicter (அணங்கியோன், the man) go unnamed, so the error is a favour to him.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner's naming of Murugu fixes the hill rite

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the girl is spoken of as இவள்; no addressee is named, and the household is the likely hearer

reading: The diviner has crowded on his veri rite, but the sickness the man of the hill country gave is the kind that ends as the strong tiger of the pepper-hung rock cave ends its distress, by joining its mate in the open ground.
nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard to construe: கழங்கு மெய்ப்படூஉ may belong to the diviner's casting or to the tiger scene, and the simile of the farmers' truth is obscure; the reading of the tiger's union as the cure is the plainer sense of மன்றில் பையுள் தீரும்.

thinai_evidence.note: the tiger of the rock cave and the hill farmers fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: no addressee is named; the friend speaks of the rite and the man in the third person

comparisons.tenor: the female the tiger joins

iraicchi.act: the tiger joins its female and its distress ends
iraicchi.sense: her sickness, like the tiger's, ends only in union with the man who gave it, not in the diviner's rite

reading: If the diviner mother brought, the one who is to know what will come, raises the offering within the bounds of the fine house and says it is Murugu, the speaker asks, is that the name of the man of the hard-to-reach hills?
nuance: The question half grants the diviner's word: if the god's name is the man's name, then the diagnosis is right by accident, and the joke on the rite is also a disclosure.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard hills and the name of Murugu fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

reading: If the angry diviner, having made the sand-strewn courtyard beautiful, is to find the cause by his beads, then fine indeed, says the friend, will be the beauty that is left to her.
nuance: நன்றால் அம்ம is ironic: the beauty is fading, and the friend means that the beads will leave it as ruined as it is.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner's beads and the prepared courtyard of the rite

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the girl is spoken of as இவள்; no addressee is named

reading: The diviner who casts his beads in the sand-strewn yard and tells mother it is Murugu, may he live long, says the friend, for he does not know the man of the haunted hill with shining falls.
nuance: The blessing (வாழிய) is double: mockery of a diviner who misses the cause, and real thanks, since his ignorance keeps the secret of the man of the hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the haunted hill and the naming of Murugu fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வெறிப்பத்து); speaker and addressee inferred from the poem: the friend speaks of mother and the diviner to the girl

reading: The friend tells the beads that never lie that truly the one who afflicted the girl's young ornamented breasts is not the manly victorious Vel, lord of our flowering valli forest where the young peahen dances in its haunt on the gem-bright hill.
nuance: The god is described by his own emblems, the peacock and the valli, and then denied: the friend grants the beads their truth only to say the truth they show is not Murugu.

thinai_evidence.note: the peahen and the valli forest of the hill fix kurinji

title: குறிஞ்சி குன்றக் குறவன் பத்து decade 26
theme: Ainkurunuru 251 to 260, Kapilar's kurinji decade on the hill man (குன்றக் குறவன் பத்து): every poem opens on the hill man, his shout, his hut, his sandal fire, his worship and his daughter; the decade moves from praise of the girl as a hill goddess, through the friend's pleas and the household's consent, to the ripened millet that ends the meetings.

reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the clouds, at the hill man's shout, pour fine and many drops, that the girl weeps even when she only sees the swift-falling cascade that comes down from his town on the tall hill.
nuance: The waterfall has done nothing to her: it is only water that has passed his town, and that is enough to make her cry, so the poem measures her longing by the smallest trace of him. The cloud that pours as soon as a hill man calls stands against a lord who does not come though she weeps.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man, the tall hill and its cascade fix the mountain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the friend speaks of the girl in the third person to the lord (நாட, நும்மூர்), the usual frame for urging him to wed

iraicchi.act: the cloud answers the hill man's shout at once by pouring its rain
iraicchi.sense: in his own land even a cloud answers a call, so the lord who leaves the girl's tears unanswered falls short of his hill's clouds

reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land where young rain-clouds roving over the village common hide the hill man's grass-thatched hut is a noble man: he came back ahead of the great cold north wind of autumn, mixed with sharp dew and driving rain.
nuance: He is praised for timing, not for gifts: he came before (முந்து) the cold wind that would have made the waiting unbearable, the kurinji season itself (கூதிர்) being the deadline he beat. The cloud that hides the hut on the common is the only cover the scene gives, and he arrived under it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man's hut and the cold season of kurinji fix the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the vocative தோழி and the praise of the man who has come point to the girl; whether he returned from a parting or came to wed the poem does not say

reading: The girl asks her friend whether, if the lord of the forest land, where the fragrant smoke of sandal burnt by the hill man perfumes the whole slope, comes to marry her, their mother will consent to the wedding.
nuance: வரையின் is both 'of the hill' and 'if he weds': the line can be read as the hill's wedding or as 'if he marries', and either way the question is about the mother, not the man. The smoke that fills the whole mountain from one hill man's fire is a scene, but it is the way a secret spreads.

thinai_evidence.note: sandal burnt on the honey-scented slope fixes the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the vocative தோழி and the anxious question about mother (யாய்) point to the girl in the secret stage

reading: The speaker says that the young girl with the bright forehead, around whom bees hum, has been taken by the wealthy ones to their country of hills, a land where the kaanthal smells of the fragrant smoke rising when the hill man cuts the sandal.
nuance: The kaanthal takes the scent of the sandal's smoke as the girl now takes the house of the man; the image has only that one correspondence, so it is left as scene. செல்வர் is plural, either honorific for the man or his people who came for her.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal, the sandal and the hill country fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the report that she has been taken (கொண்டனர்) to the man's country reads as the friend telling the foster mother that the marriage has been made; the speaker could also be the foster mother herself

reading: The man says that the hill man's beloved young daughter has the grace of the goddesses of the mountain: she is delicate, her breasts have budded, her mouth is red and her chest is spotted with pale gold.
nuance: The likeness to the hill goddesses is not flattery alone: in kurinji the அரமகளிர் are the beings who strike men who see them, and the catalogue that follows (budding breasts, the pale spots of a girl newly grown) says she has only just come of age.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain goddesses and the hill man's daughter fix the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: a catalogue of her body in praise is the man's voice; the addressee may equally be his own heart

comparisons.tenor: the hill man's daughter

tamil: வண்டு படு கூந்தல் தண் தழைக் கொடிச்சி
reading: The man says that the hill man's beloved young daughter, the hill girl with bee-haunted hair and a cool leaf skirt, bangled, with teeth bright as sprouts, is young indeed, yet she is a goddess who strikes hard.
nuance: ஆயினும் carries the point: her youth (இளையள்) ought to make her harmless, and instead she is ஆர் அணங்கு, a power that afflicts. The fear is the man's, and it is the old fear of a hill goddess, not a figure of speech.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl in a leaf skirt fixes kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the man explains to his companion why a girl so young has overcome him; the addressee may be his heart

comparisons.tenor: her teeth

reading: The friend tells the man that this bright-bangled young girl, whom the hill man won by worshipping the god and begging, has her long, finely veined eyes flowing with tears, because the land to which he is leaving is far away.
nuance: The first two lines set what is at stake: a daughter got by prayer from the god is the treasure the man would leave weeping, so the friend's argument is the father's long begging against the man's short leave-taking. The colophon's kurinji answers the decade's hill people; the situation is a parting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going to a far land (பிரியும் நாடே) is separation, which decides against the kurinji things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the friend speaks of the girl to the man who is leaving (நீ பிரியும்), to hold him back

reading: Of the hill man's beloved young daughter, the hill girl whose swaying walk is like an adorned peacock's, the friend says that if the lord of the great hill comes to wed her they have given her already, and that is good; yet the girl's grief has not ceased.
nuance: கொடுத்தனெம் ஆயினோம் is a past tense for a future act: the household counts her as already given, so nothing now stands between them but the man. The last line turns the good news back on him: consent has not ended her grief, because he has not come.

thinai_evidence.note: the peacock and the great hill fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: the friend, speaking for the household (கொடுத்தனெம்), tells the man the way to marriage is open and only his coming is wanting

comparisons.tenor: the girl's swaying gait

reading: The man says that the one who has stricken him is the hill man's beloved young daughter, who took a few vengai flowers from the village common, praised the mountain god who is the first of her clan, her hands wet and fragrant from making the honey offering, smelling of open kaanthal, her eyes brimming.
nuance: The girl who has just worshipped the god of the hill becomes herself the power that strikes him (அணங்கியோள்): the rite and the affliction belong to one vocabulary. Why her eyes brim (கலிழ்ந்த) the poem does not say: it may be her own love she prays about.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the kaanthal and the god who lives on the hill fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: எம் அணங்கியோள், she who struck me, is the man's voice; his companion or his heart is the listener

reading: The friend tells the man that the soft-shouldered hill girl, the hill man's beloved daughter, will be hard to win now, since they no longer chase the green-backed parrots: the millet sown in the mixed poor ground has ripened.
nuance: The harvest is the whole argument: the millet field was the only place the girl could be met, and with the grain ripe she will be kept at home. பெறற்கு அரிது says 'hard to obtain', the language of winning a bride rather than of meeting a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field and its parrots fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from the poem: telling the man that the guarding of the millet is over, so the meetings in the field end, urges him to marry; the man may also be saying it to his heart

title: குறிஞ்சி கேழற் பத்து decade 27
theme: Ainkurunuru 261 to 270, Kapilar's kurinji decade on the boar: each poem opens on the boar of the hill (grazing the millet, keeping its mate, rearing motherless young, fighting the tiger, rooting the slope like a plough) and turns to the hill lord, through the heroine's doubts of his courage and love, her pallor and tears, his flattery and leaving, to his return at the harvest's end.
source_issues: 261-270: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
267 line 1: பறிப் stands for பன்றிப் (a lost ன்), unflagged; the same formula line reads சிறுகண் பன்றிப் பெருஞ்சின in 266 and in Natrinai 386. Marked as பன்றி.
261, 264, 265, 266, 268, 269, 270: lines repaired per the text flags; the marks follow the repaired lines.
265 line 1: புலிகொல் பெண்பால் is read as the sow killed by a tiger, whose young the boar rears; a reading with the tigress as killer is possible, so marked uncertain.
262 line 4, 266 line 4, 269 lines 3-5, 270 lines 3-4: the construction is open to more than one reading; marked uncertain.

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the hill lord, of the land where the fierce-eyed boar that grazed the soft millet sleeps on the hard rock slope, stays away for fear that her father will find out, and concludes that this must be why he does not come.
nuance: The excuse she finds for him is a reproach: the boar of his own land raids the guarded millet and then sleeps without fear, while he, she supposes, is afraid of her father.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet, the boar and the rock slope fix the hill land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; எந்தை (my father) fixes the speaker as the heroine, and the secret love as the stage

iraicchi.act: the boar eats from the guarded millet field and then sleeps unafraid on the rock slope
iraicchi.sense: the beast of his own hill dares the guarded field and rests without fear, yet the man she loves stays away for fear of her father

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the love of the lord of the shining mountain, where the fierce-eyed boar that grazed the small millet stays with its mate on the slope of piled rocks, knows that his coming is the one remedy for her.
nuance: The whole sickness is turned into a question about his knowledge: his love may be real, but it does not seem to know the one medicine it could give, which is simply to come.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet, the boar and the boulder slope fix the hill land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; the vocative தோழி and her sickness that only his coming can cure fix the speaker

iraicchi.act: after feeding, the boar stays with its mate on the rock slope
iraicchi.sense: the boar keeps its mate's company, while the man stays away from the woman whose only cure is his coming

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the lord of the hill land, where a boar dark as a touchstone eats the ripened millet golden as fine gold, has come himself, and with him her beauty has come back.
nuance: The two similes belong together: gold and the black touchstone on which gold is tried, so the boar on the golden field looks like gold drawn across the testing stone. The doubled verb (வந்தனன் வந்தன்று) makes his arrival and the return of her beauty a single event. A hidden reading of the boar as the lover enjoying ripe beauty would rest on a single match of mood, so it stays simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the ripe millet, the boar and the hill fix the hill land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; the vocative தோழி and என் நலனே fix the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the ripened millet
the dark boar

reading: The friend tells the lord of the slope bright with springs, where a boar with tusks like the young crescent unites with its sow dark as the kalam fruit, that she has seen it: the eyes of the woman he loves have turned pale.
nuance: கண்டிகும் (we have seen) makes the friend a witness, so the pallor is reported as evidence, not complaint.

thinai_evidence.note: the boar and the hill slope fix the hill land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; the vocative சிலம்ப and நீ நயந்தோள் (the one you love) fix the friend speaking to the man

comparisons.tenor: the boar's tusks
the dark sow

iraicchi.act: the boar joins its mate
iraicchi.sense: the beast of his hill unites with its own mate, while the man leaves the woman he loves to grow pale, so he should come and marry her

reading: The heroine says the lord of the hill land, where the boar with curved white tusks rears the striped young of the sow a tiger killed, has forgotten her, he who left her with their son bright as gold.
nuance: The animal reverses the human case exactly: there the father rears young whose mother is dead; here the mother is left with a son whose father lives and has gone.

title: குறிஞ்சி 28 குரக்குப் பத்து decade 28
theme: Ainkurunuru 271 to 280, Kapilar's kurinji decade of the monkey (குரக்குப் பத்து): each poem opens on a monkey of the hill lord's slope (the stuffed-cheeked female, the reckless young at the honey or the bamboo top, the male who carries his mate from the tiger or beats the rain bubbles) and turns it on the lord: his constancy, his night visits, his leaving, the beauty he took, the gossip he will raise, and the marriage the friend demands.
source_issues: 271-280: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem's address.
271: the word division பகர்வர் / பக்கின் across lines 1 and 2 and the sense of பல்பசுப் பெண்டிர் are hard; the reading takes பக்கு as the traders' bag and பசு as 'fresh'.
272: line 4 அறியான் is masculine and leaves open who does not know and whether the mother's 'he will come' (line 5) means she has guessed the night visits; the reading cannot be fixed.
275: line 1 குரங்கின் தலிஅவன் looks corrupt (likely தலைவன், the troop's leader); the reading follows that sense.
279: line 4 கல்லகத் ததுஎம் and 280: line 3 மதிபுடைப் பதுபோல carry word breaks in the middle of words (கல்லகத்தது, மதிபுடைப்பது); the readings join them.
273, 274, 275, 278, 279: the shown text carries repaired lines (flags in show); the readings follow the repaired text.

reading: The friend says that the lord of the land where a female monkey that has eaten avarai beans looks like a trader's stuffed bag could have many fresh young women if he wanted them, but because he is her old kinsman he stays kind to this girl.
nuance: The comic image of the greedy monkey with bulging cheeks stands beside the claim that the lord does not grab every woman he could have: what holds him is the old tie (தொல்கேள்), so the friend grounds his constancy in kinship rather than in passion.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey and the hill lord fix the kurinji slope

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the girl is spoken of as இவள் and the lord in the third person, so the friend is taken to be vouching for him to the foster mother; she may as well be reassuring the girl herself

comparisons.tenor: the female monkey with cheeks full of beans

reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land where the untaught young of the black-fingered female monkey leaps onto the fearsome tall branch beside the sweet honey of the steep cliff does not know what coming by night means, and that her mother keeps saying 'he will come, he will come'.
nuance: The untaught young monkey (கல்லா) that leaps at the dangerous branch beside the honey answers the lord who 'does not know' (அறியான்) the danger of the night path; that is a near-miss ullurai, left as scene because the closing lines cannot be fixed: whether the mother's 'he will come' means she has guessed the night visits or expects a suitor changes the situation the image would point to.

thinai_evidence.note: monkey, cliff and wild honey are the hill's things

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative தோழி and யாய் (my mother) make the girl the speaker

reading: The friend tells the lord of the good hill, where the strong young of the dull-headed female monkey feed on the coral-bright shoots of the asoka by the path, that if he goes away, she who lives on her love for him will weep even more than the friend herself.
nuance: The friend measures the girl's grief against her own (என்னினும்): she admits she too will weep, so the plea is made from inside the shared household of the two girls, not as a go-between's tactic.

thinai_evidence.note: the asoka, the monkey and the good hill place it on the kurinji slope; the parting is the brief absence of kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

comparisons.tenor: the bright young shoots of the asoka

tamil: ஒண் கேழ் வயப்புலி குழுமலின் விரைந்து உடன்
reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the land where the untaught male, husband of the female monkey, hurries up the high slope together with her when the bright-striped tiger roars has gone away, taking with him the beauty of her soft shoulders and her sleep.
nuance: கல்லா (untaught) is pointed: the creature that has learnt nothing still keeps his mate beside him, so the lord's leaving reads as a failure of what even a beast knows.

thinai_evidence.note: monkey, tiger and the high slope are the hill's things; the parting is within kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative தோழி and என் மெல்தோள் make the girl the speaker

iraicchi.act: at the tiger's roar the male monkey, called the female's husband, hurries up the slope together with her (உடன்)
iraicchi.sense: even the untaught monkey takes his mate with him out of danger, while the lord went off alone and took only her beauty and her sleep

reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the red-furred male monkey, leader of the troop, beats the rain bubbles on the wide rock with a little cane stick that, though the girls desire him, their fine beauty would not fade if he would only be gracious.
nuance: The monkey smashing the fragile rain bubbles for play sits close to the girl's beauty that fades while the lord delays, a near-miss ullurai: only one correspondence (careless play breaking something fragile) can be named, so it fails condition 3. The friend's question turns his grace (அருள்) into the cure: marriage, not desire, keeps beauty.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the cane and the broad rock of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the leaf-eating male monkey, the female's lover, beats the swelling young clouds on the wide rock with a cool fragrant narai creeper: even if he does not love her, let him marry her before he goes, so that she is called the wife of the lord of the good hill where vengai blooms in the rock clefts.
nuance: நயவாய் ஆயினும் is startling: the friend concedes he may not love her and still asks for marriage, so what she wants for the girl is the name (பெண்டு எனப் படுத்து), the public standing that protects her, more than his feeling. The vengai in bloom is the hill's marriage season.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the vengai and the good hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

reading: The friend tells the lord of the hill, where the untaught female monkey frolics with her male on the boulder in the hunters' yard that the beasts rub against: let him never leave the girl so that pallor spreads over her eyes, which rival the blue lily growing in the pond.
nuance: The monkeys play right beside human dwellings (குறவர் முன்றில்), so the pair is a sight the lord passes every time he comes: the friend's warning is set on his own doorstep.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunters' yard, the monkey and the hill

thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; speaker and hearer are inferred from the poem's address

reading: The friend says that the lord of the land, where the jointed bamboo of the slope, once the strong young monkey has leapt off it, springs up like a fishing rod that jerks a fish out of the pool, has given the girl a sickness those who suffer it never forget and has taken the beauty onlookers never tire of.
nuance: The fishing-rod simile is the key: the bamboo does not merely spring back, it springs back like a rod that has just landed a fish, so the image already contains the taking (கொண்டனன்) the closing line names.

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo stem springing up when the young monkey leaps off

reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where the female monkey, having climbed the clinging itti tree that spreads over the rock and grazed on wild jasmine, frolics with her mate on the hillside, that if he comes, their village lies within the rocks and its whispering street will turn to open gossip.

nuance: The monkey reaching for the moon is a joke about overreach, and the friend's question turns it on herself: she spoke to her mother on the strength of his word, so if he now delays she is the one left beating at the moon.

title: குறிஞ்சி கிள்ளைப் பத்து decade 29
theme: Ainkurunuru 281 to 290, Kapilar's parrot decade (கிள்ளைப் பத்து) of kurinji: every poem turns on the parrots that raid the hill millet and the girl set to drive them off. By our reading the man blesses and thanks the birds whose raids put her in the field and envies them her glance, while the friend turns the same field against him: do not come by night, your promises are a net, how can you leave her, the reaped field still holds the parrots, and the elders may end her guarding, so marry her.
source_issues: Every colophon of the decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
284 has no vocative and no named hearer; whether the man or the friend speaks is a guess, and the poem's point turns on it (two alternatives recorded).
283 line 4 நீப்பினும் and line 5 பெண்டு தவப் பலவே can be construed as a taunt to the man or a warning about him; marked uncertain.
288 line 4 பாத்தரும் is read as பாத்து அருந்தும் (share out and eat); the line 2 reading follows tamilvu as shown.

289 line 1 கிளிசெத் தடுக்கத்து is read as கிளி செத்து அடுக்கத்து (taking it for a parrot, on the slope); செத்து as a likeness word is not one of the markers check accepts, so the comparison is recorded as metaphor.

reading: The man blesses the parrots: may they live for ages beyond counting, for they brought about the guarding of the millet by the hill girl with bright jewels, thick dark hair and broad shoulders.
nuance: The long-life blessing (வாழிய பலவே) that bards give kings is given to crop thieves. காவல் காட்டியவ்வே says the parrots 'showed' him her guarding: the raids that are the family's loss are his gain, since they set her alone in the field where he can see her.

thinai_evidence.note: parrots and the hill girl guarding millet, the native things of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man is glad of what the parrots' raids gave him; no hearer is named, so he speaks aloud to no one in particular

reading: The friend tells the man of the land where the small parrot of the grove still waits on the big-eared millet on the slope even as the hill girl with large rain-cool eyes drives it off: do not come, the thick darkness has deepened on the forest path where tusked beasts roam.
nuance: The parrot that keeps eyeing the millet while the girl chases it looks like the man who keeps coming though she is guarded, but no second pair or anchor ties it to him, so it stays scene (an ullurai near miss). The refusal is for the night only; the field by day is where she can be found.

thinai_evidence.note: hill slope, parrot and tusker

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the command வாரல் make the friend refuse the night tryst (இரவுக்குறி மறுத்தல்)

comparisons.tenor: the girl's eyes, cool and moist

reading: The friend tells the man of the land where the soft-spoken simple daughter of a hard-eyed hunter drives the green-backed small parrots from the millet sown in mixed poor soil: even if you make great promises and leave, the women caught in your net of lies are very many.
nuance: The opening sets the hard-eyed father against the soft-spoken daughter: she belongs to a house that can be fierce. The last line may be read as a taunt (you can leave her; you will find others in your net) or as a warning to the girl's side (many have been caught so); either way the friend names his promises as bait.

thinai_evidence.note: a hunter's daughter guarding millet from parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the reproach of his promises give the poem to the friend

comparisons.tenor: his false promises, which trap women

reading: Pitiable are the red-mouthed green parrots: even seeing the long field reduced to the green-stalked stubble of millet the hill hunters have cut, they have a great love that cannot learn to part from it.
nuance: The whole poem is the parrots, so iraicchi fails the deletion test (strike the birds and nothing is left); the harvest that ends the girl's guard duty is what the parrots' love outlasts. Whom the pity is aimed at turns on the unstated speaker.

thinai_evidence.note: parrots, hill hunters and cut millet

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; read as the man, who like the parrots keeps returning to the reaped field where the girl no longer comes

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; or the friend, praising the birds' constancy in his hearing as a reproach and a push to marry

reading: The friend asks the man of the land where the hill girl with plaited dark hair and fine forehead eats soft millet flour and with her clapper drives small parrots from the hill rice: how can you bring yourself to part, leaving her here, so that her full bangles slip?
nuance: The friend's picture of the girl is all small domestic ease, eating millet flour and rattling the clapper; the slipping bangle (வீங்குவளை நெகிழ) is the sign of wasting that his parting would bring, so the question யாங்கு வல்லுநையோ is a charge of hardness, not a request for reasons.

thinai_evidence.note: hill girl, hill rice and parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and ஈங்கு இவள் (her, here) make the friend speak for the girl against his leaving

reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the good, ever-yielding hill, where on the white stalks of the stubble left after the small millet was cut the bean has podded and the settling parrots are driven off, seems to have loved her without blemish, yet he carries off the dark glow of her beauty.
nuance: His land is யாணர், yielding again even after the harvest, while her own glow is taken; போலும் (it seems) holds back from blaming him, and the loss is put on his love itself, which takes as it gives. The stubble bearing beans could be read as a hidden image of renewal, but no pair ties it to the lovers, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: millet stubble, bean and parrots of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative தோழி and என் மாமை make the girl speak to her friend

reading: The friend tells the man of the land where the short-legged mountain goat on the high peak takes fright at the parrots leaping onto the millet: surely you are skilled at lying, and surely skilled at nothing else.
nuance: The two lines turn on one word: வல்லை (you are able) at lying, வல்லாய் (you are not able) at anything else, a sarcasm that grants him skill only in deceit. The goat startled by small birds may hint at a strong man made timid, but it does no act of the love situation, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: mountain goat of the peaks and parrots in the millet

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the charge of lying give the poem to the friend reproaching his broken promise

reading: The man asks his heart what they can do in return, knowing how good it was, for the help the parrots gave: while the gentle, lovely hill girl guards the many-eared millet, they come and share it out among themselves.
nuance: The language of debt (செய்த உதவி, நன்று தெரிந்து, எவன் செய்குவம்) is the language of gratitude to a benefactor, put to birds who meant no help: their theft keeps her in the field. பாத்தரும் is read as share out and eat.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl guarding millet from parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks to his heart (நெஞ்சே) during the secret love

reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hills that the elders, saying the parrots come to the green-eared millet on the slope because they take the hill girl's sweet voice for a parrot's, seem ready to stop even her guarding; so marry her and take her.
nuance: The girl's charm turns against her: her voice is so like the birds' that it calls them instead of scaring them, and that gives the household reason to take the guard from her, ending the day meetings. The accham is the girl's side's fear of the elders' command.

thinai_evidence.note: hill girl, millet and parrots in the great hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the closing வரைந்தனை கொண்மோ make the friend urge marriage (வரைவு கடாதல)

comparisons.tenor: the girl's sweet voice, taken by the parrots for one of their own

reading: The man says the parrots seem far more fortunate than a king of the just red sceptre devoted to right: they are looked at by the hill girl with bright, flower-fragrant hair, and they are driven off by her.
nuance: A comparison of excess (the ablative -இன், more than): the best a kingdom can offer is ranked below being glanced at and shooed away by her. ஒப்புதல் is the field word for driving off birds, so even her chasing is a favour he envies.

thinai_evidence.note: parrots and the hill girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man, envious of the birds, speaks with no hearer named

comparisons.tenor: the parrots, more fortunate than such a king

title: குறிஞ்சி 30 மஞ்ஞைப் பத்து decade 30
theme: Ainkurunuru 291 to 300, Kapilar's peacock decade (மஞ்ஞைப் பத்து) of kurinji: each poem sets the hill's peacock beside the hill girl, through the secret love (the man's longing, the friend's fear of his night visits, the girl's heart gone with him) to the wedding, and by the end the peacock is likened to the girl rather than she to it.
source_issues: Every colophon of the decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
295 line 3 புனவர் கொள்ளியின் புகல்வரும் மஞ்ஞை: புகல் may be the peacock's fear of the field-clearers' firebrands or its eagerness; the poem's sense does not turn on it.
298 line 1 மழைவரவு அறியா may be 'not knowing the rain will come' or 'not knowing (whether) rain comes'; the iraicchi reading holds on either.
Repaired lines flagged by show (293 lines 1 and 3, 294 line 5, 295 line 1, 298 line 4, 299 line 1) were read as repaired; no further doubt.

reading: The man points out the hill slope of piled boulders where peacocks dance and the owl calls back and forth, and says that is the fine town where his beloved lives, the girl with shoulders like bamboo and a waist where a skirt of chosen leaves sways.
nuance: The poem names nothing but a place, yet the place is all lover's sight: the dancing peacocks and the calling owl are the sounds he hears around her town, and the leaf skirt on her waist is the one ornament of the hill girl.

thinai_evidence.note: a slope of piled boulders where peacocks dance

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
