title: முல்லை விரவுப் பத்து decade 43
theme: Ainkurunuru 421 to 430, Peyanar's mixed mullai decade (முல்லை விரவுப் பத்து): the man held from going by her shoulders and her tears, the friend dissuading him with the rains and the crying son, the hurried drive home past doves and mullai, and the choice between the king's war and the wife, renounced in one poem, made conditional in another, and ended by the rains in a third.
source_issues: The colophon gives முல்லை for the whole decade with no thurai; seven poems (421, 423, 424, 426, 427, 429, 430) turn on a departure planned, dissuaded or given up, which by uri is paalai, and are marked so in thinai.
421: what the watchmen throw (வெண்காழ்) is not certain.
430: ஆன்றிசின் can be read as 'has wept her fill' or as a plea to stop weeping.

reading: The man says that the going he had planned was stopped by the full, bamboo-smooth shoulders of the young daughter of the chief of the poor scrubland, where at evening the watchmen throw their white missiles and the hare hiding in the fragrant flowered woodland bolts.
nuance: The journey is not refused by argument: her shoulders 'block' it (விலங்கின), as if they stood across the road. The hare driven from its cover by the watchmen is the one creature in the poem that does leave; the man, by contrast, stays. What the watchmen throw (வெண்காழ், a white hard thing, perhaps sling-stones or pointed sticks) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a planned departure is given up

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man speaks of the girl in the third person, to no one named, perhaps to his own heart

reading: The man says that if they drive the tall chariot fast, its strong-legged horses scattering the flowers of the long-stemmed mullai and the thalavam, she with rows of bangles on her forearm will not suffer.
nuance: Her suffering is measured by his speed: the conditional (செல்லின்) makes the charioteer's haste the remedy for her pain, and the scattered mullai and thalavam, the flowers of the waiting land, are crushed by the very return they wait for.

thinai_evidence.note: the man hurries home to the waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man urges his charioteer (pira) on the way home

reading: The friend tells the man that the great clouds have thundered and let fall their drops, yet he is set on going while her bright brow turns pale; they cannot bear to be left by him, and her kohl-dark eyes, fine as chosen flowers, are already full of tears.
nuance: The friend's argument is the season itself: a man who leaves when the rain has already come breaks the order by which men return in the rains. The rain is mullai's time set inside a scene of departure; the mixing is of time, not of native things.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is preparing to leave

nuance: The friend names the wife as her father's daughter, as if reminding the husband from whose house he took her, and then names the son as his (நின் புதல்வன்): the cost of going falls first on the child, whose mother's grief will fail him at the breast.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

comparisons.tenor: the son

reading: The man tells his charioteer that if he drives the tall chariot fast through the woodland, where the dun-backed hen dove croons like the drummers of kings to please her mate, it will be easy to end their sore pain.
nuance: The 'our' pain (எமக்கு) is shared: his road-weariness and her waiting are ended by one act, the fast drive.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan

comparisons.tenor: the hen dove's crooning

iraicchi.act: the hen dove croons to give her mate pleasure
iraicchi.sense: the man, hearing a mate call to her partner, knows his wife waits calling for him, and so hurries home

reading: The man tells his fair-browed wife that, giving up the hard task of the king of the conquering spear, he has now stopped going to the hard battle where that king sets the drums thundering and overcomes kings.
nuance: The war he renounces is painted at its height, drums and conquered kings, in the same breath as the refusal, so the giving up is shown as a real cost and not an easy choice.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (விரவுப் பத்து) names only a mixed decade; the man speaks to his wife (நன்னுதல்)

reading: The friend tells the wide-eyed girl that because she would not let him go, saying this is the season that meets the rains, he gave up the going, sending word that he would not come to the war camp of the fighting king.
nuance: The girl's argument was the season (காரெதிர் பொழுது), the same argument the friend uses in 423; here it has worked. Whose 'not coming' வாரான் அவன் reports is open: most simply, the man's refusal of the king's summons.

reading: The man tells his wife that the roaring cloud, bending its fine bow across the sky, has begun to pour so that chariots cannot move; the great task the king sent him on is over, and he has begun to stay and care for her.
nuance: The rain does the work of the return: it halts the chariots of war, so the king's task ends because the season forbids it, and the same rain that would have tormented a waiting wife now marks the start of his staying (புறந்தர).

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come and the man is home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan

reading: The man tells the woman of thick dark hair that if she puts away her pallor he would go to win the king's war, the king whose untrained elephant shattered the fortress of his foes with its conquering flags.
nuance: The condition is one she cannot meet: her pallor comes from his going, so 'if you give up your pallor' (பசப்பு நீ விடின்) makes the journey wait on a cure that only his staying brings. The wish particle தில் keeps the going a wish, not a plan.

thinai_evidence.note: the man seeks leave to depart

reading: The man says that the daughter of the chief of the wooded land, where on the high rock the short-stemmed konrai spreads bright petals like beaten gold, has wept her fill, and so he gives up the going.
nuance: The konrai in bloom is the flower of the rains, the season of return; he gives up going in the very season when a man should come home. ஆன்றிசின் may mean she has wept abundantly or be a plea that she stop weeping; either way her tears decide.

title: முல்லை புறவணிப் பத்து decade 44
theme: Ainkurunuru 431 to 440, Peyanar's mullai decade on the beauty of the forest (புறவணிப் பத்து): each poem opens 'good indeed is the road my lover took' and adds one more grace of the rainy season on it, peacocks, konrai-crowned men, rain-met forest, doe and fawn, neythal, konrai and kurunthu, mullai after hail, flowering bushes, herders' hamlets, thondri and thalavam, while the woman who says it waits at home.

reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took, she says: up on the dark rock of lovely hue it has even peacocks whose bodies are the colour of sapphire.
nuance: Every poem of the decade repeats the same first line and ends on உடைத்தே ('it has... too'), so the praise is cumulative: each poem adds one more beauty of the rainy road. Whether the praise is comfort (the road is safe and the season he promised has come) or a reproach (the road is so lovely it keeps him) the refrain does not say; the peacock on the rock belongs to the hills, not the mullai scrub.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover has gone and the woman, waiting, dwells on the road he took

reading: Good indeed is the road my lover took: it has even warriors crowned with konrai like heated gold, looking like men entering a wedding house.
nuance: The konrai that crowns the men is the rainy season's flower, so the road shows the season even on its people; கடி may be the wedding or a guarded house, and on the first reading the men look festive as if going to a marriage, a hint of the union the season should bring.

title: முல்லை பாசறைப் பத்து decade 45
theme: Ainkurunuru 441 to 450, Peyanar's mullai decade of the war camp (பாசறைப் பத்து): the married man in the king's camp in the rains, longing for his wife, wishing she knew his pain, picturing her as hostess of guests and mother of his son, and making every return hang on one condition, if the king's work ends.
source_issues: The colophon gives no thurai for any poem of the decade; the speaker and occasion are taken from the decade title பாசறைப் பத்து.
441 line 1: ஐய ஆயின is hard to fix (become wondrous, subtle, or doubtful); the reading is marked uncertain.
445: who speaks to whom is not stated; the second-person verbs (வந்தனையே, இழைத்தனையே) are read as the man addressing his heart, and the verse is marked uncertain.
447 line 3 begins யாடு, the glide of செம்முகை + ஆடு split across the line break; 448 lines 2, 4 and 6 print எதிர்ந் தனனே, எதிர்ந் தன்றே and எதிர்ந் தனமே with the word split.

reading: In the war camp the man says that the words of his red-complexioned wife have become a thing of wonder to him, for he left her helpless on a day of the rains with its thunder, and they now give him real pain; it would be well if she knew the sorrow he suffers.
nuance: The pain runs the other way from the usual mullai poem: it is her parting words that wound the man, and his wish is not to see her but that she should know his suffering, a defence against the charge of neglect.

thinai_evidence.note: parting on a day of the rains, the mullai season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; he speaks to himself

reading: If the fierce king's hard campaign subsides, the man says, his wife will be fit to receive guests in plenty, she whose chastity is like Arundhati's in the high world of the dark sky, the mother of a son who wears a gem ornament shaped like a young palm fruit.
nuance: Homecoming is pictured not as embrace but as the household's hospitality restored: the wife's role as hostess of guests waits on the king's war.

thinai_evidence.note: the man waits on the end of the king's war to return home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the wife's chastity

reading: If the king, whose earth-smeared drum has taken many forts rising to the sky, leaves off his work, the man says, then without calling the way too long he will mount the good chariot and go to see her lovely bright brow, like the young crescent of the shining moon.

thinai_evidence.note: the return hangs on the king's work ending

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan

comparisons.tenor: her bright brow

reading: We shall see the simple girl of broad shoulders, the man says, if the king of the victorious spear, his enmity calmed, may yet head back to his own land, the king whose great-tusked elephants have split their tusk-rings and blunted their sharp points charging the long walls of forts.
nuance: The blunted tusks measure how long the siege has lasted: the elephant's wear is the man's waiting made visible.

thinai_evidence.note: the man waits for the king's war to end

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

reading: The man tells his heart, which weeps each time it remembers her at the hour when the young cow comes home close by the good bull, that it left the famed and excellent beloved to lament and came to this camp of hard work, and has quickly drawn him to come as well.
nuance: The cattle going home together at evening are what the camp-bound man sees, and they set off the heart's weeping; the poem blames the heart both for leaving her and for its present grief.

thinai_evidence.note: the hour the cattle come home, the mullai evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; the second-person verbs and நெஞ்சம் suggest he speaks to his heart, though the addressee is not certain

iraicchi.act: the young cow comes home at evening keeping close to the bull
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle go home together at dusk while the man stays in the camp away from his wife

reading: The man tells his dark wife, absent, that they will see good things when, having helped the hard work of the war camp, they come back to their beloved good country, and her mullai-scented hair breathes its fragrance.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai in the hair and the war camp

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; he calls on her (மாஅயோயே) though she is far away

reading: May the king's work be released from its bond, the man prays, and then they will see the bright brow worthy of song, at the hour when the winged bee works open the red bud, shaped like a kingfisher's beak, of the thalavu that grows in the dew.
nuance: The bee prising open the jasmine bud is the evening of the rains and may hint at the reunion he waits for; it carries no act of the lovers, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the red thalavu bud

reading: The drum of deep voice sounds in the morning and the fierce king has taken up his work; the mullai blooms at the edge of the soft low field and the rains with thick heavy drops have come; and, the man says, thinking each time of her with her few fine tresses, he has met sleepless anguish.
nuance: Three parallel clauses end on the same verb (எதிர்ந்தனனே, எதிர்ந்தன்றே, எதிர்ந்தனமே): the king meets his war, the season meets the land, the man meets sleeplessness, so the war and the rains arrive together as his double trial.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains come and the mullai blooms

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாசறைப் பத்து) places the man in the king's war camp; no addressee is named

reading: The chariot is ready and strongly made, its wheels rolling so that the gravel ground breaks, yoked to strong horses weary of standing in the stall; we shall see her bright brow, the man says, if the king finishes his work.
nuance: Everything is ready but the king: the horses tired of the stall share the man's impatience.

thinai_evidence.note: the return waits on the king's work

reading: May the glorious king, his enmity calmed after the hard work where drums beat in turn, think of his own land, the man prays, so that his eyes may sleep on the young breasts of his red-complexioned wife and the sickness of his hot sighs abate.

title: முல்லை பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து decade 46
theme: Ainkurunuru 451 to 460, Peyanar's mullai decade of the wife who sees the season (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து): the rains have come and her husband, away with the king's army, has not, and she reads frogs, mullai, kondrai, pakanrai, herons and the north wind against her pale shoulders and wasted eyes.

source_issues.issue: The colophon has no thurai for any poem of this decade; speakers in thurai_akam are taken from the decade title and the poems.
நெடுங்கணவர் is run together; it divides as நெடுங்கண் அவர் (my long eyes; his chariot), on which the sense of the line turns. Marked uncertain.
உருவைல் is not a regular form; the sense (like the moon by day) wants உருவின். The word is not used as evidence.
மெலிறை looks like a dropped consonant for மெல்லிறை (soft-jointed); the word is not used as evidence.

reading: The wife asks why the men who left her helpless as the rainy season's morning came should keep back from the feast of welcome their chariot would bring, since holding out in patience, watching over an army no one can turn back, is the king's work and not theirs.
nuance: இருத்தல், the mullai word for her own patient waiting, is here handed to the king (ஆற்றவும் இருத்தல் வேந்தனது தொழிலே): she argues that endurance in the camp belongs to his duty, so her husband's share of the war ended when the rains came.

thinai_evidence.note: the morning the rains set in, and a man away with the king's army

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

reading: The roaring cloud has spread so the parched earth puts out shoots and has made the rainy season, she says, while her war-loving husband's effort to win tribute has made the pallor bloom like the gold of peerkku flowers on her soft shoulders and hidden their fine beauty.
nuance: Two clauses close on the same verb, கார்செய் தன்றே and அலர்செய் தன்றே: the cloud makes the season, his campaign makes her pallor. அலர் is both blossom and the town's talk, so the bloom on her shoulders is also what people will say.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain cloud and the coming of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

comparisons.tenor: the pallor on her shoulders

reading: Frogs crowd every hollow and harsh-voiced flocks of birds cry on every height: look, she says, the rains have begun this morning, and so my long eyes have begun to run with water, and his chariot has begun its way toward us.
nuance: Three clauses on தொடங்கு tie the season, her tears and his chariot into one beginning. Whether the tears are of grief or of relief turns on how line 4 is divided, and the poem lets both stand.

thinai_evidence.note: the first morning of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season; உதுக்காண் (look there) is said to someone beside her, taken as the friend

reading: As the mullai, clasping the green thalavam creeper and slowly tending its even buds bright as moonlight, reaches out for the rains it longs for, so the beauty of her dark skin stays waiting, longing for his chariot.
nuance: The comparison uses the mullai's longing and leaves out one thing it shows: the mullai waits clasped to a partner creeper (தழீஇ), which she does not have.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai flower reaching for the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

comparisons.tenor: the mullai's even buds
her beauty longing for his chariot

reading: So that the kings' war may cool, the loud cloud, raging with a war drum's sound, has begun the rains, she says, and pitiable, pitiable indeed are her broad soft shoulders, their glow turned pale, the bright bangles slipping, wasted and stripped of their old beauty.
nuance: The rain itself ends the campaign (அரசுபகை தணிய): the season that should free him has come, so the pity she spends on her own shoulders is also a charge that he is late.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains beginning, which halt the kings' war

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the cloud

reading: She asks her friend whether they have stopped thinking of us, those who assured us we would live here together through the cold season of hard dew and went away, now that the great white-petalled pakanrai flowers, like the moon by day, on white creepers deck the green eengai bushes.
nuance: The season named is கூதிர், the cold season, which the Tholkappiyam gives to kurinji; this decade carries the mullai wait past the rains into the dews, so his promise has already overrun its time.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting on a promise to be together through the season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season; she names the friend (தோழி, line 1)

comparisons.tenor: the white pakanrai flowers

reading: In this season hard to be apart in, when flocks of herons cry out, unable to escape the falling dew that torments them, she tells her simple heart that her lover cannot leave her and rest content, and it cannot forget him and rest.
nuance: The two halves turn on the same verb, அமைகல்லார் and அமைகல்லாது: neither he nor her heart can settle. The crying herons were not tagged iraicchi: they suffer and cry, which carries a mood, but do nothing a person of the situation does or should do.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the season for a man who will not stay away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season; the poem closes on என் மடங்கெழு நெஞ்சே, her own heart

reading: The kondrai's clustered pods have ripened into long pipe-like fruit, and its cool flowers that met the thundering rain lie wet and scattered: they look like her eyes, which lost their fine beauty when the lord of the bards went away.
nuance: The kondrai is the mullai sign that the rains, and so his promised return, have come; here it has already flowered, fruited and been beaten down, so it marks how far past the promise the season has run. The hero is named by பாணர் பெருமகன், a marutham epithet.

thinai_evidence.note: the kondrai of the rainy season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

comparisons.tenor: her eyes that lost their beauty

reading: She wonders whether she will be able to embrace, so that the pallor leaves her soft, bamboo-round shoulders, the fragrant cool chest of the man of the town of good fields, who went with the victorious king whose glorious army crossed the forts of his enemies.
nuance: The cure for pallor is not his return in general but touch (புல்லவும்); the doubt (இயைவது கொல்லோ) is whether the king's war will allow it. He is called ஊரன், the marutham man, though the decade is mullai.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting for a man gone with the king's army

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

comparisons.tenor: her rounded shoulders

reading: The fiercely angry king does not tire of his war camp, no message comes from the lord of the loud hill, and the cruel north wind beats on her too, shaking the plantain with its crowded leaves to its whole trunk: what will become of her, she asks, pitiable as she is.
nuance: The plantain shaken to the root by the north wind matches her state, but only as a single match of mood, so it is scene, not ullurai. The hero is a வெற்பன், a hill man, and the plantain is a kurinji plant, set in a mullai wait.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for word from a man held at the king's camp

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

title: முல்லை தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து decade 47
theme: Ainkurunuru 461 to 470, Peyanar's mullai decade of the friend's reassurance (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து): with the rains beginning, the friend tells the waiting wife not to grieve, discredits the konrai that flowered too early, explains the delay by spoil from the enemy, cites the king's release and his own haste, calls her out to see the rightward-rising cloud, and finally rests the guarantee on her own beauty.
source_issues: 462 lines 1 and 5 and 465 lines 1 and 2 are repaired readings from tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), agreeing with sangamtamil.com.
468 line 4 (வடி மணி நெடுந்தேர் கடைஇ) is missing from the base text and supplied from sangamtamil.com.
463 line 1: தொடரி may be the plant (thodari) or the verb 'having strung'; the reading is marked uncertain.

reading: The friend tells the heroine that the rains have begun, the pidavam buds made lovely by the spray of massed clouds and the forest taking on the drizzle, so she must not grieve: the men in the war camp of the victorious king will not rest content having left her.
nuance: The friend names the absent men only by their place, the camp of a victorious king (வெற்றி வேந்தன் பாசறை): the comfort is that a winning war ends, so the season and the campaign close together.

thinai_evidence.note: the onset of the rains and the pidavam in bud fix the mullai season of waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she answers the wife's grief (இனையல்) at the rains' coming

reading: The friend asks the girl why she still weeps on seeing the foolish konrai, which took a stray shower for the rains and put out its garlands: those who crossed the woodland of opening buds are not men to let her beauty fade.
nuance: The friend does not deny that the konrai has flowered; she denies that the flowering is evidence, calling the tree பேதை, simple, for mistaking an unseasonal shower (ஏதில பெய்ம்மழை) for the true rains. The promise is saved by discrediting the sign.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai of the rainy woodland is the sign in dispute

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she answers the wife's weeping (கலிழ்வே) at the flowering konrai

reading: The friend says their lovers will surely come to string the fragrant flowers of the bushes, made lovely by the season, into her fine hair; they have only stayed on to bring back the rich treasure that falls to them from the enemies' land.
nuance: The delay is given an honourable cause, the spoil of the enemies' land (நேரார் நாடுபடு நன்கலம்), and the return is pictured as an act of adornment, the man dressing her hair. தொடரி may be the thodari shrub whose flowers he will bring, or 'having strung'; the sense of the line turns on which.

thinai_evidence.note: the men are delayed and the friend promises their return

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she explains the men's delay

reading: The friend says that in the cold season, when the karuvilai opens like eyes and the climbing peerkku vine flowers like gold on the dark bushes, the men who ache to embrace her fine shoulders will not forget the time.
nuance: The two similes run backwards from the usual: the flowers are likened to an eye and to gold, the very things the waiting woman's eyes and pallor are elsewhere likened to, so the hedge in bloom already shows her face.

thinai_evidence.note: the blue karuvilai and the yellow peerkku of the mullai hedges

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she names the season the men cannot forget

comparisons.tenor: the blue karuvilai flowers
the yellow peerkku flowers

reading: The friend promises that he will come, driving his tall chariot, swift as falling water, through the rain-made forest so that she may embrace his chest with its tangled flowers; the war-loving chief's enmity has cooled.
nuance: The last line gives the reason after the promise: the return depends on the chief's anger being spent (தணிந்தனன் பகையே), so the lover's time is the king's time.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest the rains have made is the mullai land and season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she announces the end of the war and his coming

comparisons.tenor: the chariot's straight running pace

reading: The friend tells the sweet-spoken girl with the bright brow that the man has done the great work the king sent him on and the king of the tall-tusked elephant has let him go, so she is sure he will come within the counted days.
nuance: The friend's comfort is not the season but news: the task is done and the king has released him, so she reasons from the court's business to the date. 'Counted days' (எண்ணிய நாள்) implies the wife has been reckoning them.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend's certainty of the return inside the reckoned days

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she declares her own certainty (தெளிந்திசின் யானே)

reading: The friend begs the girl not to waste away grieving again and again till her ornaments slip: they say the king of fierce-horned elephants, victorious in war, thinking that those who went on his work have been gone too long, hurries more than they do themselves.
nuance: The comfort is reported (என்ப, they say) and puts the king on the waiting women's side: he is more eager than we are. The friend borrows the court's urgency to quiet the house's.

thinai_evidence.note: grief at the man's delay, answered with reassurance

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she answers the wife's wasting (புனைஇழை நெகிழச் சாஅய்)

reading: The friend says that the rains have begun this morning, striped frogs croaking and toads swarming, and that today their lover will drive here in his tall chariot with its well-made bells, to be a full feast for her even-jointed, bamboo-full shoulders.
nuance: The image of the lover as a guest's feast for her shoulders turns the wife into the host and the returning husband into a guest, the mullai wife's virtue of hospitality applied to her own reunion.

thinai_evidence.note: the frogs' croaking marks the first rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she announces his coming today

comparisons.tenor: the lover's embrace for her shoulders

reading: The friend calls the flower-eyed girl to come and look: the sky has begun to rain, rising on the right with thunder that shakes the wide heavens, to bring the lord of the hard country where the red quail steal the green millet set out to dry.
nuance: The rain does not merely mark the season; it rises on the right (வலன்ஏர்ப்பு), the auspicious side, in order to bring him (தரீஇய), so the friend presents the cloud as the man's escort and its rightward rising as an omen.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard upland country and the first rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she invites the wife to see the rain

reading: The friend asks the bright-jewelled girl whether, even if her lover forgot her, her dark-gold beauty, shining in its excellence, would let him forget her in this cold-dew season when the wind blows every night chilling the wide earth with hard dew.
nuance: The friend concedes the worst case (உள்ளார் காதலர் ஆயின், if he does not think of us) and moves the guarantee from the man's memory to the woman's beauty: it will not let him forget.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold dew season after the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தோழி வற்புறுத்த பத்து) names the friend strengthening the waiting wife's resolve; she argues that the wife's own beauty will recall him

title: முல்லை பாணன் பத்து decade 48
theme: Ainkurunuru 471 to 480, Peyanar's mullai decade of the bard (பாணன் பத்து): the waiting wife reproaches the bard who comes from her absent husband, doubts his promises and calls him loveless; the husband, still away on campaign, posts the bard with her and asks him again and again for her words; and in the last poem the bard renounces his lord for ignoring her tears.
source_issues: The colophon gives no thurai for any poem of the decade; speakers are inferred from the poems and the decade title.
471 line 1: எவ்வளை is hard to divide (எம் வளை, 'my/our bangles', is assumed); line 4 போலாய் is read as 'you do not seem to'; the reading is marked uncertain.
473 line 5: மறாவாதீமே may stand for மறவாதீமே ('do not forget') or be a form of மறு ('refuse'); the reading is marked uncertain.
475 line 1: நொடிநிலை is an obscure word; its sense ('firm state') is a guess and the reading is marked uncertain.

reading: The heroine tells the bard that the valiant lord has surely abandoned her, so that her bangles slip, her body withers and her painted many-petalled eyes are clouded with floods of tears; the bard seems not to grasp it and keeps on coming, and she asks what sort of decency that is of theirs.
nuance: The reproach is double: the lord is called மறங்கெழு குருசில், great in valour, in the same breath as the man who deserted her, and the bard's very persistence in coming is turned into evidence against the party he serves. The plural அவர் lumps bard and master together.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits at home while the warrior stays away and his bard keeps coming

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; she speaks to the bard who keeps coming from the absent lord; the friend speaking for her is also possible

comparisons.tenor: her eyes

reading: The heroine tells the bard of the skilled small lute that the season his people fixed has come and stands here; even if they do not learn of it from her, what pains her is that they feel no shame for the false word on their own side.
nuance: She does not ask for his return; she grieves that the promise-breaker is not ashamed. The season standing (வந்துநின்றது) is itself the accusation, so she need not speak it.

thinai_evidence.note: the appointed season has arrived while she waits

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; she speaks to the bard when the promised season has come

reading: The heroine tells the skilled bard that if, thinking of his much-praised lord, he wants to go back to him, then he should not abandon her the way the liars did who brought her this bitter, hard longing.
nuance: The bard has been staying with her and now wants to rejoin his master; she fears he too will turn out one of the பொய்வலாளர், the men skilled in lies. Whether மறாவாதீமே means 'do not forget us' or 'do not refuse us' is not settled by the text.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits in longing and fears even the bard's going

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; she speaks to the bard who wants to return to his lord

comparisons.tenor: the bard, if he leaves her

reading: The friend tells the heroine that the bard says he will bring back the absent man, driving his tall chariot with swift horses so hard that the roads are cut, with his battle-strong army that wrecked the forts of his foes, so that her flawless bright forehead may shine again; fine indeed, she says, is the bard's sense.
nuance: நன்றால் அம்ம may be plain praise of the bard's comfort or dry irony at a promise he cannot keep; the decade's other poems, which doubt the bard, lean toward the second. The war matter of lines 2 and 3 tells us the man is away on a king's campaign, the usual mullai absence.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard promises to bring back the man for whom she waits

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; the friend reports the bard's promise to the heroine; the speaker is inferred from the third-person பாணனது and the bard's words to சுடர்நுதல்

reading: The heroine says that the bard of the small lute, seeing her shoulders withered so that they lost their firmness and her eyes robbed of their shapely beauty, grieved greatly; he is not like his master, who left her for all her ardent love; the bard has the greater love.
nuance: The servant is set against the master by the master's own woman: the bard's pity becomes the measure of the lord's want of it. The word read here as நொடிநிலை is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: she wastes while the man who left stays away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; she speaks of the bard in the third person, most likely to her friend

comparisons.tenor: the bard

reading: Now that the massed clouds roar at the height of the rains and the green mullai creeper has flowered for its season, the heroine asks the loveless bard whether the land where his master went also has this loveless evening, when herdsmen with many cows put together their leaf garlands.
nuance: அன்பு இல் is used twice, once of the evening and once of the bard, so the hour and the messenger stand on the same side against her. The herdsmen coming in at dusk do what the absent man does not; they set the hour but are not tagged as iraicchi because the poem's question does not rest on their act.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season and the evening of the pasture land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; she speaks to the bard at evening in the rains

reading: The man tells the bard that if he stays a little while as comforting company for the helpless heart of her whose cool flower-like long eyes are spreading with pallor, who labours in grief full of bitterness and hard longing, he will soon see the man's chariot.
nuance: Here the decade turns to the man's side: the bard's staying with the woman, which she resented in 471, is his master's instruction, and the chariot is promised as the bard's reward.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits and the man promises his chariot's return

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; the man, still away, sends the bard to stay with his wife

comparisons.tenor: her long eyes

reading: The man asks the bard of the fine lute in the mullai mode to tell him what his beloved said, she who, saying he had stayed away too long, spread the word of his cruelty, her forehead withered, imagining something else, wasted by her great sickness.
nuance: He asks to hear the charge against himself: கொடுமை தூற்றி, she broadcast his cruelty. பிறிதுநினைந்து may mean she suspected another woman or simply feared the worst.

thinai_evidence.note: she has waited too long for the man away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; the man, still away, asks the bard for his wife's words

reading: The man asks the excellent bard to tell him again, since it is sweet each time it is told, what the woman of cool flower-like eyes said, now that he is held off by the lands between and every day the merciless north wind, thick with heavy dew, mocks his loneliness.
nuance: The wind mocks his solitude, not hers: the man is shown suffering the season too. Asking for the report again and again makes the message a substitute for return.

thinai_evidence.note: the dewy season of waiting apart

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; the man asks the bard to repeat his wife's words; மாண is taken as an address to the bard

comparisons.tenor: her eyes

reading: The bard tells the man that they are no longer his bards and he is no longer their lord, since he is not shaken on hearing the cry of his beloved, who laments in her lonely house and sheds tears from her moist-lidded painted eyes.
nuance: The bond of patron and bard is formally dissolved over the man's treatment of his wife. It closes a decade that opened with the wife counting the bard among the man's party: in the end he sides with her.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits alone in the house

thurai_akam.speaker: paanan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (பாணன் பத்து) puts the bard at the centre of the decade; the bard speaks to the absent man

comparisons.tenor: her eyes

title: முல்லை தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து decade 49
theme: Ainkurunuru 481 to 490, Peyanar's mullai decade of the man bidding his chariot home (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து): his work for the king done and the rains come, the returning husband urges his charioteer to goad the bird-swift horses and drive fast, so that his waiting wife's pining may end, her beauty return and her heart rejoice at the evening hour.
source_issues: 482 line 2: வல்விரைத்து is probably a slip for வல்விரைந்து (very swiftly), the form used in the return poems (Akananuru 204 line 8); read as வல்விரைந்து.
486 line 5: கலைமாப் (stag) where 481 line 4 has the same half-line with கலிமாப் (proud horse); as yoked to the chariot the beasts are horses, and கலைமா is probably a variant or slip for கலிமா.
490 line 1: அம்தீம் கிளவி தான்தர is open to two readings (the rains bring back her sweet words, or came as her sweet word granted); the verse is marked uncertain.

reading: Thinking of the woman of red jewels, with shoulders like bamboo sloping at the joint and a lovely lined waist, the man tells his charioteer to put the goad to the bird-swift proud horses yoked to his chariot and drive, so that the sickness may leave.
nuance: The goad (முள், a thorn) is asked for outright: the horses are to be hurt so that a sickness ends, and the poem does not say whose sickness (நோய்), his longing or hers, so the one cure serves both. The image of the horses as birds returns word for word in 486.

thinai_evidence.note: the man, thinking of his wife, hurries home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 3

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders
the horses' going

reading: Drive very fast, charioteer, so that I come as a great guest to the woman of chosen jewels: to stay even one day more with the king whose white-speared army wins and slays would be longer than an age.
nuance: The man names himself the feast (பெருவிருந்து) he will be for his wife, turning the duty of the house to receive guests into the joy of his own return. The king's victory is granted in one line and then measured against a single day, which becomes an aeon (ஊழி): royal service is honoured only as long as it lasts.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's war is done and the man hastens home to his waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; பாக, line 2

comparisons.tenor: a day's further delay with the king

reading: The roads have spread with blossom and grown lovely, the king has let us go, the horses are racing; drive on ahead, charioteer, so that the woman of fair brow may have her beauty back.
nuance: Three short clauses, each closed with ஏ, give the release in steps: the season, the king, the horses, and only then the order. Her beauty (தன்னலம்) is what separation took and what his arrival restores, so the drive is a cure for her body as much as a homecoming.

thinai_evidence.note: released by the king, the man hurries to the waiting wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; பாக, line 3

reading: Summer has gone, the rain clouds have poured, the forest has taken on its beauty and the season is at its full; drive swiftly, charioteer, for we have stayed far too long, forgetting her of fine jewels.
nuance: The man accuses himself: மறந்தே, 'having forgotten', is the charge an abandoned wife makes, here in the husband's own mouth. பாடுசிறந்து may be the swelling sound of the rain or the season reaching its height; either way the land's fullness is the measure of his delay.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come and the forest has grown lovely

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; பாக, line 3

reading: So that her hard pining grief may end and I may embrace her great shoulders as their beauty comes back, drive the chariot, charioteer, across the flower-decked scrub where the deer leap startled.
nuance: அவளும் ... யாமும் sets two griefs side by side: her pining ends and his embrace begins, so the return is said to be needed by both. ஏமதி வலவ தேரே is a stock half-line of the returning man (it opens Natrinai 21's order too), and the startled beasts are the land the chariot breaks into, not a sign.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowered scrub of the forest land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 3

reading: Why should she suffer hard pining, thinking without pause through the great dreary evening? So that the noble woman who could never have enough of embracing may see us, drive, charioteer, handling the reins with skill, your chariot yoked with bird-swift horses.
nuance: Line 3 (புல்லி ஆற்றாப் புரையோள்) may say she could never be sated with embracing, or that she cannot bear the absence even after embraces; the reading keeps the first. The last line repeats 481's horses but writes கலைமா (stag) where 481 has கலிமா (proud horse); as yoked to the chariot they are horses.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits through the evening and the man hurries home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade's title (தேர் வியங்கொண்ட பத்து) and the address to the charioteer make it the returning man's word to his charioteer; வலவ, line 4

comparisons.tenor: the horses' going

reading: This, surely, is the hour when those who are apart remember; so that the heart of her with close-set bangles may rejoice, drive the chariot, wise charioteer.
nuance: The season is pointed at (இது) rather than described: the man puts his own longing under a common law (those apart remember now) and makes her joy, not his, the reason to hurry. The praise of the charioteer's wit (மதியுடை) asks for skill as well as speed.

reading: The cloud-massed sky has begun to rain, and this is the hour my beloved thinks of me; yoke the good horses with spreading manes, mighty one, and drive the chariot so that her distress may end.
nuance: பெருவிறல் may address the charioteer (mighty one) or be the man's own title, 'the beloved of the man of great might'; the reading takes it as the address. The first rain is read as the moment she remembers him: he knows her mind by the season, so the weather itself is her summons.

reading: At the evening when mullai blooms on the soft land and swarms of striped bees with lovely wings crowd upon it, ply the fine-twisted strong reins and drive your long chariot of good horses fast, so that the girl of sorrowing heart may rejoice.
nuance: Evening and opening jasmine are the hour and flower of mullai, the hour her sorrow (பையுள்) is worst; he times his arrival to meet it. The bees crowding on the opening mullai could be read as the lover drawn to the woman, but the poem gives them no act of a person of the situation, so they stay scene.

title: முல்லை வரவுச் சிரப்புரைத்த பத்து decade 50
theme: Ainkurunuru 491 to 500, Peyanar's mullai decade on the arrival (வரவுச் சிறப்புரைத்த பத்து): the man back from war or work tells the woman he hurried home with the rains, and the friend says the season and her beauty have returned together because he came.
source_issues: 493 line 1: ஏறுமுதண் reads like a corruption of ஏறு முரண் (the bulls' contest); the sense of the line is taken that way and the verse marked uncertain.
494 line 4: திர்கினிப் is most likely தீர்கினிப் with the long vowel lost.
496 line 2: மாமலி புலம்ப is obscure in our text; the line is read only as the rains raging.
498 line 3: வேந்துகோட்டு யானை is probably ஏந்துகோட்டு யானை (elephant of lifted tusks), the வ repeated from the next வேந்து.
Decade title is printed as வரவுச் சிரப்புரைத்த பத்து; the usual spelling is சிறப்புரைத்த.

reading: The returned man tells the woman that when the season met the rains he suffered without pause, and with a heart that ached again and again he has hurried back so that her beauty may return.
nuance: The decade's frame is the arrival, but this first poem gives the man's side of the waiting: the pain of the season was his too, and the purpose of his haste is her beauty (ஏர்), not his own relief.

reading: The man tells the woman that with the peacock dancing like her, the mullai opening with the scent of her forehead and the deer gazing startled as she does, he came thinking of her, faster even than the rain clouds.
nuance: The comparisons run backward: she is the standard and the season's creatures are likened to her (நின்னே போலும் மஞ்ஞை), so every sign of the rains was, for him, a likeness of her. 'Faster than the rains' claims he beat the deadline the season sets.

reading: The man tells the woman that the rains began just as he came, thinking of her of the well-shaped forearm: the bulls grew fierce, the thunder roared back at them, and the lovely doe roamed bewildered with her fawn.
nuance: The line puns on ஏறு, bull and thunder, setting the beasts' rut against the sky's answer. The doe that wanders with her fawn is not given an act that maps onto the lovers, so it is left as scene, though a reader may hear the waiting mother in it.

reading: The friend tells the woman of large lovely eyes that, with beasts sheltering in the bushes, the millet heavy in ear and the rains crashing and lashing, he who lived apart from her has come to be the companion of her shoulders; now let her hair of opening buds long for flowers again.
nuance: Hair that 'wants flowers' is hair that may be dressed again: a woman apart from her husband did not wear flowers, so the friend's last line is permission to adorn. The sense of மாமலி புலம்ப in line 2 is not secure.

reading: Her shoulders have regained their beauty, her bangles stay in place and her long lined eyes have taken on a bright loveliness, because the king of the tusked elephants left off his war and the man of the hill country drove his swift tall chariot home.
nuance: The recovery is itemised in the order loss was itemised in the poems of separation: shoulders, bangles, eyes. The return depends on the king's release (வேந்து தொழில் விட்டென), not on the man's choice; and the hero is called வரையக நாடன், a man of the hills, in a mullai poem.

reading: The friend tells the woman of sweet speech that our lover, thinking she would grieve greatly if she saw the forest dressed in the beauty of the rains, with pidavam blooming and thalavam in bud, did not stay away for his hard work but came, bringing back her fine beauty.
nuance: He reasons from what the season would do to her, not from his own longing: the forest is dangerous because she would see it. அருந்தொழிற்கு அகலாது says he left the hard task unfinished rather than miss the season.

reading: The friend tells the returned lord of strong horses, who lingered long in the wide camp of victorious war, that the kohl-lined eyes of this woman, gone yellow as konrai flowers, have regained their old beauty like the blue lilies of a long mountain pool, now that he has come.

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 0-20
theme: The invocation to Shiva and Akananuru 1 to 20 in the anthology's fixed order of lands: paalai poems of men leaving or turning back for wealth and of mothers whose daughters eloped, Kapilar's hill courtships in which the friend presses for marriage, mullai homecomings at evening, neythal shores closed by gossip, and marutham quarrels over the husband's women. Chola, Chera, Pandya and lesser chiefs' names (Thithan's Uranthai, Thondi, Kodai, Avi's Pothini, Nannan's Pazhi) serve as measures of private beauty, guard and loss.
source_issues: akananuru:0: the last line is numbered 15 though the poem has 16 lines (flag lineation); marked on 16 lines.

akananuru:1 line 5 recurs verbatim at akananuru:356 line 9; akananuru:3 line 9 at akananuru:97 line 3; akananuru:14 line 11 at akananuru:64 line 14; akananuru:17 line 22 at akananuru:153 line 19 and 187 line 24 (formulaic lines, not errors).
akananuru:3 line 18: an unassigned character was removed in repair (read ஞான்றே).
akananuru:12: the colophon thurai begins with a stray double quotation mark ("பகற்குறி ...); copied as is.
akananuru:15: our base text has 19 lines and the commentary edition (pmuni0490_01) 20; line numbers here follow the base text.
akananuru:19: the colophon thurai breaks off at தலைமகன் without its verb (presumably ... நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது); copied as is.
akananuru:20: the colophon thurai breaks off at தோழி without its verb or addressee; the poem addresses the girl as தோழி (line 13).

reading: The god wears fresh konrai blossom as garland and chaplet, a fine thread on his chest, an unwinking eye on his brow, axe and pick in hand and a three-pointed spear; he rides the bull with Umai beside him, red as the evening sky, with crescent-white teeth, flame-bright matted hair lit by the young moon, a tiger's hide and a dark throat, and the world rests in the shade of his flawless feet, an old order no god or sage has fathomed.
nuance: The poem is a list of possessions in short clauses (மார்பினஃதே, நுதலது, கையது, ஊர்ந்தது, சேர்ந்தோள்) and gives its only verb of the world at the end: the whole world has stopped (தவிர்ந்தன்று) in the shade of his feet. Unlike the Purananuru's opening by a poet of the same name, it sets Umai beside him rather than inside him, a fitting choice for an anthology of love.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god, கடவுள் வாழ்த்து (porul 2.27)

tamil: நிழல் தேய்ந்து உலறிய மரத்த; அறை காய்பு,
reading: The woman asks her friend whether he has forgotten his word that they would never part, a bond he likened to stone set with lac at Avi's Pothini, now that he has left, her shoulders slackening, to fetch gold from a far country across a forest where the sun has stripped the trees of shade, dried the springs, parches spilt grain, emptied the road even of robbers, and where wind-tossed murungai blossom looks like sea spray.
nuance: She does not accuse; she asks whether he forgot (மறந்தனர் கொல்லோ), which keeps the fault in memory rather than in will. The promise was itself a simile of permanence, stone fixed with lac, set against a land where everything is coming loose: shade, water, people. Line 5 recurs verbatim in Akananuru 356.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman speaks of a man gone across the waste for wealth

reading: The friend tells the hill lord that on his slopes a male monkey drinks without knowing it the wine that ripe jackfruit and plantain have made in a rock pool, cannot climb the pepper-twined sandal tree and sleeps content on the flowered slope; if beasts there find unplanned joy so easily, how can the joy he plans be hard for him, when the girl's heart cannot be held back and he may yet come at night, slipping past her father's watchmen, though the vengai has burst into flower and the full moon has risen.
nuance: The friend states the moral of the monkey herself (குறியா இன்பம் ... குறித்த இன்பம்), so this is an open comparison, not ullurai; a traditional further reading makes the drunk monkey that cannot climb the lover who will not rise to marriage. The closing signs are a warning dressed as permission: the vengai's flowering is the season of the girl's confinement and the moon lights the path he would take by night.

thinai_evidence.note: secret meeting under the father's watch, on the hill slopes

comparisons.tenor: the monkey's unplanned joy set beside the joy the hero plans and delays

reading: The man tells his heart, which showed him the long road through the waste and pushed him from behind toward wealth, that its lie, which looks like truth, cannot lift his grief when on that far road the glance of the girl with the red mouth and sweet speech, eyes that rival her curved earrings, comes across his way; and the road is the one where a red-eared vulture, to feed its mate weak from laying in the omai tree, ceaselessly tears like looters at the rotting wild cow a tiger killed and left.
nuance: The heart stands behind and drives (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), the very phrase another paalai poet uses for a heart that stays behind and holds back (Akananuru 19). The vulture that forages for a nesting mate is the man's own errand seen from the road, and its carrion feast makes the wealth he is promised look like plunder.

reading: The friend shows the woman the season: jasmine has put out its tips, konrai buds open, the stag with horns like twisted iron leaps into the gravel hollows and rain has made the forest lovely; look, there comes the chariot of the lord of the low hills, its reins drawn taut as lute-strings and its bell-tongues tied so as not to startle the nectar birds asleep with their mates in the flowering boughs, as he comes thinking of her beauty, fragrant as the kanthal opening on the tall hill east of festive Uranthai.
nuance: The man's tying of the bells is the poem's proof of his tenderness: a man who will not wake sleeping pairs of birds is hurrying to his own pair. The rain does the promising before he arrives (கார்செய்தன்றே), as the friend's argument requires.

reading: The man tells his heart why he gave up the journey: when he thought of crossing the stony, useless forest where gooseberries fall like dice on the rock and sharp stones cut the toes, she came near unasked, with a faint forced smile, said nothing but stood like a painting as if assenting to the old saying that such leaving is not the way of right, and when, eyes swimming, she sighed over the garland on the head of the son held to her breast, its bright flower lost its colour; seeing that he stayed, for she grieves even with him beside her and would not live if they parted.
nuance: Her whole argument is unspoken: she refuses by looking (முன்னம் காட்டி, முகத்தின் உரையா), and the decisive sign is not on her but on the child, the garland withering under her breath. The old maxim she seems to accept, அறத்தாறு அன்று, is the poem's only statement of a rule, and it is attributed to tradition, not to her.

reading: The wife tells the husband back from a courtesan that yesterday he bathed with his beloved in the Kaveri flood at Uranthai of the generous Thithan, clasping a white reed raft, faces bright like the Poozhiyar's elephant in a pond, his garland crushed on his chest; today he comes and repeats lies about 'the mother of his son, of spotless chastity', mocking her age, which she lets pass: her youth, like Mathi's Kazhar where the otter that fed on vaalai fish among the vallai creepers goes back to rest in the old cane thicket, is long gone, so what can sweet lies do for her.
nuance: The otter that feasts in the lotus field and then returns to the old thorny cane is set inside the simile for her lost youth: she pictures him eating among new flowers and sheltering in the old thicket, which is herself. The praise he offers (மாசில் கற்பின், புதல்வன் தாய்) is the true wifely title, and she calls it a lie because it is said to placate her.

reading: The foster mother, following her daughter who has eloped, recalls her warnings (your breasts have formed, you are no child now, keep away from the old town's spirits and do not go out), and asks a doe with its herd, and a hill girl wearing a tiger-tooth tali who gathers the jackfruit seeds the grazing stag drops, whether they have seen her girl, who fled like a hind that sees a net, with a youth of white spear into this waste, while robbers raiding a cattle-pen have blocked her pursuit.
nuance: The first lines quote the very prohibitions the girl escaped; the mother's list of the signs of puberty is also her account of why the girl left. Her questions go to a doe and to a hill girl like her daughter, as if the wild had become the only household left to ask.

reading: The woman tells her friend, while her lover stands unseen nearby, that even the midnight when the bear clawing termites from the wet anthill makes snakes lose their strength would not be hard to face, if only someone would ask him: in your land, where the tiger drags the boar it killed so the jackfruit slope reeks of flesh and the cow elephant breaks a great tree to ease her mate trapped in a pit, do you who led her off the path even know this road, where she came by lightning flashes without losing her way, gathering her rain-wet hair over her back and wringing it?
nuance: She wants the danger she has run spoken to him by someone else; the poem is overheard reproach. The cow elephant crashing down a tree for her mate in the pit is the one tender act among the beasts, and it is what she herself has been doing.

reading: Returning with his work done, the man tells his heart, the charioteer listening, that it raced ahead of the sleepless chariot past the iruppai-strewn red path and the hill where pestle songs echo with the owl, and asks whether it has already reached her, standing at a corner of the tall house in the evening when calves come home, praying at every chirp of the lizard, and crept up with hand unraised to cover her eyes, touch her braid and stroke her bangled arm.
nuance: The man's homecoming is imagined from her side: the evening, the lizard's omen, the game of covering her eyes, all happen in the heart before the body arrives. The road's iruppai and red earth belong to the waste, but the poem's situation is the mullai return and the woman waiting at dusk.

reading: The friend stops the shore lord leaving after a night meeting and tells him, lord of the coast where birds settle on the old punnai whose buds look like fish eyes, that if he means to part and make the girl's neythal eyes weep he has taken on a hard thing; he must marry her properly and take her, for her beauty is like rich Thondi, where fishermen with new nets share out the horned fish on the sandy shore of the fragrant hamlet.
nuance: The friend values the girl in the currency of a Chera port: a public, famous, prosperous town, the opposite of a secret meeting. The fishermen's sharing of the catch is a picture of open, rightful taking, which is what she asks of him (உரிதினின் கொண்டு).

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிவந்து தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குந் தலைமகனை எதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லியது.

reading: The woman tells her friend that had he taken her with him through the sun-scorched forest where the leafless silk-cotton blooms like rows of festival lamps and the pools have turned to dust, he too would have had her close embrace on the sandbank of the forest stream under the drooping flowered boughs, and her eyes, which now weep every night like dripping flowers as if to fill a dry tank, would have slept.
nuance: She turns the usual argument round: the road is not too hard for her; it is the place where their embrace could have been. The colophon reads the poem as her assurance that she will bear up, but what it says is that she does not: the assurance lies in her saying it calmly, not in its content.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்தவிடத்து ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் வேறுபாடுகண்டு ஆற்றாளாய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் ஆற்றுவல் என்பதுபடச் சொல்லியது.

tamil: யாமே, பிரிவு இன்று இயைந்த துவரா நட்பின்,
reading: The friend tells the hill lord that the girl's mother loves her more than her own eyes, her father cannot bear her small feet on hard ground, and the two of them are one life like the two-headed bird; on his hill, where an elephant takes the vengai flowers strewn over the hunters' hut for a tiger and flees through the bamboo, if he comes (by night) the gentle girl will not survive.
nuance: The household's love is given as the guard itself: the closer they hold her, the less she can slip away. The elephant that bolts from vengai blossom mistaken for a tiger is a hill scene of false alarm; a reader may hear in it the danger of discovery, but it maps to no stated situation. Whether 'we' (யாமே) are the girl and her friend or the girl and her lover is open.

colophon.thurai: "பகற்குறி வாரா நின்ற தலைமகன் தோழியாற் செறிப்பறிவுறுக்கப்பட்டு இரவுக்குறி வாரா வரைவல் என்றாற்கு, அதுவும் மறுத்து வரைவு கடாயது.

comparisons.tenor: the two women (or the two lovers), one life like the two-headed bird

reading: The friend tells the man that even if the wealth he would earn were as great as the fruitful sacrifice of the Pandya's warrior, lord of Kodai, who wears the pearl of his sea and the sandal of his hill and gives to suppliants without limit except the short while it takes to teach a pit-caught elephant to obey, he should not leave his gentle companion in these days of cold dew, when the lonely north wind sways the forked paddy in the wide fields and makes the white heron on the sugarcane cry; let the wealth go, and the nights in a clean bed without embrace.
nuance: The patron's limitless giving is the measure, and the friend uses it to set a ceiling: no wealth, not even such a man's, is worth a winter apart. The two clauses of wishing (நோய் இன்றாக செய்பொருள்; கவவுஇன் புறாமைக் கழிக) can be read as bitter dismissal or as a blessing on his going, which is why the colophon allows that she consented.

reading: The bard tells his companions that the wife said to him, 'if he does not remember us even in this evening, when the stag nuzzles its doe and leaps grazing on the red-earth road strewn with kaya flowers, herders deck themselves in the jasmine land and good cows, udders dripping, low for their calves as they crowd into the common, what will become of us by morning, bard?'; unable to answer, he played his lute, praised the god, steadied his grief and went toward the husband, and now he has seen his tall chariot coming, wheels roaring like thunder-clouds.
nuance: The bard's own answer to her question is not words but music and prayer, and then a sighting; the poem moves from her evening to his seeing. Evening in the jasmine land is the hour when everything returns to its pair, which is why it is the measure of his forgetting.

reading: The mother whose daughter has eloped wishes that, if her fierce longing can be granted, the old town of the man's many hamlets may know how to welcome her, as the Kosar's Thulu country, with its peacock groves, shelters empty-handed travellers; for her soft-shouldered dear one, leaving her friends and mother lonely, has slipped the strict guard of a house like Nannan's fortress Pazhi and gone with him on the road where bears scatter the iruppai flowers and konrai pods, set on her sweet companion.
nuance: Her grief turns into a blessing on the stranger's town. The house is likened to Nannan's guarded Pazhi so that the breach looks like the fall of a fort; the girl's resolve (இன்துணைப் படர்ந்த கொள்கை) is acknowledged, not condemned.

tamil: 'வருக மாள, என் உயிர்!' எனப் பெரிது உவந்து
reading: The wife tells her husband, who claims he knows no other woman, that she saw a sharp-toothed girl find their little son alone in the chariot street, lift him to her ornamented breast crying 'come, my life!' when no one was looking; she went up and asked 'why so flustered, spotless girl? are you his mother too?', embraced her, and watched her bow her head, scratch the ground and stand ashamed like one caught in a secret; and so, she asks, did she not treat her kindly, since that goddess-like woman is fit to be his son's mother?
nuance: The proof against his denial is the courtesan's love for the child, and the wife's weapon is courtesy: she embraces the rival and then, with full irony, ranks her as fit to be the son's mother, which is the title the husband had denied anyone else could claim.

reading: The foster mother remembers that her girl, if she threw a ball a little or played jacks with her friends, would say 'mother, I am tired' and lie in her arms with sweat on her brow; now, forgetting kin and nurse, she has crossed her proud father's strict guard and given her whole heart to a stranger, and the nurse asks whether those little anklet feet can walk the waterless waste where salt-carters' calls echo in the hills and the falling silk-cotton flowers flicker like festival lamps or like stars at dawn, under the dark hill that bars the way.
nuance: The whole poem rests on one contrast: a girl too tired for a ball game now walking the waste. The silk-cotton flowers like lamps in an old town's festival bring the home town into the wilderness, the place she has left as a light falling on her road.

reading: The friend asks the hill lord whether anyone comes here at midnight, crossing like a fierce boar the dreadful ford of the forest torrent, its water hidden under fallen flowers, where crocodiles sleep in the eddies and the flood drags off a wild elephant; if her friend suffers harm even for a day she will not live after, and even on safe paths those who go often slip, so they live in fear; let him come by day and meet her in the kanthal grove below the honey-combed hill of their garden, and hold the soft shoulders, like bamboo, that her mother reared.
nuance: She does not forbid the meeting; she moves it. The danger she names is the road's, but the argument is also about discovery: the frequent traveller slips (பயில வழங்குநர் ... இழுக்குவர்), and a secret repeated becomes known.

tamil: வருந்தினை- வாழி, என் நெஞ்சே!- பருந்து இருந்து
reading: The man, on his way for wealth, tells his heart that it neither stayed with her then nor will cross the hills with him now, where the kite cries wearily from the tall yaa and the owl hoots like a drum; if it means to stay behind, let it go back, prosper, and not forget him, once it has embraced the tired drooping back of his love, who sits unmoving with a lamp for company, her dark lily eyelids gone red and burning with every thought of him, hot tears falling, bangles slipping from her wrist, wilting like a creeper that has shed its flowers.
nuance: Here the heart that stands behind (பின்நின்று) holds back toward her, where in Akananuru 3 the heart behind drives him on; the man splits from his heart and sends it home in his stead. The lamp as her only companion is the poem's centre.

reading: The friend tells the girl, while the lover stands unseen nearby, that their days of chasing birds from her father's drying fish, resting in the punnai's shade, digging out red crabs, swinging on the thazhai-root swing, playing with the waves and coming home in leaf skirts are over: mother, taking the word of the town's spiteful women, has put her under guard, because there is a chariot with fine horses that circles the moonlit sand of the great ford regardless of day or night.
nuance: The list of shore games is a portrait of a girlhood now closed by gossip, and it is spoken for the hidden lover to hear: the last line names his chariot as the cause, so the report is also a summons to marry.

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 21-40
theme: Akananuru 21 to 40, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men on the road to wealth arguing with their hearts and women counting seasons, set beside hill courtships at the millet field, marutham quarrels settled by a child or sharpened by gossip, mullai camps and homecomings, and neythal evenings. Puram fame (Alankanam, Thithiyan, Kari's Pennai, Korkai, Kolli) supplies the similes for private feeling.
source_issues: 22, 24, 37: the colophon thurai is numbered (1) but gives no second alternative.
25: line 7 reads படுநா விளியா னடுநின்று, which looks corrupt (the word division and the sense are unclear).
31: the colophon thurai breaks off (…பிறர் சொல்லக் கேட்டு) without the speaker or the verb; the speaker is inferred from the poem.
32: the text flag notes a printed line number 51 standing on line 15, a stray number in the base text.
38: line 15 has ஐ.தேங்கு with a stray full stop, and line 17 கணஃது; both look corrupt.
39: the record has no colophon thurai and no poet (the flags say the colophon and verse block were not found in the commentary section).
21, 39: stray or unbalanced opening quotation marks at line 1.

tamil: எழுஇனி, வாழி என் நெஞ்சே!- புரி இணர்
reading: Halfway across a waterless forest, the man rebukes his heart, which now wants to turn back: it was the heart that refused his plea not to leave the girl with jasmine-bud teeth and settled on the venture, so it must rise at once and help bring home wealth that will make the house glad.
nuance: The roles are reversed from the usual quarrel: the man had argued for staying, the heart for going, and now he holds the heart to its own choice. The goal is named as மனைநக, that the house may laugh, so the journey is cast as a gift to the home rather than flight from it.

reading: The girl recalls the midnight rite her mother held to cure her: old women said Murugan's power had seized her, the velan sacrificed and scattered red millet with blood, and in that very night her lover slipped past the house guards like a hunting tiger, so that in his embrace she laughed at an offering wasted on a stranger priest while the true cure of her sickness had come.
nuance: She speaks to defend the man her friend has just blamed, and the defence is a confession: he risked the guarded house on the night of the rite. Her laughter judges the rite only as a diagnosis; it does not deny the god, whose fierce presence (அணங்கு, உருகெழு) the poem keeps.

reading: Seeing her weep that spring, with its sandbanks of kaanji pollen and its cuckoos calling in turn, is surely the sign her man set for his return, her friend promises that he who crossed the hills whose falls sound like the music of Thithiyan, lord of Pothiyil, will come quickly with soft words of sorrow for her tears.
nuance: The friend puts apology into the absent man's mouth before he has come (நோவல், குறுமகள்), so her comfort is a script for his return. The spring is described as a season that even scorners cannot scorn, which makes his absence from it harder to excuse.

reading: The wife asks her friend how she could sulk with her husband: once he praised her breasts and would not stop embracing, but lately he held back for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son, so she turned to the boy in the nurse's arms saying he suits the good women and she suits the son, and at that he said he too loved the child, held her from behind and wept, melting like ploughed red earth in the rain.
nuance: The child decides the quarrel twice: he is her reason to withdraw and the man's way back to her. The rain-on-ploughed-field simile gives the melting to him, so her question (புலத்தல் கூடுமோ) means that his tears have left her no ground for sulking.

nuance: The friend argues from the girl's own beauty, which is a comfort and a reproach at once: her body should be his reason to stay. The pearl simile carries a whole Pandya world (the Venkatam elephant, Korkai guarded by aram) into a two-line image of her teeth.

thinai_evidence.note: news of a departure for wealth across the wild forest

comparisons.tenor: her shining teeth, like the pearls of Korkai's great harbour
her red-streaked, fighting eyes, like a victorious spear swinging with blood

tamil: உறற்கு அரிது ஆகும், அவன் மலர்ந்த மார்பே!
reading: With the man listening nearby, the friend warns the girl that the millet ears are bowing and harvested stalks are showing in the fields: if she, content with her hunter, does not rise and scare the parrots, her mother will say she cannot guard the crop and send others, and then his broad chest will be hard to reach.
nuance: The warning is meant for the overhearing man: the ripening millet dates the end of the field meetings, so he must turn the secret love into marriage before the harvest closes it.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது. இது, பகலே சிறைப்புறம்.

reading: Back from his work, the man answers his wife, who asks with a fading smile whether he forgot her: he left vowing that a day without thinking of her eyes would not be worth living, and in the burning waste where elephants chase mirages and wilt like boats in dried water, only his body stayed there, bound by shame to finish the task, while his foolish heart was always with her.
nuance: He splits himself to answer the charge: the body (உடம்பு) was held by நாண், the shame of an unfinished task, and the heart (நெஞ்சம்) never left. The tiger that will not eat prey fallen on its left side measures his resolve by a hunter's code of honour.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீண்ட தலைமகன் எம்மையும் நினைத்தறிதிரோ? என்ற தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

reading: The friend tells the lord of a shore where fishermen haul in their catch together like ploughmen at a threshing floor, fling fish to fill the empty pots of those who beg, and sleep on the high dunes, that greatness is not lost by coming one day to the cool punnai grove and asking how she fares, and implies that to ask once and leave is no greatness.
nuance: The two closing lines can be read as a plea (would your greatness suffer if you came and asked?) or as a reproach (is it greatness to come once, ask, and go?); the generosity of his own fishermen is set before him as a standard either way.

reading: Hearing it said that she cannot bear the parting, the woman tells her friend of the road her man took: a season of failed rain when the fiery sun scorched the land, where bowmen of the rock forts shoot travellers whose eyes the vultures pluck, beyond which lie the many hills of the land of changed speech, outside the rule of the three Tamil kings.
nuance: The road ends at the border of the language: the measure of his distance is where Tamil stops being spoken (மொழிபெயர் தேஎத்த). The sense of 'சென்றார்' என்பு இலர் is unclear to me, and the colophon thurai breaks off before naming the speaker.
