reading: She tells her friend how yesterday a jewelled man, looking like a patron but pleading like a suppliant, came to the millet field, called her a hill goddess who had stricken him and held her from behind; melting inside but afraid he would see it, she broke free like a startled doe and stood firm, and he went off like an elephant parted from its herd, so now she proposes they go and laugh at the gracious man who keeps trying, not knowing her shoulders are his alone.
nuance: Puram's pair of giver and receiver (புரவலன், இரவல்) is turned inside out: the man who looks like a patron begs. The plan to laugh at him is an assent in disguise, since in the same breath she says the claim to her shoulders is his.

reading: On the road the man tells his heart, which wants to turn back: it chose to leave the virtuous wife and to cross the land where a kite calls its mate, and now, halfway over the gravel hills, it would be better never to have parted from her with shoulders like the bamboo of Vanavan's Kolli; but to break off the work now would only win the laughter of others.
nuance: The poem does not deny the heart's longing; it concedes that never leaving would have been good (நன்றுமற் றில்ல) and then argues that turning back now is worse. Shame before others (பிறர்நகு) is the last argument, not wealth.

reading: His task done, the man urges his charioteer to hurry through the cool scrub where a stag feeds tender grass to his young doe and guards her while she sleeps, so that his heart may find ease with his shy wife, who in the house where swans play with their mates holds a parrot on her wrist and softly teaches it to say 'tell me he comes today', afraid the household will hear.
nuance: Both partners speak through creatures: his longing is shown in the stag's care, hers in the words she teaches the parrot because she is too shy to say them aloud.

tamil: துணிந்து பிறள் ஆயினள் ஆயினும், அணிந்து அணிந்து,
reading: A mother whose daughter has run off with a man prays: the girl, forgetting those who bore and raised her, left the high-walled house desolate and dared the flesh-smelling road where bowmen honour hero-stones with peacock feathers, drums and toddy; may the stranger who became her companion in an unknown land adorn her again and again and put her to sleep on his chest, her curled hair like the fine ripples of Kari's Pennai river.
nuance: The prayer hands the stranger her own office: அணிந்து அணிந்து, adorning again and again, is what a mother does. The road is marked by offerings to the dead, so the daughter's path into marriage is drawn through a landscape of graves.

reading: The wife tells her husband, lord of a town where a great striped varal fish swallows the hook, tears the water-lily leaves, crushes the blue lilies, tangles the vallai creeper and will not come to the angler's pull, raging like a roped bull as it churns the pond each day, that the gossip of his wedding with a young girl in the marutham grove on the Vaigai's sands is louder than the shout of Chezhiyan's warriors on the day he crushed seven kings at Alankanam.
nuance: The gossip is measured by the most famous victory shout the audience knew, so a private wrong is given the volume of a public war. The fish's scene is the wife's hidden charge; the battle simile is her open one.

reading: Breaking down under her friend's reassurance, the woman says that even if he has not forgotten her, this is the lovely spring: farmers thresh all night under dust like mist, rise at dawn to pluck mangoes green as parrots, drink new brew from leaf cups like oxen at a pond, eat horsegram and lentil porridge with milk, and rest at noon with their oxen in the marutham shade, a sweet season only for those who have partners to enjoy.
nuance: The farmers' full day, from night threshing to noon's rest with the oxen, is a picture of shared life; only the last line turns the whole landscape into her lack.

reading: The friend imagines the hill-man, garlanded with vengai and blue lily, bow in hand, coming to the old meeting places and finding the swing on the ashoka abandoned, the pool where lilies open like eyes, and the harvested millet field, and wonders whether he will turn back grieving, since she forgot to tell him that their village is the one on the high hill crowned by the white waterfall.
nuance: 'I forgot to tell him our village' is the real message for the overhearing man: the field trysts are over, and the way to her now runs through the village, that is, through marriage. Line 15 (ஐ.தேங்கு) looks corrupt.

thinai_evidence.note: hill flowers, a harvested millet field and the hill-man

reading: The returned man tells his wife not to speak like a stranger, asking whether he ever thought of her: in a vast forest swept by a wildfire from rubbing bamboo, where travellers lost the path and elephants fled a tiger, he lay at sunset thinking of her and dreamed he found her brooding with loose bangles, stroked her brow and smoothed her hair asking why she sulked, and the false dream left him with empty hands; it is she who has not cared for his distress.
nuance: He turns her charge round: her sulk is answered by his dream of answering her sulk, so the dispute is already rehearsed in the dream, and the empty hand he woke to is his evidence that he thought of her.

thinai_evidence.note: a wildfire across the great forest on the road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the record has no colophon thurai; speaker and situation are inferred from the poem (the returned man answers her complaint)

reading: At evening on the shore, as the backwater flowers close, the sea roars and herons crowd into the punnai nests, the woman tells her friend that though her man has gone without pity and left her heart in grief, may his friendship never break, and may her heart, which went to his breast of sweet sleep, not tire of staying there for want of kindness and come back.
nuance: She blesses the bond in the same breath as she names its cruelty. The heron that flees the reapers' drum to roost in the palmyra's inner frond is the picture of her own heart, which fled the evening's pain to his breast.

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 41-60
theme: Akananuru 41 to 60, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men away for wealth and women and mothers left behind, set beside hill courtships moving toward disclosure and marriage, marutham quarrels over the husband's other women, mullai homecomings and neythal pleas. Puram names (Venni, Musiri, Kurukkai, Pazhaiyan, Pannan) are used throughout as similes for private grief and joy.
source_issues: 44: the colophon thinai is the numbering rule's முல்லை; the commentary edition gives பாலை. The poem (a man returning from finished war to his wife) fits mullai.
47: the base text numbers the last line 15 though the poem has 19 lines, as the commentary edition shows; a misprinted number.
55: the colophon thurai reads தலமகட்கு, a misprint for தலைமகட்கு.
56: the colophon thurai has the corrupt word *வந்தசனாக, presumably வந்தானாக (the bard came to her house).
57: the base text has 19 lines and the commentary edition (pmuni0490_01) 18; marked as the base text stands.

reading: Away on his errand for wealth, the man looks at a dawn countryside in full beauty, the palasa ablaze with flowers, bees humming and ploughmen calling over the fields, and asks whether the dark-skinned, freckled woman he left is wasting, her shoulders slackening, in the loneliness of his absence.
nuance: The landscape gains its beauty (காடுஅணி கொண்ட) in the very lines where she loses hers (நலம் செலச் சாஅய்); the season that adorns the land is the measure of what parting takes from her, and he can only guess it with a question (கொல்லோ).

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த விடத்துக் கிழத்தியை நினைந்து சொல்லியது.

nuance: The friend speaks of her own joy, not the heroine's; the drought image measures how long the waiting for marriage had become, and the whole land rejoicing hints that the marriage will be public, the opposite of secret love.

reading: The man tells the heart that urged him to go for wealth that the monsoon has come, the clouds joining land and sky so that only water-clock keepers know where the sun is, and he has held his mullai-scented wife; pitiable are those who, without kindness, leave their sweet companion for a stranger's wealth.
nuance: He calls the wealth-seeker's departure மடமை, folly, the word usually kept for the woman's innocence; the cow elephant, worn by summer and now bathing with her bull in the flood, is the rains' gift to the paired, and he places himself with the pair.

reading: The king's war is done and the enemy has paid tribute, so the man bids his charioteer drive ahead of the column, that he may sleep on the breast of a wife who is like Kudavayil, a town as rich as Chenni's Azhumbil; Chenni is the king who, unable to bear the sight of Pazhaiyan's fall, when the chiefs Nannan, Etrai, Atti, Kangan, Katti and Punthurai had massed their camp, captured Kanaiyan and took Kazhumalam.
nuance: The catalogue of chiefs and the fall of Pazhaiyan fill lines 7 to 17, and the wife is reached only through a chain of likenesses, a king, his town, another town; the war that kept him away is also the stock from which he praises her. Who fought whom in lines 7 to 14 is compressed, and this reading of it is offered with caution.

reading: Told to bear up, the heroine says her lover has crossed a summer forest where dry pods rattle like dancing-floor drums and the tiger springs on the waterless track; her skin must pale like peerkku flowers, the gossip is louder than the bards' clamour the day Anni cut down Thithiyan's punnai at Kurukkai, and she will wander distraught like Aathimanthi, sleepless as a broken fort shaken by the Chera's assault.
nuance: Every likeness she reaches for is a public disaster: a battlefield's din, a famous madwoman, a sacked fort. Her private loss is told in the scale of puram events, which is how she answers the friend's claim that it can be borne.

reading: The friend refuses the man entry: he is lord of a town where a red-eyed buffalo, tired of the mud, breaks its tether in the sleeping night, pushes through the thorn fence, scatters the fish and grazes the lotus; they say he has brought another woman home and married her, and the friend will not say it herself, but her bangle, like Chezhiyan's Allur, may slip if it must; go, lord, who is stopping you?
nuance: The refusal is made as a release: யாரையோ நிற் புலக்கேம் (who are we to quarrel with you) and நிற் றகைக்குநர் யாரோ (who is there to stop you) deny her any claim on him, which is the sharpest claim she can make. The report of the wedding is put in others' mouths (என்ப).

reading: The man tells his faltering heart to rise quickly now the work is done, cross the hot wilderness where wind-whipped bamboo catches fire, the flames leap the crags and cracking joints scatter the stags, and at dusk, when lamps are lit and the male dove calls its mate in the tall house, reach her who weeps asking where he is, and embrace many times her bamboo-smooth shoulders, fragrant with the koothalam of Chezhiyan's Sirumalai.
nuance: He pictures the dusk at home before he has crossed the fire: the lamps, the calling dove and her question 'யாண்டு உளர்கொல்?' are what make the burning road crossable.

reading: The friend answers the foster mother, who asks why her daughter will not drink milk and has paled: when the girls went to pick vengai flowers and someone cried 'tiger', a garlanded young hunter came asking which way the beast went, asked if such girls could lie, gazed long at her daughter's eyes and drove away, and at sunset the daughter looked where he had gone and said 'he is a man indeed'; the wise can measure the rest.
nuance: The friend never names love. She gives the scene and the daughter's one sentence and leaves the inference to the foster mother (மதிவல் லோர்க்கே), a disclosure that keeps the girl's modesty. His question about lies plays on their silence: they hid and did not answer where the beast went.

reading: The foster mother grieves at home: she had seen the girl who loved her parrot, ball and play-seeds grow unlike herself, had come close, stroked her forehead and held her, and the girl had embraced her again and again; had she known the girl would go, praising the tall man, through a forest where tired deer chew withered marul in the rainless shade, she would have followed her like her own shadow wherever she played in her father's house.
nuance: Her regret is not that she failed to stop the girl but that she was not near enough: the shadow image (மெய்ந்நிழல் போல) makes her wish to have gone along. The girl's many embraces, read now, were a farewell the mother did not understand.

reading: The friend tells the bard that the shore lord once came often, even by day, despite the leaping fish of the backwater and the red-mouthed women's gossip, and now stays away; she asks him to go secretly to the old town and tell the hero what the bright-browed girl says as she hides her tears: 'see, the anril on the palmyra by the house cannot sleep at night if parted from its mate even once; what shall I do?'
nuance: The anril is the girl's own message, not an image the poem lodges: she uses the bird to say that she cannot sleep, so it carries the sense openly rather than as iraicchi. The friend, not the girl, chooses the bard as carrier, and asks him to go secretly.

reading: The man tells his heart, which urged him to leave, that in the peopleless summer wilderness where a male vulture with flesh-red ears sits scorched on a burnt yaa tree gazing at its hungry mate, the wealth he would toil for is not worth having if it comes only by parting from his wife: better to stay, hold her close so her jewels jingle, and be glad in the household's work.
nuance: The hinge is the play on புணர்வு: wealth is 'joined' only by parting, and staying is the other joining, with her. The vulture stays by its mate in the burning tree; the hearth (மனைமுதல் வினை) is set against the work (செய்வினை) abroad.

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the two-sided question, whether to tell mother of the hill lord whose wide chest their heart loves, a lord of a land where a girl's cry for vengai flowers brings the men running with bows for a cattle-seizing tiger, has been settled one way: even if her life leaves her body, the friend must not say that her pallor is love-sickness.
nuance: The colophon says she speaks knowing the friend will disclose; her forbidding is modesty speaking, and the oath (இன்உயிர் கழிவது ஆயினும்) shows the cost she sets on silence. The false alarm on the hill, a girl's cry taken for a tiger's threat, is how secrets get out in this land.

reading: The heroine tells the friend who urges patience that she does not know: he has crossed the waterless wilderness of drumstick flowers and cactus, where a red dog rests with its starving mate in the shade of a lettered hero-stone, because his heart cannot hide what it has when the needy say they have nothing; his love is for wealth more than for her, and the friend calls it grace.
nuance: She grants him the virtue and turns it against her: the inability to refuse the poor is what takes him away, so his generosity and his desertion are the same act. The last two lines set காதல் against காதல் and பொருள் against அருள்.

reading: The guest kings have paid tribute and the king's anger has cooled, the rains have come, so the man bids his charioteer drive over the red earth that the cochineal beetles make like a painting: at dusk, when the cattle hurry home to their calves with the cowherds behind, he wants to see his wife beckon the young moon with her finger, prattling sweet as water after gooseberries from the garden of Pannan, who lives for others, promising it milk if it brings their son a gold tali.
nuance: What he hurries home to is not her waiting but her play: the mother tricking the child with the moon (புதல்வற் பொய்க்கும்). The village whose gooseberry gives the simile is that of Pannan, praised in one line as தனக்கென வாழாப் பிறர்க்கு உரியாளன், a puram patron lodged inside an akam homecoming.

reading: The mother tells the neighbour women who console her that she does not grieve that her daughter went with a youth strong as an elephant across the sun-cracked waste; she lies sleepless, breathing hot like a forge's bellows, and quarrels with her own life, which will not leave her to go after the girl as the noble men who heard Cheralathan, shamed by his back wound at Venni, sit facing north, died to go with him.
nuance: She accepts the match (கழிந்ததற்கு அழிந்தன்றோ இலனே) and turns her anger on her own life for staying. The puram image is chosen for its followers, not its king: the companions who chose death with him are what her life refuses to be.

reading: The heroine laughs to her friend that yesterday the bard of the lord of the cool ford, where a black-horned buffalo stirs the gem-clear pond, gorges on lilies and comes home dusted with kaanji pollen, was hurrying to bring new brides to the lord's chest when a newly calved cow charged him; he dropped his lute and ran into her house, and when she hid her mirth and said 'this is not your house, that one is', he stood bewildered with folded hands.
nuance: The laugh is the weapon: by sending the bard to 'your house' she names the courtesan's house as his true home and her husband's errand-runner as a stranger in hers. The joy she hides (மெய்ம்மலி உவகை மறையினென்) is a joy in his discomfiture.

reading: On the summer road among the hills, where a small green-feathered female bird crosses the sky in the heat, finds no fruit on the bare fig whose roots hang like an elephant's trunk, and faints remembering the days of plenty, the man, alone, wonders whether his wife's beauty, bright as the full moon, has turned to the colour of peerkku flowers, as she weeps night and day like the wounded in Chezhiyan's siege of Musiri.
nuance: The bird comes to a tree that once fed it and finds it empty, as the man imagines his wife finding the days of their life together gone; the war simile of the wounded at Musiri makes her grief a casualty of the same world of kings and wealth that took him away.

reading: The heroine tells the hill lord, whose land is one where at midnight in cold-season rain the hunter father of the hill girls, finding no game, keeps to his house on a tiger-skin bed, that it is sweet when her arms clasp his back on his chest; but the cold north wind, which torments her whenever she thinks of him in his absence, waits long outside at midnight, bending the house tree, looking for its chance.
nuance: The father kept home by the rain is the danger to their meeting, and the wind that waits outside is like the lover who stood outside; the close of the poem (நெடும்புற நிலையே) may be his long waiting or the wind's, and the reading turns on which.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord and the midnight of the cold season

reading: The friend tells the heroine, whose eyes have lost their flower-like beauty, that on the road taken by the man who went far for wealth a bull elephant bends a tall yaa tree with his head so his young mate can eat its shoots, as Maal trod down a tree on the Yamuna's sands to give the cowherd girls leaf-skirts; yet those men do not remember even the mornings when they praised her back, lovely as the water-lily of Murugan's Parankunram, and have left her shoulders to slacken.
nuance: The comfort is double: the elephant who feeds his mate is meant to promise the man's return, while the friend also admits he does not think of her. The god's image of a tree bent for women's sake makes the elephant's care a divine habit.

reading: The friend tells the hero: do not crush our bright bangle, fine as Porayan's Tondi where a fisher girl brings her father rice bartered for salt, tamarind fish stew and fat fish; if the mother, who flushes at nothing and says 'playing in the sand with your friends wears away your glow', sees anything, she will shut the girl in more closely than the Chola guards the tribute stored at Kudanthai.
nuance: The threat of confinement is the argument for marriage: the friend never asks him to marry but makes the mother's guarded house the alternative. The fisher girl feeding her father in the opening is the life of the shore the heroine is about to lose.

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 61-80
theme: Akananuru 61 to 80, in the anthology's order of lands: ten paalai poems of men leaving or refusing to leave for wealth, women and mothers left behind and an elopement, set beside hill trysts at night, mullai waiting and homecoming, a marutham husband held at home by his son and a courtesan's boast, and neythal pleas for open marriage. Puram fame (Pulli, Udhiyan Cheral, the Moriyar, Aay, Pittan, Paari with Kapilar, Rama at Kodi) is drawn on throughout as likeness.
source_issues: 67: lines 10 and 11 repeat Akananuru 131 lines 11 and 12 word for word (the hero-stone couplet), as the text flag notes; marked as the base text stands.
70: line 9 carries a repaired character (an unassigned code point after ஞ் read as ஞா in ஞாழல்), per the text flag.

71: the colophon says the friend speaks to the heroine, but the poem speaks of என் உயிர் and addresses the friend (வாழி, தோழி), which fits the heroine as speaker; thurai_akam keeps the colophon's speaker.
72: the colophon thurai is numbered (1) but gives no second alternative.

73: the colophon thurai reads as two sentences and names no speaker (தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிகின்றான். குறித்த பருவவரவு கண்டு அழிந்த தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.); the poem itself addresses காதல்அம் தோழி and speaks of என்அழிபு, which suggests the heroine as speaker. The rain-cloud of the promised season makes the poem mullai on its own evidence, against the colophon's பாலை.

reading: The friend tells the heroine not to waste away watching the wall where she scratches off the days since her man left for a distant land, driven by the saying that those who fall at others' hands rather than to Death are blessed; even if he won Pulli's festive Venkatam, where bowmen barter elephant tusks and drink their daily toddy, he could not stay there forgetting her breast, rich as Avi's golden Pothini.
nuance: The man's journey is justified with a warriors' maxim about dying in battle rather than of sickness, so a search for wealth is dressed as heroic striving; the friend answers not by disputing the maxim but by setting a famous prize (Venkatam) against a famous city (Pothini) and letting the woman's body outweigh both.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்வயிற்பிரிய வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

reading: After a tryst that failed, the man tells his heart how the dark girl of their secret union, when talk broke it as loud as a war drum and meeting grew hard, yesterday clasped him to end her trembling as if she were plunging into the whirling Kaveri flood, she whose innocence is as perfect as the image the god made on the bright slopes of Poraiyan's Kolli.
nuance: Tonight's failure is answered with yesterday's embrace: the poem is a memory held against a broken tryst, and the closing likeness to a god-made image on Kolli sets the girl at once beyond reach and beyond blame.

reading: The foster mother tells her own daughter that she does not grieve that the girl left the great house and crossed the mountain with her lover; she grieves that her peacock-gentle child, sheltering for the night in a raiders' noisy hamlet in an old woman's rotting hut, will lie awake on his shoulder listening for the drum of cattle thieves.
nuance: She accepts the elopement in a single clause and spends the poem on a night she imagines in detail; at dawn on that road the red quail cock and his small hen bathe in the dust together, a pair at ease where the mother can see only danger.

reading: The friend tells the heroine to rejoice like the bards who went singing to Udhiyan Cheral, for they are free of the suspicious mother and the lying women of the street: the man has today set out with them on the very journey he once put off, saying the hard road over the hills, lit with bamboo fires like fishing boats' lamps at sea and guarded by a tusker, was too hard for women.
nuance: The friend quotes his old refusal in full, the road's beauty and danger included, so the elopement is told as his change of mind; the bards' joy before a famous giver is the measure of the girls' release.

reading: The heroine tells the friend who came on her husband's behalf that the old saying (sons bring fame here and a clean passage hereafter) has proved true: yesterday, dressed to wed another, he stopped his chariot when their little son ran out to see him, could not hand the crying boy back, came into the house with him, and, held by the memory of the kindness he once showed her among the girls at play, gave up the wedding though its drums kept calling him.
nuance: The proverb about sons is a puram commonplace about fame and the next world; she tests it on a household quarrel and finds it true in a way the proverb never meant, since the son's merit is that he keeps his father at home. Her own part is comic and rueful: ashamed to seem the cause, she makes a show of beating the boy.

reading: The heroine asks her friend what she can do, when they say the road her man took is a rainless gravel waste where marauders rush at night, hero-stones crowned with peacock feathers stand like a battle front, stone heaps mark where men fell, and the gravel glitters like fireflies beside a ghost's mirage.

reading: The friend tells the heroine how, testing whether their mother slept, she asked her whether she had heard the waterfall shaking the koothalam and the thunder that split the asoka where their swing hangs; the mother, hearing nothing, sank into sleep, all creatures slept, and the man, as their hearts had hoped, came through the cold road of torrents, crying elephants and pythons.
nuance: The friend's innocent-sounding questions are a sleep test, and the noise of the night (falls, thunder, flood) is both the cover for his coming and the danger he braved to come.

reading: The friend tells the heroine, wasted and dimmed in eye and colour, to stop weeping: though the man, wanting the joy of giving, has gone past the rock the Moriyar's chariot wheels cut, through summer wastes where deer herds strip the nelli, he will not stay long forgetting sweet sleep on her breast, fragrant as the first-day blossom of Aay's forest.
nuance: The friend grants his motive full dignity (he went for wealth to give, ஈதல் இன்பம்), and uses that dignity as her argument: a man moved by giving will not hoard his absence.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து நீட்டித்தான் தலைமகன் எனக் கவன்ற தலைமகட்கு வருவரென்பதுபடச் சொல்லித் தோழி ஆற்றுவித்தது.

reading: The friend tells the heroine that their love for the lord of the fishing shore, once broadcast by gossiping women, is now crowned by the wedding, and the noisy town has fallen silent, like the banyan whose birds Rama, victor in war, hushed for his secret counsel at the ancient Kodi of the Kavuriyar.
nuance: Gossip, the force that drives so many akam poems, is here simply shut off by marriage; the Rama legend supplies the image of a silence imposed on a whole clamorous tree.

reading: In the evening that ends the day, when bees leave pool flowers for branch flowers like graceless men who drop the poor, deer stand bewildered and the sky blooms like cooling gold, the speaker tells her friend that the evening's pain strikes like spearmen aiming at a wounded man's vital spot, her strength thins like breath in a furnace, and asks if this is the hour her life will leave her like a bird quitting a tree in a gale.
nuance: The opening simile is about bees, but its vehicle (men who leave those who are no longer useful) falls on the absent lover without naming him.

reading: With the man standing outside at the night tryst, the heroine tells her friend that the road he came by at midnight in the rain is fearful (lightning on the anthills where a bear digs, rivers with crocodiles, a tiger that killed an elephant for its pregnant mate, paths like walking a sword's edge), and that he who came with a loving heart and only a spear for company is not cruel, nor is the friend who brought him at fault: the fault is hers.
nuance: Spoken for his ears, the self-blame is a plea: by listing the road's terrors and taking the guilt on herself she tells him the night visits must end in marriage.

colophon.thurai: (1) தலைமகன் இரவுக்குறிக்கண் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

reading: One woman calls to the other (the colophon implies the friend speaks; the poem addresses the friend) that, since their pain is one, they should go and see what is coming to end it: over the land where he went the rain cloud stands, flashing like the sparks from a millet-guard's brand.
nuance: The rain cloud is both comfort and accusation: it is the season he named for his return, seen over his country, not yet over hers.

reading: The heroine tells the friend who keeps assuring her that the man, his task won, will see the startled doe of the stag in the rain-washed scrub, think of her and order his charioteer to hurry, that she could hold firm on that comfort if only the cowherds' small harsh flute did not torment her in the evening.
nuance: Almost the whole poem is the friend's comfort, quoted back; the last three lines undo it with a single sound of her own mullai land.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் அழிந்த கிழத்தி வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

tamil: தருநரும் உளரோ, இவ் உலகத் தான்?, என-
reading: Answering the woman's fear that he will leave, the man recalls the saying that effort, not grace, is a man's wealth, says that those who follow it across burnt hills only grieve ever after for beauty that wasted unembraced and that no one in this world can give back, and asks whether he could ever plan to leave her, so hard a prize to win.
nuance: The opening maxim is quoted to be refuted, and the refutation turns on a pun: the vision that decided on wealth is பொருள்அல் காட்சி, a view that misses the point (பொருள்) even as it pursues wealth (பொருள்).

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிவரென வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குப் பிரியேனெனத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: parting for wealth is debated and refused

comparisons.tenor: the warriors' strength
her dark lovely body

reading: Told that the wife's people rail at her, the courtesan says within their hearing that his women may keep on clamouring like bards' drums at a patron's morning feast; as Aathi Manthi wandered distraught asking who had seen her curly-haired dancer and the cool Kaveri held him, so she has resolved to seize the man and hold him fast.
nuance: The courtesan borrows the Aathi Manthi legend and takes the river's part in it, leaving the wife the role of the bereaved queen.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளை நயப்பித்துக் கொண்டாளென்று கழறக்கேட்ட பரத்தை தலைமகள் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the ford town visits the courtesans' street

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: spoken so that the heroine's companions (பாங்காயினார்) hear

her seizing and holding the man

reading: The man tells his heart that if it plots to cross the forest for wealth though her brow pale, it plots ill: past ruined villages where vultures pull out the guts of fallen warriors, at the dark evening in a hamlet's ithi shade, her tear-filled eyes will wound him like the spear Pittan, Chera's generous warrior, raised against hostile kings.
nuance: The parting is stopped in the imagination: the man pictures the evening of the journey, and what decides is not the road's danger but her eyes as he will remember them.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரியக் கருதிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லி, செலவழுங்குவித்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighs leaving her to earn wealth

comparisons.tenor: the vulture pulling out the guts of the dead
her tear-filled eyes

reading: The friend asks the hill-lord, back from his absence, whether in his few days away he ever once thought of them in the cold dewy season, when the tusker on the slope, afraid of the yali, wraps his trembling pregnant mate in his trunk; and she says the girl's brow smells of the new flowers of Paari's pool, Paari who with Kapilar beside him held out for years and drove the kings away.
nuance: The friend puts the right thought into his mouth (how will they fare, poor things, alone in our town?) and then asks if he ever had it; the brow fragrant as Paari's pool makes the girl a prize kings could not take.

colophon.thurai: களவுக் காலத்துப் பிரிந்து வந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: hill folk, kaanthal and the mountain slope

comparisons.tenor: the fragrance of the girl's brow

iraicchi.act: the tusker, fearing the yali, clasps his trembling pregnant mate in his trunk to shelter her
iraicchi.sense: the man should guard the girl who trembles alone through the cold season, as the beast of his own hill guards his mate, instead of leaving her

reading: Midway across the waste, the man tells his heart that it has suffered for wealth that never stays, crossing the hard ground of stone-cut wells, the red dust of the Kongar herds rushing to water, and the long road where the kite's mate calls while the Eyinar bowmen go out raiding to their drum.
nuance: The last word is the charge: the wealth that drew him is நில்லாப் பொருள், wealth that does not stay, so the hardship is spent on something already slipping away.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் இடைச் சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left her, bound by the desire for wealth

reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool shore that he has truly come by night, swimming the dark backwater where crocodiles and sharks move; asking whether they are so hard for him to reach, she says they spend the day driving birds from their father's drying fish, and bids him drive his chariot over the adumbu creepers and come by day to the punnai grove.
nuance: The invitation by day is a refusal of the night: a chariot that cuts the shore creepers leaves a track everyone can see, so the friend is asking for a courtship in the open.

thinai_evidence.note: crocodiles of the backwater and the punnai grove of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the gleaming punnai leaves

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 81-100
theme: Akananuru 81 to 100 in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men crossing the waste for wealth, of their return, and of a girl's elopement seen by her foster mother and by her lover; hill courtships under watch and a veriyattu rite; marutham marriage and infidelity, from a wedding night remembered to gossip loud as a Chola victory; mullai war camps and homecomings; and neythal confinement and pressure for marriage. Kings and towns of puram (Pulli's Venkatam, Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, Uraiyur, Koodal, Karuvur, Paruvur, Viyalur, Puranthai) serve as measures of distance, wealth and noise.
source_issues: 81: the base text numbers the last line 13 though the poem has 15 lines (flagged); a misprinted number.
84 line 12: அரிஞ்ர் is not a word; read அரிநர் (reapers), the word the sense needs.
86 line 31: மா அ யோளே is split by stray spaces; read மாஅயோளே.
89 lines 7 to 8 (காழியர் கவ்வைப் பரப்பின் வெவ்வுவர்ப்பு ஒழிய): rare words whose sense is not secure; the reading of the poem does not turn on them.
90 line 14: பாசிலை விலையே is obscure (a green-leaf courtship gift, or the girl's worth); the verse is marked uncertain.
93 line 17: a stray space before the comma (கடாஅத்து ,).
95: the colophon reads போக்குடன் பட்ட தலைமகன் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது, but the speaker is the woman (என் தளிர்புரை மேனி; the mother says என் மகட்கு of her); read தலைமகள்.
96 line 7: வீஞ்குபு is not a word; read வீங்குபு (swelling).
97: the colophon's வற்புறுந்துந் is a misprint for வற்புறுத்தும்.
98 line 22: பெண்டிற்க்கு is misspelt for பெண்டிர்க்கு.
99: the colophon thurai ends with a comma instead of a full stop.
85 line 2, 92 line 2 and 96 line 18 recur in 147, 108 and 368 (flagged): formulaic lines, not errors.

reading: The friend, having read the woman's heart, asks the man who has announced his going whether he will really cross the long burning waste for wealth made by going away, where a bear tired of sweet iruppai fruit digs out a termite mound and a kite pines alone on a sun-scorched maraa tree, while her lovely kohl-dark eyes, fair as Kadalan's town Vilangil, run with tears.
nuance: The question is put in the plural of respect (ஐய! சேறிரோ) and closes on the wealth itself, அகன்றுசெய் பொருள், wealth that is made by leaving: the friend names the price inside the word for the prize. The bear that turns from sweet fruit when it is sated to dig in a hard mound for a meal could be read as the man who leaves a sweet home for hard-won wealth, but the poem draws no pairing, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்திய தலைமகற்குத் தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து வந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer waste where the earth cracks is the road he means to take

her kohl-dark lovely eyes, as fair as Kadalan's town

reading: The woman tells her friend that the hill man's country is a stage where wind in bored bamboo is the flute, the waterfall the drum, the stag's call the horn and the bees the lute, the monkeys an amazed audience and the peacock a dancer; many saw him standing at the gap of the millet field with his bow, asking after the elephant he had hunted, so why should she alone lie through the dark night with streaming eyes and slackened arms?
nuance: Telling the friend this is the first step of disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்): she admits she met him, but in the form of a complaint that many saw him and only she suffers. The hill's whole orchestra plays to an audience of monkeys, and the one hearer it truly moves is she, alone at night.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope, the millet field and the hunter with bow fix the hill land

comparisons.tenor: the west wind in the bored bamboo, as a flute
the waterfall's sound, as a drum
the humming bees, as a lute
the female monkeys, as the assembly watching a performance
the dancing peacock, like a dancer entering the stage

reading: On the road, the man tells his heart that though he has passed the Venkatam hill of Pulli, chief of the unlettered young men who wear maraa flowers, tear an elephant calf from its wailing mother and tie it at the toddy-houses of their flag-lined town in exchange for drink, his love's virtues, her rain-moist eyes like an opening neythal flower, did not count the distance and have come all the way to reach him.
nuance: Paalai usually makes the woman the one whom memory reaches; here her qualities (குணனே) are the travellers, driven by love (அன்புமிகக் கடைஇ) across the frontier he has just crossed. The cow elephant crying in the forest for the calf the young men have taken sits behind his thought of the woman he left, but the poem does not draw the pairing.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone far from her beyond the frontier hill and is still on the road

comparisons.tenor: her lovely rain-moist eyes

reading: In the war camp the man says that the rains have come, a rainbow on the hill and drum-voiced clouds pouring till the directions vanish, and she of the bright brow is in her small village on the frontier woodland where mullai flowers drop on a sleeping boar's back; while he is in the camp of a garlanded king who, angry, will not accept even the rare tribute of a fortress set among rich fields of reapers and toddy-drinking labourers, and moves his army on to fight.
nuance: Two lands face each other across the poem: her mullai woodland in the promised rains, and the enemy's marutham fields where the harvest goes on. The rains that should send him home have come; what keeps him is the king's anger, which turns down the very tribute that would end the war (அருந்திறை கொடுப்பவும் கொள்ளான்).

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come over her mullai woodland while he is held at war

thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: he speaks his thought in the camp

comparisons.tenor: the boar's small red eyes
the many red flowers of the fields, like fire

reading: The friend tells the woman not to weep in reproach that the man who left them is without virtue while her brow pales and her arms waste: he assured them he would come back in the cool rains, when on the slopes of Thiraiyan's tall Venkatam hill the bull elephant breaks young bamboo shoots to feed the hungry calf of his soft-stepping mate, and the peacock, bathed in vengai pollen, calls its mate from the kurunthu branch; that is the season, and the rain has spread.
nuance: The comfort is built from his own words: the friend quotes the promise, scene and all, and then points to the sky. The elephant feeding his mate's calf is inside that promise, so the man himself had chosen the image of a male who provides.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிய வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heart of the poem is waiting for a return promised for the rains, which is mullai's situation

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant breaks young bamboo shoots and feeds them to the hungry calf of his mate, who has lately given birth
iraicchi.sense: the man who named this scene in his promise is one who provides for his own, so his word to return can be trusted

reading: The man recalls the wedding: rice cooked with black gram heaped high, sand spread under the cool pandal, lamps and garlands, the auspicious dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet; matrons with pots and bowls passing things in order; four mothers of sons pouring water with petals and paddy on her hair and blessing her never to fail in chastity and to love the man who took her; her kin then giving her as lady of the great house; and the first night, when she lay curled in her new cloth with her face hidden, and asked what her heart felt, she only bowed her head in deep joy.
nuance: The blessing (கற்பினின் வழாஅ, நற்பல உதவிப் பெற்றோற் பெட்கும் பிணையை ஆக) is the karpu ideal spoken by women who have kept it. By the colophon's first reading the man tells all this to the friend who has shut the door on him, so the memory of the wedding becomes his plea against a quarrel the poem never names. Her answer to his question is a gesture, not a word.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் மறுத்த தோழிக்கு தலைமகன் சொல்லியது தலைமகளைக் கூடி இன்புற்றிருந்த தலைமகன் பண்டு நிகழ்ந்தது சொற்று இன்புற்றிருந்ததூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is a household wedding with no landscape; its situation is union, and the marutham placement rests on the colophon's door refused

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: with his wife, recalling the first night

comparisons.tenor: her shy, wondering glance, as a deer's

reading: Coming home with his work done, the man tells his heart that it suffered long on the road, lodging for the night in a poor hamlet of grass huts where a calf sucks the churning stick hung in the yard, leaving at the cock's first call, and passing hill forks where the drum of fierce marauders from their rock forts makes travellers' hearts quake; now let it rejoice, for they will praise her breasts and lie in her bamboo-smooth arms in their tall house where the lamp burns all night.
nuance: The hamlet's small homely detail, a calf mouthing the curd-stick under a creeper pandal, is the first sight of a home on the way back and foreshadows his own; the heart, not the man, is the traveller who suffered (நனிநீடு உழந்தனை).

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem looks back on the waste road of marauders he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: her arms, smooth and long as bamboo

reading: With the man listening outside, the friend wonders whether the good man who came guided by the torch a hunter had set on his platform to watch for the boar stealing to the red millet, and who ended their trembling grief, has gone back by that path no one can tread, where a tiger-killing elephant's musth draws bees whose hum the asunam takes for a lute, where snakes crowd the bamboo thicket and the bear digs at deep anthills.
nuance: The catalogue of dangers is spoken for the listener outside: a road this perilous cannot be walked every night, and only marriage ends the need. The torch set to catch a thief is the light the lover came by.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

comparisons.tenor: the bees' hum at the musth, taken by the asunam for a lute

he approaches by stealth, reading signs

reading: The foster mother, after the girl has gone off with her man, asks whether she can walk on her soft red feet across the wide burning land where the rains failed and the mirage runs, where the owl booms like struck stone in the crevices, cicadas shrill in the thorn trees, and marauders who have eaten pale meat cut down the guards of a donkey caravan and share out the loot to the beat of the drum, she who would not drink honeyed milk even when coaxed and played under the sand-strewn pandal.
nuance: The road is all violence and the man does not appear at all: the mother can only measure the girl's feet against the land. The last lines bring the reader back into the house, to the milk she refused and the pandal where she played, so the loss is set in the very place the girl has left.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl gone off with her lover through the waste, grieved by the mother left behind

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the owl's booming cry

reading: The friend meets the man leaving after a day tryst on the shore where white-crested waves like old men wreck the sand houses of the young girls, and tells him that gossip of their union, known to few, has risen and the girl has been shut up at home; she cannot tell him to go away while he suffers so, but her people would not take even the rich market of the dark-eyed Kosar east of Chellur as enough for her.
nuance: The waves likened to old men (மூத்தோர் அன்ன) that break the play-houses of the young are the elders who have shut the girl in and broken off the lovers' meetings, and the friend never says so. The closing bride-price line turns on பாசிலை, whose sense here (a green leaf of a courtship gift, or her worth) the text does not settle.

thinai_evidence.note: the waves, the screwpine grove and the shore ford fix the seashore

comparisons.tenor: the white-crested waves
the Kosar market's noise, as the roar of the sea

ullurai.tenor: the girl's elders, who have shut her in and ended the meetings

pairs.situation: the old ones of her house
they break up the young lovers' play of meeting

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the waves of their own shore, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

reading: The friend tells the wasting woman that though the man left for rare wealth across a waste where the sun has dried the falls, and an elephant that found no water in the dread pool ate moss and shrank together with his hungry mate, he has great love: even if he gained Kuttuvan's Kudanadu beyond the marauders' scrub, a land of drums that knows no hunger, where the buffalo tired of lotus rests in the shade of old jackfruit trees, he would not stay there forgetting her beauty.
nuance: The wealth the man went for is measured by the richest land the friend can name, and the claim is that he would refuse it. The elephant pair is on his road, the buffalo in the land he would refuse.

thinai_evidence.note: the falls have dried and the wide land shimmers in the heat

iraicchi.act: finding no water, the elephant eats moss and shrinks together with his hungry mate
iraicchi.sense: even beasts in the drought keep together, so the man who crossed that land has not stopped loving her

reading: The friend tells the man not to come on such nights, when lightning blinds the slopes and in the pouring midnight rain a striped tiger strikes an elephant and roars; tomorrow she and the girl will be guarding millet, and in a grove so thick that not even the monkeys know it, by a cool fall where red kanthal has opened, he may have the sleep of her soft dark hair, by the light of a gem from a snake that thunder has struck.
nuance: The day tryst she offers is made of impossibilities, a grove unknown to monkeys and a lamp from a thunder-killed snake's gem, so that the man hears what the colophon says she means: marriage, not meetings (வரைவு கடாயது).

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சென்று தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குத் தலைமகனைப் பகற்குறி நேர்ந்த வாய்பாட்டால் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarding and the kanthal by the fall fix the hill

comparisons.tenor: the snake's gem, as a lamp

reading: Coming home with his work done, the man tells his heart: to end the kin's ruin, feed the relatives and make friends of strangers, he went with zeal for effort and won rare treasure as fine as the just assembly of the Cholas at Uraiyur; now let them go and embrace, more times than the sands heaped on the banks of the Porunai at Kothai's Karuvur, the dark woman whose brow smells like the morning market of Vazhuthi's Koodal, in their sky-high house on a bed soft as gathered foam by the tall lamp, till her ornaments print their marks on her.
nuance: The opening gives the paalai journey a household reason: wealth is for the kin, the relatives and the stranger made friend. The three crowned houses each lend one simile: the Chola court for wealth, the Pandya market for her scent, the Chera river's sands for the count of embraces.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளலுறுந் தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the return from a parting for wealth

her fragrant brow
their tall house, as if carved from a mountain
the soft flower bed, like gathered foam
the number of their embraces

reading: Returning, the man tells his charioteer that her town, the town of the woman of thick dark hair and loving gentleness, lies in the hard woodland country where at midnight the musundai blooms white like the sky, a goatherd with a leather bag, wearing a dripping garland of mullai and thondri, warms his palms at a sputtering brand and whistles long into the dark where the jackal howls, together with the black horn the field-guards blow to drive off herds of boar.
nuance: Her town is reached through its night sounds, the herdsman's whistle and the guards' horn, heard as one; the herdsman out in the dark, warming his hands far from home, is a figure of the man himself.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது தலைமகன் பாங்கற்குச் சொற்றதூஉமாம்.

tamil: புரைய அல்ல, என் மகட்கு' எனப் பரைஇ,
reading: The woman tells her friend that her brow has paled, her leaf-tender body thinned and her grief shows for all to see, and thinking can end it only with her life; the town, fond of gossip, will not say she grieves for one who crossed the wastes where a bear and her cubs carry off the hail-like iruppai flowers, and her mother has answered the women of the town that their harsh words do not fit her daughter: before such a mother, who understands and is calm, what can she do in this state?
nuance: The mother here does not scold; she defends the girl against the town, and that is what the girl cannot bear, since the mother's trust is what she is about to betray. The colophon says the speaker is தலைமகன், but the poem's first person is the woman (என் தளிர்புரை மேனி, என் மகட்கு in the mother's mouth).

reading: The friend, refusing the man entry, calls him lord of a kaanji town where in the field-pond prawns leap like a bow sprung loose, and a thorny cane, its long stem toothed like a file, catches the broad leaves of the water lily and, swung by the north wind, swells and slackens like a forge's bellows; they say he has chosen one young girl out of all the bangled band, and that news has spread through many mouths like the uproar of elephants taken on the day the Chola, father of Aqthai, beat both great kings on the battlefield of Paruvur.
nuance: The friend matches his private conquest to a royal victory's din: what he thought hidden is as public as a war. The cane that catches the lily and swells and slackens with every wind is his way with women.

reading: The woman answers her friend, who tells her not to weep thinking of the cruel man who crossed a waste where the spotted stag's horns fall in the drought and vultures and kites gather at a stench the tiger left, like marauders cutting up meat in rock clefts after a night raid on cattle: how can she easily stop her tears, hearing the sated koel call in spring, when the kuravam blooms, the cold season is over, marutham trees crowd the river ford and new mango flowers crown the boughs under smoky mist?
nuance: The friend's comfort carries a compliment (her bosom fair as Nannan's Viyalur, a court that cherished bards), and the answer sets against it the joy of spring: the koel is நுகர்குயில், a bird that has had its fill, and it is the season's plenty, not the waste, that makes tears impossible to stop.

tamil: பண்டையின் சிறக்க, என் மகட்கு' எனப் பரைஇ,
reading: With the man standing by, the girl tells her friend that her mother does not know the ache of his withheld grace can be eased only on his chest; seeing her bangles slip, the mother asked the old lying women, who said it was Murugan's seizure, and so a velan dances in the decorated pandal to restore her beauty: if after all that her wasted body does not recover the secret will become gossip, and worse, if the god relieves her and the hill man hears that her sickness was something else, living will be harder still.
nuance: The rite is described with care and mocked in the same breath (மையற் பெண்டிற்க்கு நொவ்வல்): the women are deluded, the velan dangles like a puppet. Her deepest fear is not exposure but that the rite might work, and the man conclude she never pined for him.

reading: Leading the girl who has gone off with him, the man coaxes her to look at the forest, strewn with palasa buds red as a tiger's claws, kongam opening like jewelled breasts, athiral and paathiri petals and maraa blossoms, lovely as the flower-strewn town of a dread god, and asks whether it also has hills of all heights that look like her father's war elephants, tusk-rings broken, crowded by their mates.
nuance: This is the same kind of road that the foster mother of 89 fills with marauders; the lover makes it a temple town of flowers. His last question teases and reassures at once: even the hills are her father's elephants, so she has not left home behind.

reading: The friend tells the man that it is sweet to her too that he comes, wipes off his sandal, embraces the girl till her breast is marked, and leaves in the dark; but the gossip has come true, loud as a newly arrived flock of storks at the punnai-grove ford of Puranthai, town of the bards' patron Periyan, where fishers' lamps on the stilled sea at night shine like the face-lamps of a king's dancing war elephants; theirs is a sorrowing town of screwpine gardens where the buffalo that went out at cold dawn feeds on fresh neythal flowers.
nuance: Line 4 is irony: what is sweet to the friend is exactly what she is ending. The buffalo that goes out at dawn and grazes the fresh neythal flower of their own town is the man who takes the girl's youth and leaves before light.

title: களிற்றியானைநிரை 101-120
theme: Akananuru 101 to 120, in the களிற்றியானைநிரை section: ten paalai poems of roads through raider country, a heroine doubting an old proverb, two mothers grieving for eloped daughters, set beside kurinji night trysts pressed toward marriage, marutham quarrels measured against Chezhiyan's wars, two mullai homecomings and two neythal scenes. Puram names (Ezhini, Evvi, Erumai, Ahthai and the Kosar, Vaanan, Chezhiyan at Koodal) serve as similes and settings for private grief.
source_issues: 110: line 20 reads பல்லோர் ருள்ளும், a word split by a stray space and doubled consonant; read பல்லோருள்ளும். Line 1 recurs as Akananuru 218 line 18 (a formula).
111: the colophon thurai reads தலைமளை, a misprint for தலைமகளை.
114 and 117: the poet's name is not preserved (the commentary edition prints dots).
118: the colophon thurai breaks off at வரைவு; it presumably ended வரைவு கடாயது.
120: the colophon thurai breaks off after வந்து, without saying to whom the friend speaks; the poem's பெரும (line 9) shows it is the hero.
115: line 7 recurs as Akananuru 227 line 13 (a formula).
103: line 11 was repaired (a stray space before a dead consonant).

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the old proverb that no harm comes in this life to those who do good has turned false today, since the man who crossed the many dewy hills, by a vast forest where red-eyed Mazhavar raiders with fire-sticks and bows drive off herds with their calves and where the whirling midday wind shakes the murungai's spent flowers down like cold hail, has gone though she did nothing to deserve his displeasure.
nuance: The proverb is about this life (இம்மை), not a reward hereafter: she asks whether right conduct protects anyone now. The image of cool hail made out of flowers shaken down by scorching wind turns the comfort of rain into a sign of heat.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட கிழத்தி, தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது; தோழி கிழத்திக்குச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of a man who has crossed the waste and left her

comparisons.tenor: the raiders' curled matted hair, like a ram's horn
the sun crossing the wide sky like a boat
the murungai's spent flowers dropping in the hot wind like cold hail

reading: Speaking to her friend so that the hero standing outside will hear, the heroine recalls how the man of the country where a fierce young elephant falls suddenly asleep to a hill girl's kurinji song, while the millet watcher lies drunk on his platform, came softly past the guards through the unbarred door, bees humming on his sandal-smeared chest, embraced her and left with sweet words; and she asks what this pallor is that has now come over her brow along with the gossip, because he has not given her more.
nuance: The speech is aimed at the overhearer: the night visit is told as past and tender, the pallor and gossip as the present cost. The fierce elephant lulled by the girl's song and the drunk watchman asleep set a hill where every guard is off duty, which is what made the visits possible; a reader may also hear in the lulled elephant the hero lulled out of his purpose, but no part-by-part match is stated.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret night meeting that evades the guards

reading: The heroine tells her friend that, thinking the man would have finished his work and come back across the hot, hard waste, past a cattle village whose people have left the tall wide hill, she lay at midnight with pallor as her only companion, and asks whether the one they love will not give back the beauty that went away with him of its own accord.
nuance: She does not ask for him but for her beauty, which she says went with him of itself (தம்மொடு தானே சென்ற நலனும்); the deserted cattle village on his road mirrors her own emptied state. Lines 1 to 4 (the spotted cock and what it watches) are obscure in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the shadeless waste the man must cross

comparisons.tenor: the bird's fine spots, as if sprinkled on it

reading: The friend blesses the hero who, his king's war finished, drove his swift four-horsed chariot through the cool, bee-loud woodland, leaving behind many small villages where white kids with hollow bellies like empty avarai pods and drooping ears frisk with the children and nibble the aar tree's shoots on the common, and arrived at evening to set flowers in the hair of his bangled wife, who had lived in tears and many reproaches.
nuance: The friend praises the return by one act (இனிதுசெய் தனையால்): setting flowers in the wife's hair, the ornament she had given up while he was away. The playful kids of the small villages show the settled domestic life he rides through to reach his own.

thinai_evidence.note: the woodland and the evening of the homecoming

comparisons.tenor: the kids' hollow bellies, like empty avarai pods
the kids' long ears, drooping as if wilted

reading: The mother wonders how her daughter, who would not drink the sweet milk her nurses held to her in a jewelled bowl and gave no thought to the family's wealth in their great house cool as a shaded pool, but believed false words, will manage the many-pathed summer journey with the hill man who praises her and weaves her a garland of vengai leaves, through a scorched forest of hot stones where bowmen fulfilling the commission of Ezhini of many spears and the rhythmic-stepping horse drink honeyed toddy and drive off herds of full-uddered cattle across the frontier.
nuance: The mother's doubt is about fitness, not morals: a girl who would not even take milk from her nurses now walks a road of cattle raiders. பொய்ம்மருண்டு (deceived by falsehood) is the mother's only judgment of the lover, and the vengai garland he weaves is a hill thing carried into the waste.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's journey away with her man

reading: Hearing that the wife of the man of the bright ford, where an old kingfisher too spent to fly rests on fragrant lotus leaves in a fire-red lotus pond, waiting to eat small fish that leap like popped rice, quarrels with her husband on their account, the courtesan tells her friend that since they cannot escape the blame though they did nothing, they should go there swinging their tight bangles and stroll a little, and let the wife beat her own belly like the drum the bard, who is fed on elephants, beats each time Chezhiyan of the shining-sword army wins a battle.
nuance: The courtesan's mockery is in the landscape before it is in her words: the old kingfisher that cannot fly and only waits for the leaping fish is her picture of the wife. Chezhiyan's war drum, beaten at every victory, turns the curse into a public spectacle.

reading: The friend tells the hero, who is preparing to leave, that to end the grief she has borne each time she heard of his going, her friend with thick parted hair will go with him: across the hard frontier of the Vadukar, men of strange long speech with fierce dogs who eat white rice cooked with fat on teak leaves, where travelers rejoice at venison a tiger left on the black rock, past the steep slope where a lamed ox left alone is fed iluppai flowers by boys of a hill hamlet who drive the deer off with their bows, she will be his sweet companion at evening, and at dawn the forest will smell like a wedding house as fresh blossoms fall on the gravel.
nuance: The friend turns the paalai road into a feast and a wedding: travelers' venison, the Vadukar's rice, a hamlet's evening and a forest that smells like a marriage house. The lamed ox left alone yet fed by strangers stands quietly against the fear of being left behind, though the poem does not draw that sense.

reading: Speaking to the heroine so that the hero outside will hear, the friend says that pitying the pain of those one has joined is fitting for those who understand, yet the lord of the cloud-capped mountain, where kaanthal flowers rise like cobras spreading their hoods at a peacock and a bee at their pollen looks like a spinning top, shows no such pity, for he comes alone through midnight dark of pelting rain, where hail struck from an elephant's face streams on the rock like scattered pearls, lightning flashes like sparks of a whirled firebrand, and beasts of prey roam.
nuance: The friend turns his courage into a want of kindness (அருளான்): by braving the night path he makes the women suffer fear for him, so true pity would be to stop coming that way, that is, to marry. The snake-hooded kaanthal carries the path's dread into the closing praise of his hill.

reading: Halfway along the road, the man tells his heart that the town where she lives, she of soft eyes like many-petalled flowers and words as sweet as a well-tuned yazh string, is now cut off by many dry hills: a wide land of tall groves and bamboo where herds of tusk-ploughing elephants gather, forked tracks heaped with countless cairns over men felled by white-tipped arrows, where travelers are killed though they carry nothing, and which a king without aram rules, taking great tusks and striped hides.
nuance: Three lines give her, twelve give the road; the killing ground is described so fully that it explains why the hills 'lie across' (விலங்கின) his way back. Lines 11 to 13 (whether the robbers kill to stop witnesses escaping, and whether the king takes tusks and hides as tribute) are hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste and the dry hills between him and her town

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, like soft many-petalled flowers
her sweet words, like the sound of a good yazh string

reading: Disclosing the secret to the foster mother, the friend says let the mother know and let the gossiping street hear, and swears before the god of the whirling river mouth that there was nothing else: while the girls rested after bathing in the sea, building sand houses and heaping play rice, a man came, said the day was done and he was very tired, and asked whether he might eat with them on spread leaves and stay in their noisy hamlet; they, heads bowed, said the fish food was not fit for him; when the others ran off, crying that a ship with a tall flag was in sight, he looked at her alone and asked, 'Bright-browed one, shall I stay?', and when she said 'go', he stood holding the pole of his tall chariot, gazing — and she says he seems to stand so before her eyes even today.
nuance: The friend tells the meeting in her own first person (என்னே குறித்த நோக்கமொடு, என் கட்கே), as if the man had looked at her; whether she speaks for the heroine or shields her by taking the story on herself is left open. The oath before the river-mouth god and the girls' modest refusal (இவைநுமக்கு உரிய அல்ல) are the proofs offered that nothing improper happened.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore games, fish food and ships of the meeting place

reading: The friend assures the heroine that the man who crossed the sky-touching hills will not stay content where he is and, ashamed of the scornful words of hostile men, will come back; she pictures his road, where a spider's web on a withered nemai tree swings in the hot wind like the cloth banner on a royal elephant, weary elephants mistake it for a rain-cloud and breathe through their aching trunks like the pipes of performers, and vultures feeding on a boar the red dog has killed show red ears like the lamps carried at night over a battlefield to search out the wounded.
nuance: The comfort rests on shame, not longing: he will return because staying away invites scorn. The thirsty elephants deceived by a cobweb into hoping for rain sit uneasily beside a promise of return. Lines 1 to 3 (whose mockery, and why he would be ashamed) can be read more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot wind and the waste road he travels

comparisons.tenor: the spider's web swinging in the wind, like a royal elephant's cloth banner
the weary elephants breathing through their trunks, like performers' pipes
the vultures' red ears, like lamps searching the wounded on a night battlefield

reading: Meeting the hero who has come at night, the friend tells him he has done wrong to come here, not thinking of them alone, through the cold dark grove where at midnight a hunchbacked bear tears open a termite mound and a tiger whose mate is hungry after giving birth kills a tusked elephant and roars; if a day passes without him her friend will not live, and he too desires her embrace, but the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame, so why not marry? Then, not knowing of the union already made, they will watch the ancient rite and see her new shyness like strangers come as guests.
nuance: The closing joke turns the secret into a performance: at the wedding the friend will pretend, like a stranger, not to know that the union already happened, and enjoy the bride's shyness. The maxim on the worthy (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்) is the friend's lever.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the night tryst and the friend's demand for marriage
