reading: The woman tells her friend that they say he will go alone through the summer desert, where a dead leafless tree is netted with spider webs, heat shimmers like spread silk and dark fruits like gem-coins fall, and they say that she, aching like a calf tied apart from its mother by heartless herdsmen, will only speak bitter words; what has confused their lover?
nuance: Twice 'they say' (என்ப): the plan to leave reaches her as report, and so does the prediction of how she will take it. The calf penned away from its mother is a mullai image brought into the desert to name her helplessness.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரியக்கருதிய தலைமகன் குறிப்பறிந்து தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது. தலைமகனாற் பிரிவுணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: summer heat of the desert

comparisons.tenor: the dead tree netted with spider webs
the shimmering heat
the unripe fruit
the ripe dark fruit

comparisons.vehicle: பண்பில் கோவலர் தாய்பிரித்து யாத்த நெஞ்சமர் குழவி
comparisons.tenor: the woman left behind, aching

reading: To the friend who urges patience as the season comes, the woman says that after the thunder and downpour, with karuvilai flowers wet like the eyes of women left by their lovers, eengai shoots glistening as if dipped in ghee, avarai thick in flower and ripe paddy bowing in the fields, at midnight in the dewy season, lashed by the north wind and wondering whether the men who know nothing of her pain, kept in the angry king's war camp, will ever come, she cannot bear her loneliness.
nuance: The season she was promised has come and every plant shows it, including the flowers that look like weeping women; the comfort the friend offers is undone by the very signs that were meant to bring him. The king's camp names a war, not wealth, as the cause of his absence.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits in the rains for a man kept in the king's camp

comparisons.vehicle: காதலர்ப் பிரிந்த கையறு மகளிர் நீர்வார் கண்ணின்
comparisons.tenor: the rain-wet karuvilai flowers
the wet tender eengai shoots

reading: The friend tells the woman whose shoulders have taken on affliction that though he has crossed the waterless forest where a tusker that beat a tiger stands weary beside its cow, the salt-merchants' well dug for passing travellers, the hill of Pulli and the land beyond where the Vadugar archers shout over toddy and the language changes, he will bring back her flawless beauty.
nuance: Pulli's hill is the edge of the known world in these poems; beyond it the speech itself changes. The friend's comfort measures his distance precisely in order to say it does not matter.

thinai_evidence.note: springs dried in the lingering summer

comparisons.tenor: her red-cornered rain-wet eyes

iraicchi.act: the weary tusker, its musth spent, stays beside its cow in the dry forest
iraicchi.sense: even in drought the beast keeps by its mate, so the man who went through that land is bound to her and will return

reading: The friend refusing the man entry says he slept yesterday in the fragrant grove with the dark girl who wears kaanchi pollen in her hair, bathed with her today in the great Vaigai, and comes with his chest still wet: can he hide it from them, when it has fallen into many mouths and become gossip like the swelling clamour of Koodal, the hill-high city of Chezhiyan, lord of Korkai where pearl oysters are traded for toddy?
nuance: The proof against him is bodily (the undried chest), and the gossip is measured against the ordinary noise of the Pandya capital, not a battle: his affair is as public as Madurai's markets.

colophon.thurai: வாயில்வேண்டிச் சென்ற தலைமகற்கு வாயின்மறுக்குந் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend reproaches a husband who has been with another woman

occasion.words: வாயில்வேண்டிச் சென்ற தலைமகற்கு வாயின்மறுக்குந் தோழி சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about him
the tall houses of Koodal

reading: Going for wealth, the man asks his heart what will become of her grief, which overflows at midnight and the dull evening, and of the shy glad look of the girl who said she would come with him through the fearful forest where travellers pass by an old hero-stone without stopping to read its worn inscription, a wildcat's kitten follows its mother like stars round the moon, and the warriors' raiding drum makes the vulture shift its wings.
nuance: The hero-stone's letters, carved to keep a name, are now passed unread by weary travellers: the road is a place where even fame is forgotten, and he fears forgetting is not what she will do. Her offer to come with him is the elopement he refused.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the fearful forest with its old hero-stones

occasion.words: பொருள்வயிற் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the wildcat's stripes
the kitten's bristling fur
the kitten keeping close to its mother

iraicchi.act: the wildcat's kitten keeps close at its mother's side as stars ring the moon
iraicchi.sense: she wanted to keep as close to him on this road, which is why her offer to come haunts him

reading: At a midnight meeting the woman tells the lord of the hill, where vengai shoots glow like the sun rising from the full sea, that his coming here through the tusker-haunted forest path, white spear in hand and bees on his garland, is sweet, yet out of fear that her mother would learn of it she has kept her love unspoken, and the sleepless friend who shares her nights has gladly assured her he will not delay.
nuance: The lines are tangled: she seems to weigh his dangerous night visit against the friend's comfort that he will soon come for good. What she will not say aloud is the point: her love is guarded by fear of the house.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, tusker and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the bright shoots of the flowering vengai
the dark evening

tamil: திருந்துக மாதோ, நும்செலவு' என வெய்து உயிராப்,
reading: On the road the man tells his heart that though they might live forgetting home, they cannot forget how she took the news of his going through the forest where wind-blown teak leaves fly like screaming kites: her face bowed like the waning moon, tears falling on her breast, unable to stand, she hid in her hair and, sighing, wished his going well in faltering words.
nuance: Her blessing on his journey is the most painful thing he remembers: she says what a wife should say, with every sign of her body saying the opposite.

colophon.thurai: இடைச்சுரத்துப் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wide desert way

occasion.words: இடைச்சுரத்துப் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the teak leaves whirled up by the wind
her face dimmed and bowed
her dark rippling hair

reading: The friend tells the man leaving a day meeting on the shore that the girl wept bitterly when he bade her go home, and she fears that if he parts like a stranger the girl will come to harm; so let him arrive at their busy hamlet as if from afar, and their kin will receive him, say the ford is dark and the tide brings sharks and press him to stay, and they will make him a welcome guest of the house, if he will only consent.
nuance: The friend writes a little play: the lover arrives as a stranger and is kept for the night as a guest, a way of bringing him under the family's roof before marriage. Hospitality is turned into a step toward varaivu.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, the shore grove and sharks of the sea coast

occasion.words: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: his parting coldly
his arrival at the hamlet

title: நித்திலக்கோவை 301-320
theme: Akananuru 301-320 (from the Nithilakkovai) alternate paalai poems of the man gone for wealth and the road he takes (bandits, carrion crows, a dove that will not leave a ruined hall) with kurinji and neythal poems in which the friend refuses or redirects the secret meetings and presses for marriage, two marutham poems on the courtesan quarrel, and two mullai poems of the rains and the return; wandering performers and the fame of Paari, Pulli, Vaanavan and the Pandya Vazhuthi supply the similes.
source_issues: 304: the colophon thurai begins with a stray numeral (1பாசறைக்கண்), a footnote marker left in the text.
304: line 12 spells peacock மஞ்ஜை with the grantha ஜ; the usual form is மஞ்ஞை, probably a digitisation error.
305: line 5 is missing from the base text and was supplied from the commentary edition (flag); marked as supplied.
319: the base text prints the poem number as 318 (flag); read as 319.
301: line 26 மறுவினம் is obscure; the comparison of the evening to the emptied commons turns on it.
311: line 11 தீரத reads oddly before தேக்கிலை (one would expect தீரத்); possibly a misprint, marked as it stands.

reading: Answering the friend who says she has borne her absent lover's memory fairly well, the heroine says each returning evening is as desolate as an old town's commons on the day after a troupe of wandering performers, who spend their wages without saving and roam with drums, pipes and flower garlands from town to town, has danced there and moved on; so how could the love he gave be forgotten just because he stays away long?
nuance: Twenty lines celebrate the performers' rootless, music-filled life only so that their absence can be felt: the joy is drawn at length to measure the emptiness it leaves. The troupe always leaves, as evening always comes back, so the desolation is a daily one. The word மறுவினம் (line 26) is obscure to me; I read it as the evening that comes round again.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine endures her lover's absence; the performers' road is a wasteland road

comparisons.tenor: the heroine wilting in longing, like a crop in a field struck by drought
the open mouth of the performers' grass-roofed cart
the long and short pipes joined with the drum
the beat they set, like frogs croaking on the water when the rain clouds thunder

comparisons.vehicle: புன்றலை மன்றங் காணின் வழிநாள் அழுங்கன் மூதூர்க்கு இன்னா தாகும் அதுவே
comparisons.tenor: the evening that returns each day

reading: With the hero listening outside, the friend tells the heroine that bathing in the falls with the lord of the hills where plantain leaves stroke a sleeping elephant's back, picking blue lilies in the pool and playing in the fragrant vengai grove all seem to have become hard, for though the millet their brothers sowed has ripened enough to draw the parrots, their unkind mother shows no sign of sending them out to guard it and keeps looking at the girl's swelling breasts and thick hair.
nuance: The millet and the girl ripen together, and both end the field-guarding that made the day meetings possible: the mother's watching eyes mean confinement at home. Spoken for the hero to overhear, the friend's complaint tells him that only marriage is left. The plantain leaf stroking the sleeping elephant (lines 1 to 3) may suggest the tenderness of the hills' lord, but the leaf moves with the wind and does no act, so I leave it as scene.

colophon.thurai: பகலே சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field guarded from parrots and the hill falls

comparisons.tenor: the tall millet with heavy ears, handsome as sugarcane

reading: The heroine scolds her foolish heart: their love, hidden from all like a ghoul's dream, was exposed by gossip loud as the cascade on Porayan's Kolli hill, and the man left; yet the heart believed he would come back as surely as the sparrows of Paari's Parambu fly off at dawn for red paddy and return together at dusk; let it be rid of that doubt, for she has resolved to follow his road across the wasteland, as fish leave a draining pool.
nuance: The Paari simile is turned against the heart that made it: sparrows return every evening, he has not. The last image reverses the direction of the poem: not he comes back to her, but she leaves, as fish leave water that is running out, the town that gossip has drained. The resolve is spoken to her own heart and may not be meant to be carried out.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேட்கை மீதூர்ந்த தலைமகள் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a heroine left behind, resolving to cross the wasteland after him

occasion.words: வேட்கை மீதூர்ந்த தலைமகள் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: their hidden love, unseen by others

comparisons.vehicle: கொல்லி யுச்சித் தாஅய்த் ததைந்துசெல் அருவியின் அலர்எழ
comparisons.tenor: the gossip that rose about them
the elephants Paari gives, huge as hills
his expected return
the cicadas shrilling on dead trees
her going after him

reading: In the war camp, as the first rains fall at dawn and the land takes on the season's beauty, the doe with her fawn resting with the stag in the kurunthu shade, peacocks dancing and kaayaa flowers strewn among red velvet mites like coral set among sapphires, the hero tells his heart that his dark wife, not knowing his own pain, must be saying that a man who lingers abroad on the king's work has no righteousness and no grace, and sulking at him.
nuance: He hears himself judged in her words (lines 18 and 19: அறவர் அல்லர் நம் அருளாதோர்) and does not argue; his only defence, that she cannot know his pain, is also a confession that the season's beauty is hurting him too.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season and the scrub flowers of the forest

comparisons.tenor: the hailstones
the red earth, as if wrought
the clear pooled water
blue kaayaa flowers among red mites on the sand

iraicchi.act: the doe with her fawn rests beside the stag in the shade when the rains come
iraicchi.sense: even the deer are together at the season of return, which is exactly what makes his staying away graceless in her eyes

reading: The heroine tells her friend that on these cold midnights of north wind and drizzle, when the night will not pass, even lovers locked in an embrace that seems to drink each other and enter each other's bodies feel lonely; so how is she to live, now that the graceless man is going away for wealth, when the pained cry of a lone anril on the palmyra stirs her smouldering heart and the herdsmen's sweet flute blows it into flame?
nuance: An argument from the stronger case: if the embraced suffer such nights, the one left alone cannot bear them. The flute-players are நினையா மாக்கள், people who do not think: the music is innocent and only her heart turns it into a bellows. The lone anril, a bird famed for never leaving its mate, may carry more than its cry, but it acts here only as a sound, so I leave it as scene.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is leaving for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' desire, as if drinking each other
the embrace, as if entering the body
the flute fanning her smouldering longing

reading: Turning the reveller away from the door, the friend mocks his fine reputation: a woman with a moon-bright forehead has just scolded him, looked at him with reddened, tearful eyes, torn off his cool garland in a quarrel and walked away through their own street.
nuance: The rival performs in public the oodal that the wife is refused, and does it in front of the wife's house; the friend needs no other reason to shut the door. The well-fed heron asleep under stroking mango shoots and the tortoise basking on the cane (lines 2 to 7) may hint at the pampered hero, but only one correspondence maps clearly, so I keep them as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: a quarrel over another woman, in the watered fields

comparisons.tenor: the other woman's bright forehead

reading: The friend asks the man set on his work whether he can leave without thinking how the girl here will suffer, her forehead pale, her shoulders thin, her tears falling like rain on flowers, when the mountain road he means to take runs past a ruined hall overgrown with bushes where, on the black pillar the god has abandoned, a dove still calls with its mate, unable to leave because they have lived there together so long.
nuance: The dove clings to a home that even its god has deserted; the man is about to desert a living one. The road's other creatures, the must-maddened tusker that killed a tiger and the bears digging out termites, make it frightening; the dove makes it a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend tries to stop a departure for work

comparisons.tenor: her tearful eyes

iraicchi.act: the dove stays with its mate on the pillar of a ruined hall and will not leave it, because of their long life there together
iraicchi.sense: a bird will not desert an old shared home even when its god has gone, so a man should not leave the woman he has lived with

reading: The friend asks the lord of the rain-washed hills, where a tusker still carries the long wound of its fight with a tiger and white clouds wrap the mountain like smoke from a potter's kiln, why he comes at night: let him come by day, chase parrots from the millet with them on the high platform of their spear-bearing father, sleep pillowed on her hair dressed with lilies from the rock pools, and at dusk slip past the guards like a raiding tusker back to his village of kurinji shrubs.
nuance: The opening wounded tusker shows the night road's danger without saying so. The day offer is not simple: the field is guarded, the father carries an 'unfailing spear', and the hero must leave like a crop-raiding elephant, so the day meeting carries its own risk. The colophon names only the request to come by day.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet platform and the parrots of the hill field

comparisons.tenor: white clouds wrapping the mountain
the hero slipping away from the guarded field

reading: The heroine asks her friend, who has grown sad at seeing her change, why they should not set out, as wandering performers set out for the Chera Vaanavan's feet without counting the forest long, through a land where Mazhavar raiders drive off milch cattle and feast on a cow killed at the god's neem tree, to the country beyond the hills where he went, where a night-raiding elephant takes fright at dawn.
nuance: She borrows the performers' courage: the gift-seekers cross the raiders' forest for a patron, so she can cross it for her man. The closing lines (the cracking bamboo, the sling and the elephant afraid of the thicket) are obscure to me and the reading of them is a guess.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு வேறுபட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heroine proposes to follow the man across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the white seeds of the silk-cotton scattering

comparisons.vehicle: கோடியர் பெரும்படைக் குதிரை நற்போர் வானவன் திருந்துகழற் சேவடி நசைஇப் படர்ந்தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the heroine's going after her man

reading: Having agreed to help the man who has sent his chariot and men away and come humbly pleading for many days, the friend tells him that the girl too is deeply moved, but as a daughter raised in love in her mother's house she is still shy and innocent, so he must not press here today; let him go to the calling-place under the palmyra above the flowering punnai, near their small village fenced by the roaring sea.
nuance: The friend grants his suit by naming a place, not by bringing the girl: the meeting is set within call of the village, where the girl's innocence and the friend's control are both kept. Where exactly she sends him (கூஉம்கண், the bird of line 15) is not clear to me.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore, its trees and salt traders

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes
the heaped dunes, looking like hills

reading: The friend reminds the heroine how he once waited at the painted, guarded door like gift-seekers waiting for an elephant, came in at midnight when the guards slept, swore that no one in this world surpassed her and stroked her hair for days; so though he has crossed the scorched wasteland beyond Pulli's good land, where herdsmen share sweet tamarind food with travellers on teak leaves, the man who left her with gracious assurances will not stay long.
nuance: The friend's proof is the past: a man who waited at the door like a suppliant for a gift will not linger away from the gift itself. The herdsmen's hospitality softens the road she fears.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: his waiting at the door of her house
the strong door, as if painted

reading: The friend, letting the hero overhear, says that if he means to marry and end the hardship of night visits they will rejoice, and tomorrow, careless of the village's gossip, bathe in the flood coming down the hill with his chest for their float, for the rain has come down over the bamboo slopes, roaring like a drum and flashing lightning like the spear the victorious Pandya Vazhuthi raises in battle.
nuance: The public bath with the lover is promised on a condition (வரையக் கருதும் ஆயின்): only marriage makes the gossip harmless. The storm borrows a king's victory to make the coming flood, and the union it stands for, triumphal.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது. தலைமகள் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill village and its slopes

comparisons.tenor: the hero's chest as their float
the thundering rain

comparisons.vehicle: வெல்போர் வழுதி செல்சமத் துயர்த்த அடுபுகழ் எஃகம் போல
comparisons.tenor: the lightning

reading: The friend tells the heroine, who weeps night and day, sighs hot breaths and has lost her forehead's glow like a moon swallowed by the snake, that the man who held her close saying 'what else is there now? do not fear', though he left for wealth across rock-piled hills where starving snakes shrink like emptied purses and crows drink the blood of travellers shot down by bandits, will come back out of grace.
nuance: The friend's comfort rests on his own quoted words (line 1); the road she describes in full is the danger she argues past. The crows that drink quietly, like spies in a deserted place, are the poem's chilling detail.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: her tear-filled eyes
her dimmed forehead
the starving snake, shrunk
the crows' hushed calls

reading: The friend welcomes the hero home from finished work: in the rains, as the stag frisked in the green crops with his doe and fawn and the lute played its evening melody of grief, his wife of godlike chastity had asked the bard what would become of her if he did not come now, and he arrived in time to end her grief; so may his garland flourish and his chest, held by the young woman whose hair smells of the white mullai on the fence, last for ever.
nuance: The mullai on the fence comes back in her hair at the end: the flower of the land of waiting becomes the scent of the embrace. Her question is reported in her own words, so the friend's praise is also a record of how near the despair was.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season in the scrub forest

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds

iraicchi.act: the stag holds close his doe with her fawn and frisks with them in the green crops when the rains come
iraicchi.sense: the season that keeps the deer family together is the season the husband was bound to come home to his wife

reading: The mother whose daughter has gone off with her lover blames herself: she saw the girl's hair curl and breasts swell and even yesterday suspected, yet did not shut her in; and now the girl, who had not yet stepped out of a house guarded like Vazhuthi's city of Koodal, follows the lying spearman over a summer path strewn with green gooseberries like crystal beads from a broken string, and will sleep, perhaps, in a forest hamlet where meat is cooked before huts like heaped teak leaves.
nuance: I read சிலம்புங் கழியாள் (line 8) as 'she whose anklets were not yet removed': the girl has gone before the anklet ceremony that comes before a wedding, so the mother counts the rite the elopement skipped. She calls the young man a deceiver (பொய்ப்ப), which is her view, not the poem's verdict.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's going away with her lover across the wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: the mother speaks her grief aloud

comparisons.tenor: her rising breasts, rivalling caskets
her well-guarded home
green gooseberries dropping on bare ground
the forest-dwellers' huts

reading: The friend, having agreed to let in the hero, whose chariot keeps bringing courtesans, asks the wife whether she can afford to sulk in vain because he cannot give them up, since women who were able to keep up their sulking ended alone when fortune left them, sifting and cooking a little food for themselves while their sweet-voiced sons sucked shrunken breasts, and others still do not learn from it.
nuance: Unusually blunt: the friend argues from the household's livelihood, not from love. The opening buffalo, which grazes the lilies, sleeps in the mud and comes home at dusk crowned with pakanrai, carries the hero's conduct without naming it.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்கு வாயில் நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளை நெருங்கிச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan quarrel of the watered country

comparisons.tenor: the buffalo striding into the old town

ullurai.tenor: the husband who spends his days with courtesans and comes home at evening

pairs.situation: he has taken his pleasure among the courtesans
he lies at ease in their quarter all day
he comes home at dusk wearing their garlands

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a marutham buffalo of the hero's own town in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

reading: The friend tells the heroine that while they sat looking out and wondering whether the season he had named had failed to come where he was, the season he promised when he said he would come back to hear the koel in the mango with her, in lovely spring when the palasa buds redden like dyed nails and bees and humming insects shake down the kuravam and kongu blossoms, her lover has come and stands here, as swiftly as the heart goes to what it longs for; so where now is the pallor that spread on her forehead for so many days, until even her mother noticed?
nuance: The long spring catalogue (lines 1 to 17) is the hero's own promise, quoted, so the description of the season is also the evidence that his word was kept. The final question treats the pallor as already gone.

thinai_evidence.note: the spring term set for the return from a parting

comparisons.tenor: the daytime gloom of the cold season
the sharp red palasa buds
blossoms falling as the bees work them
the humming of the thumbi
the mango thick with blossom
the lover's sudden arrival

reading: The friend tells the lord of the rich hills, who comes alone at night by a narrow path where elephants walk, thunder roars and snakes and tigers make it fearful, that marriage he can have if he wants it, but from today he must not come; and if he does come, then when he has left her and reached his own rocky village, he must blow the horn that calls together his hunting dogs, so that they, left here in anxiety, know he is safe.
nuance: The ban and the care sit in one breath: the friend who forbids the visits still needs to hear the horn. மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை makes marriage sound easily granted, which takes away his reason for the night road.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை வரவு விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill path, its beasts and falls

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை வரவு விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது

comparisons.tenor: the bees humming to the song of the falls

reading: The friend tells the man who has announced his journey that if he means to leave her, the girl whose look strikes like a goddess, slim-waisted, her breasts freckled like new vengai blossom, for a wasteland where flocks of crows on the banyan call over the hunters' forts and carry off the corpses of travellers shot by raiders, then may he get his rare wealth: she, tender as a fresh shoot, young and full of love, has not even the boldness to answer his 'we will go' with 'then we will stay behind'.
nuance: The blessing (எய்துக மாதோ நுமக்கே) is a curse in form. The two descriptions weigh against each other: the carrion road and her beauty. The last line may also be read as 'she cannot say she will die', since ஒழிவேம் can mean both; either way it is her silence that the friend speaks for.

thinai_evidence.note: a departure for wealth that the friend tries to prevent

comparisons.tenor: her glance
the freckles on her breasts
the girl herself

reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore, where the fishermen's catch is cried for sale by their well-dressed sisters in the festive streets, why he shows no grace to free her friend's grief from gossiping mouths: even if he lies now, was the oath also false that he swore on the day he first came in his tall chariot, its wheels crushing the girls' sand dolls, to the ford dusted with punnai pollen where the swan preens on the dunes, and first held her? The sea knows; it was the witness.
nuance: The chariot that ruins the girls' sand dolls (line 12) on the day of the first meeting reads to me as the end of her girlhood, though nothing in the poem says so. Calling the sea as witness makes the shore itself the court where his oath stands.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishing hamlet and the shore grove

comparisons.tenor: her friend's kohl-lined eyes

title: நித்திலக்கோவை 321-340
theme: Akananuru 321 to 340 (Nithilakkovai): men on the wealth road arguing with their hearts by the desert's robbers and dying travellers, wives waiting through the promised rains, night trysts at the elephant's plantain slope, courtesans boasting by Chola victories and a mother following an eloped daughter in thought; the fame of Thithiyan, Pazhaiyan, Thiraiyan, Athiyan and the three crowned houses measures private feeling.
source_issues: 325, 327, 328, 332: the colophon thurai carries a stray footnote numeral (1கொண்டு, 2நெஞ்சினை, 1தலைமகள்); 325's (1) has no second alternative.
331 line 8: பிறக் கெரழிய looks like a misprint for பிறக்கு ஒழிய (the vowel sign ொ split into ெ and ர).
335 line 7: மராஅத்துக் பொளிபிளந்து has க் before ப, an irregular sandhi; probably a misprint for மராஅத்துப் பொளி.
337: the colophon thurai names the speaker தலைமகள், but the one who went for wealth, came back and speaks to his heart is the man; read தலைமகன்.
332 line 12: the text flag records a repaired stray space before a dead consonant.
325, 327, 333, 337: opening single quotation marks at the start of the speech are never closed.

reading: After the girl has eloped, her foster mother pictures the summer road of dry springs, a stag calling its doe to food, cowherds' muddy wells where elephants come with their calf, and asks whether the girl will rest in some hamlet shelter with her companion or walk on into the night with the bold youth, since she slipped off her pebble-filled anklets so her mother would not hear and crossed the bamboo hills.
nuance: Taking off the anklets (சிலம்பு கழீஇ) is done so their sound will not betray her, but it is also the act that marks a girl's passage to marriage; here she performs it herself, in secret, so the sign of the wedding and the sign of the flight are one act.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl has left home with a young man across the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks her grief aloud

comparisons.tenor: the clear call of the summer wind over the dry spring
the sound echoing in the clefts of the rock

iraicchi.act: the stag leaves the iluppai flowers uneaten and calls in a male voice for his doe to come and feed
iraicchi.sense: the creatures of the road she took show a male who feeds his mate before himself, so the mother's fear holds a hope that the youth will so tend the girl

reading: Turning back at midnight in a storm from a tryst whose signal proved false, the man asks his heart whether it will languish alone, trembling like one falling from a broken cliff, and says the girl who torments him is as hard to win as Thithiyan's Pothiyil, whose honey-hung peak no climber can finish.
nuance: The simile turns puram fame to akam use: Thithiyan's war elephants and spears are named before his hill, so Pothiyil is hard to enter not only for its steepness but because a fierce lord guards it, as her people guard her.

colophon.thurai: அல்லகுறிப்பட்டுப் போகின்ற தலைமகன் தன் னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover at midnight who cannot reach the girl

comparisons.tenor: the heart trembling with unsated desire
the heart left alone through the night
the girl, hard to obtain

reading: The friend bids the heroine, whom she hails as one who excels in wifely virtue, to step out gently on her small feet and see: the cloud, dark as her hair, has come down over the bamboo slopes with thunder and hail like a moving herd of elephants, so the town's gossip will wither and the word that her lover will come will prove true.
nuance: The friend reads the rain as proof because the returning season was his pledge. The colophon files the poem under paalai, but its matter is waiting through the promised rains, which porul 1.6 gives to mullai.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife waits and the promised rains have broken

comparisons.tenor: the dark rain clouds moving over the sky
the rain cloud, dark as her hair

reading: Reading their lord's mind after the campaign, his attendants say that his wife will now even have guests to feed, for his chariot is racing through the rain-fed forest, past brimming pools and flower-strewn sand, its wheels cutting tracks where the water runs like a snake, to reach town in the jasmine evening.
nuance: விருந்தும், 'guests too': with the husband away the house could not receive guests, so his homecoming restores her duty as host as well as her joy.

thinai_evidence.note: forest after the rains at jasmine evening

thurai_akam.speaker: ilaiyar
thurai_akam.note: the speakers are the hero's attendants (உழையர்), speaking among themselves

comparisons.vehicle: கிள்ளை இனிதின் எடுத்த வளராப் பிள்ளைத் தூவி
comparisons.tenor: the green crops grown by the long rains
each brimming pool
the black sand streaked by the water
the water rushing in the wheel tracks

reading: The heroine tells her friend that her lover, seeing their secret love become gossip and her mother on guard, promised to take her with him once a day of cool rain had tamed the desert and asked her to wait a few days; instead, hardening his heart for his venture, he went alone at evening through the elephant-haunted waste toward Paanan's land in the north, and she asks what blame can fall on the fate that brings her this pain.
nuance: The desert is measured by a fallen patron: the hill lost its waterfalls as Athiyan's great drum went dead after him. She lays the broken promise on fate (பால்), not on him.

colophon.thurai: 1கொண்டு நீங்கக் கருதி யொழிந்த தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he promised to take her and went alone

comparisons.tenor: the hill whose beauty of waterfalls has died away

reading: Refusing the husband entry, the friend praises the young woman he courts, with her freckled lips, wide cool eyes and small forehead, lovely as the paddy fields by the bannered gate, says she must go to the festival in her finery, and adds that her eyes never miss whoever looks at them, as the spear Pazhaiyan of Por raised never missed.
nuance: The praise is ironic: eyes that never miss make the husband a target, not a chooser. Who the குறுமகள் is turns on reading: most likely the rival, though the lines could praise the wife's own beauty as wasted on him.

thinai_evidence.note: paddy fields and the watered Kaveri country

comparisons.tenor: the young woman's beauty
her eyes, which never miss

reading: The man rebukes his heart, which has resolved to go for wealth: if it knows that joy and grief, union and parting come by turns like midday and night, why should it cross a desert of mirages, withered marul and crows tearing at corpses, where killers pity no one and grieve only when their arrow misses; and if it goes, will it ever think of him again?
nuance: The opening is a sage's premise, that joy and grief alternate, used not to counsel acceptance but to argue against the journey: if hardship comes anyway in its turn, there is no need to go seeking it for wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: a man arguing with his heart against the journey for wealth

comparisons.tenor: joy and grief, union and parting, which come by turns
the striped slough of the snake

reading: Speaking to her friend while the lover stands unseen nearby, the heroine says that had they known the man who came through the midnight storm, treading on snakes, to embrace her would grow weary of her, they would have held his chest again and again and never let it go: the chest of the man of the hill where a tusker strokes his mate as she sleeps among the plantains after calving.
nuance: Spoken to be overheard, the regret is a warning: the lover learns that his nights are being read as waning love, and the elephant pair beside its new calf shows the settled life he should offer.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover who comes by night to embrace her

comparisons.tenor: the thunder over the hill

iraicchi.act: the tusker tenderly strokes his young mate as she sleeps after bearing her calf
iraicchi.sense: the man of that hill, overhearing, is shown a male who stays and tends the mother of his young, the married life the heroine's words press him toward

reading: Her eyes and forehead pale with longing, the heroine tells her friend that if her lover can bear to live apart while she suffers, she wonders whether he will really go, resting only briefly, along the dusty road where salt merchants' carts wear out their oxen and over the hills of dry springs where a tigress whelps and a cub bites the trunk of a thirsty elephant.
nuance: She voices no fear for him on that violent road, only the question whether he can bear to live apart: the danger is set down as the land's own law, and the doubt is about his heart.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது. பிரிவுணர்த்திய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: he has resolved to leave across the waste

reading: Pleading the lover's case, the friend tells the heroine how he picked backwater flowers, lingered in the seaside grove, played at sand dolls, delighted them and humbled himself, and now goes away dejected because they have not understood his pain; her own unruly heart ran after him to stop him, and she wonders if it reached him and was too shy to speak, while his chariot over the white dunes rises and vanishes like a fisherman's boat in the open sea.
nuance: The friend speaks of her own heart running after him, lending her longing to win the heroine's; the chariot sinking and rising among the dunes shows the lover already slipping out of reach.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: seaside grove, dunes, screwpine and fishermen

occasion.words: தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது

comparisons.vehicle: சிறுகுடிப் பரதவர் பெருங்கடன் மடுத்த கடுஞ்செலற் கொடுந்திமில்
comparisons.tenor: his chariot rising and vanishing among the dunes

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man who left is without love: he went past many hill hamlets where women in leaf skirts carry from street to street the white iluppai flowers a bear has left, and across a waste as cruel as the sword Thithiyan, generous host of bards, drew against the Velir.
nuance: Two kinds of giving frame her complaint: hill women live on what the bear leaves, and Thithiyan fills bards' hands in his daily court; the waste the lover crossed is likened to that same giver's sword, his other face.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the waste and left her

comparisons.tenor: the white iluppai flowers
the bear's brood spread over the ground
the empty waste he crossed

reading: Speaking so the lover outside can hear, the heroine tells her friend that the words she once said lovingly, that the man of the hill where a tusker kills a tiger and then sleeps beside his mate among plantains is a man of grace fit for her, have come true: his embrace, which leaves no room even for a bee, and his love are as on the first day.
nuance: Praise spoken for the lover's ears: the tusker that kills the tiger and then rests with his mate gives the hero both faces the heroine claims for him, protector and constant companion.

thinai_evidence.note: bamboo, elephant and tiger of the hill slope

comparisons.tenor: his garlanded chest, to those who desire it
his embrace and love now

iraicchi.act: the tusker kills the tiger that lay in wait, then goes slowly to embrace his mate and sleeps beside her
iraicchi.sense: the man of that hill is one who both guards and stays, the grace the heroine says she found in him

reading: Answering a friend who scolds her for wasting with pallor and blaming him, and who says he would hurry home if told of her grief, the heroine prays the friend's sweet words come true, but says that even if he stays beyond the hills where elephants lift their trunks like withered summer palms, her pallor would easily fade if only a messenger came while he finishes his work, bringing his eager wish to return.
nuance: She asks for less than his return, only a messenger: what wastes her is the silence, not the distance.

thinai_evidence.note: he is far beyond the hills on his venture

comparisons.tenor: the pallor spreading over her body
the herd of elephants raising their trunks to the sky

reading: His campaign done and tribute taken, the hero tells his charioteer that the rains have begun, falling in streams like tuskers' trunks, with hail like girls' play-beads, and bids him drive the four horses, swift as a line of swans, without slackening through the peacock-filled fields, so that he may see at once his wife's kohl eyes, thick hair and small forehead.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains begin over the forest fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the rain
the streams of rain falling to the ground
the dark clouds gathering
the hailstones
the four horses running yoked together

reading: The man grants his heart that even the most compassionate cannot give without wealth, but says the cracked, lonely summer waste, where a tusker breaks his tusk stripping marā bark to feed his mate, would not be hard for them if they went taking the bright-bangled girl, whose red mouth, sweeter than the young areca of Chezhiyan's walled old town, flows with nectar; and so he gives up going alone.
nuance: The opening concedes the moral case for wealth in a maxim's terms: giving (ஈதல்) needs means. The answer is not a counter-maxim but the elephant, which provides for its mate at her side. Most of the poem is a description of the areca palm by Madurai's walls; how it maps onto her mouth is my reading.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பொருள்கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சினைக் கழறிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the cracked summer waste

comparisons.tenor: the crown of the areca palm
the sheath of the spathe
the new flower cluster
the flower cluster opening for the bees
the white flowers spread below
the hail-like young fruit
the sweetness of her red mouth

iraicchi.act: the tusker breaks his own tusk prising bark off the dry marā so that his mate may eat in the cruel summer
iraicchi.sense: the male provides for his mate at her side, at his own cost, so the man sees that providing need not mean leaving her

reading: The courtesan the lord now favours says, for the other mistress's companions to hear, that the women who came in his chariot mock her beauty, but they go about as if they mattered only because she stays away from the festival, as a mahout lives on only by the killer elephant's mercy; if she comes and the lord of the otter-haunted ford does not turn with her as the nerunji turns with the sun, may her bangles break as the Aryan army broke at Vallam.
nuance: She stakes her bangles in the form of a warrior's oath on a Chola victory; but the bangle that slips or breaks is the sign of a woman abandoned, so the boast carries a fear.

thinai_evidence.note: otter, vaalai fish, kaanji shade and the pond's ford

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: she speaks for the hearing of the companions of the mistress kept in the house (இற்பரத்தை)

comparisons.vehicle: பாகன் நெடிதுயிர் வாழ்தல் காய்சினக் கொல்களிற்று யானை நல்கல் மாறே
comparisons.tenor: the rival women's going about as if they mattered
the lord turning with her
her bangles breaking

iraicchi.act: the male otter rises to bring the day's food to his mate, who lies unfed and weary with her young
iraicchi.sense: in the lord's own town a male provides for a mate weak with young, which recalls the wife and child he owes, against which the courtesan's boast is made

reading: When his heart again presses him to go for wealth, the man reminds it how once, finding it no joy to stay apart from her, it said 'let wealth stay where it is' and came back alone through the burnt, rainless waste where fierce Mazhavar cut down a starving brahmin messenger in case he carried gold, left in disgust at his rags, and a jackal dragged his entrails into the kalli shade, all because it feared she would suffer when the cold north wind came with the rains.
nuance: The murdered messenger is the poem's argument: on the wealth road a man is killed for what he might carry and found to carry nothing. The colophon names the speaker தலைமகள், but the one who went, came back and is tempted again is the man.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்துப் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்துவந்த தலைமகள் பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot forest the rains have deserted

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan

occasion.words: பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக் கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: the colophon reads தலைமகள்; the poem's speaker is the man

comparisons.tenor: her body
the low hills crossed by many paths

reading: After a tryst that failed, the man tells his heart that even if he cannot have the embrace of the dark girl whose forehead smells of kaanthal on the slope of the Pandyan's sacred hill, may their love last like the Porai's Kolli and may messages to her never stop, more numerous than the waves at the Chola's busy port.
nuance: Each crowned house lends a measure: the Pandyan's hill for where she lives, the Chera's Kolli for how long love should last, the Chola's sea for how many messages; what he asks is modest, that love and messages last, not union.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal on the hill slope where she lives

occasion.words: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: their love, which must not perish
the messages to her

reading: Setting out as the cold season comes, when wheel ruts run with water like a snake and pulse pods split like loosening fingers, the man tells his heart that, pulled by manly duty and held by love, he is like an ant on a firebrand burning at both ends, and wonders whether she will suffer, she whose bond with him is as life joined to the body, whose love is like living and whose parting is like death.
nuance: Both ends of the firebrand burn, so the middle is no refuge: duty and love are equally fire. The closing triad gathers in three similes what the Kural says in two couplets (1122, 1124).

colophon.thurai: போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a man leaving for work, torn by the parting

occasion.words: போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the water rushing in the wheel ruts
the pulse pods splitting open

comparisons.vehicle: இருதலைக் கொள்ளி இடைநின்று வருந்தி ஒருதலைப் படாஅ உறவி
comparisons.tenor: the man torn between duty and love
her bond with him
her love
parting from her

reading: As evening falls after a day meeting in the punnai shade, the friend asks the lover to give up leaving, since the tide has filled the backwaters, snakes and fierce fish crowd the path and the girl, lovely as Thiraiyan's Pavaththiri, is fading, and to stay the night in their fishing village, where they will feed him rice and curd porridge bought with fresh fish and anoint him with sandal paste, where the shark-torn nets hang idle on the screwpine.
nuance: Fed and anointed as a guest, the lover would be received openly by her people: the invitation to stay is the friend's push toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai grove, fishermen and sharks

comparisons.tenor: the girl's fresh beauty

title: நித்திலக்கோவை 341-360
theme: Akananuru 341 to 360, from the நித்திலக்கோவை section: paalai partings dominate, with heroines blessing or reproaching the man who left for wealth and the hero arguing with his heart on the road and at home, set among kurinji and neythal poems of secret meetings pressing toward marriage, two mullai homecomings and one marutham refusal; puram names (Cheralathan, Nannan, Anji, Pulli, Killi Valavan at Koodal) recur as measures of fame, noise and giving.
source_issues: akananuru:341: the flag reports 13 lines in our base text against 12 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the poem reads complete as it stands, but the lineation differs.
akananuru:347: line 16 is repeated as line 24 of akananuru:389 (flag); both poems are Mamoolanar's, so it may be the poet's own formula rather than a copying error.
akananuru:348: the colophon thurai has a stray footnote numeral, '1சிறைப்புறத்தானாக'; copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:358: the colophon thurai has தலைமட்குச் for தலைமகட்குச்; copied as is in `colophon`. Line 2 is repeated as line 5 of akananuru:378 (flag).
akananuru:359: lineation flag: a printed line number 5 stands on line 10; the base text has 16 lines against 15 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534).
akananuru:360: the colophon thurai has இரவுக் கறி for இரவுக் குறி; copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:344: line 3 has முடககாற் for the expected முடக்காற் (a missing pulli).
akananuru:356: lines 11 to 17 (the Chola lord of Vallam, the enemies at the door) do not construe clearly in our text; the reading there is uncertain.

reading: The heroine tells her friend there is no way through: the kongu has leaves fit to pluck, the koel calls from the mango, and on the Kaveri's sand after the flood has fallen the bull drinks with his cow and sleeps with her under the kaanji's falling pollen; this rich season is for those who have their partner beside them.
nuance: The last line turns the whole riverside scene into a list of what she lacks: every couple in it, animal and human, has a companion to enjoy the season with. The season's signs are spring's, so the poem implies that he had promised to be back by now.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman left behind laments the season she must spend alone

comparisons.tenor: the dark streaks of the river sand after the flood

iraicchi.act: the bull drinks with his cow and they lie down together to sleep on the sand
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle spend the season with their mates, while her husband stays away

reading: The hero rebukes his heart, which neither stops when checked nor stays when held: am I not your kinsman? Cherish me as if we had already embraced; she is harder to reach than the mountain goddesses hidden in the rock caves of the untouched waterfall, in the land of the victorious Pandya, while I cannot lie on her lovely waist.
nuance: The long middle (lines 4 to 11) praises the Pandya, called தென்னன் and of the கவுரியர் line, as the destroyer of a cattle-raiders' stronghold; it serves only to place the cave of the hill goddesses, the image of a woman out of reach. The poem is the hero's half of the kalavu when the friend has said no.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover longing for an embrace not yet granted

occasion.words: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்ட தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: how the heart should treat the hero
the Pandya's striking hand
the heroine, out of reach

reading: On the road for wealth, the hero tells his heart, which wants to turn back to the girl with shoulders like bamboo, that it has taken up a high endeavour and should not now look back: the path runs past a hero-stone whose top was chipped by the salt-carriers' cart wheels, its garland withered and its letters worn, through a forest where under the yaa's shade the salt-traders unload their donkeys.
nuance: The hero-stone with its worn inscription, which travellers use for another purpose (வேறுபயம்), is part of what the heart must pass: the dead are marks on a trade road. Lines 13 and 14 (the traders' load and the companion in distress) are compressed and their construction is not certain.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்து மீளக் கருதிய நெஞ்சினைக் கழறிப்போயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the glaring forked paths of the forest and the passing sun

comparisons.tenor: her rounded shoulders
the shade of the yaa tree

reading: His task done, the hero tells his charioteer to drive fast, bells ringing and horses leaping, through the forest where rain has fallen on the white saline ground, the pidavu buds open like moonlight in the cool wind and peacocks gather, so that before evening falls his beloved, worn with the pallor of longing, may show a smiling face.
nuance: The rain season has come, which is the time he promised, so speed is a matter of keeping his word as much as of desire. The peacocks are compared to something the bright-browed women make or play with (கைமாண் தோணி), and that object is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-soaked forest and the pidavu of the rainy season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (பாகன்)

comparisons.tenor: the opening white pidavu buds
the peacocks moving slowly
the horses' leaping speed

reading: The heroine tells her friend that he promised to go only when rain had cooled the land, and to spend a few days first with her wearing vengai garlands from Ezhil hill, which a famous poet sang; though he has broken that word, she wishes his road well: may the forest grow lovely with nunavu flowers on the red sand path and trees putting out dark shoots for his young spearmen to wear, and may they rest in the itti's shade.
nuance: Complaint turns to blessing in the middle of the poem: she names his lie and in the same breath prays that the road be cool for him. Ezhil hill is fixed by its fame in song (a poet given horses by the grace of the forest goddess), so a place in praise poetry measures her lost happiness.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone on the dry road before the promised season

reading: The friend turns the husband away with a laugh: lord of the town where the heron, its back like wet plaster, waits watching the overflow of the dam the toddy-glad farmers built of kaanji stakes, sugarcane and sod, eyeing the silver kayal fish, we no longer care; the day you went to her house with your lute-player, drum and drinking friends, that bangled girl rejoiced more than the Chera with the kothai garland when Pazhaiyan Maran routed Killi Valavan's army at Koodal and seized his horses and elephants.
nuance: The scale of the other woman's joy is a historical defeat: a Chola camped before Madurai, beaten, his horses and elephants taken, and a third king delighting in it. The friend's mockery (நகைநன்று) frames both the heron and the victory as the rival's gains.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband went to another woman's house

comparisons.tenor: the heron's back
the kayal fish
the other woman's joy

ullurai.tenor: the other woman lying in wait for the husband

pairs.situation: she has marked the husband as her catch
she waits patiently for him to come within reach
she profits from a household others laboured to build

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the heron and fish of the marutham field in a marutham poem without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

reading: The heroine tells her friend that though he left her, with her shoulders losing their old beauty, pallor eating her looks and the harsh street's gossip loud as the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadambu, may his work succeed; he has crossed the mountains where, after a tiger's leap, a young cow-elephant frightened by the tusker's roar has lost her calf and searches with her trunk on her head like a woman who has lost her child.
nuance: The blessing (வாய்க்கதில்) is spoken in the middle of her own wasting. The cow-elephant searching like a bereaved mother is a picture of the road's terror, and also of a loss being searched for, which is her own state.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainless slope where bamboo withers

comparisons.tenor: the gossip of the street
the cow-elephant searching for her calf

reading: With the lover listening, the heroine asks what will become of her heart, which trusted the fine but unstable words of the lord of the land where the hill folk drink toddy of jackfruit and honey matured in bamboo, offer it to the god's high peak, and forget their millet field until elephants take the grain and young and old gather angrily with their bows.
nuance: The friend has started the talk and the heroine speaks for the man to hear: the drunken hill folk who let the field go and then rouse the whole clan are her warning of what his delay invites.

reading: The heroine asks her friend what he was thinking of, letting the old beauty of the arm he bound in marriage fade, when he crossed into the land of strange speech, through the country of Nannan, whose word is true as a balance beam and who gives the spoils of broken forts unasked to weary bards, where on the beautiful hill a tusker that has eaten flame-red vengai rests its tired trunk on its brow like a snake climbing a rock.
nuance: வரைந்துதாம் பிணித்த says it was he who bound her arm in marriage, so the loss is a broken undertaking, not only a sorrow. Nannan's unhesitating giving stands against the husband who left to get wealth.

reading: To the lover leaving after a daytime meeting, the friend says the backwater's flowers are closing with the tide, the ford is silent with no one passing and the crab gone from its burrow: do not yoke your mules to the chariot, but for her sake stay and then go; see, there is our little town, on the long sandbank where the fishermen who dive for conch come in to Korkai's welcome, blowing their shells.
nuance: Pointing to her own town at dusk is an invitation to stay and also a hint to come openly to the village, which is how the friend nudges the lover toward marriage.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

reading: Returning with wealth won abroad, the hero asks his heart whether she knows yet that his task is done: she who counts each day the marks drawn on the wall for the days he set, with tears falling on her gold earring, chin on her hand on the bed, worshipping the bird omens, may hear at her ear the lizard that chirps whenever she thinks of him, as a medicine for her aching shoulders.
nuance: The man imagines the woman's waiting in close detail, the tally marks, the omens of bird and lizard, so that what he hopes to bring home is the end of a routine he knows she keeps.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்முற்றி மறுத்தராநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

reading: The bride tells her friend that she spoke well and truly in praising the hill lord, where the male monkey clasps a pot-sized jackfruit as a drummer clasps his drum behind a dancing girl, with a dancing peacock before him, and calls to his sweet mate by the waterfall, as a man of good family who would not leave her nor speak falsely: the friend is sweeter to her than the new mode the bard composed for Anji's famous song, and sweeter even than the wedding day.
nuance: The friend's earlier speech is quoted, with its own scene of the monkey keeping its mate, so the poem confirms after the wedding what the go-between promised before it. The second alternative of the colophon puts the speech before the wedding, when it is only arranged.

colophon.thurai: வரைந்து எய்திய பின்றை மணமனைக்கட் சென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது. வரைவு மலிந்து சொல்லிய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

reading: Home again with wealth, the hero answers his heart, which urges a second journey: the days of waking life pass like a dream, age comes, and love's rare joy has its season; even if you do not see this, will you not think, crossing the treeless summer waste where a stag embraces his drooping doe and both turn from the leaves for want of water at a dried pond, of the virtue of the long-haired woman who tends weary guests in our cool hall and speaks sweetly with us in bed?
nuance: The argument against going is made from impermanence: time and age are reasons to stay with love and household, not to renounce it. Her virtue is defined by the guests she feeds, so the home he would leave is a place of giving.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்துப் பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் பொருண்முற்றி வந்திருந்த காலத்து மீண்டும் பொருள் கடாவின நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

iraicchi.sense: even the stag keeps by his mate in hardship, so the man should not leave his wife again for wealth

reading: The attendants tell the hero, his work done: the king has won and raised his flag in the camp where elephants clashed, cows frisk with their calves in every grove and herdsmen raise their flutes; if you would enter home in the joy of victory, sandal dust on your gold-garlanded chest that poets praise, where then will the pallor go from the brow of your faultless lady with flower-like eyes?
nuance: The victory and the cowherds' evening are both reasons to go now; the question at the end means her pallor will vanish the moment he arrives.

reading: Told that he is going, the heroine answers her friend: when spring comes of itself, when the mango puts out shoots, the koel calls and bees hum on the budding branch like the strings of a paalai lute touched by a master, the season in which lovers forget their rich homes in cool groves, let us go and show him the loosened bangles, quarrel with him and come back, saying: while we are alone, you who love gold and have no grace have become like this.
nuance: She rehearses her reproach before he has gone, and the reproach is about the season: he will be away in the time made for lovers. The paalai lute in the simile names the very mode of parting.

thinai_evidence.note: she is to be left alone while he goes for gold

comparisons.tenor: the humming of the bees

reading: The friend tells the heroine how the lord of the town, where the tortoise at the lower ford drinks the washing water and rolls like a kinai drum with the water-hen as its player, saw me in the long street and seized my gold-bangled arm; I cried 'Mother!' and he let go, and since then, so as not to betray our old affection, I have kept a tongue like stone glued with lac and told our mother nothing; even if he showed us no grace and killed, the killing would be no fault: so what is your mind, you with hair like Nannan's cane?
nuance: The friend tells of her own encounter as a test: she has been seized and stayed silent, and she now asks the heroine to accept the man's suit. Lines 11 to 17, with the Chola lord of Vallam and the enemies at the door, are obscure in our text.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகளைக் குறை நயப்பக் கூறியது.

reading: The friend comforts the heroine: though he has crossed the great forest of Umbar, where a tiger kills a tusker to end the weakness of his hungry mate and rolls on the reddened rock, and the elephant herd turns back holding each other's trunks, he will not stay away without thinking of your shoulders; he will be kind, remembering your glance, like a blue lily swaying in the wind on a rain-filled pond.
nuance: The tiger's kill is violent, but what it does is provide for a mate weak with pregnancy; that is the reassurance, as the colophon's வற்புறீஇயது expects.

reading: By day, with the lover hidden nearby, the friend tells the heroine that she no longer plays with her companions in the deep spring, hair dressed with cool kuvalai, graceful as a blue-necked peacock dancing; if mother sees her changed colour and asks, what can the friend say of the sickness given by the lord of the high hill, where the long white waterfall looks like a flag on a war elephant?
nuance: The question is meant for the man to hear: the mother has noticed, and only marriage can answer her. The waterfall like a flag on an elephant is the hill lord's own country turned into a banner.

reading: The friend asks the heroine why she is helpless, saying he has stayed away not knowing how she hides her tearful eyes and pale shoulders: he has taken their beauty with him, rich as the Chera's Veliyam, on the mountain road of Pulli, where an elephant that has lost its beloved mate trumpets back to the clouds like the music of travelling players on a great rock, and smoke from burning fields mingles with waterfall spray.
nuance: Her beauty is not lost but carried off, held by him on the road; the friend reframes the wasting as a trust he holds. The elephant's cry for its lost mate shows that the road itself mourns a separation.

reading: Refusing a daytime meeting, the friend tells the lover that after the day spent in the flowering grove, when the sun goes behind the western hill, bees leave the neythal and sky and sea at dusk take on the joined form of the two great gods, his going leaves her desolate; so let him come at night, keeping his trained horse from neighing while the town sleeps, leaving the chariot far off and crossing the sand softly like an elephant coming down a hill, to their trysting place in the punnai grove where the anril roosts on the palm.
nuance: The friend's detailed instructions for secrecy (the muffled horse, the chariot left behind) show how dangerous the night tryst is, which is also an argument for marriage. The two gods of the simile are not named; the sky and sea joined suggest two figures of different colour.

title: நித்திலக்கோவை 361-380
theme: Akananuru 361 to 380, from the நித்திலக்கோவை section: nine paalai poems of men arguing with their hearts on the road to wealth and of wives and mothers left behind, set among kurinji night and day trysts pressing for marriage, two mullai rain poems, two marutham sulks and two neythal meetings, with Pazhi, Kaamur, Evvi, Uranthai and the Atthi legend used as scales of comparison.
source_issues: akananuru:367: the flag reports 16 lines in our base text against 15 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the poem reads complete as it stands.
akananuru:368: the colophon thurai has தலைமகட்குத் சொல்லுவாளாய், a த் before ச that is not regular sandhi, for தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய் (as in 370's colophon); copied as is in `colophon`.
akananuru:369: the flag reports 26 lines in our base text against 27 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the lineation differs.
akananuru:373: the flag reports 19 lines in our base text against 18 in the commentary edition (pmuni0534); the lineation differs.
akananuru:379: the colophon thurai has பெருண்முற்றி, probably for பொருண்முற்றி (having completed the wealth); copied as is in `colophon`.

reading: On the wide hot track he has already entered, the man tells his heart, which would not take his word that nothing surpasses the embrace of a girl who sulks if even a thread comes between them, and chose wealth instead, to stop thinking of her shoulders now, as a turtle dropped in a pot over the fire longs in vain for the shaded pool.
nuance: The argument the heart rejected is quoted in full, so the poem's real speaker is the losing side of a debate: the man has already obeyed the heart and gone, and his order to it to stop remembering is the measure of how much he remembers. The turtle in the pot pictures a longing that comes too late; the phrase about the elders in line 10 (கரியாப் பூவின் பெரியோர்) is obscure, but the turtle's plight is clear without it.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

reading: With the hero hidden nearby, the friend tells the girl that the hill streams are in flood and the path is shut by a tigress guarding her mate, wounded by an elephant, so that if the good man who came by night with his spear goes back with nothing, she will not live a day; and she asks why the moon has made the night as bright as the necklace on their breasts and the white waterfall.
nuance: Every danger she lists is the man's, and the bright moon is a further danger to secret meeting, so the speech to the girl is a warning to the listener that night visits cannot go on; it presses toward marriage without naming it. The tigress keeping watch over her wounded mate stays a sign of the path's danger here: the poem draws nothing from her care.

reading: As the sun's chariot sets behind the mountain, the friend tells the girl, faded like a flower past its hour and lying on her bed, not to grieve: the man who crossed the cruel wasteland, where the wind scatters gooseberries like gold coins on the stony path and the hawk calls its kin to men speared by waiting robbers, has done his work and is coming back, so that her eyes will regain their beauty.
nuance: The terrors of the road are given at length only to be put behind: they are the measure of what he has already passed, and so of how sure his return now is. The gooseberries that look like gold coins hint at the wealth he went for, lying on the very road of danger.

reading: The girl tells her friend that the rains have come with thunder, frogs drum in every hollow, the kondrai hangs like gold, thondri and mullai bloom and the rock pools fill, yet her lover, in the great camp of a king eager for victory, does not think of them; and the evening that comes like one bent on killing is too much to swim through.
nuance: The season he promised to return by is described as complete and lovely, and only then measured against his absence; the more perfect the rains, the plainer it is that he has broken his word. The camp belongs to a king, not to him: he stays for another man's victory.

thinai_evidence.note: the onset of the rains and the waiting wife, with the flowers of the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the croaking of the frogs

reading: At dusk in the burning wasteland, where wild elephants kick a hero-stone taking it for a man and snap their nails, and fallen bowmen lie with none to tend them, the man tells his heart, which brought him there and, unable to bear the pain it caused, now thinks of turning back, that it is the girl's soft dark hair, fragrant with the new vengai flowers of Kazhuvul's Kaamur, that draws it.
nuance: The heart that drove him out is the same heart that now wants to go home; the poem catches it in the act of changing sides. Kaamur's vengai, given by a spirit, makes her hair a thing of a famous and blessed place set against the desolate place he stands in. Lines 7 and 8 are hard to construe, and the turn in lines 10 and 11 can be read as rebuke or as relief.

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's broken nails

reading: Refusing the husband entry, the friend tells him that their lady, lovely as a goddess, wept when she learned he had wronged her yesterday by staying in a fragrant grove with the bright-browed girl whose shoulders are as comforting as the shade of Evvi, the lord who, when farmers and salt-makers came to blows over salt pans spoilt by threshing chaff, had the grey elders part them and gave toddy to the fishermen.
nuance: The long scene of the brawl belongs to the simile: it shows Evvi as a peacemaker and giver, and so makes the rival's shoulders a place of shelter and peace, a generous praise of the other woman that sharpens the wife's tears. The friend's charge is in two words, நீதற் பிழைத்தமை: you wronged her.

reading: Answering the friend who urges her to bear up, the girl says that the dreary evening, when the old bull bellows, the cattle rest by the nochchi hedge of the frontier hamlet and the male civet lies in wait by the millet store to seize the red-combed rooster and ease his hungry mate, must indeed be sweet to those who hold close their faultless companion, whose softness makes life melt at every embrace.
nuance: She never says the evening is bitter for her; she says it is sweet for the joined, and lets the friend draw the rest. Inside that sweet scene the civet hunting for his mate is the one creature that provides for a partner at nightfall.

reading: With the hero hidden by day, the friend asks the girl why, when the hill lord, in whose land the vengai flowers like a peahen's crest above the millet-guarding girls' swing, played with them like a tusker with his cow in a clear spring of a grove no monkey reaches, and went away for many days, gossip has grown in the toddy-drinking hamlet, in many mouths, like the Ulli festival of the Kongar who dance in the streets with bells at their waists.
nuance: The question is for the listener: the meeting was rare and long ago, yet the talk is already as loud as a festival, so secret love can no longer stay secret. The day tryst is at a place no monkey can reach, which makes the town's knowing all the stranger.

reading: The foster mother grieves that, since the girl went, the parrot will not drink its milk, her playmates do not play, the potted plant gets no flowers and the doll no offering; she missed the girl's purpose when she offered to wash her hair, and the girl, hurt, refused the rich wedding her kin were preparing in a house like Uranthai of the Cholas, and went over the wasteland with a young man of steady heart and long spear, and now the mother wonders whether her daughter had her anklets taken off in a poor woman's grass hut with one pillar and one cow, without honour or ceremony.
nuance: The house is described through the girl's things left without her, and the grief turns at the end from her loss to her status: what hurts is that the anklet-removal of a wedding happened in a stranger's poor hut. The words கண்டிசின் மகளே (line 1) address someone the speaker calls daughter; whether it is the girl's own mother is not clear from the poem.

reading: With the hero hidden by day, the friend reminds the girl that she once said that if, after playing with them in the punnai shade by day, he lay lovesick at night, she would fall under her father's strict guard, and that she cannot bring herself to tell him not to go yet says she will not live if he goes; so, with the girl staying in the grove like the sea goddess on the shore at dusk, the friend cannot bear to go home stripped of her own finery like a dancing girl, and says let the town talk.
nuance: Whose words are quoted in lines 1 to 9, and who will 'fall under guard', can be read more than one way; on any reading the friend's closing அலர்கவிவ் வூரே is spoken for the man to hear, daring the gossip so that he will end it by marriage.

reading: Crossing alone the scorched waste where a twist-horned stag, his mate shot by hunters, grieves with the fawns playing at his side, refuses to graze, will not drink the little water of the pond and lies down stricken like a speared man, the man asks his heart what will become of his beloved's eyes, which bees take for flowers of a clear spring, streaming tears even more than he.
nuance: He measures her grief by his own and finds hers greater: the stag, who has really lost his mate, is the image of what the man's going does to the one left. The fawns playing unaware at the stag's side make the loss sharper.

iraicchi.sense: even a beast pines when parted from its mate, so his leaving will waste the woman he leaves behind

reading: Turning back from a tryst that a false signal spoiled, the man tells his heart, which would not accept that the girl is as hard to win as the treasure the old Velir hid in their city at Pazhi under a dread god's guard, that it has swung to and fro like a swing-rope on a tall palm, tightened and slackened like the strap of a raider's war drum, and pined like a snake that has lost its gem, for she is guarded closer than a kings' fortress.
nuance: Each simile measures the hardness of the girl's guard, and each is one the hero may use openly. The poem shares its opening thought and its turn எனினும் அஃது ஒல்லாய் with Akananuru 258, which is under the same occasion.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல குறிப்பிட்டுப் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the secret lover's failed night meeting with a closely guarded girl

reading: Worn out by the wasteland and sitting alone at a desolate dusk with his hands round his knees, in the ruined hall of a village emptied by raiders where an elephant rubs against the rotting post, the man pictures the girl, who knows her own state but not his, lying on her bed at midnight sighing and sulking, flicking away with her nails the tears that soak her shoulders, and asks whether she has given up sleep like the king of a single fort besieged by many kings, poor girl.
nuance: He imagines her blaming him (புலக்கும் நெஞ்சமொடு) because she cannot see that he too is suffering: the pity of the last line is partly for himself. The besieged chieftain is an image of sleepless watching against odds.

colophon.thurai: பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.
