comparisons.tenor: the sleepless girl

reading: His campaign over, the man tells his charioteer to drive on in this lovely morning of the rains, when clouds that drank the sea flash and pour sweetly without thunder, like a bard's tuned lute, and on the sandy track the red mites run, like coral among sapphires, hiding among the fallen kaayaa blossoms, so that the slender girl may welcome him as a guest.
nuance: The rain is made gentle and musical, without thunder, because for him it is now a season of return, not of reproach. The last word, விருந்து, makes the husband a guest to be received, the honour of a homecoming.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains' morning on the woodland track, with kaayaa and red mites

comparisons.tenor: the soft sound of the rain
the red mites among the kaayaa blossoms

reading: To the friend who said he will not stay away long, the girl answers that if she knew that the man who crossed the dread wasteland, where raw youths kill even empty-handed travellers to test their arrows and feed the birds, and where the vulture, its claws wet with blood, perched on the white yaa trunk looks like the tusk of an elephant of Ilamperunchenni, the Chola who broke Pazhi's copper-strong walls and crushed the Vadukar, would come back unharmed, her eyes would not weep.
nuance: Her answer turns the friend's comfort from 'he will return soon' to 'will he return alive': her fear is not delay but death on the road. The Chola's war elephant, the vulture and the arrows make the wasteland a battlefield.

thinai_evidence.note: the wasteland of killers and vultures crossed by the absent man

comparisons.tenor: the vulture on the white trunk
the walls of Pazhi

reading: The beloved courtesan tells the lord not to go: once she owed him every duty, but now, as the Kaveri seized and hid Atthi when he danced adorned in its flood at Kazhar before Karikal and his crowd, he has been taken from her; she will not sulk at him, but let him see her paled brow, give back her beauty, which was like Kuttuvan's Maranthai, and then go.
nuance: The Atthi legend is here turned around: the woman who loses the man to the river is not his wife but the courtesan, and the river that keeps him is, by implication, his household. The closing demand நலம்தந்து சென்மே is the same as Akananuru 396's, also a courtesan's. The first two lines are compressed and their sense uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the paddy fields and river town, with a courtesan's sulk

comparisons.tenor: the man kept from the courtesan
the courtesan's beauty

reading: The man tells his heart, which has urged him to go for wealth, that those who can give with renown what people who come in hope ask of them must surely pass their nights as wanderers in some corner of a haunted common hall, its dice board crumbled and its pillars eaten by termites, in a village whose families fled when bowmen raided its cattle and where ants store fallen grass seed, thinking all the while of the soft beauty of their smiling women.
nuance: The poem gives the price of the giver's fame: the wealth for giving is earned on roads of ruin, and the giver sleeps among ruins with his wife only in his thoughts. The ants' hoard in the drought-dried field is the one store the raiders could not take.

thinai_evidence.note: the long drought and the raided, deserted village of the wealth-seeker's road

reading: With the hero hidden by night, the girl answers the friend who asked how she can live through the lord's parting, her angry mother's look and the anguished evenings of the cold season, in a land where wind shakes gold-like vengai pollen into brides' hair and the peacock cries sweet as a festival trumpet among the swaying bamboo: though the man who left after an oath does not think of her, she lives because the sky-touching peak of his hill, crowned with a singing waterfall where monkeys snatch jackfruit and frolic with their mates, is in sight.
nuance: The friend's question is put so that the hidden man hears the full list of what the girl bears, and the girl's answer, that she lives on the sight of his hill, is a reproach he cannot miss. The pair of monkeys at play in his own land is the togetherness he has denied her.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி சொல்லெடுப்பத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

comparisons.tenor: the vengai pollen
the peacock's cry

iraicchi.act: the female monkey, holding the jackfruit she snatched, frolics together with her mate
iraicchi.sense: in his own land even the monkeys keep their mates by them, while he who swore not to leave lives apart from her

reading: The man, home once with wealth and now pressed again by his heart, tells it that even sole rule of the sea-girt earth passes like a dream of the night, that he has not yet had his fill of her clinging embrace as she sleeps on his shoulder with her flower-crowned hair, and that if it makes him break his word and go, it will rest in the dappled shade of a burnt leafless forest, be struck by her many virtues, and pine on the endless road where a cow elephant trumpets for her tusker wounded by a tiger.
nuance: The argument against going is the impermanence of wealth, a puram commonplace, put to an akam use: since wealth passes, the embrace, not the treasure, is what should be held. The cow elephant crying for her wounded mate is what he expects to hear when the memory of the wife strikes him on the road.

colophon.thurai: முன்னொரு காலத்துப் பெருண்முற்றி வந்த தலைமகன் பின்னும் பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

comparisons.tenor: the passing of wealth
the embrace

iraicchi.sense: a mate cries out for the partner in danger, as the wife left behind will grieve for him on that road

reading: The friend, having agreed to help the hero, tells the girl that the lord of the shore who came alone, leaving his chariot far off, and drew near asking the name of their town, went away yesterday thoughtful after showing them a crab that tore a naaval fruit at the ford and carried it to its mate in its burrow under the screwpine, saying 'this is a fine way'; now his chariot is in sight, and he is so modest that if they do not receive him today he may resolve on that; should she hide behind the long white dune?
nuance: The man's comment on the crab is his only open speech, and it carries his intent: the crab that brings food home to its mate is the life he offers her. What he 'may resolve on' (அது) is left unsaid, and the friend's last question hands the decision to the girl.

title: நித்திலக்கோவை 381-400
theme: The last twenty poems of the Akananuru (Nittilakkovai 381 to 400), in the fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men gone for wealth and fame and of daughters gone with lovers, as heard by wives, friends and mothers; hill poems of night meetings, the diviner's rite and the pleading lover; mullai returns and invitations; a salt-girl met on the shore and a wedding chariot; and two Paranar courtesans who measure a lover's broken oath against the puram legends of Eyinan, Aththi and Vanji.
source_issues: 382: the colophon thurai reads தலைமகட்கச், a misprint for தலைமகட்குச்.
384: line 4 reads அறிந்தன்றொ இலெனே, apparently for அறிந்தன்றோ இலெனே.
386: the colophon thurai reads வாயின் மறத்தது, a misprint for வாயில் மறுத்தது.
387: the colophon thurai reads செலவபங்கச், a misprint for செலவழுங்கச்.
388: the colophon's second alternative reads தோழ தலைமகட்குச், a misprint for தோழி.
398: the colophon thurai carries a bracketed phrase (விரைவிடத்துக்கண்), apparently an editor's insertion.
400: lines 15 and 16 read பால்கண்ட டன்ன and கால்கண்ட டன்ன with a doubled ட, apparently for பால்கண்டன்ன and கால்கண்டன்ன.

reading: Halfway across the wasteland the man tells his heart that she at home must be suffering more than they who crossed it: her body wasted like an enemy fort the Chera Vaanavan's army razed, sighing long, her eyes like a pair of blue water-lilies brimming with tears.
nuance: The road is built of killers (the yali tearing the elephant's tusk, the sun that has eaten the shade, the Vadukar with their dogs, the blood-bathed vultures that make the sky look like dusk), and the turn at line 13 (நம்மினும்) makes all of it a measure of her pain rather than his danger. Line 3 (குருகருந்தும்) and line 7 (கற்றுரிக் குடம்பை) are hard words in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the man parted from her, crossing the wasteland

her body fallen to ruin

reading: With the lover listening outside at night, the friend tells the girl that their kin have resolved to hold the possession rite for Murugan, with kadamba tied, garlands, and many-voiced instruments, and that he, lord of the hill where a monkey floats down a waterfall on a jackfruit to the town's ford, must be told of it.
nuance: The opening maxim (others feel another's trouble; one's own trouble is one's own to bear) is aimed at the man: the rite would publish a sickness that is his doing, and the friend sends the news to him so that he will act. The monkey riding the jackfruit down to the big town's ford can be read as a hidden image of the girl carried into public talk, but no second correspondence is anchored, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the jackfruit and Murugan's rite of the hills

reading: The mother whose daughter has run off with a youth speaks to the vayalai creeper the girl watered every day and stripped for her leaf-skirt: the girl who never thought of the mother who raised her has crossed many lands with him amid the town's gossip, and now no one will water the withering creeper.
nuance: The mother cannot address the girl, so she addresses the plant, and its needs become an inventory of the daughter's lost daily life: the full water-pot, the jumping bangles, the ringing anklets, the glance at her mother's face as she came back. Line 5 suggests the creeper's leaves were also sought for the youth's garland.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has eloped across the wasteland

reading: Home from the king's campaign, the man asks his charioteer whether he yoked the wind or his own mind as horses, since he knew only that he mounted the chariot and then heard 'get down' at his wife's house in the mullai woodland; then he embraces him, takes him in, and the wife receives a guest.
nuance: The return is told as a lapse of time: longing has abolished the road. The last line turns the charioteer into the household's first guest, so the reunion is completed as hospitality.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai woodland, its millet village and its hares

comparisons.tenor: the speed of the horses
the charioteer's mind as the horses
the man's chest

reading: The foster mother grieves that the girl, who said nothing while her playmates and mothers prepared a festival in their house rich as the Chola's Uranthai, has gone off with her lover, swinging joyfully on a banyan's root in the wasteland as he pushes her, and that she should shed her anklets for him and go to an unknown land is cruel.
nuance: The swing scene is imagined, and imagined as happiness: the cruelty the foster mother names is not the girl's danger but her forgetting. The anklet removal (சிலம்பு கழீஇ) belongs to the wedding at home; the girl performs it, in the mother's mind, for the youth on the road. How lines 6 to 7 and 17 attach is not certain in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has left with her lover

comparisons.tenor: their rich mansion
her hair tossing as she swings

reading: The woman tells the husband, lord of a town where the otter hunts vaalai fish each day, that she felt the shame Kanaiyan felt when Paanan broke the Aariya wrestler, when his mistress came in secret by day, called herself a neighbour and a younger sister, stroked her brow and hair, and left.
nuance: The shame is double: she was flattered and touched by the rival who now has her husband, and she recognised the trick only after. The comparison to Kanaiyan's shame is a public one: a patron watching his champion fall in the ring. The otter's daily hunt for fresh fish is the husband's appetite.

reading: The friend tells the man leaving while his wife's jewels slip and her eyes weep to say, if he can, that he will come back, for the forest he goes to is one where a quail hen, frightened by the hunters' call, cries to her mate, and where at a lizard's small cry among the hero-stones even lords with elephants halt and turn back.
nuance: மன்னோ makes the request ironic: on a road ruled by omens no traveller can promise a return. Lines 4 to 8 (the washerwoman's starched cloth) seem to describe the quail's striped markings, but our text does not settle the construction, and the last line is obscure.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளது குறிப்பறிந்து தோழி தலைமகனைச் செலவபங்கச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave across the forest

iraicchi.act: the quail hen, frightened by the hunters' decoy call, calls her mate to her
iraicchi.sense: even the hen in danger calls her mate close, so the wife, afraid, needs the man beside her and he should not go

reading: The girl tells her friend, with the lover listening, how a young hunter with a hound came to their millet platform asking whether a wounded tusker had passed, and how, aching for him, she is now held by the mother's diviner, who says his god caused the sickness; she would ask the velan whether his god goes hunting with a bloodied arrow on a deer's track.
nuance: The question is a joke with a point: the 'god' who seized her is the hunter, and asking it would tell the truth to the household without a confession. The hunter's pretext (a wounded elephant) is the usual opening of the day meeting.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது. தோழ தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: guarding millet from a platform in the vengai, and Murugan's diviner

comparisons.tenor: the vengai's pollen
the hunter's flesh-smeared arrow

reading: The wife tells her friend that the man who once dressed her hair, painted her brow and breasts and shoulders, reddened her feet and would not leave her bed even by day has gone, to fill beggars' hands, silence his scorners and fix his fame, beyond the Chera Vaanavaramban's land into summer forest where a tiger that has killed a tusker roars like thunder.
nuance: She gives his reasons in her own voice, and they are the puram virtues (giving, honour, fame); the complaint is that those virtues are what took him. The adornments she lists are acts of his hands, so the memory is of being cared for, not only of being loved.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left her to seek wealth

occasion.words: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

comparisons.tenor: the tiger's roar

reading: The man tells his companion, or his heart, that his heart is lost to a salt-trader's girl who went from street to street calling 'paddy for salt, measure for measure', who, when he blocked her way and joked that he could not price the salt of her body, looked at him angrily, asked who he was to stop her, and walked off smiling.
nuance: The opening question (is the salt-carriers' wandering life a good one, then?) is the lover's envy of the people she belongs to. Her look is war and her smile is release, in one movement; the joke about the salt 'living in your body' is a flirtation she rebuffs and enjoys.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பாங்கற்குச் சொல்லியது; நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லிய தூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: salt from the brine pans and the salt-traders

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders

reading: The wife tells her friend that each time she sees the tuft of hair her lover dressed with athiral flowers the sellers could not sell and with mullai, she remembers the old adornment; even if he returns in a few days her eyes will not sleep, for he crossed summer wasteland where an elephant's limp trunk looks like a snake entering a hill.
nuance: The flowers he chose were the cheap ones the hawkers threw away, which makes the memory more intimate, not less. The elephant too weak to lift its tusks is the hot land's exhaustion, set against the care she remembers.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover has crossed the wasteland away from her

comparisons.tenor: the athiral buds

reading: The friend, having agreed to help the pleading lover, asks the girl to consent: his wasted body is like a tusker's that has lost its mate and refuses fodder, it would hurt to send him away ruined, and the lord of that roaring hill will hardly leave her; if he ever did, she herself would stand fast like Nannan and restore her beauty.
nuance: The night scene (a sling's crack scattering millet-raiding elephants, the tiger's roar, the jungle fowl's cry, the peacock dancing, the whole mountain afraid) shows a land in which one sound sets everything moving, as the friend hopes her word will. The story of Nannan holding his spear against a besieging king is told too briefly to be sure of.

reading: The friend tells the wife that though he has gone beyond Venkadam, past the land of Pulli where herders cook varagu millet and share it with milk among hungry travellers, he will not stay long, having forgotten the sweet sleep of her hair washed with thagaram and dressed with blue lily and athiral.
nuance: Most of the poem is the herders' cooking, told step by step (threshing on the rock, pounding, boiling in a stone hearth), and its point is that travellers on that road are fed: the comfort is that he is safe there. The closing memory of her dressed hair answers 391, where the wife looks at the same flowers.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone far on a journey for work

comparisons.tenor: the husked varagu grain
her thick hair

reading: Having brought the girl to the night meeting, the friend invites the lover, lord of great gifts, to come one day to their little home in the poor-soil village where a hare hides at the goatherd's whistle, and, after his young men have eaten termite-rice with curd and butter, to eat milk rice that his wife prepares there.
nuance: Line 1 is a pun: களவும் புளித்தன says the karanda fruit has soured, and also that the secret love has gone sour. 'Your wife' (நின் மனையோள்) names the girl as what she would be once married, so the invitation to a meal is a demand for marriage.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறித் தலைமகளை இடத்துய்த்து வந்து தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாஅயது.

reading: The wife tells her friend it would be good if he came back now to end the tears of eyes like rain-filled blue lilies, he who crossed the bamboo hills of dry forest where a stag, chasing a mirage and lost off the path, calls its grazing doe in a broken voice that travellers mistake for a man's.
nuance: The stag that ran after a mirage and lost its mate is set on his road: it is an image of what that land does to partners, and of the cry he will hear there.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has crossed the wasteland, leaving her

the stag's forked horns

reading: The courtesan holds her lover and will not let him go: Aay Eyinan died fighting Minjili at Paazhi to keep his word to those Nannan drove out, but he, after swearing before the god and taking her wrist, has become another's; she fears his wife will snatch him as the Kaviri snatched Aththi from Manthi, so he must give back her beauty, splendid as the Chera's Vanji, before he goes.
nuance: Each legend is chosen against him: Eyinan kept a promise of refuge with his life, the river's seizing of Aththi stands for the wife's claim, and Vanji, seat of the king who carved his bow on the northern mountain, prices the beauty he owes her. Line 10 (மார்புதரு கல்லாய்) can also be read as 'you who never learned to give your chest'.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan's quarrel with a married man

comparisons.tenor: the lover who broke his oath

reading: The foster mother says the hasty youth, instead of taking her daughter in marriage at their festive house, decided the cloudless wasteland would be easy for the girl and led her off before the cool season, through forest where a kite perches on a yaa tree, taking the red gash an elephant tore in an omai trunk for flesh.
nuance: Her grief is set against the wedding that should have been: the house where the drum never dries is named so that the elopement reads as a festival refused. The kite's mistake (red bark for meat) is the land's hunger. Line 2 is hard to construe in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the youth has led the girl away across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the red wound in the omai's bark

reading: Wasting with longing, the girl speaks to the flooding stream from her lover's hill: she reproaches it for slipping away ashamed under his hill's flowers instead of telling him of her pallor and tears, and asks what harm there would be if it rested a while in her father's flowering forest, before going back to the country where a spent elephant groans as it embraces its tired mate.
nuance: The stream is a messenger from his hill that she blames for his silence, and she offers it the hospitality she cannot offer him. The elephant that, wounded and spent, still holds its mate is the care his land knows and he withholds. Several lines (9 to 16) are hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: காமமிக்க கழிபடர் கிளவியால் (விரைவிடத்துக்கண்) தலைமகள் தலைமகன் வரையினின்றும் போந்த ஆற்றொடு புலந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country, its vengai and elephants

comparisons.tenor: her pallid body

iraicchi.act: the elephant, spent and wounded from fighting a tiger, still embraces its tired mate
iraicchi.sense: even the elephants of his hill hold their mates in distress, yet their lord leaves her to waste

reading: The friend tells the wife, whose hair smells like the Himalayan forest, that her husband will not stay away without coming back to embrace her as if drinking her in, though he crossed sun-scorched hills where a doe, chewing nelli fruit, listens to the lonely notes of herders' bamboo flutes as they rest their cattle in konrai shade.
nuance: The herders' flute is called lonely (புலம்புகொள்) and the doe listens to it: the road he is on is full of sounds of solitude that will turn him home.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband is away across the hills

comparisons.tenor: the nelli fruit
his embrace

reading: After the wedding the friend tells the bride it is laughable now that they once feared gossip even if she ran off with him: the day the lord of the shore came, his strong chariot racing over milk-white sand and mud like water down a ford, their old town of palmyras by the roaring sea looked new, the neythal buds opening and smelling of new toddy.
nuance: The chariot passage is the same apparatus akam uses for the lover's secret night visits, here driven openly to the wedding, so speed now means eagerness rather than stealth. The town that gossiped (அழுங்கல் ஊர்) is the town that looks new.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைந் தெய்திய பின்றைத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

title: பாலைக்கலி 1-18 (1/2)
theme: The invocation to Shiva the dancer and the first eighteen poems of Palai Padiya Perunkadungo's paalaikkali: nearly every poem is a debate over leaving home for wealth, in which the friend or the wife sets love, youth and the household against the giving, conquest and gain that wealth promises, often with long argued refrains and moral similes drawn from kingship and impermanence; several end with the man turning back, and one (9) has ascetics defend an elopement as the way of virtue.
source_issues: kalittokai: the core records carry no colophon thurai for any poem, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.
kalittokai:1: the invocation has no colophon thinai (the review notes some sources label it paalai); copied as null.
kalittokai:10 lines 5 and 21, kalittokai:16 line 9: ஃ restored from the old encoding (flag repaired).
kalittokai:16 line 14: a damaged word was replaced by the sangamtamil.com reading இடை (flag repaired); the sense (ஆர் இடை, the hard road) fits the refrain of lines 6 and 10.
kalittokai:5 line 9 (நாளும் கோள்மீன் தகைத்தலும் தகைமே) and kalittokai:1 line 17 (ஆணம்) are obscure; readings marked in nuance.

tamil: ஆறு அறி அந்தணர்க்கு, அருமறை பல பகர்ந்து,
தேறு நீர் சடைக் கரந்து, திரிபுரம் தீ மடுத்துக்,
கூறாமல் குறித்ததன் மேல் செல்லும், கடும் கூளி,
மாறாப் போர் மணி மிடற்று எண் கையாய்! கேள் இனி;
படு பறை பல இயம்பப், பல் உருவம் பெயர்த்து நீ
கொடுகொட்டி ஆடும்கால், கோடு உயர் அகல் அல்குல்
மண்டு அமர் பல கடந்து, மதுகையால் நீறு அணிந்து,
பண்டரங்கம் ஆடும்கால், பணை எழில் அணை மென்தோள்
வண்டு அரற்றும் கூந்தலாள், வளர் தூக்கு தருவாளோ?
கொலை உழுவைத் தோல் அசைஇக், கொன்றைத்தார் சுவல் புரளத்
தலை அங்கை கொண்டு நீ காபாலம் ஆடும்கால்,
முலை அணிந்த முறுவலாள் முன் பாணி தருவாளோ?
ஆணம் இல் பொருள் எமக்கு அமர்ந்தனை ஆடி.
reading: The invocation asks Shiva, who spoke the Vedas to the brahmins, hid the Ganga in his matted hair, burned the three cities and goes eight-armed and dark-throated with fierce goblins behind him, whether, when he dances the kodukotti, the pandarangam and the kapalam, his consort does not keep for him the beat, the measure and the rhythm; and says that with her keeping them he danced for us.
nuance: The three dances are named in the order of the three musical terms the goddess supplies (சீர், தூக்கு, பாணி), and line 15 gathers the terms back in reverse; the god is made a dancer who needs a partner to keep time, a fitting opening for an anthology in the kali metre, which was sung. The last line (ஆணம் இல் பொருள் எமக்கு அமர்ந்தனை ஆடி) turns on the rare word ஆணம், and its sense is not settled.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his dances, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து of paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the goddess, her waist slender as a creeper

tamil: அடங்காதார் மிடல் சாய, அமரர் வந்து இரத்தலின்,
மடங்கல் போல் சினைஇ, மாயம் செய் அவுணரைக்
உடன்றக்கால், முகம் போல ஒண் கதிர் தெறுதலின்
ஏறு பெற்று உதிர்வன போல், வரை பிளந்து, இயங்குநர்
ஆறு கெட விலங்கிய அழல் அவிர் ஆர் இடை -
மறப்பு அரும் காதல் இவள் ஈண்டு ஒழிய,
தொலைவு ஆகி, இரந்தோர்க்கு ஒன்று ஈயாமை இழிவு என
மலை இறந்து செயல் சூழ்ந்த பொருள் பொருள் ஆகுமோ -
முலை ஆகம் பிரியாமை பொருள் ஆயின் அல்லதை;
இல் என இரந்தோர்க்கு ஒன்று ஈயாமை இழிவு எனக்
கல் இறந்து செயல் சூழ்ந்த பொருள் பொருள் ஆகுமோ -
தொல் இயல் வழாஅமைத் துணை எனப் புணர்ந்தவள்
புல் ஆகம் பிரியாமை பொருள் ஆயின் அல்லதை;
இடன் இன்றி இரந்தோர்க்கு ஒன்று ஈயாமை இழிவு எனக்
கடன் இறந்து செயல் சூழ்ந்த பொருள் பொருள் ஆகுமோ -
வடமீன் போல் தொழுது ஏத்த வயங்கிய கற்பினாள்
தட மென் தோள் பிரியாமை பொருள் ஆயின் அல்லதை;
புன்கண் கொண்டு இனையவும், பொருள் வயின் அகறல்
அன்பு அன்று, என்று யான் கூற, அன்புற்றுக்
காழ் வரை நில்லாக் கடும் களிற்று ஒருத்தல்
reading: The friend tells the woman that when the man resolved to cross a waste split and burning as if Shiva had struck the three forts, she asked him three times whether wealth sought across hills because refusing a suppliant is shameful is truly wealth, unless it be not leaving the breast of the chaste wife who will not live without him, and that, told this is not love, he bowed like a tusker that no post can hold yet stops at the sound of the lute, and stayed by her word, afraid her old beauty would fade.
nuance: The friend grants the man the most honourable motive the Sangam knows, wealth to give to those who ask (இரந்தோர்க்கு ஒன்று ஈயாமை இழிவு), and still sets the wife's shoulders above it; the triple refrain changes only the word for what he crosses (மலை, கல், கடன்) and the word for her body. The tusker that breaks every tether but stops for the lute makes her speech the music that tames him.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's resolve to leave for wealth and its prevention

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend reports to the wife how she dissuaded the man (lines 9 to 22 are her speech to him)

comparisons.tenor: Shiva's anger against the asuras, like a lion's
the sun's burning, like the face of the three-eyed god in anger
the hills split by the heat, like the forts falling when struck
the wife's chastity, worshipped like the northern star

comparisons.vehicle: கடும் களிற்று ஒருத்தல் யாழ் வரைத் தங்கியாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the man checked by the friend's words, as a wild tusker is held by lute music

tamil: அறன் இன்றி அயல் தூற்றும் அம்பலை நாணியும்,
வறன் நீந்தி நீ செல்லும் நீள் இடை நினைப்பவும் -
இறை நில்லா வளை ஓட, இதழ் சோர்பு பனி மல்கப்,
பொறை நில்லா நோயோடு புல்லென்ற நுதல் இவள்
விறல் நலன் இழப்பவும், வினை வேட்டாய்! கேஎள் இனி;
'உடை இவள் உயிர் வாழாள், நீ நீப்பின்' எனப், பல
இடை கொண்டு யாம் இரப்பவும், எம கொள்ளாய், ஆயினை;
கடைஇய ஆற்று இடை, நீர் நீத்த வறும் சுனை,
'வல்லை நீ துறப்பாயேல், வகை வாடும் இவள்' என,
ஒல்லாங்கு யாம் இரப்பவும், உணர்ந்து ஈயாய் ஆயினை;
செல்லு நீள் ஆற்று இடைச், சேர்ந்து எழுந்த மரம் வாடப்,
புல்லு விட்டு இறைஞ்சிய பூங் கொடி - தகைப்பன.
'பிணிபு நீ விடல் சூழின், பிறழ்தரும் இவள்' எனப்
பணிபு வந்து இரப்பவும், பல சூழ்வாய் ஆயினை;
துணிபு நீ செலக் கண்ட ஆற்று இடை, அம்மரத்து
அணி செல, வாடிய அம் தளிர் - தகைப்பன.
யாம் நின் கூறவும் எம கொள்ளாய் ஆயினை;
ஆனாது இவள் போல் அருள் வந்தவை காட்டி,
மேல் நின்று மெய் கூறும் கேளிர் போல், நீ செல்லும்
reading: The friend tells the man who is set on his venture that, since he would not heed their pleas that she, shamed by the gossip and wasting, will not live if he leaves, the things he will meet on the road (a dried spring with its flowers withered, a flowering creeper drooping from a withered tree, scorched young leaves) will themselves stop him, showing him, like kin who speak the truth, what has suffered as she has.
nuance: The friend gives up on persuasion and hands the argument to the landscape: each stanza pairs a plea refused with a withered thing that will stop him (தகைப்பன), so the paalai land, usually the danger, becomes her advocate. Because the poem states the likeness itself (இவள் போல்), the withered things are an open comparison, not a hidden one.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave her for his venture

comparisons.tenor: the spring, creeper and leaves on the road, which have suffered as she has
the forest that will check his going, like kin who tell the truth

tamil: வலி முன்பின், வல்லென்ற யாக்கைப் புலி நோக்கின் -
அற்றம் பார்த்து அல்கும் - கடுங்கண் மறவர் தாம்
புள்ளும் வழங்காப் புலம்பு கொள் ஆர் இடை,
வெள் வேல் வலத்திர் பொருள் தரல் வேட்கையின்,
தாழ் கதுப்பு அணிகுவர், காதலர்; மற்று, அவர்
'முள் உறழ் முளை எயிற்று அமிழ்து ஊறும் தீ நீரைக்
கள்ளினும் மகிழ் செயும் என உரைத்தும் அமையார், என்
ஒள் இழை திருத்துவர், காதலர்; மற்று, அவர்
'நுண் எழில் மாமை சுணங்கு அணி ஆகம் தம்
கண்ணொடு தொடுத்து என நோக்கியும் அமையார், என்
ஒண் நுதல் நீவுவர், காதலர்; மற்று, அவர்
'கழி பெரு நல்கல் ஒன்று உடைத்து!' என, என் தோழி
ஒழிக இனிப் பெரும! நின் பொருள் பிணிச் செலவே.
reading: The friend tells the man that the woman knows he means to cross for wealth the waste where tiger-eyed bowmen kill travellers even with nothing to take, only to watch them writhe: she says that, not content with embracing her, he dresses her hair, not content with praising her mouth as sweeter than toddy, he sets her jewels straight, not content with gazing, he strokes her brow, and that this excess of tenderness hides something; she would not live a day without him, so let him give up this journey.
nuance: The woman reads the leaving in the caresses themselves: each refrain begins with what he does too much (அமையார், 'not content') and ends 'what is he thinking? I do not know'. The bowmen of the opening kill those who carry nothing, so the friend quietly answers the wealth motive in advance: on this road wealth protects no one.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's planned journey for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the bowmen's gaze, a tiger's
her budding teeth, sharp as thorns
the sweetness of her mouth, more delighting than toddy

tamil: பாஅல் அம் செவிப் பணைத் தாள் மா நிரை
இறந்து, நீர் செய்யும் பொருளினும், யாம் நுமக்குச்
நீள் இரு முந்நீர் வளி கலன் வௌவலின்
கல்லெனக் கவின் பெற்ற விழவு ஆற்றுப்படுத்த பின்,
புல்லென்ற களம் போலப் புலம்பு கொண்டு, அமைவாளோ?
ஆள்பவர் கலக்குற அலை பெற்ற நாடு போல்,
நீர் நீத்த மலர் போல, நீ நீப்பின், வாழ்வாளோ?
அந்நாள் கொண்டு இறக்கும், இவள் அரும்பெறல் உயிரே.
reading: The friend tells the man that if he knew they were dearer to him than the wealth he would win across a waste where herds and elephants mingle with bowmen and paths are lost, he would not be like traders ruined when the wind seizes their ships; she asks whether the woman will bear it, desolate like a festival ground after the festival, like a land ravaged by its own rulers, or live like a lotus a night out of water, and says that on whatever day he goes her life will go.
nuance: Line 9 (நாளும் கோள்மீன் தகைத்தலும் தகைமே) is obscure; on one reading the friend says that holding back even the planets on their course would be fitting for such a man, an ironic concession. The close does not ask him to stay: it makes the date of his leaving the date of her death, so that he must choose a day knowing what it names.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighing a journey across the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the man who leaves love for gain, like sea traders whose ships the wind took
her desolation, like a festival ground after the festival
her ruined face, like a land harried by those who rule it
her life without him, like a lotus a night out of water

tamil: வரை ஓங்கு அரும் சுரத்து ஆர் இடைச் செல்வோர்,
சுரை அம்பு மூழ்கச் சுருங்கிப், புரையோர் தம்
உள் நீர் வறப்பப் புலர் வாடு நாவிற்குத் -
என் நீர் அறியாதீர் போல இவை கூறல்?
அன்பு அறச் சூழாதே, ஆற்று இடை நும்மொடு
துன்பம் துணை ஆக நாடின், அது அல்லது
reading: The woman answers the man who has painted the waste to her (antelope eating marral, the rains failed, travellers shot and shrunk, tongues dry for water, tears the only wetness) by asking why he speaks as if he did not know her: it is unlike him; if he would think of her with love and take her along with hardship for a companion, what other pleasure could she want?
nuance: She turns his deterrent catalogue round: the harder the road, the more it needs a companion; துன்பம் துணை ஆக makes hardship itself the shared thing. The plural எம் may be the friend speaking for her, as often in this book.

thinai_evidence.note: she asks to share the road he fears to take her on

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman (or the friend in her voice) answers his description of the road

comparisons.tenor: the man speaking as though he did not know her nature

tamil: வேனில் உழந்த வறிது உயங்கு ஓய் களிறு
வான் நீங்கு வைப்பின் வழங்காத் தேர் நீர்க்கு அவாஅம்
கானம் கடத்திர், எனக் கேட்பின், யான் ஒன்று
நீயே, செய் வினை மருங்கில் செலவு அயர்ந்து, யாழ நின்
கை புனை வல் வில் ஞாண் உளர்தீயே;
மை இல் வாள் முகம் பசப்பு ஊருமே;
நீயே, வினை மாண் காழகம் வீங்கக் கட்டிப்
இவட்கே, சுனை மாண் நீலம் கார் எதிர்பவை போல்,
இனை நோக்கு உண் கண் நீர் நில்லாவே;
நீயே, புலம்பு இல் உள்ளமொடு பொருள் வயின் செலீஇய
இவட்கே, அலங்கு இதழ்க் கோடல் வீ உகுபவை போல்
இலங்கு ஏர் எல் வளை இறை ஊரும்மே;
செல் நவை அரவத்தும் இனையவள் நீ நீப்பின்,
reading: The friend asks the man, who means to cross a forest where a tusker worn by summer craves mirage water, one thing: as he plucks his bowstring her bright face darkens like the sun's disc clouded, as he binds his quiver and picks his arrows her eyes overflow like spring lilies meeting rain, as he strokes his chariot wheel her bangles slip like falling kodal petals; she suffers at the very noise of his going, so can the wealth he toils for in that land give her back her life?
nuance: The three stanzas pair each of his war-like preparations with a sign in her body (நீயே ... இவட்கே), so that the leaving happens twice, in his gear and in her; line 18 makes the point that she is undone by the noise of the preparations (அரவத்தும்) before he has gone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man preparing to leave for wealth across a summer forest

comparisons.tenor: her face growing pale, like the sun's disc darkened

comparisons.vehicle: சுனை மாண் நீலம் கார் எதிர்பவை போல்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes brimming with tears, like spring lilies taking the rain
her bangles slipping, like kodal petals falling

tamil: நடுவு இகந்து ஒரீஇ நயன் இல்லான் வினை வாங்கக்,
கொடிது ஓர்த்த மன்னவன் கோல் போல, ஞாயிறு
உறல் ஊறு கமழ் கடாத்து ஒல்கிய, எழில் வேழம்
வறன் உழு நாஞ்சில் போல் மருப்பு ஊன்ற, நிலம் சேர,
விறல் மலை வெம்பிய போக்கு அரு வெஞ்சுரம்,
வீழுநர்க்கு இறைச்சியாய் விரல் கவர்பு இசைக்கும் கோல்
ஏழும், தம் பயன் கெட இடை நின்ற நரம்பு அறூஉம்
பிரியும்கால் பிறர் எள்ளப், பீடு இன்றி புறம் மாறும்
புரை தவப் பயன் நோக்கார் தம் ஆக்கம் முயல்வாரை
வரைவு இன்றிச் செறும் பொழுதில், கண் ஓடாது உயிர் வௌவும்
இன் உறல் வியன் மார்ப! அது மனும் பொருளே.
reading: The friend tells the man, who resolved without a word to cross a burnt hill-waste where the sun scorches like the sceptre of an unjust king and a weakened elephant leans on its tusks like a plough, that wealth is less stable than a lute whose seven strings fail when the middle one snaps, than Fortune who leaves those she embraced to be mocked, than a king who kills without mercy; he should not desire it and should stay, for to live in his own house under the king's protection, feeding guests, is wealth indeed.
nuance: Line 9 uses இறைச்சி in its plain sense, the delight the lute gives its lovers, not the poetic device. The poem ends by redefining wealth (அது மனும் பொருளே): the household that feeds guests under a just king is already what the journey seeks, which lets the friend oppose the journey on the householder's own terms.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's resolve to cross the waste for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the sun's scorching, like the rule of a king who has chosen cruelty
the elephant's tusks dug into the ground, like a plough in dry earth
wealth, less lasting than a lute whose strings fail
wealth, less lasting than Fortune who deserts those she held
wealth, less to be trusted than a king who kills without pity

tamil: எறித்தரு கதிர் தாங்கி ஏந்திய குடை நீழல்,
உறித் தாழ்ந்த கரகமும், உரை சான்ற முக்கோலும்,
நெறிப்பட சுவல் அசைஇ, வேறு ஓரா நெஞ்சத்துக்
குறிப்பு ஏவல் செயல் மாலைக், கொளை நடை அந்தணீர்!-
வெவ் இடைச் செலல் மாலை ஒழுக்கத்தீர்; இவ் இடை
என் மகள் ஒருத்தியும், பிறள் மகன் ஒருவனும்,
தம் உளே புணர்ந்த தாம் அறி புணர்ச்சியர்;
ஆண் எழில் அண்ணலோடு அரும் சுரம் முன்னிய
மாண் இழை மடவரல் தாயிர் நீர் போறிர்;
பல உறு நறும் சாந்தம் படுப்பவர்க்கு அல்லதை,
மலை உளே பிறப்பினும், மலைக்கு அவை தாம் என் செய்யும்?
நீர் உளே பிறப்பினும், நீர்க்கு அவை தாம் என் செய்யும்?
தேரும்கால் நும் மகள் நுமக்கும் ஆங்கு அனையளே!
ஏழ் புணர் இன் இசை முரல்பவர்க்கு அல்லதை,
யாழ் உளே பிறப்பினும், யாழ்க்கு அவை தாம் என் செய்யும்?
அறம் தலை பிரியா ஆறும் மற்று அதுவே.
reading: A mother following her eloped daughter asks brahmin ascetics with umbrella, water-pot and triple staff whether they saw a girl and a boy joined in a love only they knew; they answer that they did, and, calling her the girl's mother, tell her that sandal is no use to the hill it grows on, pearls none to the sea, music none to the lute, but to those who wear and play them: so her daughter is to her; let her not grieve for a girl of surpassing chastity who has gone to follow the man she chose, for that is the way that never leaves virtue.
nuance: The answer comes from renouncers, the people least bound to household claims, and they judge the elopement by aram: following the chosen man is itself the righteous way (அறம் தலை பிரியா ஆறு). The three images all say that a thing's worth lies in its use by another, which cuts the parent's claim at the root.

thinai_evidence.note: a mother tracking a daughter who has eloped across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the brahmin ascetics on the road answer the mother, whose question (lines 1 to 8) is quoted; tradition gives the search to the foster mother, but the text says என் மகள்

comparisons.tenor: the daughter, who belongs to the man she goes with, not to the house she was born in
the daughter, of use to the one who wears her, not to the waters that bore her
the daughter, whose music is for the one who plays, not for the lute

tamil: சிறியவன் செல்வம் போல், சேர்ந்தார்க்கு நிழல் இன்றி,
யார் கண்ணும் இகந்து செய்து இசை கெட்டான் இறுதி போல்,
வேரொடு மரம் வெம்ப, விரி கதிர் தெறுதலின்
அலவுற்றுக் குடி கூவ, ஆறு இன்றிப் பொருள் வெஃகிக்,
கொலை அஞ்சா வினைவரால், கோல் கோடியவன் நிழல்
உலகு போல், உலறிய உயர் மர வெஞ்சுரம் -
இடை கொண்டு பொருள் வயின் இறத்தி நீ எனக் கேட்பின்,
உடைபு நெஞ்சு உக ஆங்கே ஒளி ஓடற்பாள் மன்னோ!
படை அமை சேக்கையுள் பாயலின் அறியாய் நீ
புடை பெயர்வாய் ஆயினும், புலம்பு கொண்டு இனைபவள்?
முனிவு இன்றி முயல் பொருட்கு இறத்தி நீ எனக் கேட்பின்,
பனிய கண் படல் ஒல்லா படர் கூர்கிற்பாள் மன்னோ!
நனி கொண்ட சாயலாள் நயந்து நீ நகை ஆகத்
துனி செய்து நீடினும், துறப்பு அஞ்சிக் கலுழ்பவள்?
பொருள் நோக்கிப் பிரிந்து நீ போகுதி எனக் கேட்பின்,
மருள் நோக்கம் மடிந்து ஆங்கே மயல் கூர்கிற்பாள் மன்னோ!
இருள் நோக்கம் இடையின்றி, ஈரத்தின் இயன்ற நின்
அருள் நோக்கம் அழியினும், அவலம் கொண்டு அழிபவள்?
'வினை வெஃகி நீ செலின், விடும் இவள் உயிர்' எனப்
புனை இழாய்! நின் நிலை யான் கூறப், பையென,
reading: The friend tells the woman that she warned the man that the waste, its trees withered like a poor man's youth, shadeless like a mean man's wealth, burnt to the root like the end of one who harmed all and lost his name, dried like a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill, would break her who weeps if he only turns in bed, frets if he lingers in play, and grieves if his kind look fails; told that she would die if he went, the spear-bearing lord gave up the journey, so let her bangles sit tight again.
nuance: Each simile for the waste is a moral failure: the poor man's wasted youth, the mean man's wealth, the infamous man's end, the tyrant's realm. The paalai land is drawn from the ethics of the state and of giving, so the man who crosses it for wealth is shown the fate of wealth misused before he sets out.

thinai_evidence.note: a journey for wealth across the waste, now given up

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend reports her plea to the man (lines 8 to 19) and his giving up the journey

comparisons.tenor: the withered branches, like a poor man's youth that bears no fruit
the shadeless trees, like a mean man's wealth that shelters no one
the trees burnt to the root, like the end of one who lost his name by harming all
the dried waste, like a land under a crooked-sceptred king whose agents seize and kill

tamil: பெரிது ஆய பகை வென்று பேணாரைத் தெறுதலும்,
புரிவு அமர் காதலின் புணர்ச்சியும் தரும்' எனப்
பிரிவு எண்ணிப் பொருள் வயின் சென்ற நம் காதலர்
வருவர்கொல், வயங்கு இழாஅய்! வலிப்பல், யான்; கேஎள் இனி:
'அடி தாங்கும் அளவு இன்றி, அழல் அன்ன வெம்மையால்,
பிடி ஊட்டிப், பின் உண்ணும் களிறு, எனவும், உரைத்தனரே;
மென் சிறகரால் ஆற்றும் புறவு, எனவும், உரைத்தனரே;
'கல் மிசை வேய் வாடக் கனை கதிர் தெறுதலான்,
தன் நிழலைக் கொடுத்து அளிக்கும் கலை, எனவும், உரைத்தனரே.
புனை நலம் வாட்டுநர் அல்லர்; மனை வயின்
reading: The woman tells her friend she is sure their lover, who left for wealth saying it brings the means to give to the deserving, victory over enemies and the joy of union, will return: when he said the forest was too hot to tread, leafless and burning, he also said that in it the tusker lets his mate drink the little muddy water before him, the dove fans its tired mate with its soft wings, and the stag gives its own shadow to the shadeless doe; such a forest will not make him wither her beauty, and the house lizard has chirped well and her eye throbs.
nuance: Three pairs carry the same iraicchi (the tusker that lets his mate drink first, the dove that fans its mate, the stag that shades the doe); the schema holds one carrier, so the elephant is tagged and the dove and stag are marked with the same role. Deleting any of them leaves her conclusion and the omens of lines 21 and 22 standing. Lines 1 to 3 name the three ends of wealth, giving, conquest and love, so the absence is justified by aram, porul and inbam at once; and she reads his own warnings about the forest against him.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman waits for the man who has gone for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the forest's heat, like fire

iraicchi.act: the tusker feeds his mate the little muddy water first and drinks after her
iraicchi.sense: the man who saw such care on his road will keep faith and come back to care for her

tamil: இடு முள் நெடு வேலி போலக், கொலைவர்
கடு நவை ஆர் ஆற்று, அறு சுனை முற்றி,
உடங்கு நீர் வேட்ட உடம்பு உயங்கு யானை
கடும் தாம் பதிபு, ஆங்கு கை தெறப்பட்டு,
வெறி நிரை வேறு ஆகச் சார்ச் சாரல் ஓடி,
சிறு நனி நீ துஞ்சி ஏற்பினும், அஞ்சும்
நறு நுதல் நீத்துப் பொருள் வயின் செல்வோய்!
உரன் உடை உள்ளத்தை, செய் பொருள் முற்றிய
கடை நாள் இது என்று அறிந்தாரும் இல்லை;
reading: The friend tells the man, who would leave her of the fragrant brow, who fears even if he sleeps a little apart, to cross a road where cairns over men killed by bowmen stand like a thorn fence and thirsty elephants lose their way among dried springs, that he calls the yield of his work true wealth, but youth and love will not stay in his hand; let him not let the days of embrace pass, for no one knows which day is the last, and he who spoils love for wealth goes the way of those who forget death and age.
nuance: The cairns (பதுக்கை) heaped over travellers killed on the road are memorials of violent death, not hero-stones, so they are scene here. The argument is a memento mori turned toward love: because the last day is unknown (கடை நாள் இது என்று அறிந்தாரும் இல்லை), the present embrace, not future wealth, is what must not be wasted.

thinai_evidence.note: the man about to leave her for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the line of cairns over the slain, like a long fence of thorn
the man who sets wealth above love, alike with those who forget death and age

tamil: செரு மிகு சின வேந்தன் சிவந்து இறுத்த புலம் போல,
எரி மேய்ந்த கரி வறல் வாய் புகுவ காணாவாய்ப்,
திரி மருப்பு ஏறொடு தேர் அறற்கு ஓட,
மரல் சாய மலை வெம்ப, மந்தி உயங்க,
உரல் போல் அடிய உடம்பு உயங்கு யானை,
ஊறு நீர் அடங்கலின், உண் கயம் காணாது,
சேறு சுவைத்துத், தம் செல் உயிர் தாங்கும்
புயல் துளி மாறிய, போக்கு அரு, வெஞ்சுரம் -
எல் வளை! எம்மொடு நீ வரின், யாழ நின்
அல்லி சேர் ஆய் இதழ் அரக்குத் தோய்ந்தவை போலக்
நலம்பெறு சுடர் நுதால்! எம்மொடு நீ வரின்,
இலங்கு மாண் அவிர் தூவி அன்ன மென் சேக்கையுள்,
துலங்கு மான் மேல் ஊர்தித் துயில் ஏற்பாய், மற்று ஆண்டை
விலங்கு மான் குரல் கேட்பின், வெருவுவை அல்லையோ?
கிளி புரை கிளவியாய்! எம்மொடு நீ வரின்,
தளி பொழி தளிர் அன்ன எழில் மேனி கவின் வாட,
முளி அரில் பொத்திய முழங்கு அழல் இடை போழ்ந்த
வளி உறின், அவ் எழில் வாடுவை அல்லையோ?
பிரிகுவர்' எனப் பெரிது அழியாது, திரிபு உறீஇக்,
reading: The friend tells the woman not to despair that he will leave: the man said that if she came with him across the burnt waste (black as a field a raging king has fired, where spotted does and stags run to mirages, monkeys droop and mortar-footed elephants suck mud) her lotus soles would blacken on the stones, she who sleeps on swan-soft beds would start at the cries of beasts, and her leaf-like body would wither in the wind off burning brush; unless the forest is truly hard he will not leave her; he said it in jest, to see her tremble.
nuance: The friend reinterprets the man's catalogue of dangers as a lover's teasing (நகை குறித்தனரே), so the same speech that elsewhere announces a parting is here a test of her fear. Line 16 (துலங்கு மான் மேல் ஊர்தி) is unclear: மான் may be the lion-carved bed or a mount.

reading: The friend asks the man, who would cross a road where bowmen with bowstrings that roar like lions and beards curled like a stag's horns, who do not flee even from kings' armies, wound men for gain without mercy, whether fresh wealth can restore her beauty, like young asoka leaves, once pallor eats it, whether learning and pure penance can restore her moon face once pallor covers it like the snake on the moon, whether lasting union can restore her lily eyes once they drip like a lamp spitting oil: wealth can be made any day, but will it bring back her youth once it has gone?
nuance: The three questions pit three goods the man might gain abroad, wealth, learning and penance, and lasting union, against three losses that none of them can restore. title: பாலைக்கலி 19-36 (2/2)
theme: The second half of Perunkadunko's paalaikkali (19 to 36): seven poems in which the woman or her friend argues against the man's leaving for wealth (his false promises, wealth moving by former deeds, love as a loan repaid with another face, the deer and elephant that keep together on the waste), then eleven spring poems in which the season's flowers, bees and cuckoos torment the woman left at home in Madurai by the Vaigai, most ending with the friend announcing that the man has come back on the promised day; the similes are drawn heavily from kingship, friendship and virtue.

தாள் நிழல் கைவிட்டு யான் தவிர்தலைச் சூழ்வலே?
கணை கழிகல்லாத கல் பிறங்கு ஆர் இடைப்
reading: The woman answers the man who warns her off the waste where the sun's rage has dried the land, elephants languish, the hill burns and the pools are dust: to his 'can your feet bear a forest that never knew rain?' she says the days of life stay less than wind and she has his chest as her grace, so why perish in grief; to his 'there is no water on the road' she says youth runs off like river water and she has his heart for clear water, so why stay here bewildered; to his 'there are no shady trees there' she says she knows her colour will fade like shaded leaves, so why leave the shade of his feet; and to his 'the forest is too hot to approach' she asks whether he will not see, on the rocky track where no arrow passes, the doe following the handsome stag, and whether they part.
nuance: Each of his warnings flatters a part of her (parrot speech, nectar mouth, bamboo shoulders) and each answer turns it: her life is shorter than wind, her youth flows away like the river, her colour already fades; the poem ends not with argument but with the deer pair he will meet on the very road, which she makes his own witness against going alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man leaving for the waste and the woman refusing to stay behind

tamil: ஈர் நறும் கமழ் கடாஅத்து, இனம் பிரி ஒருத்தல்
ஆறு கடி கொள்ளும் வேறு புலம் படர்,
பழ வினை மருங்கின், பெயர்பு பெயர்பு உறையும்;
அன்ன பொருள் வயின் பிரிவோய் - நின் இன்று
அமை கவின் கொண்ட தோள் இணை மறந்தே.
reading: The friend tells the man that he has spoken two things, the graceless word that he must leave for wealth to the far land where a lone tusker, cut off from its herd, with milk-white tusks and mortar-like feet, guards the road, and the kind word, stroking her brow, that he will not leave her and she must not fear; which of them is true, she asks, when wealth does not stay with those who call themselves its owners but moves from one to another by former deeds; for such wealth he leaves, and without him the girl will not live the space of a blink, forgetting the beauty of her shoulders.
nuance: The friend turns the man's reason against him: if wealth comes and goes by பழ வினை, no journey can earn it, while the girl's life cannot be had again. The lone tusker that has left its herd (இனம் பிரி ஒருத்தல்) is a near miss for iraicchi: it mirrors the man who leaves his own, but it stands inside his own description of the road and does nothing a person of the situation does beyond being alone.

tamil: உண் கடன் வழிமொழிந்து இரக்கும்கால் முகனும், தாம்
பண்டும் இவ் உலகத்து இயற்கை; அஃது இன்றும்
நலன் உடையார் மொழிக் கண் தாவார்; தாம் தம் நலம்
தாது தேர் பறவையின் அருந்து, இறல் கொடுக்கும்கால்,
ஏதிலார் கூறுவது எவனோ நின் பொருள் வேட்கை?
நறு முல்லை நேர் முகை ஒப்ப நிரைத்த
செறி முறை பாராட்டினாய்; மற்று, எம் பல்லின்
நெய் இடை நீவி மணி ஒளி விட்டன்ன
குளன் அணி தாமரைப் பாசு அரும்பு ஏய்க்கும்
அடர் பொன் அவிர் ஏய்க்கும் அவ் வரி வாடச்,
சுடர் காய் சுரம் போகும் நும்மை யாம் எம் கண்
படர் கூற நின்றதும் உண்டோ - தொடர் கூரத்,
reading: The woman tells the man that a borrower's face when he asks and when he repays differ, as the world has always known; women of beauty go where their lovers' word leads them, like dolls a mother has given life to, and once their beauty has been sipped as a bee sips pollen, what is this wealth strangers talk of? He praised her teeth set like jasmine buds, her hair glowing like gems through oil, her breasts like the green lotus buds of the pond; did he ever praise the teeth falling, the hair's later care, the slack breasts? And as he goes to the sun-scorched waste while the gold-bright lines of her skin fade, she asks whether they ever stood before him telling their grief when want pressed hard.
nuance: The opening proverb makes love a loan: he borrowed her youth with one face and will repay it with another. Each praise is answered by the same part grown old, so his catalogue of beauty becomes a contract for her whole life. The closing question seems to say they never complained to him of poverty, so his journey answers a need they never voiced; lines 5 to 8 and 19 to 22 are hard and this reading is not settled.

tamil: புலம் கடி கவணையின், பூஞ் சினை உதிர்க்கும்
விலங்கு மலை வெம்பிய போக்கு அரு வெஞ்சுரம்
reading: The woman tells the man that for him to cross alone the burnt waste of blocking hills, where elephant-scarers' slings knock the flowers from the boughs, while she stays behind, would make her a mockery to this gossiping town; she will neither eat nor live, for women whose beauty is enjoyed and then abandoned are like a leaf cup once its water is drunk, like a town its dwellers have left, like a flower thrown away once worn, and she is such in his heart; so let him keep her heart, which runs to him like a young doe that, hunted by killing dogs, takes refuge with the netters, and not send it back to her.
nuance: The doe that flees the dogs into the hunters' nets is the poem's sharpest figure: her heart goes for safety to the very man whose leaving hurts her, and she asks him to keep it rather than return it. குடை in line 9 seems to be a leaf cup thrown away after drinking; வேள் நீர் is not clear.

thinai_evidence.note: he crosses the waste alone and she is left behind

tamil: அஞ்சியது ஆங்கே அணங்கு ஆகும்', என்னும் சொல் -
இன் தீம் கிளவியாய்! - வாய் மன்ற; நின் கேள்
'இது ஒன்று உடைத்து' என எண்ணி, அது தேர,
மாசு இல் வண் சேக்கை மணந்த புணர்ச்சியுள்,
பாயல் கொண்டு என் தோள் கனவுவார்; ஆய் கோல்,
கடி மனை காத்து ஓம்ப வல்லுவள் கொல்லோ?
செய் பொருள் முற்றும் அளவு?” என்றார்; ஆய் இழாய்!
தாம் இடை கொண்டது அது ஆயின், தம் இன்றி
யாம் உயிர் வாழும் மதுகை இலேம் ஆயின்,
reading: The woman tells her friend that the saying 'what one fears, hearing it and suspecting it with a trembling heart, becomes the very affliction' is true: when her man kept praising her as if she were new, she sensed something and, to find it out, lay with him on the clean wide bed; asleep and dreaming of her shoulders he said, 'Will she of the bangled wrists bear it without breaking and guard the house while I cross the long-hilled waste, where tusked elephants run to the mirage, and stay until the wealth is won?'; if that is his mind, since she has no strength to live without him, and lest small people blame him as the man who left her, her life has gone with him: let the friend tell him so.
nuance: The departure is learned from sleep-talk: he says in a dream what he will not say awake, and the proverb that opens the poem (அஞ்சியது ஆங்கே அணங்கு ஆகும்) frames it as a fear made real by being looked into. Her life leaving with him is offered to save his name, not hers. Line 11 is supplied from another witness (see source_issues).

thinai_evidence.note: the man's planned journey for wealth, overheard in his sleep

tamil: கை புனை அரக்கு இல்லைக் கதழ் எரி சூழ்ந்தாங்குக்,

ஈங்கு நீர் அளிக்கும்கால் இறை சிறந்து, ஒரு நாள் நீர்
நீங்கும்கால், நெகிழ்பு ஓடும் வளை எனவும் உள அன்றோ?

ஒல்கு இடத்து உலப்பு இலா உணர்வு இலார் தொடர்பு போல்;
ஒரு நாள் நீர் அளிக்கும்கால் ஒளி சிறந்து ஒரு நாள் நீர்
பாராட்டாக்கால் பசக்கும் நுதல் எனவும் உள அன்றோ?
பொருந்திய கேண்மையின் மறை உணர்ந்து, அம் மறை
பிரிந்தக்கால் பிறர்க்கு உரைக்கும் பீடு இலார் தொடர்பு போல்;
யாம் நின் கூறுவது எவன் உண்டு? எம்மினும்
துளி மாறு பொழுதின், இவ் உலகம் போலும் - நின்
அளி மாறு பொழுதின், இவ் ஆய் இழை கவினே.
reading: The friend tells the man that he would cross the waste where fire rings a hill of dry bamboo with rutting elephants inside, as fire ringed the lac house built by the plot of the blind king's eldest son with the five kings within, and where the bull elephant, as the wind's son broke the lac house and went out with his kin, tramples a path through the smoke and leaves with his herd; let him hear her state: her eyes, flower-like while he is near, weep when he is a little away, like the bond of base men who praise to the face and slander behind; her bangles, firm while he loves her, slip when he goes, like the bond of those who eat a man's wealth and fail him in decline; her brow, bright when he praises her, pales when he does not, like the bond of mean men who tell a secret once parted; he knows all this better than they do: her beauty when his grace is withdrawn is like the world when the sky withholds its rain.
nuance: The opening retells the burning of the lac house from the Bharata story, with Bhima, the wind's son, breaking out with his kin; the elephant that leads its herd out of the fire is the hero of that simile, and the man is about to do the opposite. The three refrains make her eyes, bangles and brow behave like false friends, loyal only while he is near and betraying her state once he goes. The phrase for the Kauravas' father in lines 1 and 2 (வயக்குறு மண்டிலம் வடமொழிப் பெயர் பெற்ற முகத்தவன்) is obscure.

பருதி அம் செல்வன் போல், நனை ஊழ்த்த செருந்தியும்,

போது அவிழ் மரத்தொடு பொரு கரை கவின் பெற,

இசை பரந்து உலகு ஏத்த, ஏதில் நாட்டு உறைபவர்;

திறல் சான்ற பெரு வனப்பு இழப்பதை அருளுவார்!
ஊறு அஞ்சி நிழல் சேர்ந்தார்க்கு, உலையாது காத்து ஓம்பி,
ஆறு இன்றிப் பொருள் வெஃகி அகன்ற நாட்டு உறைபவர்;
பொரு முரண் யானையர், போர் மலைந்து எழுந்தவர்,
reading: The friend recalls the woman's lament: spring has come to pain her, the kadamba in clusters like the god of the single earring, the seruntti in bud like the sun, the kaanji loud with bees like the fish-bannered god, the gnaazhal bright like the other god, the silk-cotton like the bull-bannered god, so that the bank is lovely like the five together; in this season when bees drink new honey, will he think of her shoulders that have lost their beauty; he who guards unfailingly those who come weary to his shade and is praised by the world lives in a stranger's land; will he pity the fading of her beauty at the holy Marudam ford, the change of her brow; and she tells her not to fret: the true word of their lover, with fighting elephants and victorious in battle, has come by messenger that he will come.
nuance: Each flowering tree is matched to a god by colour: the white kadamba to the one-earringed god, the seruntti to the sun, the kaanji to Kama of the fish banner, the gnaazhal to the other (probably the dark god), the red silk-cotton to Shiva of the bull banner. The refrain sets the man's public virtue, shelter to all who come to his shade, against his neglect of the one at home.

மாதரார் முறுவல் போல் மண மௌவல் முகை ஊழ்ப்பக்
பேதையோன் வினை வாங்கப்ப் பீடு இலா அரசன் நாட்டு,
நிலம் பூத்த மர மிசை நிமிர்பு ஆலும் குயில் எள்ள,
நலம் பூத்த நிறம் சாய, நம்மையோ மறந்தைக்க;
கலம் பூத்த அணியவர் காரிகை மகிழ் செய்யப்
புலம் பூத்துப் புகழ்பு ஆனாக் கூடலும் உள்ளார் கொல்?
கல் மிசை மயில் ஆலக், கறங்கி ஊர் அலர் தூற்றத்
தொல் நலம் நனி சாய, நம்மையோ மறந்தைக்க;
ஒன்னாதார்க் கடந்து அடூஉம், உரவு நீர் மா கொன்ற,
வென் வேலான் குன்றின் மேல் விளையாட்டும் விரும்பார் கொல்?
மை எழில் மலர் உண்கண் மரு ஊட்டி மகிழ் கொள்ளப்,
வையை வார் உயர் எக்கர் நுகர்ச்சியும் உள்ளார் கொல்?
'நாம் இல்லாப் புலம்பு ஆயின், நடுக்கம் செய் பொழுது ஆயின்,
காமவேள் விழவு ஆயின், கலங்குவள் பெரிது' என
நாம் அமர் காதலர் துணை தந்தார், விரைந்தே.
reading: The friend tells the woman that spring has encamped like an enemy army in the land of an unworthy king whose foolish minister lets it in, with the riverbank trees flourishing like the wealth of a man who gives without stint and walks in virtue, mouval buds opening like women's smiles and the cool sand-stream streaked with pollen like the loosened hair of women joined with their lovers; she recalls the woman's laments (has he forgotten us while the cuckoo mocks and our beauty fades; does he not remember Koodal and its jewelled women; nor the play on the hill of the victorious spear-god who killed the sea-mango; nor the high sandbanks of the Vaigai where girls play) and tells her not to grieve with her pained heart: thinking she would be lost in loneliness, in the trembling season, at Kama's festival, their beloved drove his chariot fast and has come to her.
nuance: The similes are drawn from statecraft: spring is an enemy army let in by a foolish minister, and the trees thrive like a just giver's wealth; the season attacks the woman as a foe attacks a badly ruled land. The places of Madurai (Koodal, the spear-god's hill, the Vaigai) make the man's absence a loss of the city's shared pleasures.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman left behind in spring fears he has forgotten

the women's eyes, a doe's

the sand-stream strewn with pollen and leaves

comparisons.tenor: spring settling in, an invader in an undefended land

tamil: நாடினர் கொயல் வேண்டா, நயந்து தாம் கொடுப்ப போல்,
தோடு அவிழ் கமழ் கண்ணி தையுபு புனைவார் கண்
தோடு உறத் தாழ்ந்து, துறை துறை கவின் பெறச்,
செய்யவள் அணி அகலத்து ஆரமொடு அணி கொள்பு,
தொய்யகம் தாழ்ந்த கதுப்புப் போல் துவர் மணல்
வையை வார் அவிர் அறல், இடை போழும் பொழுதினான்;
விரிந்து ஆனா மலர் ஆயின், விளித்து ஆலும் குயில் ஆயின்,
பிரிந்து உள்ளார் அவர் ஆயின், பேதுறூஉம் பொழுது ஆயின்,
அரும் படர் அவல நோய் ஆற்றுவள் என்னாது
வருந்த, நோய் மிகும் ஆயின் - வணங்கு இறை! அளி என்னோ?
புதலவை மலர் ஆயின், பொங்கர் இன வண்டு ஆயின்,
அயலதை அலர் ஆயின், அகன்று உள்ளார் அவர் ஆயின்,
மதலை இல் நெஞ்சொடு மதன் இலள் என்னாது,
நுதல் ஊரும் பசப்பு ஆயின் - நுணங்கு இறை! அளி என்னோ?
தோயின அறல் ஆயின், சுரும்பு ஆர்க்கும் சினை ஆயின்
மாவின தளிர் ஆயின், மறந்து உள்ளார் அவர் ஆயின்,
பூ எழில் இழந்த கண் புலம்பு கொண்டு அமையாது
பாயல் நோய் மிகும் ஆயின் - பைந் தொடி அளி என்னோ?
நாம் தூது மொழிந்தனம் விடல் வேண்டா; நம்மினும்
reading: When boughs and pools give their flowers as if unasked, garlands hang to the wearers' ears and the Vaigai's long clear stream parts the red sand like the hair of the lady of the lotus hung with ornament, the woman complains that if the flowers bloom, the cuckoo calls and he does not remember, he cannot think whether she can bear her grief, and what pity is that, as pallor creeps over her brow and her eyes lose their flower-beauty; the answer comes: do not speak so, there is no need to send the far one a message; he can bear separation no better than they; why grieve, he will come quickly.
nuance: The three refrains end in அளி என்னோ ('what kind of grace is this?'), a complaint against his lack of pity. Who answers in lines 21 to 24 is not marked: if the friend, it is the usual consolation; if the woman herself, she refuses to send a messenger and trusts that he suffers as much as she does, the stronger reading. Hence two speech situations.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman pining in the season while the man is away

comparisons.tenor: boughs and pools offering their flowers unasked
the Vaigai's streams parting the red sand

tamil: தொல் எழில் வரைத்து அன்றி வயவு நோய் நலிதலின்,
பல் பயம் உதவிய பசுமை தீர் அகல் ஞாலம்
புல்லிய புனிறு ஒரீஇ, புது நலம் ஏர்தர;
வளையவர் வண்டல் போல், வார் மணல் வடுக் கொள,
இளையவர் ஐம்பால் போல் எக்கர் போழ்ந்து அறல் வார,
மா ஈன்ற தளிர் மிசை, மாயவள் திதலை போல்,
ஆய் இதழ்ப் பல் மலர் ஐய கொங்கு உறைத்தர,
சேயார் கண் சென்ற என் நெஞ்சினைச் - சின் மொழி! -
நீ கூறும் வரைத்து அன்றி, நிறுப்பென்மன்? நிறை நீவி,
வாய் விரிபு பனி ஏற்ற விரவுப் பல் மலர் தீண்டி,
நோய் சேர்ந்த வைகலான், வாடை வந்து அலைத்தரூஉம்;
போழ்து உள்ளார் துறந்தார் கண் புரி வாடும் கொள்கையைச்
சூழ்பு ஆங்கே - சுடர் இழாய்! கரப்பென்மன்? கை நீவி
வீழ் கதிர் விடுத்த பூ விருந்து உண்ணும் இரும் தும்பி
யாழ் கொண்ட இமிழ் இசை இயல் மாலை அலைத்தரூஉம்;
தொடி நிலை நெகிழ்த்தார்கண் தோயும் என் ஆர்உயிர் -
வடு நீங்கு கிளவியாய்! வலிப்பென் மன்? வலிப்பவும்,
நெடு நிலாத் திறந்து உண்ண, நிரை இதழ் வாய்விட்ட
கடி மலர் கமழ் நாற்றம், கங்குல் வந்து அலைத்தரூஉம்;
வருந்தினை வதிந்த நின் வளை நீங்கச், சேய் நாட்டுப்
பிரிந்து செய் பொருள் பிணி பின் நோக்காது - ஏகி, நம்
திருந்து எயிறு இலங்கு நின் தேமொழி படர்ந்தே.
reading: When spring has come, the wide earth that gave many goods shedding its spent look and taking fresh beauty like a mother lying weak after childbirth, the long sand rippled like girls' play-sand, the stream parting the sandbanks like young girls' braided hair, pollen on the mango shoots like the spots on a dark girl's skin, the woman asks her friend whether she can hold back her heart, gone to the far one, beyond what the friend says, when the north wind touching the dewy flowers torments her; whether she can hide her state, when the evening with the dragonfly's lute-like hum torments her; whether she can be firm, when the scent of night-opened flowers torments her at night; and the friend answers that the one who removes their grief has come, not looking back to the wealth that bound him, drawn by her sweet speech.
nuance: The three torments run through the day: the north wind by day, the evening's hum, the night scent; the woman's three questions (can I hold, can I hide, can I be firm) answer the friend's counsel of restraint. Lines 10 to 21 are hers, the closing lines the friend's.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman whose heart has gone after the far-off man in spring

comparisons.tenor: the earth after the rains, spent and then renewed
the long sand marked with ripples
the stream parting the sandbanks
pollen on the mango shoots
the dragonfly's hum

tamil: அரும் தவம் ஆற்றியார் நுகர்ச்சி போல், அணி கொள
விரிந்து ஆனாச் சினை தொறூஉம், வேண்டும் தாது அமர்ந்து ஆடிப்,
புரிந்து ஆர்க்கும் வண்டொடு, புலம்பு தீர்ந்து எவ்வாயும்,
துயில் இன்றி யாம் நீந்தத், தொழுவை அம் புனல் ஆடி,
மயில் இயலார் மரு உண்டு, மறந்து அமைகுவான் மன்னோ -
'வெயில் ஒளி அறியாத விரி மலர்த் தண் காவில்
குயில் ஆலும் பொழுது' எனக் கூறுநர் உளர் ஆயின்?
பானாள் யாம் படர் கூரப் பணை எழில் அணை மென் தோள்
'ஆனாச் சீர் கூடலுள் அரும்பு அவிழ் நறு முல்லைத்
தேன் ஆர்க்கும் பொழுது' எனத் தெளிக்குநர் உளர் ஆயின்?
உறலி யாம் ஒளி வாட, உயர்ந்தவன் விழவினுள்
'பெறல் அரும் பொழுதோடு பிறங்கு இணர்த் துருத்தி சூழ்ந்து
அறல் வாரும், வையை' என்று அறையுநர் உளர் ஆயின்?
தணியா நோய் உழந்து ஆனாத் தகையவள் - தகைபெற,
அணி கிளர் நெடும் திண் தேர் அயர்மதி - பணிபு நின்
reading: In spring, when bees and dark dragonflies settle on boughs flowering like the joys of those who have done hard penance, the woman asks whether he would stay forgetting, bathing in the stream with peacock-like women while she swims sleepless, if someone told him 'the cuckoos are calling in the cool grove the sun never reaches'; whether he would forget among doe-eyed women at midnight if someone told him 'the bees hum in the budding jasmine of glorious Koodal'; whether he would play with bright-jewelled women at the high one's festival if someone announced 'the Vaigai runs round the flowering islet'; and the friend tells the man to make ready his tall chariot, for she, worn by unending sickness, trembles more than his famed enemies who would not bow at his feet.
nuance: The refrain is conditional (மன்னோ ... உளர் ஆயின்): he would not stay forgetting if only someone told him the season had come, so the blame falls on the missing messenger more than on him. The closing simile flatters the warrior (his enemies tremble) while making the woman's fear greater than theirs. The festival of உயர்ந்தவன் is a spring feast at Madurai; the god is not named.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman in spring fearing the absent man has forgotten

comparisons.tenor: the bees feasting in the flowering boughs
the women he may be playing with, peacock-like in bearing
the doe-eyed women
her trembling, greater than that of his enemies

tamil: கடும் புனல் கால் பட்டுக் கலுழ் தேறிக் கவின் பெற,
நெடும் கயத்து அயல் அயல் அயிர் தோன்ற, அம்மணல்
வடுத்து ஊர வரிப்ப போல் ஈங்கை வாடு உதிர்பு உகப்,
பிரிந்தவர் நுதல் போலப் பீர் வீயக், காதலர்ப்
புணர்ந்தவர் முகம் போலப் பொய்கை பூப் புதிது ஈன,
மெய் கூர்ந்த பனியொடு மேல் நின்ற வாடையால்,
மயங்கு அமர் மாறு அட்டு, மண் வௌவி வருபவர்,
தயங்கிய களிற்றின் மேல், தகை காண விடுவதோ -
பயம் கெழு பல் கதிர் பால் போலும் பொழுதொடு,
வயங்கு இழை தண்ணென, வந்த இவ் அசை வாடை?
தாள் வலம்பட வென்று, தகை நல் மா மேல் கொண்டு,
வாள் வென்று வருபவர் வனப்பு ஆர விடுவதோ -
நீள் கழை நிவந்த பூ நிறம் வாடத் தூற்றுபு,
தோள் அதிர்பு அகம் சேரத் துவற்றும் இச் சில் மழை?
பகை வென்று திறை கொண்ட பாய் திண்தேர் மிசையவர்
வகை கொண்ட செம்மல் நாம் வனப்பு ஆர விடுவதோ -
புகை எனப் புதல் சூழ்ந்து பூ அம் கள் பொதி செய்யா
முகை வெண் பல் நுதி பொர, முற்றிய கடும் பனி?
நாள் வரை நிறுத்துத் தாம் சொல்லிய பொய் அன்றி,
நீள் உயர் கூடல் நெடு கொடி எழவே.
reading: The friend says that in this season, when the flood has cleared and the long pools are lovely, withered ingai flowers drop as if drawing lines on the sand, the beer flowers are pale like the brows of women parted from their lovers and the ponds bloom like the faces of the united, the cold dew and north wind come to confound them, beyond his vow that he would not lie; will this north wind, coming as the grain ears fill with milk, let them see him come in splendour on his elephant, having won the confused battle and seized land; will this light rain that blows on the bamboo blossoms let them see him come on his fine horse, sword victorious; will this hard dew let them see him come on his chariot with tribute; and she tells her not to be anxious: not failing the day he set, thinking she would suffer, the warriors with fierce spears have entered, as the tall flags of Koodal rise.
nuance: The season here is the cold of dew and north wind with ripening grain, not spring, and the man is away at war, not after wealth; his promised return from conquest at a set time is the mullai situation, but the woman's distress keeps the poem in separation. The three questions (விடுவதோ) fear that the season will kill her before she can see his triumph.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman waiting through the season for the man away at war

comparisons.tenor: the withered ingai flowers falling and lining the sand
the pale beer flowers
the pond's new flowers
the grain ears filling with milk
the dew wrapping the bushes

tamil: எஃகு இடை தொட்ட, கார்க் கவின் பெற்ற ஐம்பால் போல் -
மை அற - விளங்கிய, துவர் மணல் அது; அது
ஐது ஆக நெறித்தன்ன அறல் அவிர் நீள் ஐம்பால்
அணி நகை இடையிட்ட ஈகை அம் கண்ணி போல்,
பிணி நெகிழ் அலர் வேங்கை விரிந்த பூ, வெறி கொளத் -
துணி நீரால், தூ மதி நாளால், அணிபெற -
ஈன்றவள் திதலை போல் ஈர் பெய்யும் தளிரொடும்,

இன் உயிர் செய்யும் மருந்து ஆகப், பின்னிய
காதலர் - எயிறு ஏய்க்கும் தண் அருவி நறு முல்லைப்
போது ஆரக் கொள்ளும் கமழ் குரற்கு என்னும் -
reading: The woman tells her friend that spring has come, its red sand gleaming like comb-parted dark hair, vengai blossoms spread like a gold garland set in braided hair, tender leaves dripping like the spots on a new mother, boughs not yet blossoming like the restraint of the wise who spread no talk, bushes humming with bees like a master's lute, branches swaying like good women dancing, trees heavy with clusters like the giving of the discerning and creepers twined like lovers' embrace; spring is good to those in love, she says, but not to her; yet now their lover has sent word, a medicine for her life against the pallor, that he comes for the fragrant jasmine by the cool falls, buds like her teeth; the message has come with words that end grief, so let them prepare the feast.
nuance: Line 8 plays on அலர், blossom and gossip: the boughs that have not yet burst into flower are like the restrained who do not spread talk, so the season keeps the lovers' secret. The eight similes of lines 7 to 12 all draw on human virtue or love. The message in lines 14 to 17 is hard to construe; this reading takes the jasmine 'like her teeth' as the season he names for his return.

thinai_evidence.note: word comes from the absent man in spring

பொறை தளர் கொம்பின் மேல் சிதர் இனம் இறைகொள
முறை தளர்ந்த மன்னவன் கீழ்க் குடி போலக் கலங்குபு,
பொறை தளர்பு பனி வாரும் கண் ஆயின், எவன் செய்கோ?

கிளை அழிய வாழ்பவன் ஆக்கம்போல் புல் என்று,
வளை ஆனா நெகிழ்பு ஓடும் தோள் ஆயின், எவன் செய்கோ?
நின் உள் நோய் நீ உரைத்து அலமரல்; எல்லா! நாம்
reading: As the wide river, which in flood spread over the land and fed the world for the good of all living things, now runs lovely in thin streams, like men of worth who, having served one end first, turn at the last to serve another, spring has come with flowers falling and bees humming; the woman says she would hide the wrong of the man who did not fear parting, though the cuckoo calls bathed in kaanji pollen, but what can she do if her heart, withered like a tree under which a false witness sat, burns as if set on fire; if her eyes stream like the subjects under a king whose justice has failed; if her shoulders shrink and shed their bangles like the prosperity of one who lives on while his kin are ruined; and the friend tells her not to fret over her inner pain: not passing the day they counted, their lover has come with his trained horses, as a hand clears what troubles the eye.
nuance: All three refrain similes are moral and political: the tree that withers where a false witness sat (a belief also known from later texts), the people under a king who has failed in justice, and the wealth of one who thrives while his kin perish; her body's decline is a judgement on his conduct. The sense of the opening simile in lines 4 and 5 (men who serve one end and then another) is not certain.

reading: The friend tells the woman, as the trees flourish like the wealth of a man free of sloth, bees swarm in the boughs like those who share that wealth, tender leaves come like a dark girl's skin and pollen falls on them like the spots on that skin, not to sulk, looking at the mocking cuckoo with a breaking heart, that he has forgotten them: is this not the time, when bees drink the jasmine pollen by the cool falls on the Vaigai's high sandbanks, that he named when they sent him off in tears; the time of the bowman god's festival among the islands of the river; the time when the people of Koodal of tall mansions savour the new words born on the tongues of poets; and now, to ease the sickness that breaks her each time she remembers, the faultless lover, lord of the hill, has come on his bird-swift chariot with a day as true as truth.

title: குறிஞ்சிக்கலி 37-51 (1/2)
theme: The first fifteen poems of Kapilar's kurinjikkali: secret love on the hill told as scenes, from the girl's staged fall from the swing (37) and the old playmate who seizes her wrist and is shielded by her lie (51) to the friend's disclosure and the kuravai wedding (39); a run of valli songs sung while pounding grain (40 to 43) alternates reproach of the absent lover with its own refutation until the hidden listener comes to marry; and the friend's speeches to the man measure the girl's wasting by the things of his own hill, refuse his night visits and praise his giving to shame him into marriage.
source_issues: kalittokai: the core records carry no colophon thurai for any poem, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.

kalittokai:38: flagged numbering (a line starting with an unexpected number 7, expected 39) and line 8 repaired from the sangamtamil.com reading; the repaired line (நீடு இரு விடர் அகம் சிலம்பக் கூய்த், தன்) fits the sense.
kalittokai:40 lines 8-28 and 31-34, kalittokai:42 lines 11-22 and 25-32: not in the sangamtamil.com text (flag not_in_stc); marked from our single witness.
kalittokai:42 line 31 recurs as kalittokai:145 line 65, and kalittokai:50 line 14 as kalittokai:56 line 12 (repeated formula lines).
kalittokai:46: the voice shifts between the girl's first person (lines 10-21, addressing a woman) and a speaker who calls her இவள் (lines 23-27); speaker assignment uncertain.
kalittokai:48 lines 21-22 (பின் ஈதல் வேண்டும் ... பூங் கண் படுதலும் அஞ்சுவல்) are hard to construe; reading marked uncertain.

வய மான் அடித் தேர்வான் போலத், தொடை மாண்ட
பாயல் பெறேஎன், படர் கூர்ந்து, அவன் வயின்,
கண் நின்று கூறுதல் ஆற்றான், அவன் ஆயின்;
காணான், கழிதலும் உண்டு' என்று, ஒரு நாள், என்
தோள் நெகிழ்பு உற்ற துயரால் துணிதந்து, ஓர்
நாண் இன்மை செய்தேன், நறு நுதால்! ஏனல்
இனக் கிளி யாம் கடிந்து ஓம்பும் புனத்து அயல்,
ஊசல் ஊர்ந்து ஆட, ஒரு ஞான்று வந்தானை,
'தையால்! நன்று' என்று அவன் ஊக்கக், கை நெகிழ்பு,
பொய்யாக வீழ்ந்தேன், அவன் மார்பில்; வாய்யாச் செத்து,
மெய் அறிந்து ஏற்று எழுவேன் ஆயின், மற்று ஒய்யென,
'ஒண் குழாய்! செல்க' எனக் கூறி விடும் பண்பின்
reading: The girl tells her friend about a young man who kept coming with a garland and a bow, like a hunter tracking a beast, looking at her and signing but never speaking of his sickness; sleepless, and afraid he might pass on without her ever seeing, she dared one shameless act: by the millet field where they scare off the parrots she asked him to push her on the swing, let go, and fell as if by accident onto his chest; he caught her up at once, she lay there as if she had fainted, and the moment she stirred and rose he sent her off with 'go, girl of the bright locks', such is his fine decency.
nuance: Lines 8 and 9 give the rule she breaks: he cannot speak to her face, and for a woman to speak is unwomanly, so a staged fall does the work of the word. The comedy has two pretences, her fall and her swoon, and line 17 says he took the fall for real (வாய்யாச் செத்து); his sending her away the instant she stirs leaves open whether he saw through her, and it is that restraint she praises.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field guarded from parrots, the kurinji meeting place of kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the young man coming again and again with garland and bow, like a hunter tracking a strong beast by its prints

tamil: இமைய வில் வாங்கிய ஈர்ஞ் சடை அந்தணன்
உமை அமர்ந்து உயர் மலை இருந்தனன் ஆக,
தொடிப் பொலி தடக் கையின் கீழ் புகுத்து, அம் மலை
உறு புலி உரு ஏய்ப்பப் பூத்த வேங்கையைக்
கறுவு கொண்டு, அதன் முதல் குத்திய மத யானை,
நீடு இரு விடர் அகம் சிலம்பக் கூய்த், தன்
ஆர் இடை என்னாய் நீ அரவு அஞ்சாய் வந்தக்கால்,
நீர் அற்ற புலமே போல் புல்லென்றாள், வைகறை,
கார் பெற்ற புலமே போல், கவின் பெறும்; அக் கவின்
தீராமல் காப்பது ஓர் திறன் உண்டேல் உரைத்தைக் காண்!
இருள் இடை என்னாய் நீ இரவு அஞ்சாய் வந்தக்கால்,
பொருள் இல்லான் இளமை போல் புல்லென்றாள், வைகறை,
அருள் வல்லான் ஆக்கம் போல் அணிபெறும்; அவ் அணி
தெருளாமல் காப்பது ஓர் திறன் உண்டேல், உரைத்தைக் காண்;
மறந்திருந்தார் என்னாய் நீ மலை இடை வந்தக்கால்,
அறம் சாரான் மூப்பே போல் அழிதக்காள், வைகறை,
திறம் சேர்ந்தான் ஆக்கம் போல் திருத்தகும்; அத் திருப்
புறங்கூற்றுத் தீர்ப்பது ஓர் பொருள் உண்டேல் உரைத்தைக் காண்;
வீங்கு இறைப் பணைத் தோள் வரைந்தனன் கொளற்கே.
reading: The friend tells the girl how she spoke to the hill lord, in whose land a rutting elephant, taking a flowering vengai for a tiger, gores its trunk and, unable to pull its tusk free, bellows through the clefts like the ten-headed demon king straining beneath the god's mountain: when he comes by night through the hard path, heedless of snakes and the dark and the hill, she who had drooped like a field without water, like a poor man's youth, like the old age of one who never kept to virtue, grows lovely at dawn like a field after rain, like the wealth of a gracious man and the gain of a capable one; has he a way to keep that beauty from fading and from slander? and now, having heard her grief told, the good hill lord comes, seeing the vengai in flower, to marry her.
nuance: The three stanzas use the moral similes of the didactic books (the poor man's youth, the gracious man's wealth) as a scale for a girl's face, and each ends with a challenge: if he can keep this beauty, let him say how; the only way is marriage, and the close says he has understood. The elephant that wounds the vengai in error and is caught by its own tusk may glance at the hero, and the vengai flowering is the wedding season (line 25), but only one correspondence is drawn, so ullurai is not tagged.

thinai_evidence.note: a hill elephant at the flowering vengai and the hill lord's night visits
