tamil: நனவின்உள் உதவாது நள் இருள் வேறு ஆகும்
கயல் புரை உண் கண் அரிப்ப அரி வாரப்,
பெயல் சேர் மதி போல, வாள் முகம் தோன்ற,
பல ஒலி கூந்தலாள் பண்பு எல்லாம் துய்த்துத்
காமம் முனைஇயாள், அலந்தாள்' என்று, எனைக் காண,
மகளிர் தோள் சேர்ந்த மாந்தர் துயர் கூர நீத்தலும்,
நீள் சுரம் போகியார் வல்லை வந்து அளித்தலும்,
ஊழ் செய்து, இரவும் பகலும் போல், வேறு ஆகி,
தாழ்பு, துறந்து, தொடி நெகிழ்த்தான் போகிய கானம்
வறந்து என்னை செய்தியோ, வானம்? - சிறந்த என்
நுமக்கு எவன் போலுமோ? ஊரீர்! எமக்கும் எம்
கண் பாயல் கொண்டு, உள்ளாக் காதலவன் செய்த
பண்பு தர வந்த என் தொடர் நோய் வேது
புல்லென் மருள் மாலைப் போழ்து இன்று வந்து என்னைக்
ஒல்லை எம் காதலர்க் கொண்டு, கடல் ஊர்ந்து, காலை நாள்,
ஒள் வளை ஓடத் துறந்து; துயர் செய்த
கள்வன் பால் பட்டன்று, ஒளித்து என்னை, உள்ளி -
இரும் கழி நெய்தல் இதழ் பொதிந்து தோன்ற,
விரிந்து இலங்கு வெண் நிலா வீசும் பொழுதினான்,
யான் வேண்டு ஒருவன், என் அல்லல் உறீஇயான்;
ஊரவர்க்கு எல்லாம் பெரு நகை ஆகி, என்
ஆர் உயிர் எஞ்சும்மன்; அங்கு நீ சென்றீ -
நிலவு உமிழ் வான் திங்காள்! ஆய் தொடி கொட்ப,
அளி புறம் மாறி, அருளான் துறந்த அக்
வினைக் கொண்டு என் காம நோய் நீக்கிய ஊரீர்!
கனை இருள் வானம்! - கடல் முகந்து, என் மேல்
நோய் உடை நெஞ்சத்து எறியா, இனைபு ஏங்கி,
மாயவன் மார்பில் திருப் போல் அவள் சேர,
ஞாயிற்று முன்னர் இருள் போல மாய்ந்தது, என்
reading: The woman tells the townspeople, who laugh that love is like a dream that gives nothing in waking and that she wanders, weeps for the man who enjoyed and left her and then laughs as if she had forgotten him, not to laugh: that men leave the women they embraced and those gone over long wastes come quickly back is a turn, like night and day, that comes to all who live; she asks the cloud why it roars dry over his forest instead of drawing rain from the sea of her tears; the fierce day seems to foment her sickness; she begs the sun not to set, for evening will kill her, and asks whether she could bear the enmity of evening and its dew if he came over the sea at dawn; when the sea dims, the shore grows lonely and the neythal closes under the moon, she asks whether the one she wants sleeps with the one he wants, while her heart searches sky and earth; she asks the moon to go to him; the townspeople cured her love with rites, but her husband would not scorn her however they mock; let the dark sky rain on her, for the fire has caught all over; then those who sought him brought him as virtue answers a just complaint, she joined him like Sri on Vishnu's chest, and her grief vanished like darkness before the sun.
nuance: She answers the town's mockery with a general law (leaving and returning alternate like night and day for everyone), so her lament claims to be ordinary experience, not madness. The townspeople's rites to cure her (வினைக் கொண்டு, line 51) are the veri the akam heroine usually suffers at her mother's hands, here taken over by the town.

tamil: உரை செல உயர்ந்து ஓங்கிச் சேர்ந்தாரை ஒரு நிலையே
வரை நில்லா விழுமம் உறீஇ நடுக்கு உரைத்து, தெறல் மாலை
அரைசினும் அன்பு இன்றாம், காமம்; புரை தீர
பேர் அமர் உண்கண் நிறை மல்க, அந்நீர் தன்,
கூர் எயிறு ஆடி, குவி முலை மேல் வார்தர,
தேர் வழி நின்று தெருமரும், ஆய் இழை
'எல் இழாய்! எற்றி வரைந்தானை, நாணும் மறந்தாள்' என்று,
நிறைந்து என்னை மாய்ப்பது ஓர் வெள்ளமும் போலும் -
சிறந்தவன் தூ அற நீப்ப, பிறங்கி வந்து,
மிக்க என் நாணும் நலனும் என் உள்ளமும்
உக்காண் - இஃதோ உடம்பு உயிர்க்கு ஊற்று ஆகச்
செக்கர் அம் புள்ளித் திகிரி அலவனொடு, யான்
நிரை கதிர் ஞாயிற்றை, நாடு என்றேன்; யானும்
உரை கேட்புஉழி எல்லாம் செல்வேன்; புரை தீர்ந்தான்
மருள் கூர் பிணை போல் மயங்க, வெந்நோய் செய்யும்
யாமம் தலை வந்தன்று ஆயின், அதற்கு என் நோய்
யான் உற்ற எவ்வம் உரைப்பின், பலர்த் துயிற்றும்
முதிர்பு என் மேல் முற்றிய வெந்நோய் உரைப்பின்
பேர் ஊர் மறுகில் பெரும் துயில் சான்றீரே!
பொறி செய் புனை பாவை போல வறிது உயங்கிச்
வறம் கூர் வானத்து வள் உறைக்கு அலமரும்
reading: The poet says that love, which raises those who join it high and then drops them into trouble without bound, is more pitiless than a king who rules by punishment, and shows a girl, left by the man who loved her on a swan-soft bed, standing on the chariot road, shame and restraint forgotten, tears running over her breasts; she tells those who ask whether she has lost her shame that the sickness he left on her is like a sky that ended a drought and like a flood that fills and drowns her; she has not lost her shame, beauty and heart, for they stayed with him; she laughed with the red-spotted crab, remembering; he who will marry her will not leave her; she told the sun to search the sea-girt world and will go wherever she hears of him; if evening and midnight come she will sing her pain among the crowd, and the night that sends all to sleep would not sleep if it heard her; she tells the sleeping worthies of the town to dam the water, for even the rains would not cool her; staying, her heart burns, going, her body suffers, so she will go like a jointed doll; hearing her, he came, and as rain pours on the bird that cries for drops in a dry sky, his embrace ended her distress.
nuance: She denies the charge of shamelessness with a paradox: her shame, beauty and heart are not lost but left with him, so what the town sees is only the body without them. Her threat to the night (lines 36 to 41) is that her song would keep even the night awake and make the moon tremble.

tamil: ஆறு அல்ல மொழி தோற்றி, அற வினை கலக்கிய,
தேறுகள் நறவு உண்டார் மயக்கம் போல், காமம்
வேறு ஒரு பாற்று ஆனது கொலோ? சீறு அடிச்
சிலம்பு ஆர்ப்ப இயலியாள் - இவள் மன்னோ, இனி மன்னும்
புலம்பு ஊரப் புல்லென்ற வனப்பினாள் - விலங்கு ஆக,
வேல் நுதி உற நோக்கி, வெயில் உற, உருகும் தன்
தோள் நலம் உண்டானைக் கெடுத்தாள் போல், தெருவில் பட்டு,
ஊண் யாதும் இலள் ஆகி, உயிரினும் சிறந்த தன்
நாண் யாதும் இலள் ஆகி, நகுதலும் நகூஉம்; ஆங்கே
பெண்மையும் இலள் ஆகி அழுதலும் அழூஉம்; தோழி! ஓர்
ஒள் நுதல் உற்றது உழைச் சென்று கேளாமோ?
மிக்க தன் காமமும் ஒன்று என்ப; அம் மா
புது நலம் பூ வாடி அற்று, தாம் வீழ்வார்
கலைஇய கண், புருவம், தோள், நுசுப்பு, ஏஎர்
சில மழை போல் தாழ்ந்து இருண்ட கூந்தல், அவற்றை
ஆங்கு எதிர் நோக்குவன்- ஞாயிறே? - எம் கேள்வன்
ஆர் இருள் நீக்கும் விசும்பின் மதி போல,
பல் கதிர் சாம்பிப் பகல் ஒழியப், பட்டீமோ -
உறாஅத் தகை செய்து, இவ் ஊர் உள்ளான் கொல்லோ?
பெறாஅது யான் நோவேன்; அவனை என் காட்டிச்
உறாஅ அரைச! நின் ஓலைக் கண் கொண்டீ;
பனை ஈன்ற மா ஊர்ந்து அவன் வரக் காமன்
மெல் நடை பேடை துனை தரத் தன் சேர்ந்த
அன்ன வான் சேவல் புணர்ச்சி போல், ஒள் நுதல்
காதலன் மன்ற அவனை வரக் கண்டு, ஆங்கு
நகை ஒழிந்து, நாணு மெய் நிற்ப, இறைஞ்சி,
தகை ஆகத் தையலாள் சேர்ந்தாள் - நகை ஆக,
reading: The poet asks whether love has become like the stupor of those who drink strong toddy, and shows a girl who once walked with ringing anklets now in the street as if she had lost the man who ate her beauty, without food, without the shame dearer than life, laughing and then weeping; she asks who these staring people are, says her heart was caught in the net of a man who did not know the worth of her eyes, brows, shoulders, waist and cloud-dark hair, and that he who calmed her with oaths embraced her and left, the killer; she asks the sun to show where he is or else what use is it in the sky, warns it of being devoured where it appears in water like the moon, and asks whether he has gone past the forest of unmilked buffaloes or stays in this town doing wrong; she asks Kama, king of the shark banner, to write down his cruelty, and asks whether his arrows torment all who love one man; if she sees him she will look softly, seize his cloth and cry 'thief!' if he pretends not to know her; his bond has joined her life like drink and made her eyes sleepless; if the sun will not show him she will clasp Kama's feet and beg his arrows so that he comes riding the palmyra horse; then, like the swan joining his mate as she hurries to him, she saw her lover come, forgot her grief and leaned shyly on his breast.
nuance: The madal is turned around at the close: the woman does not ride it but begs Kama's arrows so that the man will ride it to her (lines 59, 60), keeping the convention that a woman does not mount the palm horse while making her the cause of his mounting. Lines 32 and 36 to 38 (the toad that eats the sun, the kite's eye, the forest of unmilked buffaloes) are obscure.

tamil: தொல் இயல் ஞாலத்துத் தொழில் ஆற்றி ஞாயிறு,
வல்லவன் கூறிய வினை தலை வைத்தான் போல்,
கல் அடைபு, கதிர் ஊன்றி, கண் பயம் கெடப் பெயர,
அல்லது கெடுப்பவன் அருள் கொண்ட முகம் போல,
மல்லல் நீர்த் திரை ஊர்பு, மால் இருள் மதி சீப்ப,
இல்லவர் ஒழுக்கம் போல் இரும் கழி மலர் கூம்ப,
செல்லும் என் உயிர் புறத்து இறுத்தந்த மருள் மாலை!
நலம் கொண்டு நல்காதார் நனி நீத்த புலம்பின் கண்
எம் கேள்வன் தருதல் உம் தருகல்லாய்; துணை அல்லை!
பிரிந்தவர்க்கு நோய் ஆகிப் புணர்ந்தவர்க்குப் புணை ஆகித்
பாய் இருள் பரப்பினை பகல் களைந்தது போலப்
சேய் உறை காதலர் செய் வினை முடித்தே.
reading: The woman tells the evening that it has come and camped outside her departing life, as the sun, its work in the old world done, goes to the hill like one who has carried out the task his master set, the moon combs the dark over the waves like the gracious face of one who destroys wrong, and the backwater flowers close like the conduct of the poor; she charges it that while it is a sweet suggestion to the happy and inflames the love of the united, it torments those left in tears and terrifies the deserted; it neither brings her husband nor keeps her company, a sickness to the parted and a raft to the joined; then, to end her grief, as day clears the spreading dark, her far-dwelling lover returned, his task done, having seized his enemies' land.
nuance: Line 9 uses the word இறைச்சி itself: the evening is the suggestive setting (இறைச்சி) for the happy, so the poem names the device by which a time of day carries love's sense and then complains that the same hour means the opposite to the parted. The three similes of sunset (a servant done with work, a just ruler's face, the conduct of the poor) all come from the life of the town and the state.

thinai_evidence.note: evening on the backwaters, the hour and land of neythal (porul 1.10)

tamil: நிரை திமில் களிறு ஆகத் திரை ஒலி பறை ஆகக்,
கரை சேர் புள் இனத்து அம் சிறை படை ஆக,
அரைசு கால் கிளர்ந்தன்ன உரவு நீர்ச் சேர்ப்ப! கேள்;
கற்பித்தான் நெஞ்சு அழுங்க பகர்ந்து உண்ணான், விச்சைக்கண்
எச்சத்துள் ஆயினும், அஃது எறியாது விடாதே காண்;
தாள் இலான் குடியே போல் தமியவே தேயுமால்;
சூள் வாய்த்த மனத்தவன் வினை பொய்ப்பின், மற்று அவன்
வாள் வாய் நன்று ஆயினும், அஃது எறியாது விடாதே காண்;
அனைத்து, இனி - பெரும! - அதன் நிலை, நினைத்துக் காண்;
reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, whose sea surges like a king on the march with rows of boats for elephants, the roar of waves for drums and the wings of the shore birds for his army, that her beauty wastes alone like the learning of a pupil who grieves his teacher and will not share, and like wealth hoarded while kin grieve in a family without effort; that failing those who helped one in want will strike the doer even in his descendants, and that a man who breaks the deed he swore will not be spared, however good his sword; let him think of her state, for she suffers with a racing heart like the distress of a town when an angry king camps outside its walls.
nuance: The friend argues entirely in the language of puram and ethics (the ungrateful pupil, the hoarding family, the oath-breaker, the besieged town), so the case for marriage is put as a duty of gratitude and of keeping one's sworn word (சூள்), not as a plea of love. The sea pictured as a king on the march frames the man as the conqueror besieging her.

tamil: அயம் திகழ் நறும் கொன்றை அலங்கல் அம் தெரியலான்
இயங்கு எயில் எயப் பிறந்த எரி போல, எவ் வாயும்,
கனை கதிர் தெறுதலின், கடுத்து எழுந்த காம்புத் தீ
மலை பரந்து தலைக் கொண்டு முழங்கிய முழங்கு அழல்
விசும்பு உற நிவந்து அழலும், விலங்கு அரும் வெம் சுரம் -
அறம் துறந்து - ஆய் இழாய்! ஆக்கத்தில் பிரிந்தவர்;
பிறங்கு நீர் சடைக் கரந்தான் அணி அன்ன நின் நிறம்
கரி காய்ந்த கவலைத்தாய்க், கல் காய்ந்த காட்டு அகம்,
'வெரு வந்த ஆறு' என்னார், விழுப் பொருட்கு அகன்றவர்;
உருவ ஏற்று ஊர்தியான் ஒள் அணி நக்கன்ன, நின்
கொதித்து உராய்க் குன்று இவர்ந்து, கொடிக் கொண்ட கோடையால்,
'ஒதுக்கு அரிய நெறி' என்னார், ஒண் பொருட்கு அகன்றவர்;
புதுத் திங்கள் கண்ணியான் பொன் பூண் ஞான்று அன்ன, நின்
பெரும் தண் சண்பகம் போல, ஒருங்கு அவர்
reading: The friend tells the woman that those who left her for gain, giving up virtue, to cross the hot waste where a bamboo fire, kindled by the sun like the fire born when Shiva of the konrai garland shot the moving forts, spreads roaring over the hill, confuses the paths and leaps to the sky, will not abandon her while her colour, like the ornament of the god who hid the river in his hair, turns pale; those who left for great wealth, not calling the road fearful, will remember her as her form fades; those who left for bright wealth, not calling the path impassable, will see her as her hair dries; and so, like the great champak that bloomed in full to adorn the lord of the Ardra star, they are sure he will not prove false.
nuance: Every simile comes from Shiva (the burning of the forts, the river in his hair, the bull-rider's ornament, the crescent chaplet, the Ardra star), so the friend's comfort is set in a frame of worship. She concedes that he left 'giving up virtue' (அறம் துறந்து) and still holds that he will not be false, separating his breach of virtue from his keeping of his word. The colophon files it under neythal, but nothing of the shore is in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for wealth across a burning waste

title: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து 0-20
theme: Kuruntokai 0 to 20: an invocation drawn wholly in Murugan's red, then short poems across the five lands; hill courtships praised and pressed toward marriage, shore laments of sleepless nights, marutham wives who hide their husbands' wrongs and the other woman who mocks him, and paalai women who would follow or who refuse to call the leavers wise; madal and puram names (Evvi, the Kosar, Katti) used as measures of private feeling.
source_issues: 9: the colophon thinai is மருதம்; sangamtamil.com gives நெய்தல் (text flag). The poem's things are all of the shore, its situation (a wife hiding her husband's wrong) marutham; I infer marutham, mixed.

10: the colophon thinai பாலை does not fit the poem, which has kaanji, ploughmen and a town-lord's wrong and nothing of the wilds; sangamtamil.com gives மருதம் (text flag), which agrees with my inference.
17: the colophon's குறிஞ்சி; the madal of excessive love is perunthinai by porul 1.51, which is my inference.
Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று); every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and is so noted.
13: line 5 is the repaired reading of tamilvu.org (text flag).

reading: The invocation: the world has come into safe days because the god of the cock banner guards it, he whose red feet are like the lotus, whose body is like coral, whose cloth is like the red kunri seed, and whose long bright spear split the mountain to its heart.
nuance: Murugan is never named; he is drawn wholly in red (lotus feet, coral body, kunri-red cloth) and known by his spear and banner, and the poem's one claim is that the world's safety (ஏம வைகல்) follows from his guarding.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the guarding god, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து placed under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: his red feet
his body
his red cloth

reading: The friend says that the hill of the Red One, who destroyed the demons till the field ran red, whose arrows are red-shafted, whose elephant is red-tusked and who wears the anklet and the bangle, is thick with kanthal in clusters the colour of blood.
nuance: Everything is red, five times over (செங்களம், செங்கோல், செங்கோட்டு, சேஎய், குருதி), and the last red is the flower; the poem does not say why the friend speaks, and the old setting (she turns away the man's gift of kanthal, since her own hill is full of it) comes only from the tradition, not the text.

thinai_evidence.note: Murugan's hill and its kanthal fix the land; no situation is stated

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is the tradition's (the hero bringing flowers), not the poem's

comparisons.tenor: the kanthal clusters, red as blood

reading: The man asks the bee that lives by searching out pollen to tell him what it has seen and not what it wants: of all the flowers it knows, is there one more fragrant than the hair of this woman of close-set teeth and peacock grace, whose love has held fast through long closeness?
nuance: He asks the bee for an eyewitness's report and forbids it to flatter (காமம் செப்பாது கண்டது மொழிமோ), which turns praise into a test of fact, and the answer is assumed in the asking; the fragrance is joined to a love already settled by long companionship (பயிலியது கெழீஇய நட்பின்).

thinai_evidence.note: a lover praising the woman he has joined; the bee and peacock are of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he addresses the bee

comparisons.tenor: her hair, set above every flower in fragrance
her bearing, like a peacock's

reading: The woman says that her love for the man of the hill country, where bees gather the flowers of the black-stemmed kurinji on the slope to build great honeycombs, is larger than the earth, higher than the sky and past measuring deeper than the sea.
nuance: The three measures are of land, sky and water, the whole world, but the poem closes on a small slow labour: honey built from a shrub that flowers rarely; the vast love is set beside the patient making that produced it, and she calls it நட்பு, not காமம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the kurinji flower and hill honey, with a love affirmed in secret

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is not named; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her love, wider than the earth
her love, higher than the sky
her love, deeper than the sea

reading: The woman, holding back tears hot enough to scorch her eyelids, tells her heart three times that it aches, because the lover who was so fitting has now become unfitting.
nuance: The refrain நோம்என் நெஞ்சே is said three times and the turn rests on one verb used twice: அமைதற்கு அமைந்த (made to be fitting) and அமைவிலர் (not fitting); the tears are held back (தாங்கி), not shed.

thinai_evidence.note: pure lament with no land named; lament is neythal's uri

comparisons.tenor: her tears, hot as if they burned the eyelids

reading: The woman asks her friend whether this is what love-sickness is: since the gentle lord of the shore has left, where herons sleep in the sweet shade of the punnai and the spray of breaking waves buds on it, her many-petalled darkened eyes cannot sleep.
nuance: She finds out she is in love from a symptom (அதுகொல்... காம நோயே); the herons that sleep in his punnai shade are the opposite of her sleepless eyes, but they only sit in the scene: they do nothing a lover does, so they are not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, waves and the shore lord, with lament at parting

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, as many-petalled flowers

reading: The woman says it is the dead of night; words have ceased, people have gone sweetly to rest, the whole wide world sleeps without care, and only she, surely, does not sleep.
nuance: Three clauses of the world sleeping end on one clause of her waking, with ஓர்யான் (I alone) and the emphatic மன்ற; nothing in the scene names the lover at all.

thinai_evidence.note: a sleepless lament with no land named; midnight alone would point to kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she speaks to no one; the night is her only hearer

reading: Onlookers on the road see a bowman with warrior's anklets on his legs and a bangled girl with anklets still on her soft feet, and ask who these good, pitiable people are, setting out into the bamboo wilds where the white vaakai pods rattle in the wind like the drum of Aryan rope-dancers.
nuance: The onlookers read the pair from their anklets alone: his கழல், and her சிலம்பு still on, which tells them she is unwed and has gone with him; their only judgement is pity (அளியர்).

thinai_evidence.note: a couple leaving together through the wilds

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the onlookers speak among themselves

comparisons.tenor: the rattling of the vaakai pods in the wind

reading: The other woman says that the man of the town where the vaalai fish of the pond snatch the sweet ripe fruit that falls from the mango in the field talks big about her in her house, but in his own home does whatever his son's mother wants, raising hand and foot as she raises hers, like an image in a mirror.
nuance: The insult is aimed at the wife's power as much as at him: he is a mirror image, moving only as she moves; the fish that takes fruit falling into its mouth is the man who takes the pleasure that comes to him without effort.

thinai_evidence.note: the other woman's jibe at a husband held by his wife

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: she speaks so that those close to the wife may hear

comparisons.tenor: the man doing his wife's bidding

ullurai.tenor: the husband who takes the other woman's pleasure without effort and goes home to obey his wife

pairs.situation: the pleasure that falls to him unsought, the other woman herself
he snatches what drops within reach, and gives nothing for it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the other woman is not bound by porul 7.26 to 7.28 and may use the mango and fish of his marutham town freely (porul 7.29)

reading: The friend says the dark woman has become the mother of the house: her body has wilted like flowers never worn and left in a well-made box, and out of shame before them she hides the cruelty of the lord of the cool shore, where neythal lilies on tall stems rise above green leaves and look like the eyes of girls diving in the pond each time the tide fills the backwater with fish.
nuance: The wilting has two halves: the flower was never worn (பெய்யா), so it was kept and not used, and that is the wife's condition; she does not complain, she conceals (கரப்பு), and the friend's speech exposes what she hides.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife hiding her husband's wrong is marutham's situation, though every thing named is of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred from துறைவன் கொடுமை: she speaks of the wife to the husband

comparisons.tenor: her wilted body
the neythal lilies above the water

reading: The friend says the wife, first lady of the festival, has become the mother of the house: because she hid the cruelty of the man of the town of kaanji trees, whose fragrant soft branches, with clusters like green gram, the ploughmen pull down to bathe in their fresh pollen, she comes ashamed.
nuance: It opens with the same words as poem 9 (யாயாகியளே) on the same act of concealment; here the shame is the cost of hiding: she leads the festival and comes to it ashamed.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife hiding the town-lord's wrong, among ploughmen and kaanji; nothing of the wilds

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred: the town-lord whose wrong was hidden

comparisons.tenor: the kaanji's flower clusters

ullurai.tenor: the husband who lets other women draw him down and take their pleasure of him

pairs.situation: low women pull him down to them as ploughmen pull a branch
they bathe in what he gives, while the wife is left with the shame

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a kaanji tree and ploughmen of the marutham town the poem is set in (porul 7.27)

reading: The woman tells her heart that rather than stay here crying, her conch bangles slipping day by day, it should rise and go: though he is in a land of strange speech beyond the country of Katti of the strong spear, past the frontier of the Vadugar who wear kullai garlands, let them set out to follow him to his land.
nuance: She does not ask him to return; she proposes to go herself, across a named frontier of foreign speech (மொழிபெயர் தேஎம்), and she frames staying as what cannot be survived.

thinai_evidence.note: he is gone far for his work and she longs to follow

reading: The woman says that the road his chariot took is said to be a forking track of tiny pools like ant-holes, where hunters with curved bows climb rocks hot as an anvil-stone to sharpen their arrows; yet this clamouring town, without grieving over that, scolds her like a stranger.
nuance: Her fear is learned by hearsay (என்ப) and the town's blame is direct; she sets what she fears for him against what the town says of her, and finds the town has no pity.

thinai_evidence.note: a hot rocky track of hunters and scanty water

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is not named

comparisons.tenor: the tiny rock pools
the rock, hot and hard as an anvil-stone

reading: The woman tells her friend that the man of the country where a great dark rough boulder, beaten by heavy rain until it looks like an elephant washed clean, rests on one side of the slope, has given her this sickness, and pallor has filled her lily eyes.
nuance: The boulder washed clean and at rest stands beside her eyes filled with pallor; the image belongs to his country, not to her, and the sense of பைதல் (sad, or cool and wet) decides whether the rock shares her grief.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill boulder, the elephant and the hill-country lord

comparisons.tenor: the rain-washed dark boulder
her eyes, as blue lilies

reading: The man wishes he may win the girl of few words, whose long bright white teeth came so that her nectar-holding red tongue is shy behind them; and having won her, may this town know it, may many in the street say 'there goes the good woman's husband', and may he be a little ashamed.
nuance: He wants the public naming (நல்லோள் கணவன் இவன்) and the small shame that comes with it (நாணுகஞ் சிறிதே); the tradition hears a madal threat in 'let the town know', but the poem's words are a wish for a public bond.

thinai_evidence.note: a lover in secret love who wants her and the town's knowledge of it

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred; the colophon names only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her tongue and speech, as holding nectar

reading: The foster mother tells a friend that the love between the youth with fine anklets and red-leafed white spear and the girl with stacked bangles on her forearm has proved true, as true as the good word of the Kosar of Nalur spoken at the common hall under the ancient banyan, with drums sounding and conches blaring.
nuance: The love's truth is measured by a public oath: the Kosar's word given in assembly with drums and conches; the foster mother vindicates the elopement by a standard of sworn faith, not of feeling.

thinai_evidence.note: the youth and the girl gone together; a foster mother's word on it

comparisons.tenor: the lovers' bond, proved true

reading: The friend asks whether they will not think of us, the men who crossed the forest of kalli, where the red-legged lizard calls to its mate with a sound like thieves flicking with their nail-tips the gold-bound arrows to test them straight.
nuance: The simile brings robbers into the very sound of the forest, so the comfort is shadowed by danger; the question form (உள்ளார் கொல்லோ) expects the answer yes.

thinai_evidence.note: the spurge forest and its robbers, with a man gone

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred: the friend calls her தோழி in line 1 and reassures her

comparisons.tenor: the lizard's call

iraicchi.act: the lizard calls to its mate across the dry forest
iraicchi.sense: the man who passes and hears even the lizard call its mate will think of his own and turn home

reading: The man says that when love hardens like heartwood, men ride the palm-stem calling it a horse, wear a garland of erukku buds calling it a flower, become a spectacle in the street, and become something else besides.
nuance: He speaks in the third person plural, as a general rule of what love does, and ends vaguely (பிறிதும் ஆகுப), which is the threat: the next step is beyond naming.

thinai_evidence.note: the madal of love grown excessive, which porul 1.51 sets under perunthinai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred; the colophon names only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the palm-stem, ridden as a horse
the erukku buds, worn as flowers
love grown hard as heartwood

reading: The friend tells the man of the slope where jackfruit, fenced with bamboo, bears even on its roots, to be timely; who knows how it stands? like a huge fruit hanging from a small stalk on the slope, her life is very small and her love very great.
nuance: The same tree serves twice: fruit low on the root, within reach and fenced (the girl ready and guarded), then fruit too heavy for its stalk; the first image is a near miss for ullurai, since the poem itself draws the second as an open simile.

thinai_evidence.note: hill jackfruit and bamboo, with the friend pressing for marriage

comparisons.tenor: her small life bearing a great love

reading: The man tells his heart to grieve, dull and bare like the flowerless heads of the bards made poor by the loss of Evvi: who is she to us now, the woman of thick dark hair fragrant as the jasmine that blooms by day on the house-tree?
nuance: The simile borrows a public mourning, bards who stopped wearing flowers when their patron died, for a private estrangement; and the question யாரளோ நமக்கே disowns her while the line before it lingers on her hair.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband shut out by his wife's displeasure

comparisons.tenor: the heart's desolation

reading: The woman tells her friend that if those who put aside grace and love and leave their companion to go after wealth are the strong and wise, then let them be the wise, and let us be the fools.
nuance: The word உரவோர் is said three times until it turns to mockery; she concedes the name of wisdom to the leavers and claims folly (மடவம்) for the ones who stay, a refusal phrased as agreement.

thinai_evidence.note: a man leaving for wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the friend as மடந்தை

title: kuruntokai 21-40
theme: Short speeches of secret love and separation: the woman refusing the rains' sign or the town's sleep, dreams and wasted beauty, the friend's comforts and disclosures (the diviner's song, the tusker on his road), the lover's madal and his vow, and the strangers whose hearts mingle like rain in red earth (21-40).
source_issues: 29: the colophon thurai reads தலைன் கூற்று; தலைவன் கூற்று is meant (the speaker addresses his own heart).
24 line 4: குளிறு is read as களிறு, elephant (எழுகளிறு); the construction of lines 3 to 6 is uncertain and the verse is marked uncertain.
34 line 4: முனாஅது யானையங் குருகின் is obscure (the bird யானையங் குருகு and the sense of முனாஅது); the Maranthai simile is read without fixing it, and the verse is marked uncertain.
33: the poem does not say whose go-between the young student is, nor whether அன்னாய் addresses the friend or the mother; marked uncertain.

reading: The woman says that even if the forest, where the new konrai flowers hang among their bee-thronged clusters like gold ornaments in women's hair, declares that the rains have come, she will not believe it, because he does not deal in lies.
nuance: She turns the season's sign against itself: if he has not come, this cannot be the rains he named, for he keeps his word. The forest is made to 'say' (கூறினும) like a witness she refuses, so her faith in him outweighs the evidence of the land.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest, the konrai and the word for the rainy season fix the mullai land and time

comparisons.tenor: the golden konrai clusters showing in the forest

reading: The friend tells the weeping woman that no one would part from her and leave her here with streaming eyes: his journey will be made with her, she whose bright brow is fragrant as the spring branches of the whorled maraa that adorns the hill slope.
nuance: 'நின்னொடுஞ் செலவே' can mean that he will take her with him or that he cannot go at all without her; either way the friend answers the fear of parting by denying that it can happen.

thinai_evidence.note: the fear of his leaving on a journey is the paalai situation

comparisons.tenor: her brow, fragrant as the maraa's spring branches

reading: The friend calls on the diviner woman, whose long fine hair is like a strung row of shell beads, to sing her song, and sing it again: the song she sang of his tall good hill.
nuance: By asking for the song about his hill, the friend lets the rite itself disclose whom the girl pines for, without naming him before the household. The triple call அகவன் மகளே and the triple பாட்டே copy the chant of the rite.

thinai_evidence.note: his tall hill is the land of the love and of the song

comparisons.tenor: the diviner's long fine hair

reading: The woman asks whether the new bounty of the dark-trunked neem's bright flowers will pass without her, and says that since her lover went away the tongues of the cruel have clamoured until she is crushed like a single fig fruit trodden by an elephant beside the river.
nuance: The neem's flowering marks a season meant to be shared; the gossip, not the absence alone, is what crushes her, and one fallen fruit under a great beast measures how small she is against the town's tongues.

thinai_evidence.note: she endures the season through while he is away

comparisons.tenor: she, crushed by the gossip that rose when he left

reading: The woman says that no one was there but the thief himself, and if he goes back on his word she can do nothing; only a heron was there, on thin green legs like millet stalks, watching the running water for aaral fish, on the day he took her.
nuance: The one witness of the union is a heron whose eyes were on the fish, a witness that saw nothing; கள்வன் names the secret lover as a thief who left no proof.

thinai_evidence.note: the secret union with no witness is the kalavu of kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the heron's thin green legs

reading: The friend says that though the man of the land where peacocks perched on the high branches of the fully bloomed dark-trunked vengai look like women plucking flowers should speak falsely, like one unworthy, what one has seen with one's own eyes does not lie; even the male monkey of the hill, sire of a sturdy young one, sharp-toothed and red-mouthed, eating sweet mango, knows that cruel man.
nuance: Against the lover's possible denial the friend calls the hill's own creature as witness. Who 'தான்' and 'தன்கண்' refer to is not fixed (the lover, or a diviner who speaks wrongly of the girl's illness), so the occasion is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the hill and its monkey fix the land

comparisons.tenor: the peacocks perched on the vengai's high branches
the lover, if he speaks falsely

reading: The woman says that her beauty, the dark glow of her mottled waist, of use neither to herself nor to her man, is left for pallor to eat, like a good cow's sweet milk that the calf does not drink and the pail does not catch, spilling on the ground.
nuance: The simile makes beauty a yield owed to someone; unshared, it is not only lost but wasted, and உணீஇயர் gives the pallor an eater's appetite.

thinai_evidence.note: beauty wasting into pallor while her man is away

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, enjoyed by no one and eaten by pallor

reading: The woman asks whether she should butt them, or strike them, or, not knowing what to do, find some pretext and cry out 'aah, help' to the town that sleeps on, unaware of the grief that torments her while the restless wind tosses her about.
nuance: Her rage is at the sleeping town, not at the man: the whole community rests while she alone keeps watch with her pain, and the wind is the only thing awake with her.

thinai_evidence.note: the grief of a woman left alone

reading: The man tells his heart that, passing over good counsel and spreading worthless talk, it has plunged like a fresh unfired pot set out in the rain into a flood the mind cannot hold, and is in hard straits; its clamour would be very great indeed, if it found anyone to hold it close and listen, as a mother monkey on a high branch holds her young.
nuance: The unfired pot dissolves in the very water it takes in: the heart is unmade by the desire it receives. The second simile is a wish that sharpens the loneliness: no one will hold and hear him as the monkey holds her child.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey on the high branch is of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the heart that took in a flood of desire it cannot hold
one who would hold the heart close and listen

reading: The woman tells her friend to listen: last night a lying dream that seemed true, of the embrace of the man so skilled in lies, deceived her, and she rose and felt over the bed; now, wasted like a kuvalai flower that the bees have visited, she is alone and truly to be pitied.
nuance: The man is called a master of lies and the dream a lie that looked true, so the dream repeats his falseness; waking is the moment of loss, her hand finding the empty bed.

thinai_evidence.note: she wakes alone in his absence

comparisons.tenor: she, wasted and alone after the dream

reading: The woman says that neither at the festival where warriors gather nor in the thunangai dance where women hold one another can she find the noble one anywhere; she too is a woman of the dancing ground, and the proud chief who loosened her bright conch bangles is a man of the dancing ground as well.
nuance: The poet is Aathimanthiyaar, and the lost man of the dancing ground is the dancer whom other poems name; she searches the festival grounds because they are his own place, and the two parallel lines (ஆடுகள மகளே, ஆடுகள மகனே) claim an equal bond.

thinai_evidence.note: the town's festival and its dance are marutham settings

reading: The man says that if one can tell the hours apart, morning, day, helpless evening, the midnight when the town sleeps, and dawn, then love is a lie; to appear in the street on the palmyra-stem horse and proclaim it openly is shame, and to go on living is shame too, once parting comes.
nuance: The two shames are made equal: riding the madal disgraces him, but living apart from her is no less a disgrace, so the threat is the lesser of two dishonours. Tholkappiyam files madal under perunthinai; here it is threatened, not yet done, and the poem stays in kurinji.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover in secret love threatens madal to win her

comparisons.tenor: the palmyra stem ridden as a horse

reading: The woman says to her companion that this young student, his body never filled by the food he begs, who comes into town as a guest, such a great noble fellow, must be someone of standing at the common ground of his own town.
nuance: The praise is mockery: the go-between who comes begging as a guest is called a great man, so the heroine shuts him out with laughter instead of anger. Whose messenger he is, and whether அன்னாய் addresses the friend or the mother, the poem does not say.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no land; the colophon's marutham and the refusal of a go-between are followed

reading: The friend says: let this town, which would not stop when we rebuked it nor believe when we denied, now that its gossip that we sleep alone is over, hear the sweet news and rejoice: the lord of our girl, whose bright brow with its shining ear-rings is lovely as Kuttuvan's Maranthai, where the great flock of herons in the seaside grove takes fright at the roar of the warriors, is that very man.
nuance: The gossip ends by coming true: the man the town whispered about is now her lord (கிழவனும் அவனே), so the friend invites the town to the very news it guessed. The brow is measured by the beauty of a Chera port town.

thinai_evidence.note: the gossip of the town ends when the man is owned as her lord

comparisons.tenor: the girl's bright brow and beauty

reading: The woman says her eyes are shameless indeed; and the cold north wind, coming with fine drizzle that opens the folded bud of the dense sugarcane, swollen like the belly of a green snake heavy with young on a branch, is fire to those who have been parted.
nuance: The cane's flower opening in the drizzle is a sign of fruitfulness that burns the parted woman; her shameless eyes weep openly and betray her.

thinai_evidence.note: the pain of the one parted from her man

comparisons.tenor: the folded flower-bud of the sugarcane

reading: The woman tells her friend that the man of the hill land, where the dark maanai creeper climbs an elephant asleep beside a boulder, swore an unfailing vow, 'with my heart as witness I will not leave you', on the day he took her shoulders; is the grief then yours, friend?
nuance: The creeper that climbs the sleeping elephant as though it were the boulder beside it is a near miss for ullurai: one correspondence (a clinging thing on a body unaware of it) but no second pair, so it stays scene. His vow is called வஞ்சினம், the warrior's word.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, its boulder, creeper and elephant

reading: The friend tells the woman that he has great desire for her and will surely be gracious; the road he took is a loving one, where the big-trunked tusker strips the soft branches of the yaa tree to ease the hunger of his mate.
nuance: The friend calls the road itself 'loving' (அன்பின) because of what is done on it: the hero cannot pass such care without being reminded of his own.

thinai_evidence.note: the yaa tree and the hungry elephants of the dry road

iraicchi.act: the tusker strips the yaa tree's soft branches to ease his mate's hunger
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees such care on his road will remember his own wife and return to cherish her

reading: The woman says, bitterly, that the friendship of the hill man, in whose land the young of the sun-basking langur roll the eggs the forest peahen laid on a rock, is good indeed for ever, friend, for those who can bear it without thinking of him while their kohl-lined eyes are spent with tears.
nuance: The praise is irony: his bond is good only for one who can forget him. The langur's young rolling the peahen's eggs on bare rock is a near miss for ullurai (one correspondence, careless play with a fragile thing left exposed, but no second pair), so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the peahen, the langur and the hill

reading: The woman says they tell her that the road taken by him who tired of lying between her breasts is the hard mountain waste where, when the fierce strong wind sweeps through the grove, the dried ripe pods of the uzhinjil rattle.
nuance: 'என்ப', they say: she knows the road only by report, and the rattling pods are the sound she imagines on it. முனிநர், the one who tired of her, makes his leaving a rejection, not only a journey.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard dry waste with its rattling dead pods

reading: The man asks what his mother and hers were to each other, how his father and hers are kin, and how he and she ever came to know each other; yet like rain falling on red earth, their loving hearts have mingled into one.
nuance: The three questions strip away every tie of kin and acquaintance before the simile, so the union owes nothing to family; rain on red soil takes its colour and cannot be separated out again. The poet is known only by this image (செம்புலப் பெயனீரார்).

thinai_evidence.note: the first union of two strangers in secret love

comparisons.tenor: two loving hearts mingled into one

title: kuruntokai 41-60
theme: Short poems of the five lands in many voices: the woman desolate when he goes (41, 43, 46, 50, 54), the friend testing or holding the man to his word (42, 47, 53, 55), the foster mother on the eloped girl's trail (44), vows that reach past death and birth (49, 57), the consent of kin and gossip (51), the lover's sickness his friends cannot cure (58), and the pleasure of merely seeing him (60).
source_issues: 46 lines 6-7 recur word for word as Kuruntokai 330 lines 6-7 (flagged); marked as written, as a shared closing formula.
48 lines 1-4: the construction is uncertain (who gives the warning about the pollen doll, and whether நினை in line 4 is 'thinking' or 'you'); the verse is marked uncertain.
52 line 5: பரிந்தனென் may be 'I pitied' or 'I pleaded'; the addressee is taken as the girl named in lines 3-4; the verse is marked uncertain.
56 line 5 is the repaired reading of tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), flagged by show; marked as repaired.
The Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (X கூற்று), so every addressee in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and occasion.stage is left null.

reading: The woman tells her friend that while her lover is near she delights like a town holding its festival, but since he went away she is desolate and dull, like an empty house in a little hamlet by the wasteland whose people have left and in whose yard squirrels play.
nuance: Both similes are places, a crowded festival town and an emptied yard; the squirrels playing freely in the yard are the sign that no one is left, so her emptiness is measured by what now moves in it. The poet is named after line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of the time after he has gone away

comparisons.tenor: her delight while he is near, like a town in festival
her dull desolation since he left

reading: The friend asks the man of the hill land, where after the cloud-massed rain falls at midnight the waterfall goes on sounding in the clefts, whether, even if desire should end, our bond with him could ever wane.
nuance: The friend grants that kaamam may end and asks only whether the bond will; தேயுமோ, 'will it wane', is the moon's verb. The image sits in the address to him, where the hill lord's own land answers her question before he can.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill clefts, the waterfall and midnight

ullurai.tenor: desire and the bond that should outlast it

pairs.situation: desire, which comes down in one burst and is spent
the bond, which should go on sounding after the desire has passed

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the rain and waterfall of the hero's own hill in a kurinji poem, without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

reading: The woman says she made light of it, thinking he would not go, and he made light of it, thinking she would not bear it; caught in the clash their two great prides made, her troubled heart writhes as if a cobra had seized it.
nuance: Avvaiyar gives the same verb to both (இகழ்ந்தனனே, இகழ்ந்தனரே) and calls the silence of both ஆண்மை, a word of manly pride, used here of the woman too: each was sure of the other, neither spoke, and the parting happened between them. The poem does not say what the snake seizes; the moon in eclipse is one reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going away, which neither spoke of

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

comparisons.tenor: her troubled heart writhing

reading: The foster mother, following the girl who has gone off with her lover, says her legs are worn out and her eyes have lost their light from looking and looking, and that the others in this world, none of them her girl, are surely more than the stars of the wide dark sky.
nuance: The poem never says whom she seeks; the speaker and the eyes that have lost their light from looking make it the search. பிறரே, 'others', is the last word: everyone she has looked at is someone else.

thinai_evidence.note: the search on the road for the girl who has gone with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee in the poem; she speaks to herself on the road

comparisons.tenor: the strangers she has looked at in her search

reading: The friend says that the lord of the rich town rose at dawn, yoked his swift chariot and went to embrace women of bright jewels, and when he stays out long the mother of his little son grieves; how searing it is, she says, to be born into this station.
nuance: திணை here is birth or station, not landscape: what burns is being born to a family whose wife must keep the house while the man goes to other women. The friend names the wife only as the mother of the little son, the title that binds her to stay. எல்லினன் is taken as 'he is late'.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the rich town goes to other women and his wife grieves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: he is spoken of in the third person, so the friend answers someone sent by him

reading: The woman asks her friend whether, in the land where he has gone, there is no grieving, lonely evening like this one, when the house sparrows with folded wings the colour of water-lily ash, having eaten the grain drying in the yard and bathed in the fine dust of the dung in the common ground, settle with their young in the nest under the eaves.
nuance: The colophon's thinai is marutham, the land of the village yard the sparrows live in; the situation, a man gone to another land and a woman alone at evening, is paalai's. The question is whether evening exists where he is: if it did, he would feel what she feels and come.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone to another land and she bears the evening alone

comparisons.tenor: the sparrows' folded wings

iraicchi.act: the sparrows come back at evening to the nest in the eaves and stay there with their young
iraicchi.sense: even the house sparrow is home with its young at nightfall, while he stays away in another land

reading: The friend tells the long white moon that, in the forest where the boulder strewn with the falling blossoms of the black-trunked vengai looks like a great tiger's cub, it does no good to those who come at night for secret love.
nuance: The moon does two harms at once: its light shows the lovers to watchers, and it makes the rock under the vengai look like a tiger, so the night path is both seen and fearful. The man is not addressed; he is meant to understand that the night meetings cannot go on. The poet is named after line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai and the tiger of the hill forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the moon; by the usual reading the man, standing by, is meant to hear

comparisons.tenor: the boulder spotted with fallen vengai blossoms

reading: The friend asks whether the lover will not send even one word of the kind she longs for, to clear the pallor from her fair forehead, though she suffers greatly in this way even after hearing her playmates at the oorai game tell her to beware the grief of the morning, when the cool dew-wet doll they made of pollen will wilt.
nuance: The playmates' warning about the pollen doll that wilts by morning reads as said of her: her beauty is as perishable as the toy. இன்ன பண்பின், 'of such a nature', joins the two, but the construction of lines 1 to 4 is not certain. One kind word is all the friend asks of him.

thinai_evidence.note: her pallor while the lover is away and sends no word

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: unclear: she speaks of the girl and of the lover in the third person

comparisons.tenor: the girl's beauty, which wilts as she grieves

reading: The woman tells the lord of the shore of dark sapphire waters, where the water-thorn's blossoms with ripe pollen are like a squirrel's teeth, that even when this life turns into the next, may he be her husband and may she be the one close to his heart.
nuance: The vow stretches the marriage past this life and asks for two things, not one: that he be her husband, and that she be the one his heart agrees with (நெஞ்சு நேர்பவள்). The second wish admits a doubt the first does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-thorn and the lord of the strand; the situation is a vow, not a lament

comparisons.tenor: the water-thorn's blossoms with ripe pollen
the dark great waters of the shore

reading: The woman says the ford of his town is adorned with small nyaazhal blossoms like mustard seeds strewn with the spent flowers of the fresh marutham, while the shoulders he embraced, wasted so that the bright bangles slip past the wrist, are adorned with loneliness.
nuance: The same verb closes both halves: அணிந்தன்று, 'is adorned', for his ford and for her shoulders. His place wears flowers and hers wears loneliness; the parallel is the reproach. The colophon says marutham; the uri of lament, with the shore tree nyaazhal, points to neythal.

thinai_evidence.note: her lament as her body wastes is irangal, though the ford mixes neythal and marutham trees

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

comparisons.tenor: the small nyaazhal blossoms

reading: The friend says that the lord of the shore of pure sand, where the cold dewy flowers of the bent-thorned water-thorn, blown by the wind like pearls from a broken string, spread over every ford, is loved by her too; their mother is very fond of him, their father wants to give the girl to him, and the gossiping town too speaks her name with his.
nuance: Each one who might stand in the way is turned in his favour: the friend, the mother, the father and at last the town, whose அம்பல் usually threatens secret love and here pairs the girl with him. யானும் காதலென், 'I too love him', is the friend speaking as one with the girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the water-thorn on the sands and the lord of the strand

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the man is spoken of in the third person

comparisons.tenor: the water-thorn blossoms scattered by the wind

reading: The friend tells the girl with thick dark hair smelling of naranda and rows of bright white teeth that when she saw her trembling, like one desired by the spirit of the water-bright slope trampled by the feeding elephant, she felt for her, little by little, did she not?
nuance: சூர் நசைந்தனையை, 'like one the spirit has desired', is how a girl's lovesickness looks to those who do not know its cause; the friend says she saw it and understood. Whether பரிந்தனென் is pity for the girl or a plea made on her behalf is not settled by the verse.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant, the hill slope and its spirit

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the girl named in lines 3-4 is taken as the one addressed

comparisons.tenor: the girl trembling with love

reading: The friend tells the man of the fields that what afflicts us is the oath he swore at the broad ford of our town, holding the girl's forearm with the hill-goddesses as witness, by the sand dune where the yard's punku blossoms lie on the white sand like the bright puffed red rice the velan scatters on every ground of his possession rite.
nuance: அணங்கு is turned round: what afflicts them is not the goddess but the oath sworn before the goddesses, which will punish its breaker and, the friend fears, those he swore to. The velan's scattered rice brings the possession rite into the scene, as if the ground of the oath were already a ground of veri.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend holds the man of the fields to the oath he has broken

comparisons.tenor: the punku blossoms fallen on the white sand

reading: The woman says she is here, but her beauty has stayed there with the man of the forest land, where the green bamboo the forest elephant lets go, frightened by the sling-noise of the millet-field watchmen, springs up like a rod that has struck a fish.
nuance: Line 1 splits her in two, I am here and my beauty is there, so nalam becomes a thing that can leave with him. The poet is named after the simile of line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, its watchmen and the forest elephant

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo springing up when the elephant lets go

ullurai.tenor: the man who lets her go for fear of the watch kept on her

pairs.situation: the watch and talk that frighten him off
he lets go of her, who is left behind
she is left shaken, her beauty gone with him

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the millet field she herself guards and the elephant of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The friend says that as the sapphire flowers of the great backwater close, and the stroking cold wind comes bringing mist with the spray of the white waves to leave us helpless, this small good town has become, for these few days, a painful place to live.
nuance: The closing flowers mark the evening without naming it. The town is called small and good (சிறுநல்லூர்) and painful in one breath: the place has not changed, only the season and his absence have.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the waves and the cold wind at nightfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred: the complaint is meant to make him hasten

reading: The man on the waterless road says: let her of the bangled hands come and drink with me this little rotten water swarmed by wasps, left over when the hunting wild dogs dug and drank; she is to be pitied, pitied, she who dwells in my heart.
nuance: The wish holds two readings: he would have her share even this water, so that love would make it sweet, or he pictures her drinking it and pities her for it; அளியளோ அளியள் keeps both. கிளைத்து, 'dug', can also mean 'with their kin', which would make the dogs a pack sharing the water as he would share it with her; that reading is too doubtful to tag.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunting wild dogs and the fouled water of the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks of her to himself

reading: The woman wishes that, with a love that never slackens and cannot bear parting, like the union of the water-dwelling makanril pair for whom even a flower slipping between them seems a year gone by, their two lives might go out together, so that in this world where they live as two who know their duty they may escape the misery of one being left alone.
nuance: கடனறிந்து இருவேம் ஆகிய, 'we two who live knowing our duty', places the wish inside married life: the fear is not of a journey but of one death before the other.

thinai_evidence.note: the fear of parting and of being left alone is lament

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from நாம் and இருவேம், which include him

comparisons.tenor: a flower's moment between the birds, felt as a year
their love that cannot bear parting

reading: The man tells the friends who rebuke him that it would be well indeed if they could hold back this sickness for his sake, but it has spread like butter melting on a sun-scorched rock, watched over by a handless mute with only his eyes, and it is hard to bear.
nuance: The image stacks three helplessnesses: the keeper has no hands to gather the butter, no voice to call for help, and only his eyes to watch it melt. The rebukers are granted their good intent; the reply is that rebuke cannot reach what has already spread.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's love-sickness in secret love, which his friends rebuke

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the companions who rebuke him (இடிக்குங் கேளிர்)

comparisons.vehicle: கையில் ஊமன் கண்ணிற் காக்கும் வெண்ணெய் உணங்கல் போலப்
comparisons.tenor: his love-sickness, spreading past holding

reading: The friend asks whether he could forget her fragrant forehead, which smells of wild jasmine bundled with blue water-lilies from the deep wide-mouthed spring of Athalai hill, ruled by the lord of the gift-seekers who beat the pathalai drum; and since rare wealth beyond many wastelands is never filled up however one strives, she says, he will not stay long.
nuance: The comfort has two arguments: he cannot forget her, since the scent of a named hill's flowers is the memory he carries, and wealth is never complete, so there is no point in his staying to complete it. The second turns the reason for his journey against its length.

thinai_evidence.note: he has crossed the wastelands in search of wealth

reading: The woman says that, like a dark-legged cripple who sees a great honeycomb on the high cliff where short-stemmed koothali sways and, sitting below, cups his palm into a little bowl, points and licks it, even if her lover does not grace her or desire her, seeing him often is sweet to her heart.
nuance: The cripple never tastes the honey: he points at it and licks his empty cupped hand, so the simile makes the sweetness of seeing him an imagined taste. நல்கார் நயவார் ஆயினும் concedes the worst before claiming the sweetness.

thinai_evidence.note: the koothali and the honeycomb of the high cliff

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred; the poem names none

comparisons.vehicle: முடவன் உட்கைச் சிறுகுடை கோலிக் கீழிருந்து சுட்டுபு நக்கி
comparisons.tenor: her pleasure in merely seeing him

title: kuruntokai 61-80
theme: Short speeches of the five lands: women waiting through the rains and the cold for men who went far (64-68, 75-77, 79), men praising the girl's body and eyes (62, 70-72), the friend's stratagems and refusals (61, 66, 69, 73, 74), the companion on love's folly (78) and a courtesan's taunt (80).
source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (தலைவி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
75 line 2: தெளிய was repaired from a TSCII leftover (தௌிய); the repair reads correctly.

Thinai differs from the colophon in 68 (mullai: black-gram fields and deer), 71 (kurinji: a hunter's daughter; the colophon's paalai implies a journey the poem does not state), 75 (mullai: waiting for news of his return) and 76 (paalai: his going decides it among hill things).

reading: The friend says that, like small boys who cannot ride the little cart a carpenter made yet delight in dragging it by hand, we take our delight in mere kinship with the man of the pond-rich town of good chariots, though we do not enjoy his embrace, and the bangles have grown tight again.
nuance: The boys' toy cart is a pleasure taken without its proper use; the friend makes the household's dignity out of a love that has been reduced to a name, and the tightened bangles answer the gossip that she is wasting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is named by the ponds of the watered town

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the man is spoken of in the third person, so most likely his messenger

comparisons.vehicle: தச்சன் செய்த சிறுமா வையம் ஊர்ந்தின் புறாஅர் ஆயினுங் கையின் ஈர்த்தின் புறூஉம் இளையோர் போல
comparisons.tenor: the women, who cannot have his embrace but are content with the bond itself

reading: The man says that her body, fragrant as a finely made garland of upturned kodal buds, fresh mullai and sweet-petalled kuvalai woven in alternation, is softer than tender shoots and sweet to embrace.
nuance: The garland mixes flowers of three lands, hill, woodland and water, so her one body gathers the scents a single landscape cannot give.

thinai_evidence.note: the embrace of lovers is the union of kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he speaks of her in the third person, after their meeting

comparisons.vehicle: கோடல் எதிர்முகைப் பசுவீ முல்லை நாறிதழ்க் குவளையொ டிடையிடுபு விரைஇ ஐதுதொடை மாண்ட கோதை போல
comparisons.tenor: her body, fragrant with mingled scents
her body, softer than tender shoots

reading: The man asks his heart: you reckon that the work to be done must be pressed hard because there is neither giving nor enjoying for those who have nothing; but will the lovely young woman come along on that work, or will you send me off alone? Tell me.

reading: The woman asks her friend whether they do not think of us, the men who crossed the forest of kalli on scorched land, where the bright neem fruit held in the parrot's curved beak looks like a gold coin that a man with sharp fine nails threads on a new string.

reading: The man says the young girl of the gathered, glossy hair and bright brow is fragrant and cool and a great enchantress; I cannot measure her adornment to say she is such; her few words are soft, and she is soft as a pillow when I embrace her.
nuance: 'I cannot say she is such' is the lover's refusal to describe, and then he describes only what touch knows: coolness, fragrance, soft words, a soft body.

nuance: The girl's work is to drive off small birds with her cries, but it is her eyes that strike; and 'everyone knows' marks the moment his private wound becomes public talk.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl guarding the hill millet from sparrows

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he explains his visible sickness, likely to his companion

her eyes, which wound like arrows

reading: The friend tells the woman: you long for your lover's chest; do not despair, may you live; like the Kosar of the single word, who cut down Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land, a little hard-eyed scheming is needed.
nuance: The scheme is not named: whether it is to withhold meetings so he must marry, or something else, the poem leaves open. மகிழ்நன் for the lover is a marutham word in a poem filed under kurinji.

reading: The friend says that the man of the hill where green bamboo touching the sky springs up with the speed of a horse let loose, not knowing how we pined for him, has himself, they say, wasted like a bull in summer, longing for our fine beauty.
nuance: The friend gives the heroine the comfort that the wasting is mutual; the summer bull, a beast of the pasture brought into the hill poem, makes his thinness a matter of season and hunger, the very terms of her own.

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo springing upright with force
the man, wasted with longing as a bull in the dry season

reading: The woman asks: did you see it yourself, or hear it from someone who saw? Tell us one clear thing, for we long to know; may you win Pataliputra rich in gold, where white-tusked elephants bathe in the Son; from whose mouth did you hear that my lover is coming?
nuance: The blessing, may you win Pataliputra, is the richest reward a Tamil poet could name, and it is offered before she knows if the news is true, so her hunger shows in the price she would pay.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman waiting for news of his return

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the one who brought news of his coming

reading: The woman asks whether they say he will go, the man with a chest like a rock face, of the good land of high hills fenced with kaanthal, in the hard-dewed early winter when the cold north wind sways the big leaves of the taro on the slopes like the ears of a great tusker, and sets us shivering in distress.
nuance: The season is the argument: no one should leave in the cold of அச்சிரம், and the shiver she names is both the weather's and her own.

thinai_evidence.note: the news of his going decides it, though the things are of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the swaying taro leaves, like elephants' ears flapping

reading: The woman tells her friend there is no fault in him at all; if fault there is, it is that the broad soft shoulders became easy to leave for the man who went to the hard forest, where in the cruel waste the leaf-heaped cairns of dead travellers give shade to the tall elephant.
nuance: She clears him and blames her own shoulders, but the desert of dead men's cairns he chose over them is a reproach she leaves standing; the elephant resting in the shade of graves is the land's indifference to death.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

reading: The companion tells the man of the shining hill, where the long white waterfall on the great peak resounds like the drum of the skilled old players as it pours down the slope: love is a painful thing; with great folly it goes and stands even by those who do not think it good.
nuance: The companion does not blame the girl but love itself, which stands by those who do not value it; the drumming fall frames love as something that pours down unbidden.

thinai_evidence.note: the high hill and its waterfall

reading: The courtesan says: with whole stalks of water-lily fastened in our hair we will go to bathe at the broad ford where the great flood has come; if she fears that, let her and her kin guard her husband's chest, like the great herds at the front of Ezhini of many spears, who wins fierce wars till the yoke breaks.
