comparisons.tenor: the husband, whom the wife must guard as closely as a war-chief's cattle

title: kuruntokai 81-100
theme: Kuruntokai 81 to 100: short poems of hill courtship and its dangers (the night path, the town's talk, the friend testing and pressing the girl), set beside wives waiting through the rain season, a husband's go-between mocked, and a foster mother who reads her daughter's flight too late. Puram names (Aay's Pothiyil, Anji's raids, the Kolli of Porayan and of Ori) are used as measures for private feeling.
source_issues: 81: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but the poem is all shore (கடல், கானல், ஞாழல், பெண்ணை); marked neythal.
84: line 5 is the repaired tamilvu reading, as show flags.
94: line 3 is the repaired tamilvu reading, as show flags.
81 and 85: the poet's name is spelt வடம வண்ணக்கண் in 81 and வடம வண்ணக்கன் in 85; the colophons are copied as they stand.

reading: The friend tells the lover that the girl, who believed her word because it carried his, now sits alone in a corner under the many-branched njaazhal with its fresh buds, her new beauty gone; then she points: look over there and keep it in mind, our small good town of drooping palmyras, where the sea of smelling waves and the shore grove show side by side like moonlight and darkness.
nuance: The friend admits her own part: the girl yielded because the friend's word stood surety for his (நின்சொற் கொண்ட என்சொல்). Pointing out the town and its landmarks is a way of telling him where to come openly, that is, to ask for her.

thinai_evidence.note: shore grove, njaazhal and palmyra are neythal things; the colophon's kurinji has no support in the poem

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she calls him நின் and speaks of the girl as இவள்; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: the pale sea and the dark grove seen together

reading: The woman asks her friend what sort of man he is, the one who used to stroke her long curled hair, hold her and wipe her weeping eyes saying 'do not cry', and who has not come back in the bitter-dew season, when the plump avarai creeper flowers on the second-sown millet of the hill farmer's wide field.
nuance: The tender gestures she recalls are his own, so the question 'who will wipe my eyes?' is also an accusation: the comforter is the cause. The avarai flowering on the millet's second sowing dates the broken promise on the field itself.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits past the season he named, which is mullai's situation, though every thing in the poem is of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி)

reading: The friend blesses the mother: may she win the world of great name with rare ambrosia for her food, because she said that the lord of the high hill, where sweet jackfruit hang from every branch like one's own food eaten in one's own house, will come.
nuance: The blessing is extravagant (the gods' food, the world above) for a single sentence, 'he will come'; the size of the gratitude shows how long the waiting has been. The simile of eating one's own food in one's own house anticipates the household the coming promises.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit hill and its lord fix the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem; she reports the mother's words to the girl

comparisons.tenor: the jackfruit hanging ripe and sweet on their own branches

reading: The foster mother recalls that when she turned the girl over to embrace her, the girl said 'I am sweating'; only now does she understand that it was distress; yet that girl, fragrant with the vengai and kaanthal of Aay's cloud-crept Pothiyil, was cooler to the touch than the water-lily.
nuance: The last line undoes the first: the girl was cool by nature, so the 'sweat' was an excuse to slip the embrace of the woman who raised her, already turned toward another. The foster mother's memory of her daughter's fragrance is all hill-country flowers, the lover's land.

thinai_evidence.note: the foster mother reads the sign only after the girl has gone, the paalai situation of the elopement

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks her discovery aloud, and the girl's going is inferred from the colophon's paalai

comparisons.tenor: the girl's coolness to the touch

reading: The friend says that the lord of the rich town, where the hopping sparrow cock of the village plucks the scentless white flowers of the sweet-jointed sugarcane to line a nest for his hen near her laying, is sweeter than anyone and full of great love: in his bard's mouth.
nuance: The praise collapses on its last word, வாயே: the great love exists in the bard's telling. The sparrow's flowers are scentless (நாறா); whether that is a further slight on the husband's gifts is doubtful and not tagged.

thinai_evidence.note: the sugarcane and the lord of the rich town are marutham's

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the bard comes as the husband's go-between; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

iraicchi.act: the sparrow cock gathers cane flowers to build a nest for his hen as her laying nears
iraicchi.sense: even a village sparrow provides for his mate in her time, while the husband's care for his wife exists only in the bard's words

reading: Her red-streaked cool eyes overflowing like a breached dam, sick with an unbearable illness and shaken by loneliness, the woman asks whether anyone else is listening, at midnight in the cold season when the north wind flings the heavy rain, to the thin, poor voice of the curved bell with its tongue that clangs each time the lonely cow stirs.
nuance: 'Does anyone else hear?' means 'is anyone else awake?': the only other wakeful thing is a cow whose loneliness (புலம்பு) rings out in the same word the poem uses for hers (புலம்பலை).

thinai_evidence.note: the cold season and the midnight watch are kurinji's time

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: her tears overflowing like water breaking a dam

reading: The woman says people hold that the fearsome old god in the kadamba tree of the village common destroys the false; her hill lord is not false in the least; yet her forehead has paled with longing and her broad soft shoulders have grown slack as his care slackened.
nuance: She clears him before the god so the god will not strike him for a broken oath; but the punishment the poem shows has landed on her own body, so the defence carries its own accusation. The doubled verbs (பசைஇப் பசந்தன்று, ஞெகிழ ஞெகிழ்ந்தன்று) tie each loss to his loosening.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country of the lover fixes the land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the high hill of loud white waterfalls comes even at midnight across the hard slope where the small-eyed great tusker, struck by a strong tiger, loses its old fierceness; and they, for their part, will not shrink from the shame of scandal.
nuance: The last line can be read as resolve (we will not let fear of talk keep him in danger: the love should be made known and the marriage pressed) or as a reckless 'we are past caring for blame'. The tusker that loses to the tiger shows what the path can do even to the strongest; it carries the danger, not an act of the lovers, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: waterfall, tusker and tiger are the hill's things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: Strangers sing the open-mouthed pounding song at their broad-footed mortars and nobody minds; what harm can come to this foolish town if this soft young girl, like the lovely figure that the dark-eyed goddess drew on the western face of fearsome Kolli of Porayan of the great ornaments, sang as she pounded?
nuance: The friend's point is the double standard: the same pounding song is harmless in strangers' mouths, but from this girl it is taken as a sign (presumably because she sang of the lover's hill). The town is called பேதை, the word usually given to an innocent girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the town's talk about an unmarried girl's song is the secret love of kalavu; the poem has no fields or ford for the colophon's marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of the town in the third person, perhaps for the lover or the mother to hear

comparisons.tenor: the soft young girl

reading: The friend exclaims to the girl: what a thing it is! the friendship of the hill lord, from whose slopes where pepper vines climb, after the dark rain-cloud has thundered all night and fallen, the falls carry down to the drinking ford a fragrant jackfruit that a shaggy stag touched and loosened, has wasted your soft shoulders and yet has brought forth your constancy.
nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the fruit that the stag loosens and the stream carries to a common ford invites a mapping (the girl won by the lover, then exposed to everyone), but the poem never anchors a second correspondence, so the scene stays scene. சால்பு is given a double edge: the friendship 'yielded' wasting and, with it, endurance.

thinai_evidence.note: pepper slopes, stag and jackfruit are kurinji things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: The woman tells herself that if she is to be the wife of the lord of the cool ford, where kendai fish in the deep pool snap at the ripe striped fruit of the tangled rattan, then let the cares in her heart be many and her nights of sleep few, like those of a town on the deadly frontier at night that fears Anji of the tall chariot and hard-driving elephants, whose hand gives like unceasing rain.
nuance: A near miss for ullurai: fish snapping at whatever fruit drops into the pool can be read as the husband taking every woman who comes his way, but the poem never states his straying, so there is no anchor. The wife's curse on herself borrows its measure from war: her marriage will be a frontier town under raid.

thinai_evidence.note: the pool, its fish and the lord of the cool ford are marutham's

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses herself in the second person (நின் நெஞ்சு, நீ துஞ்சு நாள்); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: her own nights of little sleep as the husband's wife
Anji's giving hand

reading: The woman says the curve-winged birds in the wide sky where the sun has set are to be pitied: carrying food to push into the mouths of their young in the tall kadamba beside the path where they roost, they hurry on their way.
nuance: Her pity for the birds is pity for herself turned outward: their haste home at dusk with food for their young is what her own man does not show. The birds are the whole poem, so striking them leaves nothing; it fails the deletion test and is not tagged iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the sunset hour is neythal's time

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: The woman tells her friend not to speak against him even if her fine beauty fades, she wastes away and her sweet life leaves her: is he not mother and father to them? and what is sulking worth when love is gone?
nuance: Two refusals in four lines: she will not let the friend blame him, because he is her whole family; and she will not sulk, because sulking presumes a love that would notice it. The second refusal is the bitterer.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem turns on whether to sulk against an erring husband, marutham's situation

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி), who urges her to quarrel; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: the husband, on whom she depends wholly

reading: The woman tells her friend that the buds of the foolish pitthikam, deceived by the great cold rains, have reddened even earlier than before, and she is bewildered: what will become of the man who left her, if he too hears alone at midnight the thunder of the massed storm clouds that shakes the great hill of waterfalls?
nuance: The bud is 'foolish' for blooming to rains that are not the promised season, and she half admits she is like it. Her fear is turned toward him: she imagines him, not herself, alone under the thunder.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season of waiting is mullai's time

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: The man says that the grace of the broad-shouldered young daughter of the hill farmer of the small hamlet, on the flowered slope where the pure white falls from the great hill brim in the rock hollows, is like water, and it has put out his strength, which was like fire.
nuance: The two similes are one action: water does not defeat fire by being stronger but by being what fire cannot survive. Softness (சாயல்) is set against will (உரன்), and the soft wins.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill farmer's daughter on the slope fixes the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the companion is inferred: the man answers a reproach for his changed state; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: the girl's gentle grace
the man's strength of will

reading: The woman says to her friend: you ask 'what can I do about the lord of the great hill of waterfalls and vengai trees?'; if I had not taken that as a joke, what would have become of you, fine-browed one?
nuance: The friend's question tests her (shall I refuse him?); the woman answers that she chose to hear it as a joke, and that if she had taken it seriously the friend would have had to answer for the consequence. Who would suffer, and how, is left unsaid.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill of waterfalls and vengai names the lover's land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (நன்னுதல்); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: The woman says she is here; her beauty is there in the shore grove with an unending sickness; the lord of the shore is in his own town; and their secret, turned to open talk, is out in the common square.
nuance: Four things in four places: herself, her beauty (left where they met), him, and the secret. The love has come apart into its parts, and the only part that has gone public is the talk.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the lord of the shore fix the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

reading: The woman tells her friend it would be good if they could find someone who would go close to him, carrying a few flowers of the rainy-season peerkam that grows thick in the wet green bushes of their garden, and tell him 'the fine-browed one has become like this'.
nuance: The message is the flower: the yellow peerkam, held up with 'she has become like this', shows her pallor without a word of complaint. That it is the rain-season flower also reminds him that the season of his return has come.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season flower and the waiting at home are mullai's

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: her pallor, shown by the yellow flower held up with 'like this'

reading: The man says: did I not remember? remembering, did I not think hard? thinking, was I not bewildered? but such is the way of the world, and my great desire held back to the end, like the flood that once touched the branches of the tall kadamba and has sunk until one must scoop it to drink.
nuance: The three questions climb (remember, think, be bewildered) and each takes the last verb as its start. The flood simile can be read two ways: his desire was once as high as the treetops and shrank under duty, or it was a flood he held back to the last; the sense of மீண்டு கடைக்கொள is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the man, back from his duty, answers whether he remembered her while away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he answers a charge of forgetting, most likely put by the friend; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: his great desire held in check by duty

reading: The man says that the girl of the kaanthal-fenced hamlet, where people sow mountain rice on the spread of the falls, weed out the broad-leafed kulavi and the green maral, and when hungry trade the tusks of fierce elephants for food, has the innocence of the figure on the western face of Kolli of Ori of the strong bow, and her broad shoulders, like bamboo, are hard to win.
nuance: The girl comes from a hamlet that lives by elephant tusks, yet she is as unknowing as a painted figure; the hardness of her people's life and her innocence make her hard to win.

thinai_evidence.note: mountain rice, kaanthal fences and the hamlet are kurinji's

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the companion is inferred; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

comparisons.tenor: the girl's innocence
the girl's broad shoulders, as bamboo

title: kuruntokai 101-120
theme: Kuruntokai 101 to 120: short speeches of the love situation in every land. Men weigh earth and heaven against one day of embrace, or find a strong man undone by a slip of a girl; women burn whether they remember or try not to, curse the cock that ends a night beside the husband, hang between love and the town's talk, and face evenings and north winds that bring no one; the friend fixes trysts, mocks the mother's diviner and turns slipping bangles into a jibe.
source_issues: 115: lines 3 and 4 (இலைகவர் பாடமை ஒழுகிய) are hard to construe; the slope's description is read only as cool and fragrant, and the verse is marked uncertain.
105: the repaired line 6 (the poet's name moved to `poet`) reads cleanly as the end of the poem.

reading: The man says that the sea-girt world and the hard-won land of the gods, weighed together, are not worth the day he lies arm in arm with the young girl whose kohl eyes are like flowers and whose body is like gold.
nuance: தூக்கின் is the language of the balance: he does not say heaven is bad, only that both worlds on one pan do not lift a single day (வைகல்) of embrace on the other.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the joy of union itself; no native thing is named

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he states it as his own verdict

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes
her body's colour

reading: The woman says that if she thinks of him her heart burns, and not thinking is beyond her strength; this love has grown till it touches the sky, and the man she has clung to is not one of the noble.
nuance: The bind is closed on both sides (உள்ளின் ... உள்ளாது இருப்பின்), and the last line turns from her pain to a judgment on him: சான்றோர் அல்லர், not noble, because he lets a love this large burn her.

thinai_evidence.note: lament in absence, with no native thing to place it

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the size of her love

reading: The woman tells her friend that in the shivering mire gathered by the flood, where even the red-beaked egret hunting its food is pained by the spray the cold north wind drives, he seems not to be coming, and she seems not to be going to live.
nuance: The two lines end alike (வாரார் போல்வர் / வாழேன் போல்வல்): his not coming and her not living are set as matching guesses. The egret, which only suffers and does no act of the lovers, sets the mood and is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the egret in the flood-mire of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the egret's red beak

reading: The woman tells her friend that her lover left in the dew season, when cold drops fall like pearls from a broken string and the cool thaali creeper is grazed at dawn, and the days of parting will be many.
nuance: The season is the cruelty: he left not in summer but in the cold, when the pearl-like dew and early grazing mark each morning she counts alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone away; the things are of the cold pasture

comparisons.tenor: the cold dew drops

reading: The woman says that the bond with the man of the dread hill, where a peacock that unknowingly ate the rich millet ears set aside for the god trembles in the heat like a possessed dancing woman, has become something she remembers with streaming eyes.
nuance: The peacock's fault is innocent (அறியாது உண்ட): it took what belonged to the god of the hill and now shakes like one seized. Her own wasting would be read at home as the god's seizure, and the hill is named சூர், the dreadful.

thinai_evidence.note: hill millet, the peacock and the hill god

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: the trembling peacock

ullurai.tenor: the girl who took the hill man's love

pairs.situation: she took his love without knowing what it would cost
what she took belonged to the dread hill and its man, not freely hers
she now burns and trembles, eyes streaming

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses a peacock and millet of her own hill field, things she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The woman tells her friend that word has come from the man of the land where the white roots of the itti, climbing the rock, look like a waterfall coming down the slope, spoken from a heart without guile, and they should take it up as fire takes ghee and send back word that they are as good as wedded to him.
nuance: தான் மணந்தனையம் claims the standing of a wife while love is still secret; the eager fire of ghee is hers, the friend is drawn into the reply (நாமும்).

thinai_evidence.note: the fig on the rock and the hill waterfall

comparisons.tenor: the itti's white roots on the rock
how eagerly they should receive his word

reading: The wife curses the cock with its crest like a cluster of thondri flowers: may it fall prey to the young wildcat that watches for house rats at midnight and come to cruel harm, for it woke her from the safe sweet sleep she slept beside the lord of the rich, well-watered town.
nuance: The curse is elaborate and patient (the cat that waits at midnight for rats), which measures how sweet the broken sleep was; ஏம இன் துயில், safe sweet sleep, is the sleep of a wife at home, and the cock's crow is the dawn that ends it.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the rich watered town, and dawn

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the cock (நீயே)

comparisons.tenor: the cock's red crest

reading: The woman tells her friend that in the little village under the hill where rain clouds play, as the milch cows head back to their calves, the bright jasmine of the green-leaved scrub has taken on the beauty of the red sky, and she thinks she will not survive.
nuance: The poem never says 'evening' or 'he has not come': the cows turning to their calves and the jasmine opening red in the sunset do it for her, and the last line is the whole of her speech.

thinai_evidence.note: scrub forest, rain and the red evening

iraicchi.act: the milch cows go back to their calves at dusk
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle return to their young at nightfall, but her man has not come back to her

reading: The friend says of the lord of the shore, where the waves bring in a great swarm of thorny-legged, bent-backed prawns, that even in the days when the two were together the beauty of the girl's fine forehead was not as it is now.
nuance: மன்னோ marks something past and gone: her forehead was lovely then, and is pale now; said in the third person, it is a reproach meant for the man's hearing. The prawns that the waves bring are only the shore's plenty here; reading them as a hidden picture fails the two-pair test.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns cast up by the sea at the lord's shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she speaks of both lovers in the third person; no addressee is named

reading: The woman asks her friend what he is to them now, come or not, the man who never asked what had become of her in the cold cruel north wind that ruffles the blue water-lilies, sways the karuvilai spotted like peacock feathers and scatters the soft flowers of the thorny eengai.
nuance: Her dismissal (யாராகியரோ, who is he to us) is the measure of her hurt; what she holds against him is not absence but the question he never asked (என்னாயினள்கொல்).

thinai_evidence.note: bush flowers of the scrub under the wind

comparisons.tenor: the bright spots of the karuvilai flower

reading: The friend says that if the mother too takes the diviner's word that victorious Neduvel caused the sickness that has loosened the girl's soft arms, then let the man of the hill, where dark boulders look like a stub-tailed cow elephant with its trunk tucked in, come quickly, so they may see the household's great foolishness laughed at.
nuance: The friend wants the man's arrival to expose the rite: the household will be the joke (பெருநகை) once its god-sickness turns out to be love. சிறிதே at the end keeps the mockery mild.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner of Murugan and the hill man

comparisons.tenor: the dark crowded boulders of the hill

reading: The woman tells her friend that if she fears the town's talk her love will waste, and if she lets restraint go only shame is left; she is like the fibrous branch a great elephant has bent, broken but not fallen to the ground; see what he has done to her beauty.
nuance: The branch is held up by its own bark fibre (நாருடை): what keeps her from falling is the thread still joining her to him, which is also what the gossip would cut.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill elephant bending a branch; secret love under the town's talk

comparisons.tenor: the woman caught between love and shame

reading: The friend tells the man the place: the pond is near the town, the little forest stream not far from the pond, and the grove there is visited by nothing but the white heron looking for food; she and the friend will go there to fetch rich clay for their hair, and the great simpleton will come there too.
nuance: The directions are laid out as a chain (town, pond, stream, grove), and the heron is both the grove's only visitor and the sign that no one else will see. பெரும்பேதை, the great simpleton, is the friend's fond word for the girl who will come.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend fixes a secret tryst, the uri of kurinji, among things of the town's fields

reading: The friend tells the man of the well-made chariot that she has come to his trysting place leaving her doll lying in the neythal field, and asks leave to go, since every evening the egret, its belly full of aaral fish, tramples her little daughter's forehead.
nuance: The 'daughter' is the doll she has left on the shore, a playful pretext to leave the lovers alone; the reading of என்மகள் as the doll is ours and the joke depends on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flats, the egret and the aaral fish

reading: The friend tells the man of the good hill, where the soft-gaited wild cow sleeps on the cool fragrant slope, that even those who do great good may be slighted, but though she has only one good in her, he should be kind with a perfected love so that her sulking ends, for she has no one but him.
nuance: The wild cow sleeping unafraid on his slope stands for the safety she should have in his grace; the opening maxim is a warning turned gently against him.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild cow on the hill slope

iraicchi.act: the wild cow sleeps unafraid on the man's slope
iraicchi.sense: as the creatures of his hill rest secure there, the girl who has no one but him should rest secure in his kindness

reading: The man says that the honey-dripping hair of the woman he loves and lives with is like the fine sand drawn into ripples at the great ford of Uranthai of the rich Cholas, well parted, fragrant and cool.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the beloved in union; no native thing places it

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

comparisons.tenor: her dark, wavy hair

reading: The friend says of the lord of the shore, where a wet crab, frightened by the watch of the heron white as a rain-season lily, rushes to its hole among the mangrove roots like a herdsman's bull that has snapped its rope, that if he does not come, let it be: there are bangles here in the sellers' hands, small ones too.
nuance: The jibe is that her bangles slip as she wastes, so she will need smaller ones, and these can be bought: the friend makes light of his absence to sting him. Read as a hidden picture (the crab fleeing the heron's watch as the girl hiding from the town's eyes) it has two pairs, but the poem names no watch or gossip to anchor them, so it fails condition 4.

thinai_evidence.note: crab, mangrove and the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person; the jibe reads as meant for his hearing

comparisons.tenor: the white heron
the crab rushing to its hole

reading: The woman tells her friend that in the loveless evening that has come down thick, when birds and beasts settle in loneliness and those shutting the much-used gate call out whether anyone else is coming, her lover does not come.
nuance: The gatekeepers' call (வருவீர் உளீரோ) is the cruel detail: the house asks every evening who is still to come, and the one answer she waits for never comes.

thinai_evidence.note: lament at nightfall; the evening and the shut gate are all the setting

reading: The man says that as the striped young of a small white snake can strike down a forest elephant, so this young girl with teeth like sprouts and bangles on her hands has struck him down.
nuance: அணங்குதல் is what a god or demon does to a person; the scale of the simile (a hatchling snake, a wild elephant) is the hero's own wonder at being undone by someone so small and young.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest elephant of the hills

thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named

reading: The man tells his heart that it has longed for something hard to get, like a poor man longing for pleasure: it knew the beloved was good, but did not know she was hard to reach.
nuance: The two knowings are set against each other (நல்லள் ஆகுதல் அறிந்து / அரியள் ஆகுதல் அறியாது): the heart learned her worth and missed its price, which is where the simile of the poor man's wish bites.

thinai_evidence.note: the man in secret love finds her hard to meet; no native thing is named

comparisons.tenor: the heart's longing for her

title: kuruntokai 121-140
theme: Kuruntokai 121 to 140: short poems in every landscape, most of them turning on one image set against one feeling; the cost of a missed tryst borne by the woman (121), evening that brings night with it (122), the laughing rainy season (126), the fish that fears the lotus after the heron (127), a king captured by a brow (129), love as a season and not a sickness (136), the maxim that work is men's life turned against going (135) and the oath that stakes a giver's honour on staying (137), with a run of gossip poems at the end (139, 140).
source_issues: 126: line 1 (இளமை பாரார் வளநசைஇச் சென்றோர்) is flagged as not in sangamtamil.com; our text keeps it and the poem needs it, since it is the subject of வாரார் in line 2.
128: line 4 is the reading of tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), which agrees with sangamtamil.com and replaces the base text.
132: line 1 is flagged as not in sangamtamil.com; our text keeps it, and the list of her body begins there.

138: the colophon thinai is மருதம் in the base text and குறிஞ்சி in sangamtamil.com; nothing in the poem is of the fields, and the night watch fits kurinji, which is the inferred thinai here. Line 2's division (எம்மி லயல தேழி லும்பர்) hides a possible hill name ஏழில், which therefore cannot be cited as an entity.

139: the colophon gives மருதம், but அம்பல் (the first talk about secret lovers) and the man told to keep away from the street point to kalavu; the inferred thinai is kurinji, with the house hen and fence as borrowed marutham things.

139: the simile marker ஆங்கு is split by sandhi across lines 4 and 5 (தாஅங் / கின்னா), so the marker is cited as ஆஅங்; likewise 133 (தாங்கென்) cites ஆங், 133 பொன்போற் cites போற், and 129 (பிணித்தற்றால்) cites அற்றால்.

reading: The woman grants her friend that it is true: as the branch that took the miss of the black-faced langur, which leapt short on the slope, goes down with it, so for the hill man's failure to keep the tryst it is her broad soft shoulders that have turned pale.
nuance: The poem is about where the cost of a fault falls: the langur misjudged the leap but the branch bears it, the man failed the meeting but her shoulders show it. The opening மெய்யே concedes something the friend has said, probably that he is not to blame, and the simile answers it without disputing it.

thinai_evidence.note: hill slope, langur and the man of the hill country at a failed tryst

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman answers her friend after a tryst the man did not keep

comparisons.tenor: the langur's face, black as if smeared with ink
her shoulders bearing the pallor for the man's missed tryst

reading: The woman says the water-lilies of the deep water, grey as the dull back of the green-legged heron, have closed now; evening has come, and it has not come alone, for it brings the night with it.
nuance: The closing lilies are the clock: their shut buds take the heron's colour as the light goes. The last line is the sting: evening, the hour of longing, is only the first of the hours she must get through without him.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening hour and its grief on the water

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman in separation, at evening

comparisons.tenor: the closed water-lily buds, dull grey as the heron's back

reading: The friend says that the flowering grove of black-trunked punnai, with shade cool and thick as packed darkness beside white sand heaped like gathered moonlight, lies lonely: he still has not come, and the boats of our kin who hunt many fish are coming back.
nuance: Two similes make the grove a meeting place at once dark and bright. The line break sets வாரார் against வரூஉம்: the man does not come, the kinsmen do, so the time for meeting is closing. Said to the woman, perhaps for the man to hear, it presses him to come openly.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the friend; the warning that the kin are returning reads as meant for the man too

comparisons.tenor: the dense cool shade of the grove
the heaped white sand

reading: The friend tells the lord that if he calls harsh the great forest of omai trees, desolate as a wide town left waste after the salt-traders camped and moved on, then is the house sweet to those left in it alone?
nuance: She takes his own word (இன்னா) and turns it round: the abandoned camp of the simile is already a picture of the house he would leave. She does not plead; she makes the forest and the home equal in harm.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going through the waste and the woman left alone

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend answers the man who would leave

comparisons.tenor: the empty omai forest, like a town deserted after the salt-traders' camp

reading: The woman tells her friend that though her bright bangles slip and she has wasted, she is still alive; but her beauty, which outshone at festivals even the leaf-skirted women of the slope, has turned away from her along with the lord of the cool harbour where a forlorn heron, its old wing-strength gone, sits on a bent branch the waves wash.
nuance: The heron that can no longer fly and sits on a wave-washed branch is close to her own state, but she speaks as a girl of the slope about a man of the shore, so the condition that the heroine use only things she knows is not clear; it is left as scene (a near-miss ullurai). கண்மாறின்று, 'has turned its face away', makes her beauty a companion that has left with him.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron, the waves and the man of the harbour

reading: The woman tells her friend that those who went for wealth without regard for youth have not come back, and the fragrant cool rainy season, with the clustered buds of the flowering mullai the rain has fed for its bright teeth, laughs, as if asking where they are.
nuance: The season's laugh is mockery: the buds are white teeth and the question எவணரோ is put in the season's mouth. The first line is the charge: they did not weigh youth, which passes, against wealth, which can wait.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains and mullai in bud, the season he promised

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman, waiting through the season he named

comparisons.tenor: the clustered mullai buds as the laughing season's teeth

reading: The friend tells the man of the town of kaanji trees and field-plots, where the kendai fish that dived when a heron struck at it now fears the bright bud of the lotus beside it, that because his one bard proved a liar, every bard there is looks like a thief to the women he has left.
nuance: The lotus bud is harmless, but white-tipped like a heron's beak; the fish once caught at shies from it. The friend never says the women are the fish, and the line நீ அகன்றிசினோர்க்கு lays the blame on his leaving, not on the bard.

thinai_evidence.note: fields, kaanji trees and lotus pond of the town

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend refuses the man's bard as go-between

reading: The man tells his heart that, like a heron on the waves of the eastern sea that has lost its wings and longs for the rich ayirai fish of the front harbour of Thondi of Poraiyan of the sturdy chariots, it pines for one who is far away and hard to win, and that suffering is its lot.
nuance: The heron is on the east coast and Thondi is on the west, and the bird cannot fly: the simile measures the girl's distance by the width of the land and the lover's helplessness by the lost wings.

thinai_evidence.note: sea, heron and harbour

comparisons.tenor: the heart longing for a girl far off and hard to reach

reading: The man tells his comrade, the friend who gladdens boys and keeps company with poets, to listen: the small forehead gleaming beside her hair, like the fresh white moon of the eighth day rising out of the dark sea, has bound him like a newly captured elephant.
nuance: The eighth-day moon is a half disc, the shape of a small brow, and its rising from black water is the brow against dark hair. The poet is the Chola Kopperunchozhan, and the image of capture is a king's: he who takes elephants is himself taken like one.

thinai_evidence.note: the first sight of the girl that binds the man, told to his comrade

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man tells his comrade why he is changed

comparisons.tenor: her small forehead shining beside her dark hair

reading: The friend says their lover will not burrow into the earth, climb the sky or walk across the sea; if they search country by country, town by town, household by household, can he be lost?
nuance: The three denials close off every place but the peopled land, and the doubled words (நாட்டின் நாட்டின், ஊரின் ஊரின், குடிமுறை குடிமுறை) act out the search. The comfort lies in the certainty, not in any plan to go. Tradition makes the poet a woman who went in search of her husband; the colophon gives the words to the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover gone far away and the woman left behind

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend comforts the woman

reading: The man tells his heart that the town where she stays, she of broad shoulders lovely as swaying bamboo and large fighting eyes, lies very far over a hard road, yet the heart is as eager as a farmer with a single plough when his green field is wet and ready; and he grieves.
nuance: The one-plough farmer has one chance while the soil holds the rain: the simile is about timing, the urgency of a moment that will pass. The poet's name, Orerruzhavanar, comes from this line.

thinai_evidence.note: the long hard road between the man and her town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man, far from home, to his heart

comparisons.tenor: her broad shoulders
the heart's eagerness to reach her

reading: The man asks how he can forget her, fierce in embrace, of lovely beauty, with rounded soft breasts and creeper-long hair, the dark girl who looked at him with a drooping gaze like the longing of the trembling-headed calf of a good full-uddered cow to see its mother.
nuance: The list of her body ends on a look, and the look is likened not to a lover's but to a calf's need for its mother: helpless dependence is what binds him. The cow and calf are herders' things in a hill love poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the man who cannot forget the girl he has met

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man answers a comrade who would have him forget her

comparisons.tenor: her drooping, longing look
her long hair, like a creeper

reading: The woman tells her friend that, like the stubble of the hill farmer's golden millet, cropped short by parrots, which puts out leaves again in heavy rain, she is still alive in the loneliness that followed his first taking of her beauty.
nuance: The parrots that ate the millet and the man who 'newly ate' her beauty (நலம் புதிது உண்ட) share the verb உண், so the simile carries both the loss and the survival. உரஞ் செத்தும் may mean 'though my strength is dead' or 'thinking of his firmness'; the sense of line 4 turns on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill farmer's millet field and parrots

comparisons.tenor: the millet heads, golden
the woman who lives on after her beauty was taken

reading: The woman tells her friend that the friendship joined with the man of the crossing hills, where the swift waterfall strikes the flowered swaying branch of the tall vengai on the small hill till it is bare, dashes roaring on the rocks and slides down like a snake taking the ground, would be good beyond anything if only it brought no parting.
nuance: The waterfall strips the vengai of its flowers and then runs away down the hill; she names only the parting, and lets the scene say the rest.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, waterfall and hills of the man's country

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall sliding down the slope

ullurai.tenor: the man whose love has stripped the woman's bloom and who goes away

pairs.situation: his love has struck her in her bloom and left her desolate
he slips away down the hill, out of reach

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the vengai and waterfall of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

reading: The friend tells the woman not to cry: he himself told them that work is life to men and men are life to bright-browed women who keep the house, so he will put off his going.
nuance: The hero spoke both halves of the maxim; the friend leans on the second to cancel the first. If he is her life as work is his, going for work would kill what he works for.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going for work, held back

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend comforts the woman who weeps at his going

comparisons.tenor: work as men's very life

reading: The man says people keep saying 'love, love', but love is neither a possessing spirit nor a disease; it does not grow fine and flare and subside; like the musth that comes on an elephant chewing soft fodder, it has its season, when it finds someone to look on.
nuance: He answers a charge, probably his comrade's, that his love is an affliction: it is a native season of the body, latent like musth, which the sight of her brings out.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and its fodder of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man answers a comrade who calls his love a sickness

comparisons.tenor: love, which rises when it finds one to look on

reading: The man tells his soft-natured wife that if he ever leaves her and stays away so that her good breast grows lonely, may he have many days when suppliants leave him and do not come: that is what his going would deserve.
nuance: The curse he takes on is the worst a giver can suffer, to be passed over by those who ask, and men usually leave home to earn the wealth to give; so he stakes the reason for going against going.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's oath against leaving

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man swears to his wife he will not leave

reading: The friend says that though the town sleeps uselessly, they do not sleep, hearing clearly the sound of the sapphire-blue flowers dropping from the lovely soft branches of the dark-clustered nochchi with leaves like peacock's feet, beside their house on the height.
nuance: They are awake enough to hear nochchi flowers fall, the faintest sound there is, and the sleeping town is set against the two who keep watch. Line 2 may name the hill Ezhil (அயலது ஏழில் உம்பர்), but the word division is unsure. Nothing in the poem is of the marutham fields; night, watching and the waiting for a man fit kurinji.

thinai_evidence.note: the sleepless night of waiting while the town sleeps

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend tells the man of the night watch; the colophon says only that the friend speaks

comparisons.tenor: the nochchi leaves, spread like a peacock's foot
the blue nochchi flowers, like sapphire

reading: The friend tells the man not to come to their street, for the gossip there sounds as harshly as the cry of a short-legged house hen who, when a wildcat comes to the fence at evening, cannot find where to go and calls her frightened chicks together.
nuance: The simile makes the street an alarmed household and quietly casts the man as the cat at the fence. அம்பல் is the first murmur of talk about secret lovers, before it becomes அலர், so the situation is kalavu and the karu of house and fence are borrowed from the town.

thinai_evidence.note: gossip about a secret love; the man told to keep away

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend turns the man away from the street

comparisons.tenor: the harsh sound of the street's gossip

reading: The woman says her lover has gone through the waste where the old male chameleon with a saw-toothed back sits and travellers take it for an omen; how did this noisy town come to know the grief she has borne here with her strength broken?
nuance: She has kept the grief to herself, so the town's knowing is a second injury: the gossip is about a pain she never voiced.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste he went through

comparisons.tenor: the chameleon's serrated back

title: kuruntokai 141-160
theme: Kuruntokai 141-160: short speeches of kalavu and separation, most in the heroine's voice: night trysts refused and longed for (141, 150, 153), the lover's heart left behind (142, 156), the friend's comfort and the coming of marriage elders (143, 146, 159), the season and the dream that fail (147, 148, 155, 160), and three hens calling for absent mates (151, 154) beside the dawn, the storm and the elopement that part lovers (144, 157, 158).

reading: The heroine asks her friend what harm there would be in telling the lord of the slope that her mother has sent her to drive the curve-beaked parrots off the ripening millet, and in telling him not to come in the deep midnight, when a great tiger, bruised from a hard fight with an elephant, waits for its chance to kill a green-eyed red dog.
nuance: The mother's errand is reported as news, but it tells him where she will be by day, so 'do not come at night' is half of an offer. The beasts are reasons, not a mood: even the tiger on that slope is wounded and lying in wait to kill.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and the dark midnight are kurinji's land and hour (porul 1.8)

reading: The hero wonders whether the simple girl with flower-like eyes, who threads a garland of pool flowers and drives the parrots off the millet field, knows or does not know that at midnight he breathes heavily like an elephant in its resting place and that his heart is still there beside her.
nuance: He has gone home but his heart has not, and he cannot tell whether she knows: the doubt of the first days of kalavu, before any word has passed between them. The sleeping elephant's breath gives the size of his longing in a scene of stillness.

thinai_evidence.note: pool flowers and the parrots of the millet field are kurinji things

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he speaks to himself

comparisons.tenor: his heavy sighing at midnight, like the breathing of an elephant at rest

reading: The friend tells the heroine not to despair: the lord of the fruitful hill loves her greatly and fears blame, and since only impermanence is permanent, the pallor spread over her lovely skin cannot stay, any more than wealth stays with a dutiful man of kind heart who seeks good fame.
nuance: The maxim of impermanence, usually a warning, becomes comfort: what must pass includes her pallor. The simile is chosen with care, since the generous man's wealth leaves him because he gives it away: the pallor will leave by a good act, not by decay.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country names the land of the lover

comparisons.tenor: the pallor on her body, which cannot stay, as wealth does not stay with a generous man

reading: The foster mother says it was good when the girl picked water-lilies in the backwater and played in the white-crested waves of the sea; she would not even stay here to play as she should with her inseparable friends, and has gone that way, over desolate gravel, to a mountain country of sky-high ridges where moving clouds crawl over the peaks.
nuance: She measures the going by landscapes: from the sea shore of the girl's play, across the stony waste, to the mountains beyond. பிரிவில் ஆயம், the troop that never parted from her, is the first thing she has parted from.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's going over the gravel waste with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of the girl

reading: The heroine says this little harbour village is no place to live: charging the lord of the seaside grove with cruelty, she suffers in unending sorrow at midnight, and the long night here holds only people with sleeping eyes, who will not talk with those who lie awake.
nuance: Who 'raises' the lord's cruelty is open, she or the village; either way the complaint lands on the sleepers, whose sleep is a refusal of company. Line 1's உறைபதி யன்றி may mean 'not our own town' rather than 'no place to dwell'.

thinai_evidence.note: the harbour village and the seaside grove are the shore

reading: The friend asks the heroine whether the people who unite the parted have come to their town: men with staffs in their hands and white cloths on their heads, who say 'good, good' and, there in their assembly, 'today is a great day'.
nuance: The elders are seen before their errand is named, by their staffs, white headgear and stock words of approval, so the friend lets the heroine read the signs of a marriage embassy herself and gives her joy as a question. வெண்டலை may be white heads of age rather than white cloth.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of those who unite parted lovers turns kalavu toward marriage

reading: The hero tells the dream that, as if it had brought him the young woman of fine ornaments, whose lovely dark skin with its fine down is like the curved paathiri flower of summer, it wakes him from sweet sleep; those parted from their mates are not to be mocked.
nuance: He blames the dream, not waking: its gift is a trick that ends in waking, so its kindness is a kind of mockery. The last line widens his case into a rule for all the parted.

thinai_evidence.note: summer and the parted lover

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he addresses the dream

comparisons.tenor: the fine down on her dark skin, like the curved paathiri flower of summer
the dream, acting as though it had brought her to him

reading: Answering a friend who says the season has not come, the heroine asks: if this great cool time, when konrai buds like the gold coins of the frog-mouthed anklets on rich children's small feet bloom along with the kurundham, is not the rainy season, then is this a dream?
nuance: The friend's usual argument, that the rains prove he will come, is turned round: the rains have come and he has not, so the friend must deny the season and the heroine must insist on it. Her question makes the comfort an admission that he broke his word.

thinai_evidence.note: konrai and kurundham in bloom mark the rains of the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the konrai buds, like the gold coins on the anklets of rich children

reading: The heroine says her modesty is to be pitied: it struggled long beside her, but now, like a small dam of heaped sand where white-flowered reeds grow, which gives way when the sweet flood presses, it has held as long as it could and, with desire pressing, no longer stays in her hand.
nuance: Modesty is a companion that 'suffered with us' and is pitied, not a law she breaks. The dam is small and of sand and the flood is sweet: the image concedes that what breaks it is welcome.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no land; the colophon's paalai fits a restraint giving way before she goes with him

comparisons.vehicle: ஓங்குமணற் சிறுசிறை தீம்புனல் நெரிதர வீய்ந்துக் காஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her modesty, which held as long as it could and gives way as desire presses

reading: The heroine tells her friend that when she thinks of the sandal-dried chest of the lord of the high hill, where the fragrant smoking torches lit by the watchman on the platform flicker here and there like stars, the pain within her swells; when she embraces it, how is it that the pain vanishes?
nuance: Thought and embrace act on one sickness in opposite ways, and she asks why as if it were a riddle; the asking itself reports that the embrace has happened.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet watchman's torches on the high hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: அன்னாய், 'mother', is her address to the friend

comparisons.tenor: the watchman's smoking torches, flickering here and there like stars in the sky

reading: The hero says that, not counting it hard to take the narrow path through the hills where the red-legged hen, her mate felled by a hawk as he rose, cannot find him and keeps crying short flute-sweet calls, to leave behind the beloved he cannot forget and go: that is the end of youth.
nuance: 'Going is the end of youth' is a verdict, not a regret: youth is the time to be with her, and the road can wait. வங்காக் கடந்த in line 1 is hard; it may name the vangaa bird whose hen she is.

thinai_evidence.note: the question of leaving her for the road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he answers his own urge to leave

comparisons.tenor: the hen's calls, sweet and sad as a flute

iraicchi.act: the hen, her mate struck down by a hawk as he rose, cannot find him and keeps calling
iraicchi.sense: a woman left behind would call so for a man lost on such roads, so the hero who hears it will not leave his beloved

reading: The heroine says those who reproach her know nothing at all: if her lover leaves it helpless, love, like the young of the tortoise, has nothing to do but lie within and waste away, as an egg does away from its mother.
nuance: The image rests on the old belief that the tortoise leaves her eggs in the sand and the young live by her thought of them: love too lives only by the lover's thought, and withdrawn it can only shrink where it lies. தாயின் in line 2 (with or without the mother) is the crux.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no land; the friend's rebuke belongs to kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: those who reproach her are the friend's words

comparisons.tenor: love lying hidden within and wasting, like an egg left by its mother
love left helpless by the lover, like the tortoise hatchling left by its mother

reading: The heroine says her pitiable heart, which used to be afraid when the hill owl hooted or when the male monkey leapt on the dark branch of the jackfruit in the yard and shook it, now in the dense dark night never tires of going to him along the long way down the slope.
nuance: The old fears are household ones, an owl, a monkey in the yard; the journey the heart now makes is the lover's own night road. She speaks of the heart as a separate creature whose character has changed.

thinai_evidence.note: hill, slope and dark night

reading: The heroine asks her friend how they learned it, those who can part and live far away in the forest of the hard waste, where in the hour when heat shimmers like a snake's stretched slough the short-stepping hen with spotted neck feathers, thinking of the cock that went to find food, sits on the forked branch of the parched kalli and calls out in loneliness.
nuance: The cock has gone only to fetch food, the hero's own errand in small, and still the hen cries; 'how did they learn it' sets parting down as a skill learned against nature.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard waste in the hour of heat

comparisons.tenor: the shimmering heat of the hot hour, like a snake's sloughed skin stretched out

iraicchi.act: the hen, thinking of the cock gone to find food, sits on the kalli fork and calls in loneliness
iraicchi.sense: even a bird whose mate is only gone to fetch food cries out, so the man who knows that road knows what his going does to her

reading: The heroine says the hour has come when the farmers who cleared the old field with a great din bring their seed baskets brimming with flowers, but no word comes that his chariot is on its way, its clear split-mouthed bells, cast from wax moulds and poured in the furnace, ringing through the thick-treed thicket as it comes down from the waste to arrive in the evening for a great feast with guests.
nuance: The season and the hour are both here; what is missing is only the report, so she waits for news before the man. The chariot is drawn down to the casting of its bells, as if imagined over and over. விதைக்குறு வட்டி போதொடு பொதுள (line 2) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the sowing time and the evening hour he named

reading: The hero calls to the Brahmin youth, who carries a water pot hung from a staff of red-flowered palasa stripped of its bark and eats the food of his vows: among the sweet words of your unwritten learning, is there a medicine with the power to unite those who are parted, or is this madness?
nuance: எழுதாக் கற்பு, the learning not written, names the Veda by how it is kept, by mouth. மயலோ இதுவே leaves it open whether the madness is the question or the hero's own state, and so whether he mocks the Brahmin's lore or truly hopes in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero in kalavu asks for the means of union

reading: The heroine says that when the cock cried 'kukkoo' her pure heart started in fear, for dawn had come like a sword that cuts apart lovers whose shoulders touch.
nuance: The cock is only the signal; the sword is the dawn itself. Her heart is pure and still it starts as at a blow, as if dawn's cut fell on her.

thinai_evidence.note: the cock and dawn are marutham's hour (porul 1.9)

comparisons.tenor: dawn, which cuts apart lovers whose shoulders touch, like a sword

reading: The heroine asks the dark cloud heavy with rain, which came on the wind mingled with the roar of the swift thunder that strikes snakes dead on the slopes of the tall mountain, whether it has no pity: it has power to shake even the famed Himalaya, so what is this against women who are pitiable for want of a companion?
nuance: The storm's might is granted and then turned into a reproach: a power that can shake the Himalaya has no need to try itself on a lone woman. The strong thing that leaves her unprotected stands for the absent man.

thinai_evidence.note: the tall mountain in the storm of night

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the rain cloud

reading: The friend says that the girl's slender waist, too small to bear the leaf skirt on her hips, is in distress, for her soft chest has filled out and her round streaked breasts have risen to rival caskets, while this foolish town, full of worry, keeps saying with sorrowful hearts 'what will become of her, the girl with flower earrings?' and consults no one.
nuance: Her coming of age is told as a burden on her waist and as worry in the town; both mean she will now be watched and kept at home, so said in the lover's hearing it presses him to marry. உசாவா in line 6 may mean the town will not consult her family, or will not talk to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the leaf skirt of the hill girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred from the matter: the girl's coming of age told in the lover's hearing

comparisons.tenor: her breasts, risen to rival caskets

reading: The heroine tells her friend that at hushed midnight, when the fire-red-headed anril cries with its prawn-beaked hen from their nest on the tall branch, making the parted helpless, and the great cold north wind blows as well, he does not come: so this is our lover's coming!
nuance: The last line is bitter irony: the cries and the wind are all that came. The anril pair in one nest is the measure of her single bed.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight is kurinji's hour (porul 1.8) and the cold north wind its season

comparisons.tenor: the anril's red head, like fire
the hen's curved beak, like a prawn

iraicchi.act: the anril keeps with its hen in their nest on the tall branch through the cold midnight and cries
iraicchi.sense: even the birds keep their mates through the cold night, while her lover, who said he would come, stays away

title: kuruntokai 161-180
theme: Kuruntokai 161 to 180: short speeches across all five lands. A hill man stands in the night rain at a wakeful house; the jasmine laughs at a lonely man in the rains; a girl hears her own sleeplessness in the sea; a courtesan swears by the sea that she has no claim; a man rides the palmyra horse; a young wife cooks for her husband's one word of praise; a wife curses her own laughing teeth; and in the wasteland poems the woman and her friend weigh wealth against grace and ask whether the absent man has hardened.
source_issues: 176: line 1 (ஒருநாள் வாரலன் இருநாள் வாரலன்) is not in sangamtamil.com's text; line 5 (ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ) repeats as Kuruntokai 325 line 4, and its first words are hard to divide.
177: line 5 varies (ours நாந்தப், tamilvu.org நாம் நகப், sangamtamil.com நாம் தம்); the sense of the closing lines depends on it.
173: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but the poem is a madal speech, which the Tholkappiyam places under perunthinai; the disagreement is recorded in thinai.

180: the poet's name, printed at the end of the verse in the source, was moved to the poet field (per the text flag); lines 1 to 4 are a dense description whose construction (what the herd does to the bamboo) is not certain.
170: line 5 கேண்மை தலைபோகாமை can be read as a bond that will not end or one that will not reach completion; the reading taken is the first.

reading: On a night when daylight has gone dark, the rain will not stop and a wind blows that would chill even a ghoul's eyes, while her mother clutches the boys with tiger-tooth pendants and cries out in alarm, the girl wonders what could have possessed the hill man, his chest smelling of sandal, to come and stand outside like an elephant in the rain.
nuance: The danger is doubled: the storm outside and the wakeful mother inside. The elephant standing silent and soaked in the rain gives his bulk and his patience at once; the cry அன்னா is the household's alarm, which the girl must hear while knowing who is out there.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man, the tiger-tooth pendants and sandal fix the hills, and the night visit is kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the girl speaks of the night visit, most likely to her friend

comparisons.tenor: the lover standing outside the house in the night rain, like an elephant standing in the downpour

reading: In the wide watered land the rains have nursed, at the dull evening when everyone goes home, the man alone hails the jasmine and asks whether it is fair to put on a smile with its small white buds and seem to laugh at those who are by themselves.
nuance: The buds are not called like a smile; they have taken the smile from someone (முறுவல் கொண்டனை), so the flower wears the absent woman's laugh. The evening when many come home is the mullai hour of return, which makes his being away the sharper.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season, evening and the jasmine are mullai's time and flower

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he addresses the jasmine; he is away from home in the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the jasmine opening its buds, as if laughing at the lonely man
the small white buds as a smile

reading: The girl asks the sea who has hurt it, since on the great shore of the grove, where fish-fed herons spread like a flock of the Puzhiyar's small-headed white sheep and the waves toss the white-flowered thazhai, she hears its voice even in the dead of night.
nuance: The question is turned outward but answers itself: she hears the sea at midnight only because she is awake, so the sea's unrest is the mirror of her own, and யார் அணங்குற்றனை asks of the sea what others might ask of her.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and a sleepless night of lament are neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the sea

comparisons.tenor: the white herons spread over the shore, like a flock of the Puzhiyar's small-headed white sheep

reading: The man's courtesan tells her friend: may the cool great sea east of the hill town of the ancient Velir, where the vaalai fish and its heavy-bellied young mate snatch the sweet fruit of the clustered mango, strike me, if I am the one the wife sulks over in her simplicity, if I am anything to her husband.
nuance: An oath sworn by a named sea is a public statement: the courtesan disowns any claim on the man so that the wife's quarrel falls back on him. The fish pair feeding on fallen mango has been read as a hidden image of the man and his pregnant wife at ease, but it is the oath-place's description, with no second pair to anchor it, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking over the husband and another woman is marutham's quarrel

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her own friend (தோழி, line 4); the oath is meant to reach the wife

reading: The man tells his heart that, like drinking toddy on top of being already merry, it has burned on top of its desire, and has given way like a salt cart standing on a steep bank that melts away in a heavy downpour, from seeing her thick dark hair and natural grace.
nuance: Both images make the sight a second blow on an earlier one: toddy on top of joy, rain on top of salt. The salt cart is a coast and trade thing brought into a hill poem, and its cargo does not break, it dissolves, which is how he says his resolve went.

thinai_evidence.note: a man undone by the first sight of a girl is the meeting of kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the நீ of line 2 is his own heart

comparisons.tenor: the heart's fresh desire coming on top of its earlier joy, like toddy drunk by one already merry
the heart giving way at the sight of her, like a salt cart that dissolves in a heavy downpour

reading: Where the waves of the cool sea draw back and the white-winged storks move off in a line to feed on ayirai fish, the town of Maranthai is good indeed, says the friend, but for one who stays there all alone it turns to desolation.
nuance: The storks move and feed in a row (நிரை), the company the speaker lacks; the praise of the town is granted only to be withdrawn by the last line. ஒருதனி doubles the word for alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea's waves, storks and ayirai fish are the shore's things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; read as the friend telling the man that the woman left alone in his town will suffer; who stays alone is not stated

iraicchi.act: the storks move off together in a line and feed side by side
iraicchi.sense: even the storks of the shore feed in company, so a town, however good, is misery to the one left to live there alone

reading: The foster mother reports that the young wife, wiping her soft kanthal-like fingers that had kneaded thick curd on her unwashed garment and with her lily-like kohl eyes filled with seasoning smoke, stirred and cooked the sweet-sour stew herself, and when her husband ate it saying it was sweet, her bright-browed face glowed with a quiet joy.
nuance: Every detail of the girl's discomfort (curd on her fingers, a dirty cloth, smoke in her painted eyes) is the price of the one word இனிது, and the joy is small and fine (நுண்ணிதின்). The foster mother, who knew her as a child, notices that she now cooks with her own hands (தான் துழந்து).

thinai_evidence.note: a wife keeping house content with her husband is mullai's karpu

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; by convention the foster mother reports the married daughter's household to the mother

comparisons.tenor: her soft fingers as kanthal flowers
her kohl-lined eyes as blue water lilies

reading: The man says she is fragrant and cool, like dripping plump buds of the rain-season pithikam packed together in a fresh palmyra-leaf basket and opened out at dawn after heavy rain, her dark body lovely and her broad curved shoulders like a raft on a flood; for him there is no joining her and leaving her, and to live apart from her is even less possible.
nuance: The raft simile is the poem's argument: shoulders that carry one across a flood are not left behind. மணத்தலும் தணத்தலும் இலமே says that with her there is no cycle of union and parting at all, so the journey he weighs is ruled out.

thinai_evidence.note: he weighs leaving her and refuses: the parting is the situation

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he speaks of her in the third person, refusing a journey

comparisons.vehicle: மாரிப் பித்திகத்து நீர்வார் கொழுமுகை இரும்பனம் பசுங்குடைப் பலவுடன் பொதிந்து பெரும்பெயல் விடியல் விரித்துவிட் டன்ன
comparisons.tenor: her fragrance and coolness, like rain-season pithikam buds packed in a palm-leaf basket and opened at a wet dawn
her broad shoulders, like a raft on a flood

reading: The wife tells the man: may the bright white teeth that laughed with you snap off at once like an elephant's tusk struck on a rock on the wasteland road; like the bowl in which bards poured fresh fish, we too reek to ourselves and cannot have you, so may our life break.
nuance: புலவு (the stink of fish) carries புலவி (the sulk): she reeks to herself as the bards' fish bowl does. The curse falls on her own teeth, the part of her that once laughed with him, so the anger turns inward.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's bitter sulk at a husband who is not hers is marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses him as ஐய

comparisons.tenor: her teeth snapping off, like the tusk of an elephant on the wasteland road that strikes a rock
her own reek to herself, like the bowl the bards poured fresh fish into

reading: Let many say it, those who do not know, says the girl; I know well that the bond of the man of the hill country, where an elephant seeking a pool gulps a mouthful of the fresh-spiked eruvai grass the waterfall has brought down, will not come to an end.
nuance: The elephant takes what the falls bring it without labour, which suits a love she counts as given; but the line that carries her claim, கேண்மை தலைபோகாமை, can be read either as a bond that will not break or one that will not reach its end in marriage, and the poem's confidence rests on that reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterfall, the elephant and the hill man are kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; she answers the talk of the many

reading: Look now, friend, says the girl: like a great beast caught in a fish net set in the long pond on the bank of the new fierce flood, what will come of the strangers' suit?
nuance: A fish net cannot hold a large beast; it tears and the catch is lost. The strangers (நொதுமலர்) who have come asking for her are the net, and the girl who already belongs to another is what they cannot hold, so her question mocks their effort.

thinai_evidence.note: the flood, the pond and the fish net are field and river things

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her friend (தோழி, line 1) while strangers seek her in marriage

comparisons.tenor: the strangers' marriage suit, like a great beast caught in a fish net that cannot hold it

reading: In the aching evening when the bat with its soft flapping wings makes for the fruiting tree, the woman asks whether those who left her alone here are happy being alone themselves, while her heart toils without limit like the trodden bellows of a forge one village set up for the common work of seven.
nuance: The bellows is worked by everyone and rests for no one, so the heart is pumped by every hour of the evening. Her question imagines him as lonely as she is and stops short of saying he is not.

thinai_evidence.note: the lament at evening, left alone, is neythal's hour and uri

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of those who left her

comparisons.vehicle: ஏழூர்ப் பொதுவினைக் கோரூர் யாத்த உலைவாங்கு மிதிதோல் போலத்
comparisons.tenor: her heart toiling without rest, like the trodden bellows of a forge one village keeps for the work of seven

iraicchi.act: the bat flies at evening to the tree where its fruit is
iraicchi.sense: even the bat goes at dusk to where its food and rest are, yet the man stays away from her

reading: The man says that, mounting the palmyra horse hung with a many-stranded garland of fresh gold-like avirai flowers, its bells ringing, casting off shame as the pain within him grows ever worse, he is ready to go there, knowing that this town will stand before her and name her fault, saying 'such a woman did this'.
nuance: The madal works through the town's tongue: his shame is to become her blame (அவள் பழி), which is what forces her kin. The garland of avirai is the madal rider's own sign; நாண் அட்டு says shame is killed, not merely set aside.

thinai_evidence.note: riding the palmyra horse with shame cast off is madal, which belongs to perunthinai, not to the hill land the colophon gives

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the madal threat is conventionally spoken to the girl's friend

comparisons.tenor: the fresh avirai flowers, golden like gold

reading: If he leaves us for wealth, not saying the roads are hard through the lonely wasteland the rain has forsaken, where the dried pod of the forked-thorn cactus bursts with a crack and scatters a pair of soft-feathered doves, then in this world wealth alone is wealth, and grace is something no one has.
nuance: The doves are a pair (துணைப் புற) driven apart by a sound, a picture of what his going does, but they do nothing themselves, so they stay scene. The verdict is about the world, not only the man: பொருளே மன்ற பொருளே and அருளே மன்ற ஆருமில் லதுவே are built as a pair, wealth affirmed and grace orphaned.

thinai_evidence.note: parting for wealth across the dry waste is paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; she speaks of him in the third person

reading: Of the lord of the wide waters, on whose wave-beaten shore of packed sand swarms of many-winged bees, wanting the season's honey, crowd the dark branches of the wet punnai, the girl tells her friend that she will not go about telling everyone 'I do not grieve; what is wrong here?'; let things be as they will, what is the gossip to her?
nuance: The friend's advice to hide her pain is refused: the pretence that would quiet the town is what she will not perform. The construction of lines 5 and 6 is loose, and whether she refuses or grants the friend's request turns on how கூறல் is taken.

thinai_evidence.note: the wave-beaten shore, the punnai and the lord of the coast are neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her friend (தோழி, line 5)

reading: The friend says: he did not come for one day or two, but came for many days, spoke humble words and softened my good heart, and then went off like honey ripe on the high cliff; where is he now, he who was our support, while my heart runs muddy like thundering rain poured out on another land?
nuance: The friend speaks of her own heart because the lover first won the go-between: his humble words were addressed to her, so his absence is her betrayal too. The rain falls on another country, wasted where it is not needed, and so her heart's flood reaches no one.

thinai_evidence.note: the cliff honey is a hill thing, and the lover is the one courted in kalavu

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of her own heart and asks where he is

comparisons.tenor: the lover gone beyond reach, like honey ripened high on a cliff

comparisons.vehicle: வேறுபுல னன்னாட்டுப் பெய்த ஏறுடை மழையிற் கலிழும்
comparisons.tenor: her heart running muddy, like thundering rain poured out on another land

reading: The sea's roar has died down, the shore grove has dimmed, the dark backwater of the ford looks forlorn, and the anril that lives on the fronds of the palmyra in the common ground calls softly; will he come today, friend, the man who, afraid even of parting when we sulked, pressed on us a love hard to leave?
nuance: The stilled sea, the dim grove and the hushed anril are all evening's quiet, and the friend sets against them the man's old fear of any parting. Line 5's reading differs between editions (நாந்தப், நாம் நகப், நாம் தம்), and whether the sulk was theirs or his changes the last two lines.

thinai_evidence.note: the stilled sea, shore grove and backwater at dusk are neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her friend the heroine (வாழி தோழி, line 5)

reading: The friend tells the man: like those who pluck the hollow-stemmed water lily in the cool field where ayirai fish spread and yet thirst for water, you once trembled lying between her breasts; now that we have become as hard to see as the crescent moon one worships, you have borne a great deal, and I grieve for it.
