nuance: The irony is in the reversal: he who shook at the gap between two breasts now endures a long absence with ease. The lily-pickers stand in water and thirst, which was his old love: desire even in possession. நோகோ யானே pities him only in form.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool field and the lily-pickers are marutham's, and the barb at a neglecting husband is its quarrel

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses him (நீர், நுமக்கு)

comparisons.tenor: his old trembling even when lying close to her, like lily-pickers who stand in water and still thirst
the women now rarely seen by him, like the crescent moon that one sees only to worship

reading: The friend tells the hunter: you have chased the wild beast through the noisy forest, the day has darkened and your dogs are worn out; do not go, sir; that is our village, there in the curve of the high hill among the stunted bamboo that a foolish soft-mouthed elephant chewed after eating green clustered bamboo that had torn the sweet honeycomb.
nuance: The invitation to stay is given as plain hospitality, a tired man and tired dogs at nightfall, and the village is placed by a landmark only a local would use. The young elephant tasting honey-smeared bamboo has been read as a hidden image of the sweetness waiting there, but no situation in the poem anchors it, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunt, the dogs, the hill slope and the elephant are kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses him as ஐஇய

reading: The friend wonders whether the man has reached his wealth, having crossed the waste where, when the herd of great broad-footed tuskers comes, with nails thick like a demon's teeth, the lone pining bamboo, like a sugarcane joint that has died and fallen on the rock, stands tall; and whether those who left, letting the lovely lines of her waist fade, have grown hard of heart in the land they went to.
nuance: The lone bamboo is the waste's emblem of what survives alone, worn like a dead cane joint; the friend's two questions move from the road (did he arrive?) to his heart (has it hardened?), and the second is the one she fears.

thinai_evidence.note: a man gone across the waste for wealth is paalai's parting

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she wonders aloud about the absent man, with the heroine in mind

comparisons.tenor: the elephants' thick nails, like a demon's teeth
the lone wasted bamboo, like the joint of a sugarcane that has died and lies on the rock

title: kuruntokai 181-200
theme: Kuruntokai 181 to 200: short poems mostly in the wife's voice waiting through the rains (the mullai budding, evening, thunder, the cold season as Death), with a threatened palm horse, a fisher girl's net of eyes, a husband's turned taste for the wife at home, and a lover who promises his pain will outlast this life.
source_issues: kuruntokai:182 line 6: our text reads கலிந்தவிர்; tamilvu.org has கலிழ் கவின், sangamtamil.com கலிழ்ந்து அவிர் (flag). The word qualifies her gait and does not change the poem's sense.
kuruntokai:183 line 3: repaired from tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), agreeing with sangamtamil.com (flag).
kuruntokai:189: colophon thinai பாலை in the base text, முல்லை in sangamtamil.com (flag); the poem can be read as a man setting out (paalai) or returning (mullai). Base kept; marked uncertain.
kuruntokai:194 line 2: வானோர் பிரங்கும் is hard to divide (வான் ஓர்பு இரங்கும?); read as the sky roaring. Marked uncertain.
kuruntokai:198 lines 6-7: கானத் / தார is ஆரம் (sandal) split across the line break; the karu form is given as written on line 7.
kuruntokai:191: colophon gives no poet (None).

reading: The wife asks her friend what good there is in the harsh word 'that is how she is', spoken in the quarrel, against women like them who have grown old as matrons carrying the many duties of the great house of the man from a town where a newly calved buffalo grazes the green crop near the calf the ploughman has tied, never moving away from it.
nuance: She calls herself and her kind பெருமுது பெண்டிர், the old matrons who bear the house's many burdens, so the sting of the word is that it is said to a wife whose years of service should have earned better. The mother buffalo that will not leave its tied calf is read by some as the hero kept near home by his son while he grazes elsewhere; only one correspondence (staying near the child) can be made firm, so it fails the two-pair condition and stays scene. Who spoke the harsh word (the hero, or someone of the parathai's side) is not said.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, the ploughman and the crop field belong to the watered fields

reading: The lover asks whether it will bring her to him if he ties a great garland hung with bells to the palm-stem horse cut from a fine-crowned palmyra, wears white bones, shows himself so that others mock, throws off his great shame for one day and goes down the street, since the simple girl of the swaying gait has not softened to the messenger they sent.
nuance: The verb is a question (தருவது கொல்லோ): he weighs the madal as a last resort and counts its cost in the mockery of others before he has mounted it. The contrast ஒருநாள் / பெருநாண் sets one day's display against a lifetime's shame.

thinai_evidence.note: a threatened, not yet ridden, palm horse after a failed message keeps the poem inside the courtship

reading: The wife wonders whether, in the land he went to, where the fresh konrai blossoms turn pale as she does, her man will see the stag with twisted horns parted like himself from its small-headed doe, there in the poor forest tract where the great flowering branch of the kaayaa shows like a peacock's neck.
nuance: Two similes run in opposite directions: the flower is like her (நம்போல்), the stag is like him (தம்போல்). The season marks both partners, and her hope is that the sight of a parted pair will teach him what she feels. The stag is the subject of her question, so striking it removes the poem's sense; it is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: forest scrub and the konrai's bloom set the land and the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the konrai blossoms that yellow as her skin pales

comparisons.vehicle: தம்போற் சிறுதலைப் பிணையிற் றீர்ந்த நெறிகோட் டிரலை
comparisons.tenor: the absent man, parted from her as the stag from its doe
the dark-blue kaayaa blossoms on the branch

reading: The lover tells his companions that the wise do not bear false witness and warns them off the little fishing village: his noble heart, not weighing what is fit for what, fell there and is lost in the seaside grove where the young daughter of fishermen with fine nets, a doll with a fine knot of hair like a peacock's eye, catches men in the net of her eyes.
nuance: The fishermen's fine net (நுண்வலை) and the daughter's net of eyes (கண்வலை) stand in successive lines: the girl practises her family's trade on men. The opening maxim is his reply to a companion's rebuke: he claims the evidence of his own lost heart as testimony the wise cannot doubt.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishermen and their nets belong to the shore

comparisons.tenor: the girl's fine knot of hair
the fisher girl
her eyes that catch his heart as her father's net catches fish

reading: The girl asks her friend what would come of telling the man of the land where the bright red kaanthal, closed like a striped snake that has let down its hood, ruined by the east wind, droops over the rock, that she has become like this through him: her brow pale, her spots faded, her long soft shoulders thinned, her bangles slipping, and her fine dark body in a state of ruinous grief.
nuance: The kaanthal beaten down by the wind and hanging over the rock is the traditional figure of her own ruined beauty and, some say, of the man as hard as the rock it hangs on; only one firm pair (flower to her beauty) can be named, so it is not tagged ullurai. Her question is a refusal: she will not use her wasting as a reproach.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal on the rock of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the kaanthal flower folding shut after the storm

reading: The girl tells her friend that for the man of the land where the soft mullai creeper of the forest field, wedded by the rains with their loud thunder, has put out buds like teeth, her eyes have given up sleep.
nuance: The rains 'wed' the land (மணந்த), and the creeper buds like a row of teeth, as if the season smiles at her: union and laughter in the land, sleeplessness in her eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the first rains on the forest field

comparisons.tenor: the mullai buds, white and pointed like teeth

reading: The girl tells her friend that the man of the land where the kid of the mountain goat, bedded on red rock, drinks its fill of the sweet milk pouring from the udder and leaps in the shade of the great hill is harder than stone, yet her heart, never calling him hard, melts.
nuance: Kapilar sets வலியன் against மெலியும்: the man is hard as stone, her heart grows soft, and the same root (வலி) is turned three ways in two lines. The kid nursed full and sheltered in the hill's shade is the care his own land gives its young and he withholds from her.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain goat and the great hill

comparisons.tenor: the man's hardness of heart

iraicchi.act: the kid is fed to the full from its mother's udder and plays safe in the shade of the hill
iraicchi.sense: in his land even the young of beasts are nourished and sheltered, yet he leaves her uncared for

reading: The wife says the mullai buds have ripened, and with the mullai the wide field of the cool rains has come to its beauty; the man who loosened her bright bangles has not come, and evening has come, aiming at her fine beauty.
nuance: The verb முற்றின is repeated for the buds and for the field's beauty, and then answered by வாரார் and வந்தன்று: the land has come to fullness on time, he has not come, and evening has come in his place.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool rains, the field and evening

comparisons.tenor: evening as an enemy coming against her beauty

reading: The man says the errand is one of going today and coming back tomorrow: his white chariot will race like a waterfall coming down the hill, its bright wheel like the young crescent cutting the green crop like a firebrand falling from the sky, and travelling like the wind it will reach her by evening, and he will embrace the many-graced body of the young girl with few rows of white bangles and be glad.
nuance: The addressee is not named; the chariot images suggest the charioteer. All the poem's speed belongs to the return: the parting is reduced to one day by the man, and the speed of the images measures his longing. Whether he speaks before setting out (a short parting, paalai) or on the road home (mullai) is open, as the colophon variants show.

thinai_evidence.note: a man setting out on a short journey, reckoning his return

comparisons.tenor: the white chariot racing
the bright wheel
the wheel slicing the crop
the chariot's speed

reading: The wife asks her friend whether the man who stroked her dark curled hair and great shoulders and left to make wealth, loosening her close bangles, knows of the single bell of the stall of many cows that rings each time the good bull moves, at the midnight of half-darkness when the mighty thunder roars to sever the green head of the angry spotted snake.
nuance: That she hears the bull's one bell at every step is the proof that she lies awake; the thunder that kills the snake is the night's terror, the small bell its loneliness. His parting caress (நீவி) is remembered as the act that loosened her bangles.

thinai_evidence.note: the herders' cattle stall in the rains at midnight

reading: The wife says, look there, what shall I call this: a flock of dark-winged birds perched on a strong branch, having paired, call in sweet voices into the hearts of the parted; hearing them, she would have said to the stranger who left, should he come here, 'do not dress my thick hair with flowers, do not touch me', if only she could.
nuance: மன்னே marks the resolve as one she knows she will not keep: she rehearses refusing his touch and his flowers, and the particle concedes she will yield. ஏதிலாளர், 'strangers', is her word for her own husband.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for one who has gone, in the season of mating birds

iraicchi.act: the birds pair and stay together on the branch, calling
iraicchi.sense: even the birds keep with their mates in this season, while he has gone off like a stranger

reading: Told 'he will come right here, do not grieve', the wife asks whether she should not weep now, she who lives wasting with this pain, when the dark koel with glossy feathers, like a touchstone streaked bright with gold, tears at the fragrant pollen on the mango branch, and at this hour she strokes her hair empty of flowers.
nuance: வறுங்குரல் கூந்தல், hair empty of flowers, says without saying it that she has not dressed her hair since he left; stroking it is all the touch it gets. The touchstone simile turns the koel into the assayer of the season: gold on black, the proof that spring has come.

thinai_evidence.note: the koel in the mango blossom marks the spring of parting

comparisons.tenor: the black koel dusted with yellow pollen

reading: The girl says the man of the land where the open-mouthed frog in the narrow-mouthed pool, like a gem-bowl filled with toddy, croaks like a clapper drum, embraced her long shoulders in the long white moonlight of last month; today the mullai buds are fragrant.
nuance: The poem's whole lament is in the two time-words: தொல்லைத் திங்கள், last month's moon, when he held her, and இன்று, today, when only the mullai is fragrant. The tattai is the clapper used to scare birds from the millet, so the frog's croak is a sound of the hill fields she remembers him by.

thinai_evidence.note: the passing of a month and the mullai's bloom set a time of waiting

comparisons.tenor: the small rock pool
the frog's croaking

reading: The girl asks her friend what this can be called: the sky roars with lightning flashing, that is one thing; against it the forest peacock cries out fiercely; for these two strangers that have joined together, her foolish heart is thrown into great turmoil.
nuance: ஏதில, 'things that are nothing to me': the cloud and the peacock answer each other, a pair that has met while she has not, and her heart is shaken by a union that has no business with her. The peacock answers the thunder, so the bird is the subject of the poem, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: lightning and rain-thunder over the forest

reading: The wife asks where they are now, the men gone to finish the work they wanted, as the sun, its anger cooled, reaches the hill in the sorrowful evening that rises bearing grief; alas, they do not say 'she suffers, she laments', not knowing that her body, like a crafted doll through which the caressing, swaying wind passes, has become something else.
nuance: The wind is caressing (தைவரல்) where he is not, and her body has become an object it plays over. The plural verbs make her charge general: the men who go for their work do not say the words that would show they know.

thinai_evidence.note: sunset and the grief of evening

comparisons.tenor: her body, lifeless and changed

reading: The friend tells the husband that once, when her friend gave him the green fruit of the neem, he called it a lump of sweet jaggery, and now, when she gives him the cool clear water of the cold spring on Pari's Parambu in the month of Thai, he says it is hot and brackish; such, sir, is the way of love.
nuance: The irony is in the last line: அற்றால் அன்பின் பாலே presents his fickleness as a law of love itself. Nothing she gives has changed; what he tastes has, and the friend's two examples make the bitter sweet and the sweetest bitter.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's love that has turned, reproached by the friend

reading: The wife asks her friend what they can do: painfully, Death in the shape of the cold season, with clustered rain-clouds that have drawn up the sea's water and gathered, confused and wild with the cold north wind, is coming, aimed at her who is parted from her lover.
nuance: Season and Death are fused in one phrase, கூதிர் உருவில் கூற்றம், Death wearing the cold season as its body, and it aims at her alone (எற் குறித்து), as evening aims at the wife's beauty in 188.

thinai_evidence.note: a parted wife's helpless lament

comparisons.tenor: the cold season, seen as Death come for her

reading: The friend tells the man with a chest fragrant with sandal from the forest of Malaiyan, whose great hand shines with the spear of killing war, that they are going to drive off the parrots settling on the red millet sown where the yaa trees were felled and burned, millet with green stems and bases like sugarcane and dense green ears, dripping milk like the trunk of a young cow-elephant and bowed on their dark stalks; he should not come here, for her mother is coming.
nuance: The refusal carries an invitation: telling him where they are going (to the millet field to scare parrots) while forbidding him the house names the place he may meet her. Malaiyan's war epithet is spent on a forest that perfumes the lover's chest.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field guarded from parrots on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the millet's thick base
the drooping millet ear

reading: The lover tells his heart that even if it does not come to winning her, one thing is sure: this love-sickness for the dark woman with curled, oiled hair fragrant with the wind that touches the forest of Ori of the strong chariots and generous hand will, with a closeness like today's, have no end and will last on in the other world.
nuance: He takes comfort not in winning her but in the endlessness of the pain: the illness (நோய்) itself is promised continuance in the next world, a consolation turned into a vow.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's longing in courtship, unsure of winning her

comparisons.tenor: the bond continuing as it is today

reading: The wife tells her friend that even the cool, flower-scented torrent that comes down from the hill where rain has fallen, carrying flowers strewn on the heights, has come, but he has not; surely he has forgotten, though she does not forget; the dark evening clouds of the season's rain rumble with their sweet-voiced thunder, the season before which he promised to come back when he left.
nuance: The -உம் of புனலும் ('even the torrent') makes the flood a rival traveller: water from the hills keeps its time and arrives, he does not. மறந்தோர் மன்ற மறவா நாமே balances the two verbs of forgetting in five words.

thinai_evidence.note: the seasonal rains at evening

title: kuruntokai 201-220
theme: Kuruntokai 201-220: short speeches of the love situations, waiting under the promised rains, the friend's comfort drawn from beasts on the man's road, and love argued as feast and as pain.
source_issues: 201 to 220: the colophon thurai names only the speaker (தலைவி கூற்று and the like), so thurai_akam occasion words are null and addressees are inferred from the poems.
201: the colophon names no poet.
209 line 1: அறந்தலைப் பட்ட and line 4 குறுநடை பல உள்ளலமே are hard to construe; the reading is marked uncertain.
213 lines 3 to 5: ததரல் and தெறித்துநடை மரபின் are rare, and who leaves food for whom is unclear; marked uncertain.
219 line 7: our text was replaced by the tamilvu (Swaminatha Aiyar) reading; the phrase எந் நீரிரோ is construed as 'who are you?', which is uncertain.
216: our thinai (mullai, from the rains) differs from the colophon's paalai.

reading: The heroine blesses the woman next door, may she eat ambrosia, because she brought word that the lord of the hill land will come, the land of tall bamboo groves where a soft blue-winged, sharp-clawed creature that has eaten honey-sweet mango like mixed milk gulps sour nelli and hangs from the thornless bamboo nearby.
nuance: The blessing of food (அமிழ்தம் உண்க) repays the bearer of good news, as Kuruntokai 210 repays the crow; the creature that hangs from the bamboo is the bat. Its meal of the sweet and then the sour may be read as a hint of the hero's mixed dealings, but no second correspondence is anchored, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: bamboo groves and the hill-land lord fix the hills

comparisons.tenor: the honey-sweet mango, sweet as milk mixed (with honey)

reading: The heroine tells her aching heart that, as the small-leaved nerunji thick on poor ground first gives a new flower sweet to the eye and then bears thorns, her lover who once did sweet things now does cruel ones.
nuance: The refrain நோம் என் நெஞ்சே opens and closes the poem, so the simile sits inside the pain; the point of the nerunji is the order of its gifts, flower first and thorn after, which turns the comparison into a story of a love.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's turn from kindness to hurt is the household grievance of marutham

comparisons.tenor: the lover who did sweet things and now does painful ones

reading: The heroine says her man is not from a land beyond the hills nor from a town too far to see its treetops; he lives within sight, yet keeps apart from her like those who have gone over to the god, and once she would not have grieved for him so.
nuance: The two negations measure distance by what can be seen (hills between, treetops out of sight), so the pain is a nearness without contact; the simile of those who have reached the god makes his avoidance a kind of vow. The last line's மன் gives a past that is lost: before, she had no cause to pine.

thinai_evidence.note: he lives in the same town yet keeps away, the marutham estrangement

comparisons.tenor: the man who lives near but keeps apart from her

reading: The companion tells the broad-shouldered hero that people cry 'love, love', but love is neither a possessing spirit nor a disease: think of it, and it is like an old cow nibbling the young unripe grass that has sprung on old upland, a feast always new.
nuance: The old cow can only lick at grass too short to graze, and gets pleasure without fullness; so the companion's 'feast' (விருந்து) is also a gentle deflation of the hero's suffering. அணங்கு and பிணி name exactly the two explanations, spirit and sickness, that akam poems give for a lover's state.

thinai_evidence.note: the companion answers the hero's lovesickness in the secret stage

comparisons.vehicle: முதைச்சுவற் கலித்த முற்றா இளம்புல் மூதா தைவந்
comparisons.tenor: love, a pleasure ever new that never fills

reading: The heroine asks her friend how the pallor spreading over her fragrant forehead came to know it so soon, when the lord of the heaped-sand shore has only now left, mounting his white chariot bright with gold, rising like sky-going swans under lightning-laden rain clouds, its wheels wet with spray from the churning sea.
nuance: The question gives the pallor a mind of its own (யாங்கு அறிந்தன்று), so the body knows the parting before she has taken it in; the white chariot rising like swans against dark rain cloud is the last thing she sees.

thinai_evidence.note: sea spray and the sand-shore lord fix the coast

comparisons.tenor: the white chariot rising away swiftly

reading: The hero says that if even the qualities of a woman so sweet, whose lovely words are like ambrosia, can bring such unbearable grief, love is hard to live with, and he warns the wise to keep from coming near it.
nuance: The argument runs from the best case: not a cruel woman but a sweet one causes the pain, so love itself is the cause. The plural அறிவுடையீர் may be his companions, which makes the poem a reply to counsel like the companion's in Kuruntokai 204.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero's lovesick grief before union is settled belongs to the secret stage

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the wise (அறிவுடையீர்), probably his companions

comparisons.tenor: her lovely sweet words

reading: The heroine says many who love her told her he went without telling her, thinking that if he spoke the going would become hard, along the old narrow path beside the rocky hill, printing his fine footsteps, where the clear lonely cry of a kite parted from its flock, perched in the fork of a dry omai, is the only companion in grief for those who cross the wasteland.
nuance: She knows the road only by report, yet she pictures his footprints on it; the kite separated from its kind is a companion to the traveller, which may hint that he too is now alone, but the bird only cries, so it carries a mood and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the wasteland road and the dry omai of the waste

reading: The heroine tells her friend she is not one who will refuse: she will be one with the lord of the land where the vengai, its trunk crushed by fighting elephants, blooms low enough for the hill women to pluck its flowers standing, for their hair; with anyone else she will not be one.
nuance: The poem turns on ஒன்று, to be one, to agree, in five forms; the last line can be read as refusing another match the family proposes. The crushed vengai that blooms within reach can be taken as the heroine, hurt but still giving, but only one pair can be anchored, so it is a near miss and stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, the vengai and the hill people's women

reading: The hero, having crossed the hard hill where green nelli lies on the path and the tiger cub's kill-ground roars, says he does not count the many short steps (of the way), for he carries the love of the young woman whose dark thick hair smells of the many opening buds of the bent-branched vetchi growing in the forest at the path's edge.
nuance: The sense of குறுநடை பல உள்ளலமே is unsettled: it may be that he does not think of the short stages of the road, or of her short-stepped walk; அறந்தலைப் பட்ட may mean the nelli has become a charity for travellers. The vetchi at the path's edge brings her scent into the wilderness.

thinai_evidence.note: the man speaks after crossing the hard way, away from her

reading: The friend tells the returned hero that even if she offered in seven bowls hot white rice grown entire in Thondi with ghee from the many cows of the herdsmen of Nalli's forest, Nalli of the strong chariot, it would be little as the offering due to the crow that cawed to bring a guest and so ended the grief that wasted her friend's broad shoulders.
nuance: The guest the crow called is the husband himself, now at the door, so the thanks to the bird is praise of his return said to his face. The meal is priced by the two most famous sources of plenty the poet knows, Nalli's herds and Thondi's rice; the poet's name, Kakkai Padiniyar, comes from this poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsmen and their cows of the forest pasture

reading: The friend tells the heroine that they have stopped fearing for the man who, unkind, agreed to leave her as her chosen bangles slipped, and crossed the waterless wasteland where a bee, sucking honey from the single summer cluster on the hot bough of a scorched kadamba, goes away unsatisfied.
nuance: அஞ்சல் எஞ்சினம் is bitter: they have given up even fearing for him. The bee that leaves the one cluster on a burnt tree still hungry is what he has chosen over her full love.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless waste and the scorched tree

iraicchi.act: the bee sucks at the one cluster left on a scorched tree and goes away unsated
iraicchi.sense: the man who left her full love has gone where nothing can satisfy him, so his leaving gains him nothing

reading: The friend says the long chariot with curved rail that the lord of the shore drives comes, its clear bells ringing on the shore of the clear sea, only to be seen and then goes back leaving shame; pitiable is such love, it will surely die, and she grieves.
nuance: காண வந்து நாணப் பெயரும்: the visit gives sight and then shame, and nothing lasting; the friend's grief is a push toward marriage, since a love that only shows itself is one that will fade.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and its lord

reading: The friend tells the heroine that the man has deep love for them, since on the road taken by those who spurned their sweet sleep, they say, the old fork-horned stag pulls down with its foot the big dry leaves bent low and eats only if (its mate and young) leave any, and failing that stands as shade for its fawn and lets the sun pass.
nuance: The words of lines 3 to 5 (ததரல், தெறித்து நடை மரபின்) are hard, and who leaves food for whom is not certain; the sense of a stag starving to shelter its young is clear. என்ப makes it hearsay of the road, which is how the friend can promise what he must have seen.

thinai_evidence.note: the stag sheltering its young from the sun on the wasteland road

iraicchi.act: the stag eats only what is left and stands as shade over its young in the sun
iraicchi.sense: the man who sees such care on his road will remember his own and come back to shelter her

reading: The friend says this noisy town has been thrown into confusion since the hill girl of soft gait and lovely hair down her back, who guards the shining-eared millet the forest man sowed after clearing his plot, was given a great leaf skirt for her jewelled waist, stripping the asoka to its trunk, and crowned with a garland of the arali that grows nearby.
nuance: The stripped asoka is the evidence: a gift that took a whole tree cannot be hidden, and the town reads it. ஏமுற்றன்று may also mean the town is deluded, taking the signs for a god's possession; the subject of the giving is not named, and the reading of the confusion is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarded by the hill girl in the forest man's plot

reading: As grief spreads and the sun slowly withdraws to hide behind the great hill of summer, the friend asks whether he will come today, he who crossed the wasteland by the tall mountain where the elephant with crossed tusks, having searched the dry pool, embraces his beloved mate beside the low rock while the great striped tiger lies in wait.
nuance: The sunset and the question 'will he come today' make it an evening of waiting; the tiger that 'guards' the elephants is a watcher of prey, so the road is both a picture of faithful pairs and a danger to him.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer heat and the crossed wasteland

iraicchi.act: the elephant, finding the pool dry, holds close to its mate on the hillside
iraicchi.sense: even in drought and danger the beast keeps to its mate, so the man who sees it will turn back to her

reading: The heroine says he has crossed the forest of green-leaved, never-wilting valli to bring flawless wealth, while she, her rows of bright bangles slipping, has sighed and sunk in grief on the bed made for sleep; and the great cloud, without saying 'she is pitiable', still pours, thunders and flashes, friend, with her sweet life as its aim.
nuance: அவரே and யானே set the two halves against each other, his errand and her bed; the rain, the season he named, comes as an attacker rather than a promise. The poem is spoken under the rains, so the waiting is mullai though the colophon files it under the journey.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain of the season he named has come and she waits

reading: The friend says she told the hill lord that if they were sent to drive parrots from the millet they could meet by day, but she feared his coming by night, and asked what they could do for their trouble; he took all she said for something else and surely sighed; love is delicate, and she had spoken only of great prudence and of blame.
nuance: She proposes the day tryst for safety and he hears a refusal; ஐதே காமம் admits how easily a word can wound it. The last line is hard: முதுக்குறைமை is mature prudence, and she may mean the girl's or her own.

thinai_evidence.note: guarding millet from parrots, and the hill lord

reading: The heroine says that she will make vows to the victorious goddess of the cleft hill caves, tie the sacred thread on her wrist, heed the birds and stand for chance words, and still think of him, friend, since he is like life to her life, he who once could not bear to be parted even for a blink and now can forget her and stay away.
nuance: The list of rites is everything a woman could do to bring him back, and it closes on the one she cannot stop, thinking of him. The contrast is inside his own past: the man for whom a blink was too long a parting is the one who can now stay away.

thinai_evidence.note: he stays far off, forgetting her

comparisons.tenor: the man, dear to her as life to her life

reading: The heroine says her body is pale, her longing is with the unkind-hearted man, her restraint has gone far off, and her mind keeps saying 'rise, let us go to him', saying what cannot be done; but there will be no place for her, friend, with the lord of the shore of thorny-leaved broad-trunked screwpine, if he asks 'and who are you?'
nuance: Each part of her is somewhere else (pallor on the body, longing with him, restraint far away, reason urging her out); the only thing that holds her is the fear of being met as a stranger. The phrasing of line 7 is restored from Swaminatha Aiyar's text and its sense is not settled.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine shore and its lord

reading: The heroine tells her friend to see: in the woodland of fragrant flowers, where the stag has cropped the new varagu sprung from the old rain to stubble and the jasmine blooming by the straw has loosened its small buds like a wild cat smiling, even the evening ringed with bees has come and those who left for wealth have not.
nuance: The varagu has been sown, grown and cropped since he left, so the scene is a clock of the seasons; the jasmine buds opening like a wild cat's bared teeth make the promised season's smile a sneer.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening in the jasmine woodland after the rains

comparisons.tenor: the jasmine buds opening

title: kuruntokai 221-240
theme: Kuruntokai 221 to 240: short akam poems of waiting and lost beauty, in which the mullai season arrives without the man (221, 234, 240), the friend demands back the beauty the man has consumed (236, 238), the woman's wasted body leaves no shame to keep (239), and onlookers credit fate with marrying childhood rivals (229).
source_issues: kuruntokai:225 line 7 and kuruntokai:237 line 2 are repaired readings from tamilvu.org (flags); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:231 line 6 reads வில்லுமிழ் கணியிற், where the sense (an arrow shot from a bow) wants கணையின்; marked with the arrow sense.
kuruntokai:223 line 3 (நல்லோர் நல்ல பலவாற் றில்ல) is hard to construe; the reading is uncertain.

kuruntokai:221-240: the colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so thurai_akam addressees are taken from vocatives in the poems where present and given as pira otherwise, and occasion.words is null.

reading: The woman says he has not come though the mullai has bloomed: the goatherd who leaves his lambs, comes into the village with milk and goes back with gruel, wears nothing on his head but small green mullai buds.
nuance: The season's proof is put on the humblest head: even the goatherd is crowned with the buds the man was to come back by. The goatherd also comes and goes back every day; a reader may hear a reproach in that, but nothing in the poem draws it, so the herdsman stays scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits through the season he promised to return in

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The man says that in the water-play she takes the head of the raft when he does and the tail when he does, and if he lets the raft go and drifts with the stream she will seemingly come there too, she whose rain-cool eyes have corners red as the streaks of a wet jasmine bud and who is like a tender shoot drops have fallen on.
nuance: The doubled lines (தலைப்புணை ... கடைப்புணை) move the way she moves, copying his every hold; the third conditional pushes the play to the point of risk, letting go into the current, and still she follows. The bud of the rainy-season jasmine is a mullai thing in a kurinji poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the union of lovers who cannot be parted

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the red-streaked corners of her eyes
the girl, fresh and tender

reading: The woman reminds her friend that the friend kept saying 'let us go' to the festival that filled the big town, and that on that day, here, he gave her the bird-scaring rattles and tender leaves, said falsely that they suited her, and took the fine beauty her mother had guarded, so that she is now as she is.
nuance: She turns the blame on the friend: while the friend wanted the town festival, the union happened 'here', in the field, through small gifts of the millet-guard's own tools. Line 3 (நல்லோர் நல்ல பலவாற் றில்ல) is hard to construe, so who 'the good ones' are is not fixed.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet-guarding rattles of the hill field

reading: The woman tells her friend that brooding on the cruelty of the man who went down the long road of forking paths makes her sleepless sickness worse than sickness, and that like a mute man who saw at night a cow suffering in a well she cannot bear the pain and cannot speak it.
nuance: The simile has two sufferers: the cow in the well and the mute who sees it and can neither help nor call for help; she is the second, so the pain is doubled by being unspeakable. உயர்திணை, 'of the higher class', marks him as human, set against the animal he watches.

thinai_evidence.note: she suffers the absence of the man who went on the hard road

comparisons.vehicle: கூவற் குராலான் படுதுயர் இராவிற் கண்ட உயர்திணை ஊமன்
comparisons.tenor: the woman who sees her own pain and cannot speak it

reading: The friend tells the man of the great-rock country, where a she-elephant eats the millet in the yard while her calf drinks at her rich udder, that if he does not forget kindness, as a king forgets the help he received in ruin once he has gained the glory of the throne, then the girl's thick soft hair, like the spread tail of a proud peacock, is his.
nuance: The gift of her hair is conditional: it is his only if he is not the ungrateful king, so the friend presses for marriage by naming the vice in advance. The she-elephant eating the household's millet while she suckles has been read as the lover taking freely what is not yet his, but the scene gives only one pair, so it stays scene (a near miss on ullurai condition 3).

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant in the millet yard of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the lover who might forget the help of the girl's love once he has what he wants
the girl's thick soft hair

reading: The woman tells her friend that her flower-like eyes, her shoulders lovely as bamboo and her forehead that could be mistaken for the crescent were truly fine before she laughed with the lord of the wide-water shore, where every night white screwpine buds struck by the waves open like herons.
nuance: The praise of her beauty is all in the past tense (நல்லமன், 'were good indeed'): the catalogue of eyes, shoulders and brow is an inventory of what she has lost. The screwpine bud that looks like a heron is a thing that seems what it is not; some read the hero's look of constancy in it, but the poem gives no second pair, so it stays a simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine and waves of the shore

comparisons.tenor: her eyes
her shoulders
her forehead
the white screwpine bud as it opens

reading: The friend says that here in the seaside grove the chariot-man drove away from, there are even stubby neythal flowers with their broad petals cut off, sliced by the bright face of the golden-rimmed wheel that looks like a wrought jewel.
nuance: The poem says only that there is evidence: the lilies cut by a chariot wheel prove the man came to the grove. To whom the friend shows this sign, and why (to tell the heroine he came, or to let the household learn of the affair), the poem does not say, so the situation is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flowers of the seaside grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the golden rim of the chariot wheel

reading: The woman says that though the man of the cool sea left us and belongs to a far country, he is near to her heart, in the land where, they say, the waves come up to the yard of the little hamlet by the seaside grove and go back, and the ripe screwpine bud opens its petals like a heron preening its feathers.
nuance: She knows his land only by report (என்ப, 'they say'), and what she chooses to repeat is the coming and going of the waves. The far country and the near heart are set side by side (நெடுஞ்சேண் ... நெஞ்சிற்கு அணியர) with no complaint.

thinai_evidence.note: the screwpine, the grove and the waves of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the screwpine bud opening its sheaths

iraicchi.act: the waves come up to the doorstep of his hamlet and go back again
iraicchi.sense: even the sea of his own country comes and returns, so his going is not the end of his coming

reading: Onlookers say that the two who once fought small senseless fights, he pulling her plaited hair and she pulling his thin tuft while their loving nurses tried and failed to stop them, have been shown the joy of marriage by fate, which has done well to join them like a garland of paired flowers.
nuance: The childhood fights are the evidence of the match: those who could not be kept apart even to fight are now joined by பால், the portion fate deals. The poem has nothing of the paalai land; its paalai filing presumably follows the onlookers' frame of the couple seen on the road.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem gives no land or season; paalai is the colophon's

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the onlookers address fate (பால்), which the last line calls காட்டியோயே

comparisons.tenor: the couple joined in marriage

reading: The friend asks the woman whether she herself, in her simplicity, did something to hurt that noble man when they met, for the lord of the shore is not one to resolve on such a thing, yet he no longer knows the way of coming, as he did in those few days, over the water path where fierce sharks move.
nuance: The friend blames herself (யான் என் பேதைமையால்) rather than the man, a polite way of saying he has stopped coming without accusing him; the shark-haunted water reminds that his earlier visits braved danger, so their stopping cannot be fear.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the shark-haunted waters

reading: The woman says that though they live in one town he does not come to her street, and if he comes he does not embrace her fully, but passes by without looking, as one passes a stranger's burning-ground; and her desire, having killed shame and lost good sense, has gone far like an arrow loosed from the bow.
nuance: The stranger's burning-ground is a place one passes with averted eyes, so the simile says he treats her as an unlucky sight. The closing turns from him to herself: her own desire has already gone, past shame and sense, and cannot be called back. Line 6 reads கணியிற், where the sense wants கணையின், 'arrow'.

thinai_evidence.note: the neglect of a man who lives in the same town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the man passing her by without a look
her desire, gone beyond recall

reading: The friend asks whether they have not thought of us, or whether, thinking, they do not come for lack of a fitting chance, those who crossed the hill of dark groves where a dark-necked stag, weary for want of the marul to graze, sleeps in the striped shade of a yaa tree left after a mortar-legged elephant broke and ate it.
nuance: The two questions give the absent man two excuses, forgetting or lack of chance, and the friend leaves both open. The stag that sleeps in the thin, striped shade left over by an elephant shows a land where even rest is a remnant; it carries a mood and does nothing a lover does, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the absence of those who crossed the hills

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's legs, thick as a mortar

reading: The man says that the town of the father of the girl with rows of small bangles is in the forest that has met the rains, where bright konrai flowers spread in small wide pits dug up by digging, like opened gold-filled caskets of the rich, and where the rice left after water-poured offerings to the great knows no limit to anyone.
nuance: He praises her by her father's house: its leftovers are shared with everyone without limit, which makes her family the generous household the ethical books describe. The konrai fallen into pits like gold in caskets makes the rainy forest itself look rich. Whether he speaks returning or on the way to ask for her, the poem does not say.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest that has met the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The woman says that those who call evening the hour when the sky reddens as the sun goes and the mullai blooms as the light fails are confused: for those without a partner, the great breaking dawn when the crested cock calls through the tall house is evening too, and so is the day.
nuance: She uses the definition of evening (மாலை என்மனார், 'so they say') as a learned premise and refutes it from experience: the hour is not fixed by the sky but by the absence of a companion. It is a poem about the mutal itself, the time proper to mullai, overturned.

thinai_evidence.note: evening, the mullai hour, made the frame of her waiting

reading: The man asks the north wind to guard it: near the high rock with its pure white waterfall hanging like a snake's cast skin, the town of his good woman is a grass-thatched hut in whose yard herds of marai deer feed on nelli.
nuance: Her town is only a grass hut, but he names it as the one place he wants protected. The north wind, which brings the cold season, is asked to be gentle where she is: the season that makes her suffer is the one he appeals to. Everything he sees in her place is kurinji; the paalai is only in his being away.

thinai_evidence.note: the man far from her asks the wind to keep her place

reading: The friend tells the lord of the cool sea, where a stray stork roosts on the low branch of a punnai standing on the shore of sand heaped like hills, to let the day of his leaving come if he has agreed to it, but first to give back the beauty he has consumed and then go.
nuance: The demand is impossible on purpose: beauty that has been 'eaten' cannot be handed back, so the only way to settle the debt is not to leave. The friend speaks in the girl's person (என் நலன்).

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, the stork and the cool sea

comparisons.tenor: the heaped sand of the shore

reading: The man says that though his heart, which knows no fear and has embraced its beloved, has left him for her, it matters little if the bond of his hands, all that is left, should loosen; for the space between the two of them is very great, and he cannot count what now stands in the way of their embrace: groves where the killing tiger roams to the right, roaring like the waves of the great sea.
nuance: The heart has already crossed to her; only the body, held back by its grip, is here, and the obstacle between them is reckoned in forests and tigers. Lines 1 to 3 are compressed and line 2 is a repaired reading, so the exact turn of the argument (whose hands, what bond) is uncertain; மலைவு in line 7 may mean the hills between them or the obstruction itself.

thinai_evidence.note: the distance of a man gone from her

reading: The friend tells the lord of the fields to give back her beauty, which was like Tondi, where girls with bright bangles play at sand-houses after laying to sleep on the ridge of the ripe paddy the black-cored pestle that pounded green flattened rice, and then go, keeping his oath.
nuance: The pestle 'put to sleep' on the field ridge and the girls at play describe a town so secure its work stops for games; that ease is what her beauty was. 'Go, keeping your oath' is bitter: the oath he swore is what he is breaking by going.

thinai_evidence.note: the paddy ridges and the lord of the fields

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, rich and at ease like the port town

reading: The woman tells her friend that her bangles have slipped and her shoulders wasted, so is there any shame left to give up for the lord of the hill hedged with bamboo, where the short-winged bee sucking the fragrant pollen of the swaying kanthal that scents the hill at the cleft looks like a gem spat out by a snake?
nuance: Her body has already published what modesty would hide, so there is no shame left to lose by speaking; the line prepares the move from secrecy to disclosure. The bee at the kanthal, a creature on a bloom shaped like a snake's hood, is a dangerous-seeming beauty; some read the lover in it, but no second pair is given, so it stays a simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the kanthal and bamboo of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the dark bee in the red kanthal bloom

reading: The woman tells her friend to see how, on top of the north wind's coming, when the many bright avarai flowers like parrots' beaks crowd on the bush with mullai buds like a wild cat's teeth, at evening his tall blue hill shows like a ship sinking into the sea and then vanishes, so that her sickness strikes.
nuance: The one thing of his she can see is his hill, and evening takes even that: it does not vanish at once but sinks like a ship, a slow loss watched to the end. The sinking ship is a neythal thing in a mullai poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the north wind and evening of the waiting season

comparisons.tenor: the avarai flowers
the mullai buds

title: kuruntokai 241-260
theme: Kuruntokai 241 to 260: short akam poems in which the body and the land are read as evidence: eyes that weep or block a chariot (241, 256), a forehead restored by a look at his hill (249), shoulders that swell as an omen (260), peacocks and stags that misread or mark the season (250, 251), and the mother's watch and the town's talk that hem the lovers in (244, 246, 248, 257).

source_issues.issue: TSCII repair at line 6 (தெளி form); text reads as repaired. Line 1 (ஆய மாய்ந்த) and line 4 (மாலைவேல்) divide uncertainly.
Line 1 is repeated verbatim as Kuruntokai 313 line 1; a formulaic opening, not an error.
Colophon gives the friend as speaker, but the poem addresses தோழி; read as the friend addressing the heroine, though the heroine as speaker is also possible.
தாரனின் றாரே is read as தாரல் நின் தாரே; line 5 (அரியலம் புகவி னந்தோட்டு) is obscure.
கன்றி லோரா விலங்கிய does not construe with confidence.

reading: The woman tells her friend that while she herself bears her love, her eyes, out of their own intimacy with him, have wept: the eyes that saw the man of the hill country, where the small-headed boys who have herded the calves home raise a guarding shout at the vengai blooming in the village common, without climbing it, and the shout echoes in the sky-touching clefts.
nuance: She splits herself: she bears the desire in silence and the eyes break down. கெழுதகைமை is the closeness of old intimates, so the eyes weep out of their own bond with the man they saw, not on her orders. The boys' shout at the flowering vengai is the cry raised to bring its flowers down without climbing; the vengai's bloom also marks the millet harvest and the time for marriage, but the poem does not draw that out, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill, its vengai and its herd boys place the love in the kurinji

reading: The foster mother says the girl lives in a small village in the flower-scented scrub, where the jungle cock with its calling voice, cool drops dripping from its bright-spotted neck, sweeps the water off the bushes; and even when the young lord goes to another town on work the king sends, his chariot does not know how to stay the night away.
nuance: The proof of the marriage is negative: the chariot does not know how to stay away. The king's business, which elsewhere takes a husband away for whole seasons, cannot keep this one for a night. The wet cock of the rainy scrub sets the season of waiting that this household is spared, which is why the mullai uri is here only to be denied.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-wet scrub and its jungle cock set the mullai household

reading: The woman says she will not think of the lord of the great sea shore where birds cry, where girls with bright bangles play at sand houses after plucking the bright flowers, like the bells on a garland, of the adumbu whose forked leaves are like a deer's hoofprint: let my eyes sleep, friend.
nuance: The vow not to think is made so that the eyes may sleep, which concedes that thinking of him is what has kept them open. The girls at their sand houses are the play she has left behind, and she places them on his shore.

thinai_evidence.note: the adumbu and the sea shore are neythal, and she laments alone

reading: The friend tells the man that they are not people who failed to hear him, in the dense midnight when everyone sleeps, trying the door at night like a strong elephant: they heard, lord, but like a fine peacock caught in a net, its crest ruffled and its plumes drooping, we lay held, because the unfair mother embraces us each time we stir.
nuance: The mother's embrace, the sign of her love, is the trap: அறனில் யாய், the mother without fairness, holds the girl closest exactly when she would rise. The friend answers the man's force (the elephant at the door) with the girl's helplessness (the netted peacock, crest and plumes spoiled, as her beauty will be by the wait).

thinai_evidence.note: the midnight tryst at the door is kurinji union

reading: The woman says that worse than the loss of her beauty, which her companions in the seaside grove admired, would be for the unkindness of the lord of the soft shore, where the screw-pine with lush, sword-edged spathes stands as a fence like spears planted in a row, to spread wide and come out for many to know.
nuance: She ranks two losses and chooses the private one: her wasted beauty she can bear, the public knowledge of his unkindness she cannot, since it shames them both and closes the way to marriage. His shore is one where even the screw-pine stands armed as a fence, yet he guards nothing of hers; that is a single correspondence, so it is not tagged as ullurai. Whether மாலை in line 4 is a row (of spears) or evening, and how ஆய மாய்ந்த in line 1 divides, are not certain.

reading: The woman says that because people say a chariot came and turned back at midnight for one who was alone, when the small white crow of the great sea's shore, stirring the green leaves broad as an elephant's ear, searches the cold backwater, her mother torments her; yet there are other girls, young and simple, with braided hair and bright jewels, the lucky ones, whose mothers do not torment them.
nuance: The rumour is true and the punishment falls on her alone, and she complains to fate: நற்பாலோர், those of good portion, are not better girls but girls with gentler mothers. The crow searching the cold backwater is awake at the hour the chariot came; it is witness and setting, and does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the crow of the backwater sets the shore, and she laments

reading: The friend says she knew then that the flawless friendship from the chest of the man of the country, where the vengai sheds blossom from its soft unwithering branches and the elephant's deep sleep is heard, has great beauty, comes to sweet fruit, is righteous like the work of the able, and is a raft for people with kin.
nuance: A secret love is praised in the language of public virtue, beauty, fruit, righteousness and a raft for the kin, so the friend presents it as an alliance fit for families. The elephant asleep under the flower-shedding vengai is the hill at rest; it does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai and the sleeping elephant are of the hill

reading: The friend says the talk was sure to come: from the day he said 'embrace my chest' it has been drawing near and now it is here, friend; and the mother has learned of it, from those telling big things about the lord of the shore where the sand dune climbed by adumbu, which the west wind heaped up to bury the swaying trunks, makes the tall palmyras short.
nuance: The landscape inverts measure: the wind's sand makes tall palms short, and the town's talk makes the affair big (பெரிய கூறி against குறிய ஆகும்). That is one correspondence of size, and it is not clear what the buried palm stands for, so it is recorded here and not tagged as ullurai. Lines 1 and 2 are compressed, and what அது refers to, the talk or his coming, is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the dune, the adumbu and the palmyra are of the shore

reading: The woman tells her friend that she looked toward the hills of his country, whose slopes the heavy rain has drenched, making the grey-faced langur shiver with its young, in the thick-treed forest where flocks of peacocks call: see her forehead, is it not as it was before?
nuance: The cure is only a look at his hills from afar, and it works on her body at once: the forehead that had paled is as it was. The land she looks at is cold and wet, the langur and its young shivering in it; the pair does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: his rain-soaked hill with its peacocks and langurs is kurinji

reading: The man tells his charioteer to drive the wind-swift horses before evening comes, when the fine stag with its mate, having drunk the water in the pebbled hollow, frisks at the foot of the path: for the woman of painted eyes that rival the fighting carp of deep water, and of sweet, chosen words, is in bewildered distress.
nuance: He races the evening because evening is her worst hour; the stag with its mate is already where he wants to be. The colophon's paalai is the journey; the poem itself is the return, which is mullai's.

thinai_evidence.note: the man hurries home by evening to the waiting wife, the mullai situation

reading: The friend says the dark flocks of peacocks are foolish, bless them: thinking the season's rain had fallen, they danced to meet it, and the pidavam too has blossomed; but this is not the rainy season, friend, so let your grief end; they did it on hearing the thunder of a stray cloud that pours out the old water left from the rain that has passed so as to take in new.
nuance: The friend overturns the evidence the heroine is reading: the peacocks and the pidavam are right that it rained and wrong that the season has come. The cloud is only emptying its old store, so the thunder is not the promised monsoon. The mutal is negated: the friend says outright that this is not kaar.

thinai_evidence.note: the waiting wife grieving at the season of his promised return

reading: The woman tells her friend not to be angry for urging her, 'you are simple indeed', because when the crooked man of the hill country who loosened the armlets on her long rounded arms comes, she tends him with a chastity like a god's, her sweet face unchanged: the worthy feel shame even before praise, so how could they bring themselves to blame when they see him?
nuance: She turns a lover's weakness into a rule of the noble: face to face is no place for reproach. She calls him கொடியன் and admits the fault in full before she explains why she will not speak it. The situation, a wife urged to sulk over the man's fault, is marutham's, though the man is of the hills.

thinai_evidence.note: she refuses the sulking her friend urges on her over his fault

reading: The friend tells the heroine that the men who crossed the high-peaked, crag-ringed hill, where on the slope of rustling tall bamboo travellers on the road sleep in a rock cave reeking of flesh where a tiger has been, are not men who will fail to hear; and if they hear of you lying on the flower bed of loosened threads, your great beauty lost, they will not tarry, even if a great thing is slipping from them.
nuance: The comfort is doubled and conditional: they are not the kind who do not hear, and if they hear they will not delay. The road, where travellers sleep in a tiger's flesh-smelling den, shows both how far he is and that he has borne worse than coming home. புலிபுகா உறுத்த in line 6 is hard to construe.

reading: The woman tells her friend that the first blossoms of the kongu have come, its soft buds, lovely as breasts, opened on leafless branches loud with swarms of bees; but the message has not come saying he is here: the man who went in desire of bringing back wealth, who in the nights meant for sleep has forgotten sleep, and does not think of the bed of her hair fragrant with resin.
nuance: The kongu, flowering on bare branches, keeps its time; the messenger is the sign that fails. She counts what he has forgotten in three things, sleep, her hair as his pillow and the season, all set against the wealth.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone for wealth and she waits past the season

reading: The friend tells the heroine that on the road their beloved took, gone bound by the lovely desire for wealth and meaning to fulfil their duty, the men have seen, at place after place, the great-tusked elephant that gores the cracked-barked trunk of the solid-cored yaa tree on the path, pulls it down with its fierce broad trunk and so relieves the burning hunger of its small-eyed great herd that walks with weary steps.
nuance: The elephant feeds not one mate but the whole herd, which matches the men who left to discharge their own obligation (தங்கடன்). The friend's comfort is that a man who watched that at every halt cannot forget whom he is bound to provide for.

reading: The man says that before he could even say, 'Leaving behind the forest where the stag frisks after feeding with its doe on the soft tendrils of the dark arugu creeper, strung like gems, I will come back when the work is done; can you bear it till then, you with flower earrings?', her eyes would not stay, could not stop weeping their flood of tears, and stood across his chariot's way.
nuance: The departure is defeated before it is announced: he has the sentence ready and her eyes answer it first. தேர் விலங்கின, the eyes stood across the chariot, makes tears a barrier on the road. The colophon names no poet.

reading: The woman tells her friend that the enemy of our love comes every time the man of the roaring hill comes, the hill of jackfruit whose fruit hangs from root, trunk and branch alike as if strung together, low as the drooping thodari; and when he goes it does not go, but stays and fights.
nuance: The enemy is not named; since it comes with him and stays after him it is most likely the town's talk or the watch kept on her. The jackfruit loaded on every part is the hill's plenty; a traditional reading takes fruit hanging from the very root as a love too heavy to stay hidden, but the poem draws no correspondence, so it is not tagged as ullurai. Line 2's தொடரி and what it compares are uncertain.

reading: The friend tells the man not to come to their street and not to give his garland: talk has risen, lord, on seeing the flawless fine beauty of this girl wasting, she who is like Arkkadu of Azhisi, father of Chendan whose high-tusked elephant is tied to the marutham at the great Kaveri ford where many bathe, Azhisi, lord of young men with bright swords in rows who live on toddy and the hunt.
nuance: Refusing the garland at the street refuses his re-entry. The girl is likened to a chieftain's rich town, so her beauty is a holding like Arkkadu, and its wasting is what the street has seen. Line 1's தாரனின் றாரே divides as தாரல் நின் தாரே; line 5 is compressed.

reading: The friend tells the dark girl, whose fragrant forehead smells without end like the opened bud of the cool, fragrant kaanthal fed by the waterfalls of the rain-clouded hill, and whose rain-cool eyes are many-petalled, that whether she consents or kills, she herself has measured and knows her own worth: why tell lies that pass for truth? nuance: The friend corners the girl into the truth: she will not let her pretend nothing has happened. ஒல்வை யாயினுங் கொல்வை யாயினும், consent or kill, puts the man's life in the girl's hands, the vocabulary of a suit. reading: The friend asks whether he will come: the herons climb the wide sky, the bushes have opened their mouths as striped bees hum, and the shoulders adorned with curled bangles are growing full; will they come back, friend, who crossed the wasteland of thin-stemmed omai trees lying across the way, near the vazhai-covered slopes of the Thondaiyar of generous chariots, whose lordly elephant takes the soil of its foes?
nuance: The friend reads three signs at once, sky, bush and body: the shoulders that had wasted are filling out, taken as an omen. The return is still a question (வருவர்கொல்) and the road is hard, so the signs give hope, not news. Line 7, கன்றி லோரா விலங்கிய, does not construe with confidence, and செற்றும் in line 3 may mean the shoulders grow firm or are pressed.
