title: kuruntokai 261-280
theme: Kuruntokai 261 to 280: short akam poems that weigh one day of love against a lifetime (271, 280) and the world's wealth against death (267), set the veri rite's slander against a blameless love (263), and show the returning man in the rain (270) and the friend listening for his chariot bell (275).
source_issues: kuruntokai:269 lines 7 and 8, 270 lines 3 and 4, and 276 line 4 are repaired readings (tamilvu.org, or a TSCII leftover fixed); 273 line 8 likewise. Marked as printed.
kuruntokai:274 line 8: our text reads முயகினஞ், tamilvu.org முயங்கினம், sangamtamil.com உள்கினம்; the last would make the journey a lone one. Marked with the embrace reading and uncertain.
kuruntokai:271: the colophon says மருதம், but the poem has only hill things (அருவி, நாடன்); inferred kurinji.
kuruntokai:277: the colophon says பாலை, but the poem waits for the promised season (கடைப்பெயல் வாடை); inferred mullai.

kuruntokai:261-280: the colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so thurai_akam addressees are taken from vocatives in the poems where present and given as pira otherwise, and occasion.words is null.

reading: The woman tells her friend that at the end of the light rains, when the old downpour has rotted the sesame pods, even in the fearful midnight when the red-eyed buffalo, weary of standing in mud, lows, her eyes do not sleep, because her heart is wounded with a grief that keeps count like the watchmen.
nuance: The buffalo is a field beast lowing in a hill poem's night; it does not stand for anyone, it only makes the hour audible. Lines 6 and 7 (காவலர் கணக்காய் வகையின்) seem to say she keeps the night's count as the watchmen do, so the town's guards and the lover's wakefulness are set side by side.

thinai_evidence.note: the sleepless midnight of a secret love

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative வாழி தோழி names the friend

reading: The friend says: let the town's gossip rise and the street clamour, and let the mother, who rails without justice, keep to her own house; the girl, her sharp teeth gleaming from the gooseberry she ate, has chosen to drink with him, in a far country on the slopes of a cross-lying hill that rises to touch the sky, the water left standing in a great tusker's footprint, like a bed dug for planting sugarcane.
nuance: The gooseberry is the point: its sourness makes any water taste sweet, so the girl has already prepared her mouth for the worst water of the road. The friend sets the town's noise and the mother's anger against a choice already made.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl leaves home with her lover for a far land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the water-filled footprint of the tusker

reading: The friend says it is painful that, while the mother cuts the throat of a kid, scatters millet and, to the noise of many instruments at the forked path, praises many strange great gods who are only show and no cure for this sickness, the girl should be called possessed by a demon, when they have done no wrong to the lord of the high hill where clouds play.
nuance: The friend's complaint is double: the gods praised are 'other' gods (வேற்று), not the cause, and the rite's verdict, that she is possessed, is a slander on a love she calls blameless (பிழையேம்).

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and its lord; the rite of the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the addressee

reading: The woman says that the friendship the lord of the land, where on the high bank of the forest river gathered with roaring rain the dancing peacock walks with its long rustling plumes at rest and calls, formed with her out of desire, even when it bore fruit, brought her nothing she can bear.
nuance: The last line plays on பய: பயந்தக் காலும் (even when it yielded) against பயப்பு (yield, or the pallor of longing), so the bond's very fruit may be her pallor. The peacock only calls and walks; it carries the mood of the wet bank, not a sense of its own.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill river, the peacock and the hill lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the rock hill, where the plump kaanthal bud, its guard of no use, opens its mouth when the bee comes, as men who know their duty open to the worthy they have long known, and its petals loosen and come free, is of good heart: when she told him the girl's state he was ashamed that it should go on so.
nuance: The simile is reversed: the flower is the tenor and human courtesy the vehicle, and then the whole picture is turned onto the man, whose shame works the way the bud opens, unforced, once the right one comes.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal of the rock hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the addressee

comparisons.tenor: the kaanthal bud opening to the bee

reading: The woman wonders whether those who could cling to her broad shoulders and then leave, though they told her nothing, have also forgotten the vengai in the garden that was their sweet companion through painful nights, and the message the birds' cries carry.
nuance: She cannot accuse him outright, so she asks whether he has forgotten a tree: the vengai that sheltered their meetings is made a witness that he owes something to.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The man says that even if all the great wealth of the wide world came together at once, those who know the lawless crookedness of Death, which takes in its due order every day, would not leave the young woman with small bangles, whose white teeth hold sweet faultless water like the taste of a joint of sugarcane cut at the node, to go after work.
nuance: The argument from death, usually a reason to hurry after merit or wealth, is turned into a reason to stay: if life ends on Death's schedule, the hours with her are the only gain. The poet's name, காலெறி கடிகையார், is taken from line 3.

thinai_evidence.note: leaving for wealth, refused

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the sweet water of her teeth

reading: The friend says: we can neither say 'will you go?' nor ask 'will you come?'; what shall we do, friend, with him who, not minding that it was midnight, came with the thunder that splits the hooded heads of snakes and reached her long soft shoulders?
nuance: Both courteous questions are closed to them: asking him to go is unkind, asking whether he will come again is shameless, so the friend's helplessness is a lesson in what the secret stage forbids saying.

thinai_evidence.note: the midnight tryst in a storm

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the addressee

reading: The woman says it would be good to find someone who would go the long way without tiring and ask him, and this would be the message: father, his wound from the strong shark healed, has gone out on the blue sea, mother has gone to the salt fields to trade salt for white paddy, so if he comes now to the lord of the cold wide shore she is easy to meet.
nuance: The message is built out of the household's working day: the father's healed wound and the barter of salt for paddy are why the house is empty, so the fisher family's labour becomes the girl's opportunity.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea, the salt pans and the shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The man tells the great sky to pour now and live long, flashing to cut the deep darkness, scattering cool sweet drops and roaring, thunder on thunder, like a drum beaten hard: with the full heart of one whose work is done he has joined her and lies on the soft pillow of her fragrant hair that smells of fresh short-stemmed blue lilies.
nuance: The rain that in the waiting poems is the man's broken promise is here blessed: the same storm, once he is home, becomes a canopy for the union.

thinai_evidence.note: the return after the task, in the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man addresses the sky (பெருவான்)

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the thunder

reading: The woman says that trusting the lord of the land, where the clouds scatter rain like waterfalls and the rivers run full, what happened was a single day, but it has become a disease that for very many days confuses her shoulders and seizes their beauty.
nuance: The arithmetic carries the poem: ஒருநாள் against தவப்பன்னாள், one day of union against very many days of wasting.

thinai_evidence.note: waterfall country and the hill lord; nothing in the poem is of the fields

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the heavy rain the clouds scatter

reading: The man asks whether it will even be possible to touch the shoulders of the hill girl with dark fragrant hair, whose kohl-lined eyes are like the red-shafted arrow her brothers, when the sad young doe parted from its herd came in sight in the wide forest where whistling bowmen raised their din, drove with the bow's full force into the stag's side and drew out with its blood.
nuance: The arrow that is her eye belongs to her brothers, so the look that wounds him is also a weapon of her kin. Read as a hidden comparison (the stag shot near the stray doe as the suitor, the brothers as her guardians) it would be a near miss: the eye is the stated tenor, and the second pair is not anchored, so it is not tagged ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunt of the hill country and the hill girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes

reading: The friend tells the bright-browed girl, cool and fragrant as the gentle evening wind that stirs the great forest so that pollen and buds tremble, that if she is hurt she will tell what she has seen: this world has been fooled like the simpleton who climbed the old cliff of the great honeycomb without a ladder; while we are here he will not leave, be sure of it.
nuance: The friend laughs the rumour down: those who said he would go are like a man who climbs for honey with no way to reach it. முதுமால் பறியாது is hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the feared departure that will not happen

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative ஒண்ணுதலோயே names the addressee

comparisons.tenor: her cool fragrance

comparisons.vehicle: பெருந்தேன் கண்படு வரையின் முதுமால் பறியா தேறிய மடவோன்
comparisons.tenor: the world that expected him to leave

reading: The man says that even the cruel forest, where the ukaay with thin stems like a dove's back drops its dense fruit like coins, where hard-eyed men climb its branches with bow and arrow to watch for travellers, and where the parched chew the fruit to ease their thirst, will be sweet if he goes holding the jewelled bosom of the girl whose girdle is set with gold and gems.
nuance: Line 8 decides whether he means to take her with him: our text and tamilvu read 'embracing' (முயகினம் / முயங்கினம்), sangamtamil.com 'thinking of' (உள்கினம்), which would make it a lone journey sweetened by memory.

thinai_evidence.note: the harsh forest road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the ukaay's thin grey stem
the dense fruit

reading: The friend says: let us climb the high rock overgrown with mullai and look, friend; is that the bell of a good grass-fed cow of the bull herd coming home to town at dusk, or are those the bells of the chariot of the man who, with the full heart of one whose work is done, comes down the wet-sand forest stream with young bowmen guarding his side?
nuance: The two bells, the cow's and the chariot's, are the same sound at the same hour; the friend's question keeps hope and doubt together.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai on the rock and the returning herds at dusk

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the addressee

reading: The man says that the guards who watch the bright thoyyil painted on the rising breasts of the slim-shouldered girl, as she makes dolls and wanders round the reed pond, do not even know; if he were to take his case to the just king's court of the red sceptre what would become of her? She is truly very simple, and this clamouring town is to be pitied.
nuance: He imagines suing a child at law: the king's court of justice is the only authority he can think of for a harm that has no culprit, and he drops the idea at once because she does not know what she has done.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret love the guards do not see

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The friend blesses the mendicant who eats his fill of red rice and white butter begged at a single house, at a wide doorway with no dog in a clean street, that he may get hot water in a vessel in the cold season; he asks when the north wind of the last rains will come, the wind at which she of the lightning-slim waist trembles, and the friend answers that when it comes their beloved will come.
nuance: The blessing is precise: a man who lives on alms in the cold season would want hot water most. Whether என்றி means 'you ask' or 'you said' decides whether the mendicant brought the promise or only the question.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for the promised season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: a mendicant who begs at one house (ஓரிற் பிச்சை), addressed as நீயே

reading: The woman says they think neither of her small soft feet, like the tender shoots of the lovely mango stirred by a strong wind, nor of the small green doll; cruel are they, friend, who crossed the mountain where the male monkey shakes down the sweet ripe fruit and the mother monkey with her young sits below and eats all she can catch.
nuance: The small green doll (சிறுபசும் பாவை) is the girl's plaything, but read with the monkey's young it may also be a child, which would make this a wife's poem.

thinai_evidence.note: he crossed the mountain and does not think of her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative வாழி தோழி names the friend

comparisons.tenor: her small soft feet

iraicchi.act: the male monkey shakes down ripe fruit for the mother monkey and her young, who eat it below
iraicchi.sense: even the monkey on the mountain he crossed provides for its mate and young, while he who passed it does not think of her

reading: The woman asks whether, even at this hour, when the clear bell tied to the striped neck of the dark ram with twisted horns rings at every step in the lonely night, he will not come, he who went past many great hills where a huge boulder the rain has forgotten to wash shines like an elephant covered in dust, and did not think of her well-jointed shoulders.
nuance: Two places at one hour: her village, where the flock's bell keeps ringing at night, and his road, where the rain has failed; the season she was promised has come at home but not on the hills he crossed.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting into the night of the promised time

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the dry boulder on his road

reading: The man tells his companions, long may they live, that if he could join for one day with the young woman of broad shoulders, small soft body and fine thin tresses who binds his heart every day, he would not want even half a day of life after.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's longing for union in the secret stage

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressed to his companions (கேளிர்), who are taken to rebuke him

title: kuruntokai 281-300
theme: Short speeches of the five lands: women waiting through the rains and the seasons for men gone to the waste (281-283, 285, 287, 289, 290), men remembering and reassuring the hill-girl (286, 291, 300), the friend's curses, counsel and pleas in secret love (284, 292, 294, 297, 298), and the wife's grief at the husband's other women (293, 295, 296), with two poems weighing love against heaven and the world (288, 300).
source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
kuruntokai:283 line 3 (தெளிய) was repaired from a TSCII leftover (தௌிய); the repair reads correctly.
kuruntokai:293 line 8 is the tamilvu.org reading that replaced ours (flag); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:287: the colophon says தோழி கூற்று, but the poem addresses தோழி and speaks of காதலர், which reads as the woman's voice; the colophon is kept and the doubt recorded here.
Thinai differs from the colophon in 282 (mullai: the field facing the rains, against பாலை) and 297 (paalai: the elopement through the waste, against குறிஞ்சி).
Hard lines, marked uncertain: 282 line 7 (ஆர்கழல் புகுவ), 284 line 5 (நம்மே சுவரோ தம்மிலர்), 285 lines 5-6, 289 line 6, 293 line 1 (ஆத்திரை), 294 line 8 (காத்தோம் பல்லே), 298 lines 5-8 (the simile).

reading: The woman asks her bright-jewelled friend whether their man has gone into the forest where hills crowd together, his curly head bright with the white leaf from the crown of the palmyra that grows thick on white sand and with the pale flowers of the neem.
nuance: She sees him in his going-out dress, palmyra leaf and neem flowers on his head, the kind of adornment worn by men setting out as warriors; the whole poem is one picture and one question, and the question (கொல்லோ) lets her hold off knowing. உளைத்தலை could also be the tufted head of a horse.

thinai_evidence.note: she asks whether he has already left on the hill-forest road

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative சேயிழை names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The friend asks whether their man, seeing the cool clearing turning toward the rains, where the young fawn of the deer nibbles the dark leaf of the seedling sprung on the red ground of ripe millet, will not say that her bangles must be slipping off like the new hollow flowers of white koothalam dropping from their stems on the water-bright slope.
nuance: The friend hopes the season itself will speak for the woman: the land he crosses shows him the rains, and she wants him to read her slipping bangles there. Line 7 (ஆர்கழல் புகுவ) is hard to construe; the falling-flower sense is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the field facing the rains is the season he should come back by

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: நமர் suggests the friend speaks to the woman; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her bangles slipping off her wasted arms

reading: The woman tells her friend that he left after showing her plainly the force of what he had said, that those who waste what they have are not counted as men and that the life of the poor is more shameful even than begging, and went by the waterless road through the long old waste where a hawk watches the reeking flesh of travellers killed by bandits whose spears kill like Death.
nuance: She quotes his reasons almost as maxims and then sets them against the road: the argument that sent him is clear (தெளியக் காட்டி), and what waits on the road is a hawk over the bodies of men robbed of what they carried. The poem does not say whether she accepts the argument.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone for wealth across the waterless waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative வாழி தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the bandits' killing spears

reading: The friend says that, whether the man of the land where many bright red kaanthal open together on the boulder of the village common like the spotted face of a fighting elephant proves good or not, the people of this small village, living wretchedly in their huts below the white waterfall that drops from the hill, will blame us, or care nothing for us.
nuance: Line 5 (நம்மே சுவரோ தம்மிலர் கொல்லோ) is hard to divide, and the reading 'will they blame us' is a guess; what is clear is the friend weighing the lover's worth against the village's judgment, and finding the village careless either way.

thinai_evidence.note: kaanthal on the rock and the hill waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person (நாடன்); the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the red kaanthal massed on the rock

reading: The woman asks her friend where he can be, who crossed the sky-high mountains where a lone hawk sits on the top of the nyemai tree craving flesh: day after day passes and he does not come, every limit of time passes and he does not appear, though this is the season he named; is the bird calling again and again to its dull-backed mate for delight nothing to his eyes?
nuance: The repeated words of lines 1 and 2 (வைகல் வைகல் வைகவும், எல்லா எல்லை எல்லையும்) make the days pile up in the sound. Lines 5 and 6 are hard; the bird and its mate are read as the season's sign the man ignores. The lone hawk waiting for flesh is a mood of the road, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits for one who crossed the mountains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

iraicchi.act: the male bird calls to its mate again and again so that they may delight together
iraicchi.sense: at this season even birds call their mates, yet he does not come to her

reading: The man says he seems to see, as he thinks of it, the look of the hill-girl with wide rain-cool eyes, full of pride and soft smiling, her mouth red and lovely where nectar wells by her sharp teeth, her hair dark like rippled sand and fragrant with agil and sandal.
nuance: The whole poem is one noun phrase hanging on நோக்கே, the last word: after the mouth, the hair and the eyes, what memory finally holds is a look, proud and smiling at once.

thinai_evidence.note: the beloved is a girl of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks to himself; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her dark hair

reading: The speaker asks her friend whether their lover will forsake them even after seeing it: the time when the great roaring cloud, having drunk the sea, cannot climb the sky and holds itself back, gathering toward the many rich hills, like women heavy with a first child who, at the end of their months, cannot move and crave green tamarind.
nuance: The cloud is pregnant with rain as women are with child, and the season it brings is the one he promised; the simile makes the rain season itself a time of fulfilment he would be failing.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain clouds gather: the season of return

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names the friend as speaker, but the poem addresses தோழி and speaks of காதலர், which reads as the woman's voice; see source_issues

comparisons.tenor: the rain clouds slow and heavy with water

reading: The woman says that because the lord of the great hill country, where monkeys sit together eating tender shoots on the slope where pepper grows, is dear to her, even the hurt that comes from kin is sweeter than the world of the gods that is called sweet.
nuance: Whose kin (இனத்தின்) cause the hurt is not said: her own family's anger at the affair, or his people's coldness. The monkeys that sit together (ஒருங்கு) eating may hint at a troop that keeps its members, but the poem does not draw this, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: pepper slopes and monkeys of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The woman tells her friend that, growing day by day like the waxing moon, the grief that loosened the bangles on her wrist has left her shrunk like a crushed sprout; besides the pain of his not being near, the rain has set in thick, and this clamouring town pities her more than she pities him out in the rain.
nuance: The town here is not the hostile gossip of other poems but a chorus of pity, and its pity measures her own: she grieves for him in the rain, the town grieves for her. Line 6 (பட்ட மாரி படாஅக் கண்ணும்) is hard and the reading of it is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come while he is away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her growing grief
her wasted body

reading: The woman asks whether those who tell her to bear her love do not know what it is, or are themselves that strong: if she does not see her lover, with a heart where clinging grief has swelled, she will waste away little by little like the small foam that breaks on a rock in deep water.
nuance: The image gives no crash, only foam dissolving where it strikes; the doubled மெல்ல மெல்ல makes the dissolution slow. The poet is named from this simile (கல்பொரு சிறுநுரையார்).

thinai_evidence.note: lament of one who will fade without him

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she answers those who counsel endurance; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her slow wasting away

reading: The man says that the clapper in the hand of the hill-girl driving parrots from the millet on the burnt clearing makes a call sweeter than music, so the parrots take it for one of their own and will not rise; and her eyes, which wept in vexation at that, were like the many-petalled kuvalai of the deep hill pool, ruffled by bees and taking the cool drops.
nuance: The joke turns on her sweetness: she fails at her work because her voice is too lovely, and her vexed tears only add a second beauty. The man watches both.

thinai_evidence.note: a hill girl guarding millet from parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her tear-wet eyes

reading: The friend curses her mother: as Nannan, when a bright-browed girl who had gone to bathe ate a green fruit the stream carried down, refused eighty-one elephants and a golden doll of her weight in amends and chose to kill a woman, so may her mother go to endless hell, who, since a smiling guest came one day, has not slept, as in a town that faces enemies.
nuance: The curse is wildly out of proportion, and that is the point: one visit from a smiling guest has turned the house into a town under siege, and the friend answers with the worst story of cruelty she knows, a chief who would take no ransom for a girl's small fault.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother's watch keeps the lovers apart

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the speaker curses the mother in the third person, perhaps with the man in hearing; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the mother
the mother sleepless on guard

reading: The wife says she is to be pitied: the bright-jewelled one, lovely as the old town of Aathi Aruman where people go home with palmyra kernels from tall dark palms whose spathes give small fibrous fruit, comes there, her leaf-skirt of white lilies beating in turn on her spotted thighs, to see the husband.
nuance: The rival is praised before she is resented: the wife grants her the beauty of a famous chief's old town and then ends on herself, அளியேன் யானே. Line 1 (கள்ளிற் கேளிர் ஆத்திரை) is obscure: ஆத்திரை may be a place or a person, and the poet's name is taken from it.

thinai_evidence.note: another woman comes for the husband

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the other woman's beauty

reading: The friend says that after sea-bathing, resting in the shore grove and dancing in the garlanded troop, he came suddenly like a stranger, embraced her and went, and gossip spread; yet he never left her side, and himself gave the green-leaf skirt that swings on her spotted hips with its fresh shoots; now mother keeps her guarded.
nuance: The gift of a leaf-skirt is a lover's pledge, and the friend sets it against his stranger-like coming and going: the bond is real, and now the mother's watch makes marriage the only road. The last line (காத்தோம் பல்லே) is hard to divide.

thinai_evidence.note: sea-bathing and the shore grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the man arriving and leaving

reading: The friend tells the man that he comes with the festival in a crowd of women bright with leaves worn as skirts, strung, put on and tucked in the hair, and that this town says the festival has truly begun now that the lovely young girl of a poor house that lives on a single cow has come.
nuance: The town's praise of the new girl is reported by the friend as an accusation: 'the festival has come' now means 'your new woman has come', and the poverty of her house (one cow) sharpens the sting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man comes to the festival with other women

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend addresses the man (நீயே); the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The woman tells her friend not to stand before the lord of the cool shore, where the stork sitting on the swaying punnai bough, tired of the small fish of the creek, longs for the toddy-scented neythal among the paddy of the field, and rebuke him harshly, as she had resolved, asking whether it suits him to forsake one who is in such a state.
nuance: She forbids the rebuke while repeating it in full, so the reproach is spoken after all, through the friend's resolve. The stork leaving the creek's fish for the field is the hidden picture of his straying.

thinai_evidence.note: the stork on the punnai of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

he longs for other women away from the shore

reading: The friend says she understood surely, before he did, that the right course was for the two to go off together, speaking good words of the wide rocky waste where the cairns heaped with leaves over travellers who stood against the bow-bearing bandits and died look like a village.
nuance: The friend takes credit for the elopement plan, and lays its road out in its worst colours, a village of graves; the danger is not hidden from the girl but made part of the choice.

thinai_evidence.note: elopement through the waste land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

reading: The friend asks the woman to think of the sorrowful look of the man who comes slowly again and again to their street, rarely opens his mouth to say sweet words and stays each day with his colour changed: his long standing at the back aims at something else, like the young she-elephants that Akuthai's father, of sweet strong toddy, gave as gifts to the singing women with small white-tipped sticks.
nuance: The simile is the hard part: what the gift and the waiting share seems to be that each is an outward act aimed at something beyond itself, the chief's gift at the singers' praise, the man's patience at the girl. The friend thus casts the lover as a suppliant whose silence is a request.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover waiting for the girl's consent

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி marks the friend speaking to the woman; the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: his long waiting at the back

reading: The woman asks her friend what this is: in the shade of the clustered punnai on the dune of the shore grove where the old sea's waves play and birds cry, on the day their tryst came true, her eyes saw the lord of the shore and her ears heard his words; and now her wide soft shoulders take on great beauty when he joins her and waste when he leaves.
nuance: Eyes and ears are named as the witnesses that did the harm, each with மன் (once, and no more); the body that now swells and wastes with his coming and going is the only record left.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea and the shore grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the vocative தோழி names the friend; the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The man tells the dark girl with fine spots like the pollen of the deep-water lotus, with heaped dark hair smelling of kuvalai and a honeyed red mouth smelling of aambal, that she fears his very word 'do not fear'; but he would not think of leaving her friendship even if he gained the sea-ringed world where the short-legged swan rests on heaped sand.
nuance: The setting of நீயே against யானே divides the poem between her fear and his oath. The swan resting on heaped sand is a shore image of rest, put inside the very world he says he would refuse.

thinai_evidence.note: reassurance after union in secret love

title: kuruntokai 301-320
theme: Kuruntokai 301-320, mostly shore poems: the heroine sleepless at midnight (301, 302), pale or wasting (303, 316), stung by gossip she did not earn (311, 320), holding the man to his oath and the knotted bond (304, 313, 318); waiting through the rains and evenings (314, 319, 310); the paalai crescent and tusker (307); the friend's neythal that reblooms where it was weeded (309); and Kapilar's girl who is a thief of two faces (312).
source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (தலைவி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.

301: the base colophon gives குறிஞ்சி and sangamtamil.com gives நெய்தல் (flag); the poem's palmyra and anril support neythal, which is our thinai. This is the only verse in the chapter where our thinai differs from the colophon.
303 lines 1-2: the word வெண்குருகு is split across the line break (வெண்குரு / கு).
306 line 5: பயருங் is doubtful (perhaps பயிரும்); the sense of lines 1-2 is also open, and the verse is marked uncertain.
309 line 1: மாக்கடம் is probably a misdivision of மாக்கள் தம்; line 7 has a stray comma inside a word (நீயெமக், கின்னா).
310 line 6: கமழுஞாழல் is run together (கமழும் ஞாழல்).
313: the colophon names no poet.
314 line 3, 316 line 8 and 318 line 8 were repaired from tamilvu.org; the repairs read correctly.
316 line 6: வாய்ந்த லவன் looks like a faulty division (the crab, அலவன், is clear; the preceding word is not), and the sense of lines 5-7 is uncertain.
320 line 8: தூற்றந்தன் is probably தூற்றும் தன் run together.

reading: The heroine tells her friend that at midnight, when the pregnant female anril craving in its twig nest on the frond of the drum-trunked palmyra calls out, a sound rings in her ear as if the long chariot with its bells, cleaving the village common, were coming though it does not come, and her eyes have given up sleep.
nuance: The bird calls from inside a nest it shares with its mate, at the same hour that she lies alone; the chariot exists only as a sound her own ear makes, so the poem places the whole tryst inside her listening.

thinai_evidence.note: the palmyra and the anril of the shore village decide it against the colophon's kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 8; stage inferred from the midnight chariot of a secret visit

comparisons.tenor: the sound in her ear of a chariot that is not coming
the palmyra's trunk, shaped like the base of a drum

iraicchi.act: the craving female calls out at midnight from the nest she shares with her mate
iraicchi.sense: the bird that has its mate beside it still calls for him, while the heroine, whose lover does not come, can only lie awake listening

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether it is not wrong: she can bear hard grief, but fears more that it may turn into something worse; alas, has the man of the good hill grown afraid of the gossip that says the two are inseparable, so that at midnight, when the town sleeps, he knows no way of coming except into her heart?
nuance: பெரும்பிறிது, the greater other thing, is left unnamed; it may be death or the end of the bond, and the poem's fear lives in the gap.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is of the good hill and the visit belongs to midnight

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 1; stage from the gossip about the unmarried pair

reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where the black-legged white heron that has searched the backwater for food gathers in the thaazhai at the edge of the shore and sleeps through the roar of the breaking waves, that her friend, her bangles slipped from their old place, has grown pale here ever since the day she played with her, chasing the gold-striped crab in the spotted shade of the sweet-clustered punnai.
nuance: The heron that has fed and sleeps through the surf could be read as the man at ease while she wastes, but only one correspondence holds (his ease against her pain), so it fails condition 3 and stays scene; the crab game dates the pallor to the day of first meeting.

thinai_evidence.note: thaazhai, punnai and the shore crab

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from துறைவ in line 3; stage from the play-day meeting

reading: The heroine says that with the lord of the shore of cool kaithai waters, where, as the fishermen of curved boats hurl the sharp-mouthed harpoon on its strong shaft of dry bamboo at the horned fish in the unbearable sea, the white flock of short-legged swans sitting on the long shore scatters through the flowered grove, they have surely made a friendship that brings enmity.
nuance: The harpoon thrown at the shark scatters swans that were no part of the hunt; read as a hidden image it would make the lovers' bond scatter the innocent household, but no second pair can be fixed to the situation, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen and kaithai of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; she speaks of the man in the third person

reading: The heroine says the bright fire of love the eyes brought torments her to the bone, yet she cannot go to him and embrace him, nor does he come to remove her pain; they neither let go nor part, and like the lone fight of the dunghill cocks, which ends only when one dies, this sickness that has reached its height has no one to stop it.
nuance: The cocks fight on a rubbish heap with no one to part them; the image makes love-sickness a contest with no umpire, and 'ends only in dying' is said flatly.

thinai_evidence.note: the dunghill cock of the settled town is the poem's only native thing

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: her love-sickness, which no one parts and which ends only in death
love as a fire that burns to the bone

reading: The heroine asks her heart whether, though it said 'these are the soft, sweet, welcome, fitting words we shall speak', it will forget them once it has seen the lord of the cool sea, of the shore grove where bees fall on the pollen-filled flowers of the lovely mango.
nuance: The words may be the ones she means to say to him or the gentle words he once spoke; either way the heart's resolve is expected to fail at the sight of him. The bees dropping into the mango's pollen could figure the heart's fall, but they do no act of the situation, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the lord of the cool sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from என் நெஞ்சே in line 3

reading: The heroine says the new crescent has already been born, shaped like a broken bangle, appearing slender in the red-mouthed sky as many worship it; alas, have they forgotten, the men who left her weeping for the long wasteland where a tusker, unable to bear the pain of his young female's weary gait, gores and fells a tall yaa tree, takes its white fibre, tastes it with his trunk and looks up trumpeting with a grieving heart?
nuance: The crescent counts the months since he left; a broken bangle is also what wasting does to her own wrist.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left across the long wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; stage from his journey

comparisons.tenor: the new crescent

iraicchi.act: the tusker, unable to bear his weary mate's pain, fells a tree to feed her and trumpets in grief
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant on that road cannot bear his mate's suffering, yet the man who crossed it has forgotten the one he left weeping

reading: The friend says that the bond of the man of the great hill, where an elephant, its fearsome head stroked by the curled bud of the grove banana, loses its might and in deluded grief sleeps with difficulty on the slope of falling waters while its tender, weary female strokes its back, has slackened in the hand that gave love.
nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe (whether the banana bud grieves or strokes, and why the beast loses its might); the female soothing the stricken male could be an iraicchi of the heroine's care, but with the act and its subject unsure it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and the man of the great hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the man is spoken of in the third person

reading: The friend tells the lord that, though the field workers finishing their weeding throw down the fragrant flowers that bees feed on and leave them to wither on the high ridges, the neythal of his town does not say 'they are cruel; we will move to another land', but blooms again in the very field it was weeded from; we are like that neythal, lord: though you do us many unkind things, we cannot do without you.
nuance: The neythal is weeded out by the household's own hands and still returns to the same field, which makes the women's loyalty a matter of belonging to the soil rather than of being well treated.

thinai_evidence.note: weeded paddy fields and the field workers

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from பெரும in line 6; stage from the man's town and his many wrongs

comparisons.vehicle: பெயர்த்துங் கடிந்த செறுவிற் பூக்கும் நின்னூர் நெய்த
comparisons.tenor: the women of his house, who stay though he wrongs them

reading: The heroine says the birds have grown lonely, the flowers here have closed, the shore grove is full of loneliness, and the sky too, dazed like us, has turned dim past the day's end; friend, I may yet live in this state if I find someone to tell it to the lord of the cool ford where the cool njaazhal is fragrant.
nuance: The evening's loneliness is shared by birds, flowers, grove and sky, and against all of it she sets one practical hope, a messenger.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove at the end of day

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 5

comparisons.tenor: the sky, dimmed and dazed at evening

reading: The heroine asks her friend how the gossip can end, when the swift, rattling chariot that would not stop though its driver on the broad fish-smelling ford held it back, whether she saw it or not, was seen by the whole troop of girls plucking the pollen-laden bright flowers of the punnai bent over the high white sand.
nuance: 'Whether I saw it or not' gives up her own witness: it no longer matters what she saw, only that everyone else did.

thinai_evidence.note: the great sea and the white sand

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 1; stage from the talk about the unmarried pair

reading: The man says his beloved is a thief who knows two ways: in the thick of night she comes, filling with fragrance the forest of Mullur of Malaiyan of the red spear and hostile strength, as one of us; at dawn, having shaken out the mixed flowers she wore in her hair and smoothed her sandal-scented locks with oil, her face unmoved, she is as one of her own kin.
nuance: The thief steals nothing but herself: the scent she carries at night and the oiled hair at dawn are her two disguises, and the man admires the skill that hides him.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest tryst at midnight

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he speaks of 'our beloved' as if to his heart

comparisons.tenor: the girl at night, one of the man's own
the girl at dawn, one of her family again

reading: The heroine says that with the lord of the shore, where the small white crow of the great sea's edge searches out and eats its prey in the dark backwater of flowing water and roosts in the flower-scented grove, they tied it, and the friendship is tied: it is knotted and settled, hard to untie.
nuance: The bird's day ends in a fixed roost after its search; the bond, too, is spoken of as done, in the past tense, beyond anyone's untying.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea crow feeding in the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: the friendship, as a knot that cannot be untied

reading: The heroine tells her friend that even in this lonely evening, when the full-bellied cool-voiced cloud from the far high sky flashes bright lightning and the rain comes down darkening everything, he does not come, the man who crossed the wasteland of cruel places, who would come and press her young breasts in embrace.
nuance: The rain cloud is a promise kept by the season and broken by the man; the line on her breasts recalls the return she was told to expect.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain cloud at evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 4; stage from his journey across the waste

reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man of the high hill, where the white waterfall pours like the rising moon seen over the sea, is like the sun, and her great bamboo-like shoulders are like the nerunji.
nuance: The nerunji opens to the sun and follows it, so her shoulders flourish with his presence; but the same sun scorches the dry ground the nerunji grows on, and the pairing does not say which.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the high hill with its waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 3

comparisons.tenor: the white waterfall pouring down the hill
the man
her shoulders, which turn to him

reading: The heroine asks her friend whether she would live if her mother learned of this sickness-laden distress that loosens her chosen bangles and fills her body with faintness, now that the words of the lord of the shore, where the unceasing sea beats on the sand-heaped shore and the rising waves wipe out the fast-running crab the girls playing at orai point out, have turned to something else.
nuance: The waves erasing the crab the girls were following could image his words wiped out, but lines 5 and 6 are unsure and only that one correspondence can be named, a near miss on condition 3.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and its crab

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 3; stage from the fear that the mother will learn

reading: The friend asks whether the man of the land where the fine dark-grey bull of the wild cattle, beloved of its young cow, eats sweet-sour nelli, sighs hot breath that makes the honey-dripping flowers beside it tremble, and drinks from the green spring of the high hill, will stay away from us in the cold dewy days when the north wind's rain, beyond measure, moves south.
nuance: The bull's sour nelli followed by spring water (a taste that turns sweet after the sour) is traditionally read as the hard courtship turning sweet; the beast does nothing of the lovers' situation, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the high hill in the cold dewy season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; 'us' includes the heroine

reading: The heroine says of the lord of the shore, where fragrant njaazhal and punnai flowers strewn over the gleaming expanse of water alive with attacking sharks make it look like the ground of a frenzy rite, that though he gives no sign, shall she tell anything else to one who knows nothing else even in thought; on the day he embraced these wasted soft bamboo shoulders he swore an unfailing oath, and he himself is the thief, the one bound by it, and the raft that must carry her across.
nuance: Thief, debtor and raft are three legal and practical names for one man: he took, he owes, and he alone can save; the word வஞ்சினம், elsewhere a warrior's oath, here binds a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: njaazhal and punnai on the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; stage from the secret oath

comparisons.tenor: the shore strewn with flowers

reading: The heroine tells her friend that as the stag, clasping its young doe, shrinks in bewilderment into the bush near the forest, and the good elephant with its trunk joins its female and makes for the dark-sloped hill, the evening has come with the season's great dark rain; if those who ruined her gold-like body's beauty do not come even now, what will become of her sweet life?
nuance: The elephant pair repeats the stag's act of sheltering with a mate as the rain-evening comes; the iraicchi is tagged on the stag, and the doubling makes the heroine the only creature left without her partner.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 8; stage from the absent man's promised return

comparisons.tenor: her body before he ruined its beauty

iraicchi.act: the stag clasps its doe and takes shelter with her as the rain-evening comes
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts seek their mates for shelter at the evening of the rains, while the man who should be with her has not come

reading: The heroine says that with the lord of the shore, where the fish the sea fishermen caught, drying with the prawns taken from the backwater, make the moon-white sand reek of flesh as they spread over every dune, they have not even the blame of having laughed together one day, yet this town of the punnai street, by the punnai grove of golden clusters where flowers open and birds call, spreads idle gossip out of its own cruelty.
nuance: The drying catch is the town's own trade, and its smell spreads over sand that was clean; the heroine draws the moral without naming it.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen and their drying catch

comparisons.tenor: the gossip that sullies her name

the stuff of the talk is the town's own catch, not anything she did

title: kuruntokai 321-340
theme: Kuruntokai 321-340: night visits and their dangers on hill and shore (321, 324, 336), the friend's push for disclosure and marriage (321, 332, 333, 339), waiting at evening and midnight while the man crosses the desert for wealth (329-331), his return with the stag at its doe (338), the man's own voice on the embrace and on a girl coming of age (323, 337), and the heroine's laments for a love begun in play or broken by her own word (325, 326, 334, 340).
source_issues: 321 to 340: the colophon thurai names only the speaker (தோழி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
332: the colophon thinai is பாலை (sangamtamil.com gives குறிஞ்சி, as the flag says); the poem is all hill (யானை, குன்றச் சிறுகுடி, மலைகிழவோன், வாடை), marked kurinji.
336: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி (sangamtamil.com gives நெய்தல், as the flag says); the poem is all shore (துறைவ, இருங்கழி நெய்தல்), marked neythal.
324 line 6: கவைமக (the twin child) is a rare figure, and the poet is named after it; the simile is read as fear for two at once and the verse is marked uncertain.
325 line 4 (ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ) repeats Kuruntokai 176 line 5; its first words are hard to divide, read as 'my lord who was my support'.
333 line 4: கணவும் is a rare verb, read as hovering about; marked uncertain.
329 line 7 (TSCII repair), 331 line 5, 337 lines 3 to 5 and 338 line 5 are repaired readings, as show flags; they read correctly.
330: the colophon thinai is மருதம்; the karu is of the watered fields, but the situation is a wife waiting at evening for a man gone to another land, marked mullai.
338: the colophon thinai is பாலை; the poem is the man's return at evening with a stag and doe, marked mullai.

reading: The friend tells the girl that the man who comes at midnight wearing red hill sandal on his chest and a bee-filled garland of spring kuvalai, and then goes back from their house, is her dear companion; now that on the common ground the red-eyed tiger roars after killing the bull of the marai deer, it is no longer a time for hiding, and she will open their door.
nuance: The kill is made on the மன்றம், the village's own common ground, so the danger of the night path has come to the door; the friend's 'opening the door' turns secrecy into disclosure, the step toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: hill sandal, the tiger and the marai deer of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she addresses the girl (அரிவை, line 4)

reading: The girl tells her friend that, as the soft-eared fawn of the gentle-eyed deer, frightened from its herd when forest folk took it up and brought to the small hamlet by the forest, came to love house life once the youths reared it, nothing is sweeter than what one grows used to; so let them go, walking as they can.
nuance: The fawn was taken by force and learned to love the house; she applies it to her own leaving, so the image answers in advance the fear that she cannot live away from her mother's home.

thinai_evidence.note: she resolves to leave home on foot with him

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; the address தோழி is in line 7

comparisons.tenor: the girl, who will grow used to a new home as the captured fawn did

reading: The man says all other days are chaff; the only days he has lived are those spent sleeping on the two shoulders of the young woman whose fragrant forehead smells of the pollen of fresh mullai buds blooming in the rain-soaked field, when the thunder rises sweet in the sky like a bards' lute tuned to padumalai.
nuance: பதடி வைகல், days of chaff, gives the poet his name; the thunder that in mullai marks the man's promised return here only sweetens the days he has already come back to.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-fed field and the mullai bud

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; he speaks as if to himself or a companion

comparisons.tenor: the thunder rising in the rainy sky
the woman's forehead

reading: The friend tells the man of the great shore, where the crooked-legged male crocodile, strong at seizing, cuts off the paths, that he swims the dark backwater full of fish because of his love and comes, while she suffers because of her innocence, and the friend herself, like one whose twin children have both eaten poison, is afraid in her heart.
nuance: The friend splits the situation in three: his love brings him, her innocence makes her suffer, and the fear for both is hers alone; the simile of the twins is what holds the two lovers in one fear.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee and stage inferred from the poem; the colophon names only the speaker; she addresses him as நீ and பெரும

title: kuruntokai 341-360
theme: Kuruntokai 341 to 360: short akam poems of waiting and leaving, in which the friend and the foster mother weigh the road (343, 347, 356), the mullai season and the evening return as signs (344, 352, 358), the veri rite and night visits endanger the secret love (355, 360), marriage silences the gossip (351), and a given beauty cannot be asked back (349).
source_issues: kuruntokai:341 line 1, 347 line 1, 351 line 4, 358 line 7 and 359 line 4 are repaired readings from tamilvu.org (flags); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:341: the colophon files the poem under neythal, but the poem names only spring flowers (kuravam, punku) and the man's absence, nothing of the shore; inferred thinai paalai.
kuruntokai:352: the colophon files the poem under paalai, but it has no road or waste, only the evening hour of the waiting woman; inferred thinai mullai.

reading: The woman tells her friend that even in this season when the kuravam is spread with many blossoms and the punku with its puffed-rice flowers adorns the grove, though her lover does not cherish her, she will make her unwilling heart firm, telling it that the manly purpose great men set their hearts on is not to be faulted, and so live on by her own hardness.
nuance: She answers her own grief with the man's own argument: the great are right to pursue their manly work (ஆண்மை), so she will not blame it, and she calls the strength that lets her survive her வன்கண், a word for cruelty or hardness, as if enduring were itself a fault. The colophon's neythal has nothing in the poem to support it: the flowers are of the spring, the season of paalai.

nuance: The leaf-skirt was a lover's gift; the friend makes it the cause of the girl's suffering, since the household has noticed it. The snares set after the fruit is touched read as the guard that comes too late, which is the household watch that now keeps the girl in.

reading: The friend says that before the lord of the sky-touching hill, where the tall fine elephant that turned back from the firebrand of the watchman guarding the small millet fears even the gleam of lightning, came to unite with her, her shoulders were rounded and always earned the word 'good'; now her collyrium-lined eyes, sleepless and labouring in hateful grief, run with tears, and her shoulders, their beauty bowed, have grown thin and slip.
nuance: The elephant scared once by the watchman's firebrand that now fears even lightning may hint at a man made timid by the household's watch, who no longer comes; but the poem draws no pair beyond one mood, so it stays scene. The syntax of lines 1 to 4 is hard to fix.

reading: The friend tells the woman, who sobs here with her heavy bangles slipping, bewildered, her darting eyes, scoring lines and clinging to the wall, that the season he promised, saying he would come so that her distant grief would end, is there to see: in the cold evening when the lonely grieve, the white buds of the mullai are like the cowherds' garlands, as if they spoke it.
nuance: The scoring of lines on the wall is the counting of days, and the friend answers it with a sign outside the wall: the buds are the promise kept by the season, so he must be near. Line 7 was repaired from Swaminatha Aiyar's text and its syntax remains hard.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai buds and the herdsmen of the rainy evening

reading: The friend tells the bard to see how seemly it is: in the evening under the spreading fresh white moonlight, on the short-legged cot with its fragrant flower bed, the man, breathing like an elephant at rest, longingly embraced his son, and the son's mother embraced the victorious man's back.
nuance: No one embraces the other directly: the father holds the son and the mother holds the father from behind, so the child closes the circle. Told to the bard, the go-between of the man's other loves, the scene also says his office is no longer needed.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard's errand ends in the family's own embrace

reading: The woman tells her friend that even if today they must bear the grievous pining because their mother sees that the velan, taking it for possession, does not know the cure for the sickness, may he not come at night, the lord of the shining hill with groves that echo on the slopes, where the rattle in the hill girl's hand scares off the parrots eating the big-eared millet like a she-elephant's trunk.
nuance: She would rather suffer the mistaken rite at home than have him risk the night path: the veri rite misreads her sickness, and the one true cure she forbids for his sake.

title: kuruntokai 361-380
theme: Kuruntokai 361-380: the friend at work, mocking the diviner (362), dissuading departure (363), urging marriage through tears, gossip and a broken promise (365, 372, 379), and reporting the asking (374); girls who love beyond union (361, 371, 377); courtesans and a forbearing wife in the watered town (364, 368, 370); elopement seen by friend and foster mother (369, 378); waiting through the rains (367, 380); and the man's praise of a beloved warm in winter and cool in summer (376).
source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (தோழி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
372 line 1 carries a stray comma inside a line (பனைத்தலைக், கருக்குடை); the sense of lines 1 to 5 is hard to fix.
377 line 1 is missing from the base text and is supplied from sangamtamil.com; line 3 (தோழியாற் றலையே) is hard to divide.
375 and 379 have no poet in the colophon.
363, 365, 366 and 378 each have one line repaired from tamilvu; 374 line 2 was a TSCII leftover (தௌிய) repaired to தெளிய; the repairs read correctly.

Thinai differs from the colophon in 367 (mullai: the first rains and waiting, not marutham), 376 (kurinji: the man's delight in her body, with Pothiyil sandal; the colophon says neythal) and 380 (mullai: waiting through the rains into the cold; the colophon says paalai).

reading: The girl tells her friend that her mother is worth more than the high world itself, for she did not forbid her to clasp, crushing its soft leaves, the whole kaanthal plant that the flood of the evening rain on his hill brought down in the morning, nor to carry it home and plant it.
nuance: The mother's not forbidding is praised as above heaven because she does not know what the plant is: the girl embraces the hill of her lover in a flower the flood carried, and the mother's innocence is the girl's whole freedom.

thinai_evidence.note: a kaanthal from the lover's hill is the token of the poem

reading: The friend asks the old-mouthed diviner who came rejoicing in Murugan's rite to hold back his anger and answer one question: if he kills a small kid, offers rice-balls of many colours, strokes the girl's fragrant brow and makes his worship, will the bright-garlanded chest of the man of the sky-touching hill who afflicted her also eat the offering?
nuance: அணங்கிய names the man as the possessing power the rite blames on the god, so the question to the velan reveals the secret (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்) while seeming only to mock the rite.

thinai_evidence.note: the possession rite of Murugan belongs to the hill

reading: The household concubine says that the proud wife of the man of the town where the otter among the tangled cane gets a vaalai fish for its daily food speaks behind her back, they say; well, the days of the thunangai dance of the bright-bangled women have come, and there, when eyes clash, comes the contest of young men eager to take brides.
nuance: The otter that takes a vaalai every day is the traditional figure for the husband enjoying her without effort, but the poem names no situation it maps onto (the anchor is the wife's slander, not his pleasure), so it stays scene; the concubine answers the slander by a public challenge at the festival, not by denial.

reading: The friend says that, beyond what destiny has fixed and arranged, who are we to measure the man's worth; when I spoke otherwise the girl would not accept it, and looking at the wide-petalled blue lily that has burst open in the green-eyed dark pool, her eyes ripened with tears: this jewelled girl's resolve is not false.
nuance: பால் is the destiny that pairs lovers; the friend argues that the choice is not hers to judge, and the girl's tears at a flower like her own eyes are offered as proof. Lines 5 and 6 (உள்ளகை பழுத கண்ணள்) are hard to construe.

reading: The friend tells the girl that even if the cruel man shows no grace, her bangled shoulders may regain their beauty: look there, now that the dense dark rain has begun, his hill has come into view in his land, its cool fragrant boulders shining like a washed gem in the falls down which the noisy troop of girls slides with delight.
nuance: The sight of his hill is offered as a cure in itself: the friend does not promise he will come, only that seeing his land washed by the first rains will restore her.

reading: The wife tells her gentle friend, three times over, that she can only bear with strength the shame of a dark beauty that has lost its good modesty, and cannot say it aloud; for the sake of the town where small and great live, let them embrace him often in a blameless state, like the great tree on the firm bank of a flood that never fails.
nuance: The riverbank tree is the town's common shade, standing in a flood that comes every day: her quarrel would be a public loss, so she makes endurance a civic duty. Lines 2 and 3 are obscure, and the sense of நன்னாண் நீத்த is not certain.

reading: The friend says that in this town of passers-by gossip rose before the mound on the sand ridge could dry, a heap the sea threw up with flowing mud where the fierce wind piles long white dunes that bury the palmyras' crowns, their saw-edged fronds and shoots, in the shore grove where crested heaps bow.

nuance: The weaver's nest is a marvel of order that looks like chaos; the town that misread the secret is more tangled still, now that the truth has ended in a proper asking.

nuance: She is a counter-climate: the lotus that shuts at sunset keeps the day's warmth inside, as she keeps warmth for the cold months.

title: kuruntokai 381-401
theme: Kuruntokai 381 to 401: the last short akam poems, where one laugh with the shore lord costs a girl her beauty (381) and is then forbidden her (401), the evening and the night become floods to swim (386, 387, 398), pallor parts and closes like well-moss under the lover's touch (399), the friend denies the season to save the man's word (382), and the foster mother reads too late the refused milk of a girl who has gone (396).
source_issues: kuruntokai:382 line 3, 392 line 8 and 394 line 4 are repaired readings (flags); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:396: the colophon thinai is printed பாால; read as பாலை.
kuruntokai:383: the colophon's paalai does not fit a tryst with the man of the hills at the meeting place; inferred kurinji.
kuruntokai:398: colophon paalai; the poem is a woman waiting at evening, inferred mullai.
kuruntokai:381 and 395 have no poet in the colophon.

kuruntokai:381-401: the colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so thurai_akam addressees are taken from vocatives in the poems where present and given as pira otherwise, and occasion.words is null.
Hard lines: 383 line 3, 384 line 1, 388 line 3, 389 lines 1-2, 391 lines 1-2, 395 lines 7-8, 398 lines 6-8, 401 line 6; readings marked uncertain.

reading: The friend asks whether the girl, her old beauty gone, her shoulders wasted, her troubled heart sleepless even at night, will turn pale and die: that is all the fruit of once laughing, her bright teeth showing, with the lord of the shore, where white herons cry in the cool fragrant grove and the crosswise waves break, tangling the fresh flowers of the blossoming thicket.
nuance: The whole cost is weighed against one laugh (நக்கதன் பயனே): a moment of shown teeth is set against lost beauty, sleeplessness and death. The waves that break and tangle the fresh flowers could be heard as the man who ruined her, but that is a single match of mood, not two pairs, so the shore stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the lament of a girl wasting after the shore lord's absence

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The friend says that the green mullai creeper, made for cool drops, has opened its buds, its scent rising over the bushes with the flower-laden jasmine, because the clouds pour untimely rain: if this were not untimely but the true rainy season, would our lover not have come?
nuance: The comfort is an argument from the man's word to the season: since he promised to come with the rains and has not come, these cannot be the rains. The friend turns the proof of his failure into proof that the flowers are mistaken.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the season the man named for his return

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

reading: The friend tells the girl that because she consented, the friend brought him and the man of the hills has come and stands at the meeting place; now she says today's meeting must wait for another day, and the friend, her hands and feet going slack with distress, trembles like a shoot touched by fire, with nothing she can do.
nuance: The friend is caught between the two lovers: she arranged the meeting on the girl's word and must now face the man at the tryst. Line 3 (இன்றை யளவை சென்றைக் கென்றி) is hard to construe; the reading 'not today, another day' is a guess. The colophon's paalai does not fit a tryst on the hill.

thinai_evidence.note: a tryst arranged in kalavu with the man of the hills

reading: The friend tells the man that if he enjoys the beauty of the girls, with thick shoulders painted with sugarcane designs, long many-stranded hair and small bangles, and then abandons them, his oath is very fine indeed.
nuance: மிகநன்று is praise turned to scorn: the oath he swore is 'very good' precisely because it keeps him free to take and leave. Line 1 (உழுந்துடைக் கழுந்திற்) is unclear: it may name a town of black-gram fields or compare the shoulders to a pounding pestle, so the girls' description is uncertain.

reading: The girl says the lord of the great mountain slope, where a male monkey of the troop, full of fruit on the jackfruit tree, startled by the hunter's well-aimed bow, leaps like a war-horse so that the tall bamboo of the slope shakes, is always as friendly as on the first day; it is this town with its clamour that is new to her.
nuance: She turns the blame from the man to the town: he has not changed, the gossip has. The startled monkey leaping so the bamboo shakes could be read as the lovers disturbed by the town's aim, but only the hunter's aim and the town's talk can be paired, and the poem names no harm, so the monkey stays scene.

reading: The woman says that before the lord of the cool shore of spread white sand and crowded flowers left her, she knew evening only as the time that gathers bright-jewelled women for festival; she did not know that evening could be lonely, with a sorrow as wide as the earth.
nuance: The same word மாலை closes line 4 and opens line 5, the festival evening turning into the lonely one at the line break. Her ignorance before is part of the complaint: the evening she knew was a public time of women together, the one she learns is private.

reading: The woman tells her friend that even if, when the day's limit passes, the mullai blooms and the sun's rays cool their anger, they swim across the helpless evening and reach the night as its bank, what good is it: the flood of night is greater than the sea.
nuance: The evening is a river crossed with the night as its far bank; reaching the bank only opens a second water, the night itself, larger than the sea. The poet was named for this line (கங்குல் வெள்ளத்தார்).

reading: The friend tells the man that the row-petalled kuvalai bound to running water does not wither even if summer strikes it, and so the forest, where the dry branches stand like the long line of salt merchants' bullock carts straining at their yokes and the elephant, too weak to split them, folds its trunk and suffers, will be sweet if the girl comes with him.
nuance: The lily is never said to be the girl; the friend sets it first and lets the forest follow, and the last line supplies the match. Line 3 (கவணை அன்ன பூட்டுப்பொரு தசாஅ) is hard to construe: the comparison of the yoke is uncertain.

reading: The friend wishes, friend, that she may get a full meal with ghee-rich quail as its relish: when the man of the great hills came to ask for her in marriage, she said to him 'is it good, son?', and he answered 'it seems good'.
nuance: Who is to be feasted, and who said 'is it good, son?', is unclear: என்றனென் is first person, so the friend may be reporting her own question to the suitor, and அத்தை may be a particle rather than a kinswoman. The relish of quail is the reward of good news.

reading: Onlookers tell the man, mate of the young she-elephant, not to go on: the day has lost its light, and he should listen to the sound, for a caravan has halted because of the danger of the hostile frontier, and the drum of the guards, who come to the thorn hedge carrying long ringed spears and go back, is sounding.
nuance: The onlookers name the man only through the girl, as the tusker of a young cow-elephant, so their warning is for her. The danger is told by sound alone: the caravan has stopped, and the guards' drum carries the frontier's threat after dark.

reading: The woman tells her friend that where the bull of the salt ground lay idle without ploughing and the heat had steamed in the rainless scrub, the rain has fallen sweetly, mingled with thunder that strikes so fast the snake's hood shrinks; and in the sorrowful evening that came to leave the separated helpless, the peacock with eyed plumes, sitting on the flowering branch, calls across the wide wet land till it is desolate: they are very foolish.
nuance: The peacocks rejoice at the rain that makes her helpless, and she calls them fools for it. The snake whose hood shrinks at the thunder sits beside her own shrinking, but it does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene. Lines 1 and 2 (உவரி யொருத்தல், புகரி புழுங்கிய) are hard to construe.

reading: The friend asks the bright-winged dragonfly, which need fear nothing for carrying good news, to go to the noble one's tall mountain and tell the lord of the hills, where honeycombs hang like the hide shields of kings' marching ranks, that the sister of the weeders who hoe the small millet field crowded with wild cattle is not let out by her kin.
nuance: The message is a warning dressed as news: the girl is kept at home by her kin, so the man must come and marry. Calling her the weeders' sister names her as a hill girl of a working family, and the honeycombs like kings' shields make his hill a kingdom fit to send for her.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is a dragonfly sent as messenger

comparisons.tenor: the honeycombs hanging in rows

reading: The friend says the days on which the lover embraced, crushing a garland of mixed flowers, were few; but the gossip is louder than the shout of the Kongar with flashing swords on the day when Athikan, the skilled general of the Pandiyan with green ornaments, fell with his elephant on the battlefield of Vaakai where owls haunt.
nuance: The measure of the gossip is a defeat: the Kongar's victory cry over the Pandiyan's fallen general. Whom the husband embraced is not said, so the friend may be scoffing at the scandal of his other women or at the cost of the few days he gave the wife. Athikan, the general, is named in line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: the gossip about the husband's affairs, out of all measure

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

reading: The friend says that their laughing play with the man has turned into an enemy, as the soft-headed calf of the big she-elephant with knee-high legs, running and frolicking with the children of the low-eaved huts whom the hill woman of the toddy-rich hamlet bore, was sweet in its early days and later grazed on their millet field.
nuance: The calf does no wrong: it grows, and the same play that charmed the children ends in their field being eaten. So the affair has not changed its nature; it has only grown into a thing that costs the girl her standing.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant calf among the hill people's children and millet

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

comparisons.tenor: their laughing play with the man

reading: The woman tells her heart that restraint is beyond her: he, having no love, does not count grace as worth anything and holds firm in his hardness; even if he will not free her as the people here free the moon the snake swallows, there is no one even to say 'fear not' so that her eyes may sleep; pitiable is her shame, if she must leave it to go where he lives.
nuance: At an eclipse the people make a din to free the swallowed moon; she is swallowed and no one comes, not even to say a word of comfort. The last two lines are hard: they may mean that shame is pitiable if she leaves home for him, or that it is lost already.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman abandoned by a hard man who has gone away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the heart is addressed as நெஞ்சே

reading: The foster mother says the girl would not drink her milk or take up her ball, and was weary with her playmates; did she think it easy, then, the going with him through the land where bamboo withers, on the hot slopes of the summer hills, where the tall-tusked bull elephant that gored the dry-branched omai listens for the harsh voice of thundering clouds?
nuance: The foster mother reads the signs too late: the refused milk and the dropped ball were the girl's mind already on the road. The elephant listening for thunder that does not come is the drought she now pictures the girl in.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has left home with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore of strong waters, where the cold wind scatters the millet-like clustered flowers of the full-budded gnaazhal onto the large neythal blossoms as though pouring them, that like a baby who cries 'mother' even while its angry mother beats it, her friend, whether he does her harm or shows her sweet kindness, is within his bounds and has no one else to remove her sorrow.
nuance: The baby cries 'mother' to the one who is beating it, because there is no one else to cry to; so the girl's dependence is not a virtue to praise but a helplessness the man is asked to respect. The wind pouring one flower onto another is a gentle image set before the harsh one.
